nodes.title: Pre-Development Foundation
nodes.description: Documentation, standards, infrastructure before production code.
nodes.prompt:
CONTEXT: Pre-Development Foundation — Wave 1

You are setting up the mgit project scaffold. mgit is a safety-critical micro version control system for LLM coding agents, built in Go. It uses go-git v5 (pure Go, no shell-out to git binary) and modernc.org/sqlite (pure Go, CGO-free) as its two core storage engines.

ARCHITECTURE: mgit follows a strict layered architecture:
  cmd/mgit/ → internal/service/ → internal/store/ → internal/model/
  Dependency direction is downward only. No circular imports.

KEY STANDARDS:
  - DO-178C (avionics), IEC 62304 (medical devices), NASA-STD-8739.8
  - 90%+ line coverage overall, 95%+ for store/service layers
  - Zero linter warnings, zero race detector issues
  - TDD mandatory: write test first (red), implement (green), refactor

APPROVED PACKAGES: go-git/go-git/v5, modernc.org/sqlite, spf13/cobra, labstack/echo/v4, oklog/ulid/v2, stretchr/testify, golang.org/x/sync, log/slog (stdlib). No others without approval per PACKAGE-APPROVAL-PROCESS.md.

READ BEFORE CODING: CLAUDE.md (directives), CODING-STYLE.md (patterns), QUALITY-STANDARDS.md (coverage), TDD-WORKFLOW.md (process), APPROVED-PACKAGES.md (deps).
nodes.creator: cli

nodes.title: `mgit sandbox launch` run from inside a worktree cannot find the repo's guest base (host root is resolved from cwd/.mgit)
nodes.description:
Hit while trying to live-verify MGIT-95 from the task worktree the work was done in.

`cmd/mgit/sandbox_image.go:sandboxHostRoot()` resolves the sandbox host root as `<cwd>/.mgit/sandbox` and requires `<cwd>/.mgit` to be a directory. In a linked mgit worktree, `.mgit` IS a directory but holds only the worktree marker (`worktree`, `generated`, `shims`) — the real store is named inside `.mgit/worktree` ("store": "/path/to/repo/.mgit"). There is no `sandbox/` there, so `repoGuestBaseRef()` reports:

    Error: this repo has no guest base, so there is nothing to boot.
    Compose one from any Linux image ...
      mgit sandbox base from debian:12

...on a repository that HAS a registered, signed guest base. The message is confidently wrong, and the suggested remedy would compose a second base rather than use the existing one. Every other mgit verb run from a worktree resolves the store correctly (that is what ADR-007 / MGIT-24 established); this one path re-derives it by hand from cwd.

Consequence for the dogfood loop: an agent working in `mgit work` worktree cannot launch or re-launch its own sandbox from where it is standing — which is exactly where CLAUDE.md tells it to work.

Workaround used: build a scratch repo elsewhere and re-register a copy of the base tree.
nodes.prompt:
Resolve the sandbox host root through the same worktree-aware store resolution every other verb uses, instead of `<cwd>/.mgit/sandbox`.

1. In cmd/mgit/sandbox_image.go, replace the hand-rolled cwd derivation in sandboxHostRoot() with the repo-root resolution the rest of the CLI uses (the one that reads a worktree's `.mgit/worktree` store pointer and walks up from a subdirectory). Every caller — sandbox base/image commands and repoGuestBaseRef — must then see the repo's real images.lock.
2. Add a test that runs the base/launch resolution with cwd inside a linked worktree AND inside a subdirectory of one, asserting the registered base is found (this is the same class of bug MGIT-24 fixed for commit/log/status).
3. Check the sibling resolvers for the same assumption — anything else deriving a store path from cwd rather than from the resolved repo root.

Refs: MGIT-95, MGIT-24, ADR-007, FR-16, FR-17.17
nodes.acceptance: `mgit sandbox launch` / `sandbox base` run from inside a linked worktree (and from a subdirectory of one) resolve the repository's registered guest base instead of reporting none; covered by a test that stands in a worktree.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The FR-17.26 aggregate CONCURRENCY cap has the same flag-not-policy wiring MGIT-98 just fixed for memory
nodes.description:
Found while implementing MGIT-98 (wiring the aggregate MEMORY ceiling from host policy).

model.SandboxPolicy carries MaxConcurrentSandboxes (default 8) — the other half of the FR-17.26 fleet ceiling. Nothing reads it. cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go still wires that dimension from a flag:

    flags.IntVar(&o.maxSandboxes, "max-sandboxes", 8, "global concurrent-sandbox ceiling (FR-17.26)")
    manager := sandboxd.NewCeilingManager(selected, opts.maxSandboxes, ceiling.maxTotalMemoryMB, ceiling.defaultMemoryMB)

This is NOT the same severity as MGIT-98 and was deliberately left out of its scope. The flag's default (8) equals the policy default (8), so a default install is correctly capped — there is no fail-open here, unlike the memory dimension where the flag defaulted to 0 (= disabled).

What is wrong is quieter: an operator who edits max_concurrent_sandboxes in host policy is silently ignored. They lower it to 4, the daemon keeps admitting 8, and nothing on the log says which number is in force. That is the same class of defect (a policy field that exists, is documented, validates, and drives nothing) minus the consequence.

Ordering note for whoever picks this up: the flag's default is non-zero, so "was it passed?" cannot be inferred from its value the way --max-memory-mb's zero allowed. Use flag.FlagSet.Visit to detect an explicitly-set flag, or change the default to 0 and treat 0 as "resolve from policy" — the latter matches the shape MGIT-98 left behind for memory.

MGIT-98 also left the resolved ceiling on the daemon's startup log (event=fleet_memory_ceiling); the concurrency cap should join that record so an operator sees BOTH dimensions in force in one place.
nodes.prompt:
Wire the FR-17.26 aggregate concurrency cap from host policy (SandboxPolicy.MaxConcurrentSandboxes) instead of from --max-sandboxes alone, following the shape MGIT-98 established for the memory dimension in cmd/mgit-sandboxd/ceiling_wiring.go.

1. Resolve MaxConcurrentSandboxes from the host policy already loaded at daemon start (loadDaemonPolicy) and pass it to sandboxd.NewCeilingManager.
2. Keep --max-sandboxes as an explicit operator override. Its default is currently 8, which is indistinguishable from an explicit 8 — either detect the explicit set with flag.FlagSet.Visit, or move the default to 0 and treat 0 as "resolve from policy" (matching --max-memory-mb).
3. Report the resolved concurrency cap alongside the memory ceiling in the existing fleet_memory_ceiling startup record (or rename it to cover both dimensions), so an operator reads both numbers in force in one line.
4. Test at the CLI level, not just under it: run() with no resource flags must record the policy-derived cap. See TestRun_DefaultInstall_ResolvesALiveMemoryCeiling in cmd/mgit-sandboxd/ceiling_wiring_test.go for the pattern (it uses --backend container without the acknowledgment to terminate deterministically after ceiling resolution).
5. Keep the concurrency refusal reading as "the host is already running N sandboxes" — distinct from both the per-sandbox ErrSandboxResourceLimitExceeded and the host-too-small memory refusal.

Refs: FR-17.26, MGIT-98, SEC-09
nodes.acceptance: The daemon derives its concurrent-sandbox cap from host policy with no operator flag required; --max-sandboxes still overrides explicitly and is distinguishable from its own default; both fleet dimensions appear in the startup log record; a CLI-level test proves the default install uses the policy value rather than the flag default.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A registered-but-unbooted sandbox is lost when the daemon exits, with no audit record — `work --sandbox` containment evaporates before first use
nodes.description:
Found by DOGFOODING: the MGIT-98 agent reported `mgit sandbox status MGIT-98` -> "sandbox not found" and worked without containment. Reproduced and root-caused on host (macOS/libkrun, 2026-08-12).

WHAT HAPPENED
1. `mgit work /tmp/mgit-98-wt --task-id MGIT-98 --sandbox --image <ref> --memory-mb 6144 --cpus 4` succeeded and printed "Registered sandbox 01KZTSHTNR39JWEBAQPF4PPAB9 ... (created)".
2. Immediately after, `mgit sandbox status MGIT-98` returned `resources: 4 vCPU 6144 MB memory 4096 MB disk` — the registration was real.
3. Some time later the SAME command from the SAME repo returned `Error: sandbox: sandbox not found: task "MGIT-98"`, and `mgit run -- /bin/echo` from inside the worktree returned `no sandbox bound for /private/tmp/mgit-98-wt`.

ROOT CAUSE (measured, not inferred)
The live sandbox registry is daemon-process memory. There is NO `sandboxes` table in .mgit/sandbox/sandbox-index.db (tables: branch_locks, branches, sandbox_egress_log, sandbox_events, schema_version, task_commits, worktrees). `ps -o lstart=,etime=` on the running mgit-sandboxd showed it had been alive 39 SECONDS — i.e. the daemon that held the registration had exited and the CLI had auto-spawned a fresh one with no knowledge of it.

This is worst exactly in the lazy-provisioning window (FR-17.9/FR-17.10): `work --sandbox` REGISTERS without booting, so a sandbox that has never been used holds no VM keeping anything alive, and is the most likely thing to be lost.

SECOND DEFECT — THE AUDIT TRAIL IS INCOMPLETE
sandbox_events for MGIT-98 contains exactly one row: `created` at 2026-08-12T10:51:07Z. There is NO destroyed / killed / ttl_expired event. An auditor reading the append-only record concludes the sandbox still exists. A sandbox can therefore disappear leaving a record that says it is alive, which is precisely the traceability failure the append-only design exists to prevent.

SEVERITY — STATE THIS PRECISELY
This is loss of containment AVAILABILITY, not a containment BREACH. `mgit run` fails closed ("commands never run on the host"), so nothing untrusted was executed on the host through the wired path. But the practical effect on an agent loop is severe: the agent is told it is contained, the containment silently evaporates, `mgit run` starts refusing, and per the CLAUDE.md caveat the agent falls back to bare host commands to make progress. That is how a poisoned dependency reaches the host (FR-17, the single most consequential failure) — not by breaking containment, but by containment quietly ceasing to be there.

It also invalidates the "start every parallel task with a contained worktree" workflow now documented in CLAUDE.md, and the `work --sandbox` story told to the integrating lane.
nodes.prompt:
Make a registered sandbox survive the daemon that registered it, and make its disappearance auditable.

1. PERSIST THE REGISTRY. Add durable storage for sandbox registrations (task_id, sandbox_id, worktree path, image ref, resolved resource caps, network mode, state, created_at) in .mgit/sandbox/sandbox-index.db, and rehydrate it at daemon start. Follow the project SQL rules: parameterized queries, PRAGMAs, all writes in transactions. Do NOT touch task_commits.

2. RECONCILE ON START, HONESTLY. A rehydrated registration whose VM is gone must not be reported as `running`. Reconcile persisted state against reality at startup: a sandbox in `created` (never booted) is still perfectly valid and must come back as `created`; one recorded `running` whose VM no longer exists must transition to a state that says so, with an audit event recording the transition. Never report a state you have not verified.

3. CLOSE THE AUDIT GAP. Every terminal transition must append a sandbox_event. A sandbox that vanishes because its daemon died must leave a record saying so — the current trail shows `created` and nothing else, which actively misleads.

4. DECIDE AND DOCUMENT DAEMON LIFETIME. Find out WHY the daemon exited (idle timeout? parent exit? something else) and state it. If an idle daemon shutting down is intended, then registration must be durable (item 1) and this ticket is the fix. If the daemon exited unexpectedly, that is a separate bug — file it.

REQUIRED VERIFICATION — this defect was invisible to a green unit suite, so unit tests alone do not close it:
- Reproduce the ORIGINAL failure first and capture it, so the fix is proven against a real reproduction rather than a hypothesis.
- End-to-end: register with `mgit work --sandbox`, terminate the daemon, run `mgit sandbox status <task>` and `mgit run -- <cmd>` from INSIDE the worktree, and assert the sandbox is still there and usable.
- Assert the audit trail contains a coherent event sequence in both the survives case and the genuinely-destroyed case.
- Cover the from-inside-a-worktree path specifically. It is where the agent actually stands, and it is under-tested (cf. MGIT-100).

Refs: FR-17, FR-17.9, FR-17.10, MGIT-95, MGIT-100
nodes.acceptance: A sandbox registered by `mgit work --sandbox` is still found by `mgit sandbox status` and usable by `mgit run` after the registering daemon has exited and a new one has been spawned, both from the repo root and from inside the bound worktree; rehydrated state is reconciled against reality rather than asserted; every sandbox that ceases to exist leaves a sandbox_events row explaining it, so no trail ends at `created` for a sandbox that is gone; the original failure is reproduced before the fix and shown resolved after.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A SIGKILLed/crashed mgit-sandboxd orphans its VM children — no Pdeathsig or process-group teardown, so containment residue survives an ungraceful exit
nodes.description:
Found while root-causing MGIT-102 (durable sandbox registry). SEPARATE from that defect and not fixed by it.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (code, not inferred behavior)
`grep -rn "Pdeathsig|Setpgid|SysProcAttr" internal/sandboxd/` returns NOTHING. Every VM is a child process of the daemon — a firecracker subprocess on Linux, a libkrun re-exec child (`libkrun.ChildCommand`) on macOS — and none of them is tied to the parent's lifetime. Note the contrast: the CLI DOES set `SysProcAttr` when it spawns the daemon (`cmd/mgit/sandbox_spawn_unix.go`, `Setsid: true`) precisely so the daemon outlives the short-lived CLI. Nothing does the inverse for VMs.

Consequence: if mgit-sandboxd dies WITHOUT running its drain — SIGKILL, a panic that escapes the recover in handleConn, OOM-kill, a host crash of the daemon alone — its microVMs are reparented to init and keep running, holding their memory, their virtio-fs share on the worktree, and (in allowlist/open mode) whatever host-side networking their launch configured. Nothing supervises them and no later daemon can address them: the new process's manager has no handle, so `stop`/`remove` cannot reach them. The only recovery is manual `kill`.

The ORDINARY exits are all clean, which is why this has not been seen: idle exit and SIGINT/SIGTERM both go through `Daemon.drain`, which stops and removes every sandbox. This is strictly the ungraceful path.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE LEAK
It bounds the honesty of MGIT-102's rehydration. A replacement daemon that cannot verify a sandbox now records a terminal `killed` event with detail "unsupervised: ... its VM could not be verified by the daemon that replaced it". That wording is deliberately precise — the daemon establishes that it can no longer supervise the VM, NOT that the VM is gone. If an orphan is in fact still running, mgit's records say the sandbox ended while a VM with the worktree mounted is still live on the host. Fixing this ticket is what would let that record say the stronger thing.

Refs: FR-17.19 (no residue), FR-17.16, NFR-17.6, MGIT-102
nodes.prompt:
Make a microVM die with the daemon that supervises it, on the ungraceful exit paths where drain never runs.

1. REPRODUCE FIRST, on a backend that really boots (Linux/KVM firecracker is the cheapest; macOS/libkrun needs the hypervisor entitlement). Launch a sandbox, `kill -9` the daemon, and record what survives: the VM process, its memory, its mount of the worktree, and any host-side tap/iptables/listener state. Capture it — the fix should be proven against a real orphan, not a hypothesis.

2. TIE THE VM TO THE PARENT. On Linux, `SysProcAttr.Pdeathsig` is the direct mechanism (note it fires on the parent THREAD's exit, so the spawning goroutine must be locked to its OS thread, or the signal arrives early — this is the classic trap). On macOS there is no Pdeathsig: options are a process group killed by a supervisor, or a guest-side watchdog on the vsock control channel that halts when the host end goes away. Whatever is chosen must be a mechanism the KERNEL or the guest enforces, not a host-side cleanup that a SIGKILLed process was never around to run.

3. ADOPT OR REAP, DO NOT PRETEND. If a mechanism cannot cover a backend, then the next daemon must at least be able to FIND the orphans it inherited (the pid/socket of each VM is already reconstructible from workDir) and either re-adopt them or kill them, so `mgit sandbox status` can stop qualifying its answer. Coordinate with MGIT-102's reconciliation: it currently discards what it cannot verify, and this is the ticket that lets it say WHY with certainty.

4. DO NOT weaken the normal drain path to get there.

VERIFICATION: the reproduction above, re-run — after `kill -9` of the daemon, no VM process remains and no host networking state is left behind. Assert it in the live gate, not only a unit test; scripts/e2e/sandbox_registry_durability.sh already SIGKILLs the daemon serving one repo and is the natural place to add "…and its VM is gone".

Refs: FR-17.19, FR-17.16, MGIT-102
nodes.acceptance: A microVM launched by mgit-sandboxd does not survive a SIGKILL of that daemon: after `kill -9`, no VM process remains, the worktree is not still mounted by a guest, and no per-sandbox host networking state is left behind — demonstrated by a captured before/after reproduction on a backend that really boots, and gated in the live e2e rather than only unit-tested. Where a platform cannot enforce it, a replacement daemon can enumerate and reap the orphans it inherited, and the limitation is documented per backend rather than implied to be covered.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The memory-cap advisory fires on boot failures it cannot explain, and calls a guest that never started "stopped answering mid-command"
nodes.description:
Found live while verifying MGIT-102 (macOS/libkrun, 2026-08-12). This is a defect in MGIT-95's own OOM-visibility work — it over-fires.

WHAT HAPPENED
`mgit run` was issued against a sandbox whose daemon lacked the com.apple.security.hypervisor entitlement. The VM could not start at all. mgit printed, in this order:

    mgit run: sandbox exec: sandbox ensure-running: libkrun launch: guest never
    answered on its control channel within 15s: ... connect: no such file or directory
    guest console (tail):
    {"level":"ERROR","msg":"libkrun vm failed","event":"krun_vm_failed",
     "error":"libkrun start vm: krun_start_enter: libkrun error -22 ..."}

    mgit: the guest stopped answering mid-command.
    This sandbox (task DUR-1) is capped at 3072 MB of memory and 2 vCPU. Memory
    exhaustion inside the guest presents exactly like this, and the cap is a
    property of THIS SANDBOX, not of your project.
    If the workload needs more, declare it ... --memory-mb 6144

TWO SEPARATE INACCURACIES

1. MISATTRIBUTION. mgit had, in its own hands, a guest console tail containing an explicit VM-START failure (krun_start_enter: libkrun error -22, EINVAL — here a missing hypervisor entitlement). That error rules memory exhaustion OUT: there was no guest to exhaust. The advisory was appended anyway. The hedge "presents exactly like this" keeps the sentence technically defensible, but the practical effect is to point the reader at --memory-mb 6144 when the actual fix is to sign the daemon — and the real cause was printed three lines above.

2. WRONG PHASE. "the guest stopped answering mid-command" describes a guest that was serving and then died. This guest NEVER STARTED. The failure text immediately above even says so ("guest never answered on its control channel"). A never-booted guest and a guest killed mid-command are different failures with different fixes, and mgit already knows which it is.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS
MGIT-95 exists because a consumer's agent, given a failure and no visible ceiling, inferred the BUILD was too large and reshaped a production bundler config. This defect is the same error in reverse: a failure with a KNOWN, PRINTED cause gets annotated with a memory hint, inviting the reader to raise a cap that was never the problem. A diagnostic that points at the wrong fix is worse than no diagnostic, because it is acted upon. It also spends the credibility of the advisory in the cases where it IS right.

It is also a first-hour macOS pitfall: the missing-entitlement boot failure is exactly what a new user hits, and the memory advice sends them the wrong way.

--- WHAT TO DO ---

1. GATE THE ADVISORY ON EVIDENCE. Before appending the cap advisory, check what is already known. If the guest console tail carries an explicit VM-start failure (krun_vm_failed / krun_start_enter), the guest never ran and memory exhaustion is not a candidate — surface the start failure and its actual remedy instead. Keep the advisory for the cases MGIT-95 built it for: a signal exit (134/137/-1) or a guest lost while it was serving.

2. FIX THE PHASE WORDING. Distinguish "never started" from "stopped answering mid-command" from "exited on a signal". mgit already has the evidence to tell these apart — the same code path prints "guest never answered on its control channel" immediately before claiming it stopped mid-command. Do not print both.

3. NAME THE REAL REMEDY WHERE IT IS KNOWN. A libkrun start failure on darwin with a daemon lacking com.apple.security.hypervisor is a known, diagnosable condition and a common first-hour failure. If the entitlement is detectably absent, say that and give the fix rather than a generic start error. Prior art for the check: scripts/e2e/sandbox_cli_surface.sh and sandbox_posture.sh use `codesign --display --entitlements`.

4. DO NOT OVERCORRECT. Where the cause is genuinely ambiguous, the MGIT-95 advisory is correct and valuable and must stay, including its "do not reshape the project to fit this guest" line. The goal is to stop it firing where the cause is already known, not to weaken it.

REQUIRED TESTS
- A boot failure whose console tail contains a krun start error does NOT produce the memory advisory, and DOES surface the start failure.
- A signal exit (134/137) still DOES produce the advisory naming the cap — the MGIT-95 tests must keep passing.
- A guest lost mid-command still produces the advisory.
- The phase wording matches the phase in each case; assert the negative (a never-started guest is never described as stopping mid-command).

Verify live on macOS by reproducing both arms: an unentitled daemon (start failure, no memory advice) and an entitled one (normal operation).

ACCEPTANCE
A guest that fails to start emits its actual start failure and remedy with no memory-cap advisory; a guest that dies on a signal or mid-command still emits the MGIT-95 advisory naming the cap; the phase wording matches the observed phase in every case and a never-started guest is never described as stopping mid-command; a detectably missing hypervisor entitlement on darwin is named with its fix; verified live on both arms.

Refs: MGIT-95, R-H212, MGIT-102, MGIT-64

nodes.title: `mgit commit` has no --file/-F: a real commit message must be passed through the shell
nodes.description:
Found while committing MGIT-104 (2026-08-12).

`mgit commit` accepts only `-m/--m/--message`. git has `-F <file>` (and `-t`), and every non-trivial commit message wants it: the message this project's CLAUDE.md asks for is multi-paragraph, and a body that mentions shell metacharacters (backticks around `krun_start_enter`, `$(command -v ...)`, quotes) cannot be passed inline. The first attempt at the MGIT-104 commit died with `bash: unexpected EOF while looking for matching '`, purely because the message contained backticks inside a heredoc. The workaround is `-m "$(cat file)"`, which works but silently makes the shell responsible for the integrity of an audit artifact.

This matters more for mgit than for git: mgit commits are the reviewer's record of what an agent did, and agents compose messages programmatically. A quoting accident either truncates the record or fails the step.

WHAT TO DO
Add `--file/-F <path>` to `mgit commit` (`-` for stdin), mutually exclusive with `-m`, reading the message verbatim with no shell involved. Mirror git's semantics: the file content is the message as written.

ACCEPTANCE
`mgit commit -F msg.txt` records the file's exact bytes as the message, including backticks, quotes and `$(...)`; `-F -` reads stdin; `-m` together with `-F` is refused naming both; a missing/unreadable file is a clear error and nothing is committed.

Refs: MGIT-104
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Sibling verbs still route their message through the shell: `squash`/`merge` have no -F (and no -m)
nodes.description:
Found while implementing MGIT-105 (--file/-F for `mgit commit`), reported rather than silently widening that task's scope.

`mgit commit` now takes --file/-F (verbatim bytes, `-` = stdin, exclusive with -m). The same gap remains on every other verb that composes a recorded message:

- `mgit squash --message <msg>` (cmd/mgit/squash.go:125) — no -m shorthand, no -F. This is arguably MORE exposed than commit: the squash message is the single message that lands in the user's real git via `--to-git`, i.e. the artifact a human reviewer reads outside mgit. Composing it inline is exactly where a multi-paragraph body with backticks/`$(...)` appears.
- `mgit merge --message <msg>` (cmd/mgit/merge.go:65) — same shape, lower frequency.
- `mgit rollback --reason <text>` (cmd/mgit/rollback.go:89) — free text that ends up in the revert commit's message; same class, smallest stakes.

Not affected: the MCP surface (internal/mcp/server.go) takes message as a JSON string, so no shell is involved there.

WHAT TO DO
Give `squash` (and `merge`) the same contract MGIT-105 established for commit: `-m/--message` inline, `--file/-F <path>` reading bytes verbatim with `-` = stdin, the two mutually exclusive and refused naming both flags, and an unreadable/empty file erroring before anything is written. The helpers already exist in cmd/mgit/commit.go (resolveCommitMessage / readCommitMessageFile) and should be reused, not re-implemented — lift them to a shared file if a second caller appears. Decide explicitly whether `rollback --reason` is worth the same treatment or is genuinely short-text-only.

ACCEPTANCE
`mgit squash --task-id ID -F msg.txt` records the file's exact bytes as the squash message and they survive into `--to-git` output byte-identical; `-F -` reads stdin; `-m` plus `-F` refused naming both; unreadable file squashes nothing.

Refs: MGIT-105, R-H229

nodes.title: A GRACEFUL daemon shutdown leaves the same "killed / unsupervised" audit trail as a crash — Daemon.drain bypasses the service layer that writes `destroyed`
nodes.description:
Found while live-verifying MGIT-103 on macOS/libkrun. SEPARATE from that defect and not fixed by it.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (live, not inferred)

Booted a real sandbox, then SIGTERMed its daemon — the ORDERLY path, which runs `Daemon.drain`. The drain worked: the VM process was gone, the per-VM state dir was removed, the registration was gone. But the append-only trail reads:

    DRAIN-1 | created
    DRAIN-1 | resumed
    DRAIN-1 | killed | {"reason":"unsupervised: the daemon that supervised this sandbox exited; its VM could not be verified by the daemon that replaced it..."}

That is the record MGIT-102 writes for a sandbox whose daemon DIED — and it is now the record a clean, deliberate shutdown produces too. Compare `mgit sandbox remove --force` on the same build, which correctly yields `created destroyed`.

ROOT CAUSE (code)

`Daemon.drain` (internal/sandboxd/daemon.go) calls `d.cfg.Manager.Stop` / `d.cfg.Manager.Remove` — the BACKEND manager — directly. The `destroyed` event is written one layer up, in `internal/service/sandbox.go` (`teardownLocked(ctx, reg, model.EventDestroyed, ...)`), which drain never goes through. So a drained sandbox leaves no terminal event and no registry row update; the NEXT daemon then reconciles a registration it cannot verify and stamps it `killed / unsupervised`.

Note this is also the layering rule in CLAUDE.md inverted: the daemon reaches the store-facing manager instead of the service that owns the semantics.

WHY IT MATTERS

It is an audit-trail honesty defect in the same family as MGIT-102. The trail cannot distinguish "the operator stopped this cleanly and mgit tore it down" from "the daemon died and nobody knows what happened to the VM". Every idle-timeout exit — the daemon's own designed NFR-17.6 behavior, so the COMMON case — currently manufactures a `killed / unsupervised` record for a sandbox that was destroyed in an orderly way. That both dilutes the signal a real crash should carry and overstates what went wrong on a normal day.

Refs: FR-17.19, NFR-17.6, MGIT-102, MGIT-103
nodes.prompt:
Reproduce first: boot a real sandbox, `kill -TERM` its daemon (not -9), and read `sandbox_events` for the task. You should see the trail end in `killed` with the "unsupervised" detail, even though the drain ran and removed everything cleanly.

Then route `Daemon.drain` through the same teardown the service layer uses for `mgit sandbox remove`, so the `destroyed` event and the registry-row removal happen once, in one place. Do not duplicate the event-writing into the daemon — a second writer of the same terminal event is how the two paths drift apart again.

Watch the ordering: drain is bounded (drainTimeout) and must stay best-effort per sandbox — one stuck sandbox must not strand the rest, and a failure to write the event must not abort the shutdown. A sandbox that genuinely cannot be stopped should still end up with an honest record, not a silently-clean one.

Gate it next to its twin in scripts/e2e/sandbox_registry_durability.sh: that script already has kill_repo_daemon (SIGKILL) and reads the trail; add the SIGTERM case and assert `created ... destroyed`.
nodes.acceptance: A sandbox torn down by `Daemon.drain` (idle exit, SIGINT, SIGTERM) leaves a terminal `destroyed` event and no live registry row, so its trail is indistinguishable from an explicit `mgit sandbox remove` and clearly distinguishable from the `killed / unsupervised` record an ungraceful daemon death produces. Asserted in scripts/e2e/sandbox_registry_durability.sh, which already SIGKILLs a daemon and reads the trail — add the SIGTERM twin. The drain path goes through the service layer that owns teardown semantics rather than reaching the backend manager directly.

nodes.title: An image-store failure is reported to the agent as guest memory exhaustion — "the guest stopped answering mid-command" plus RAM advice for a missing trust root
nodes.description:
Found while live-verifying MGIT-103 on macOS/libkrun.

WHAT WAS MEASURED (verbatim CLI output)

In a repo with a sandbox registered against an image reference that cannot resolve (no trust root generated in THIS repo):

    $ mgit sandbox exec --task REG-2 -- /bin/echo booted
    mgit sandbox: sandbox exec: sandbox ensure-running: libkrun launch: resolve image
    "base@sha256:...": image store unavailable: images: load trust root
    (run GenerateTrustRoot first): missing or invalid key

    mgit: the guest stopped answering mid-command.
    This sandbox (task REG-2) is capped at 2048 MB of memory and 2 vCPU. Memory
    exhaustion inside the guest presents exactly like this, and the cause is a
    property of THIS SANDBOX, not of your project.

The first paragraph is correct and actionable. The second is appended unconditionally and is FALSE here: no guest ever started, nothing was capped, and memory had nothing to do with it. The remedy it implies — raise --memory-mb — cannot work.

WHY IT MATTERS

This is the MGIT-92-family failure mode inverted. The guest-OOM hint exists because guest memory exhaustion is genuinely hard to diagnose, but it is being attached to failures that happen BEFORE any guest exists (image resolution, trust root, backend construction). An agent under progress pressure reads the last paragraph, not the first, and will spend its next several turns raising memory limits against an image-store problem — or conclude the sandbox is unusable and fall back to bare host commands, which is the exact behavior mgit's containment story cannot afford.

The correct rule is narrow: only attach the memory hint when a guest actually STARTED and then stopped answering. A launch that failed before boot should carry its own cause and nothing else.

Refs: MGIT-92, FR-17.9, FR-17.10
nodes.prompt:
Reproduce first, because the exact wording is the defect: register a sandbox against an image reference that cannot resolve in this repo (e.g. skip `mgit sandbox image init`), then run `mgit sandbox exec`. You should get an accurate image-store error immediately followed by an unconditional paragraph about guest memory exhaustion.

Find where that advice is appended (grep for "stopped answering mid-command") and gate it on evidence that a guest actually ran — the same evidence MGIT-92 uses to decide it can quote a console tail. A launch that never reached boot has no console and no guest; that is the discriminator, and it is already available at that point.

Do not delete the hint. It was added for a real diagnosis problem and is right when a guest genuinely dies mid-command. The fix is to stop attaching it to failures it cannot explain.
nodes.acceptance: A sandbox failure that occurs before the guest boots (image resolve, trust root, backend unavailable) reports only its own cause; the "the guest stopped answering mid-command" text and the per-sandbox memory/vCPU advice appear only when a guest actually started and then stopped responding. Covered by a test that asserts the pre-boot failure output does NOT contain the memory advice, alongside one that asserts a genuine mid-command guest death still does.

nodes.title: `sandbox policy set/show/revoke` dial a VM that lazy provisioning has not booted yet — reproduced on main, NOT fixed by MGIT-102
nodes.description:
Reported from a live user walk on the v0.4.5 pin (R-H232): after a clean base re-compose, the egress-policy step failed with

    vm control channel unreachable ... /w/0Z6EAJ7X/c.sock: no such file or directory

The reporting lane hypothesised the MGIT-102/103 class (lifecycle state referencing a dead control socket). REPRODUCED AND ROOT-CAUSED HERE 2026-08-12, and that hypothesis is WRONG — which matters, because it means a release does not fix it.

REPRODUCTION ON MAIN, WHICH ALREADY CONTAINS THE MGIT-102 FIX

    mgit work /tmp/wt --task-id REPRO-EG2 --sandbox --network allowlist \
      --allow example.com:443 --image <base>
    -> Registered sandbox 01KZVK8EAYTPNRHANK7YFQVE17 (created)
    mgit sandbox status REPRO-EG2   -> REPRO-EG2  created  01KZVK8...
    mgit sandbox policy set --task-id REPRO-EG2 --allow other.example.com:443
    -> Error: sandbox: egress policy: vm control channel unreachable at
       .../w/7YFQVE17/c.sock: connect: no such file or directory
       (the sandbox may not be running, or its VM predates this capability);
       the running policy was NOT changed

Same error string, same /w/<8-char>/c.sock shape as the report. `policy show` and `policy revoke` fail identically — all three verbs share the path.

ROOT CAUSE
cmd/mgit-sandboxd/policy_wiring_libkrun.go dials the VM child's control socket DIRECTLY:

    libkrun.NewPolicyClient(c.workDir, sandboxID).SetPolicy(entries, drain)

There is no EnsureRunning and no consultation of sandbox state anywhere in that wiring. Provisioning is LAZY by design (FR-17.9/FR-17.10): `work --sandbox` and `sandbox launch` REGISTER the sandbox in state `created` and the microVM boots on FIRST USE. So immediately after the documented setup step — which is exactly where a user walk arrives at the egress-policy step — there is no VM, therefore no c.sock, therefore this error. The verb assumes a running VM that the product's own contract says will not exist yet.

WHY THIS IS NOT MGIT-102 OR MGIT-103
- MGIT-102 was registry amnesia: the sandbox was NOT FOUND. Here the sandbox is found; its state is `created` and correct. The fix is merged on main and this still reproduces.
- MGIT-103 is an orphaned VM after an abnormal daemon death. No VM ever existed here.
Both would leave the registration intact and the VM absent, which is why the symptom LOOKS the same from outside — see the diagnostic defect below, which is why it looks the same.

THE DIAGNOSTIC DEFECT, WHICH IS THE MGIT-104 CLASS AGAIN
The message guesses: "the sandbox may not be running, or its VM predates this capability". The daemon HOLDS the sandbox state and could say which. Three genuinely different conditions collapse into one string with two speculative causes:
  1. never booted (state `created`) — normal, expected, and needs no VM at all;
  2. booted then died (the MGIT-99 class: a dead guest still recorded `running`);
  3. a genuinely old VM predating the control channel.
Each has a different remedy, and the operator is handed all three as a shrug. The reporting lane's misattribution to MGIT-102/103 was a direct consequence: given that string, their inference was reasonable.

IMPACT
This is the only thing between the integrating lane and a green gate 2; their loop leg is paused on it. It is on the documented setup path, hits a first-hour user, and it will NOT be fixed by shipping the current main.</description>
<prompt>Make the egress-policy verbs honour lazy provisioning, and make the failure name the actual state.

1. CONSULT THE STATE BEFORE DIALING. The policy path must read the sandbox's registration rather than assuming a running VM. Route the three verbs (set, show, revoke) through the service layer that already knows the state, instead of constructing a vmctl client straight from workDir + sandboxID in the daemon wiring.

2. DECIDE THE `created` CASE DELIBERATELY, and write down why. Two defensible designs:
   (a) EnsureRunning — boot the VM, then apply. Consistent with every other verb under FR-17.9/17.10, where first use boots.
   (b) Apply to the pending launch options, so the VM boots WITH that policy — cheaper, and avoids booting a guest merely to configure it. This is likely the better answer for `set`, and it is strictly safer: the VM never runs with the old policy even momentarily.
   Whichever you choose, `show` on a `created` sandbox must report the policy that WILL be enforced, clearly labelled as not-yet-running rather than presented as live. Do not report a pending policy as if it were being enforced — that is the "records are truth" line this project holds.

3. DISTINGUISH THE THREE CONDITIONS IN THE MESSAGE. Never booted, booted-then-unreachable, and predates-the-capability are different failures with different remedies. Name the one that applies, using the state the daemon already has. Delete the two-cause guess.

4. KEEP FAILING CLOSED. The existing fail-closed contract is correct and must not weaken: an unreachable child is an error, never an empty policy, because an empty list reads as "nothing is allowed" when the truth may be "nothing is enforcing" (MGIT-72, ADR-012, SEC-04). Nothing in this ticket licenses a silent success.

5. CHECK THE OTHER BACKENDS. firecracker and vzf policy wiring may share the shape. Report what you find; fix what is the same defect, file what is not.

REQUIRED TESTS
- `policy set` on a `created` sandbox succeeds (or refuses with an accurate, actionable message — per your item-2 decision), and the policy is demonstrably in force once the VM boots. Assert the SECOND half live: boot it and read the enforced policy back.
- `policy show` on a `created` sandbox does not claim a running policy.
- The three conditions produce three distinguishable messages; assert the negatives (a never-booted sandbox is never told its VM "predates this capability").
- The fail-closed behaviour on a genuinely unreachable running VM is unchanged.

VERIFY LIVE on macOS/libkrun, reproducing the exact reported failure first and showing it resolved. An unsigned mgit-sandboxd cannot start a VM at all and will hand you a vacuous pass — sign it: codesign --force --sign - --entitlements build/darwin/vz.entitlements <binary>

Refs: MGIT-109, R-H232, MGIT-102, MGIT-103, MGIT-99, MGIT-104, FR-17.9, FR-17.10, MGIT-72</prompt>
<acceptance>The reported failure no longer occurs on the documented setup path: after `mgit work --sandbox --network allowlist`, the egress-policy verbs work against a registered-but-unbooted sandbox without a manual boot step, and the resulting policy is verified in force once the VM runs. A sandbox whose VM is genuinely unreachable still fails closed with the running policy unchanged, and the message names which of the three conditions applies rather than listing speculative causes. `policy show` never presents a pending policy as an enforced one. Verified live on macOS/libkrun with the original reproduction captured before and after.</acceptance>
</invoke>

nodes.title: Sandboxed Agent Execution (microVM)
nodes.description: Seamless, platform-agnostic microVM sandbox bound to mgit task-worktrees so LLM agents execute untrusted code (builds, installs, tests) with no host exposure and full per-commit provenance. Implements FR-17 per ADR-005 and both audits.
nodes.prompt: STORY CONTEXT: Build the mgit sandbox (FR-17) — one task <-> one worktree <-> one microVM. The guest is the hostile party (it runs the npm/supply-chain code); the host is the trust anchor. Read FIRST: docs/adr/005-microvm-sandbox.md, AUDIT-FR17-SANDBOX-V1.md (F-01..F-12), AUDIT-FR17-SANDBOX-SECURITY-V1.md (SEC-01..SEC-12), plus CLAUDE.md governing rules. Dependency order (do not violate): 11.1 requirements -> 11.2 model -> 11.3 store -> 11.4 daemon -> 11.5 backends -> 11.6 guest-fs -> 11.7 network -> 11.8 attestation/land -> 11.9 service -> 11.10 cli -> 11.11 agent-integration -> 11.12 verification/compliance -> 11.13 e2e/perf/fuzz. Architecture: cmd -> service -> store/manager -> model. Handlers never touch store/manager directly. DI everywhere, clock injected, no globals/init(). CGO confined to mgit-sandboxd; core stays pure-Go. STORY-CLOSURE GATE (mandatory before the story is marked done): an INDEPENDENT, detailed code review of the entire story's delivered code must be performed by a reviewer that did NOT write it (separate agent/session or human). The review covers: requirement traceability (every FR-17/NFR-17 acceptance criterion -> code -> test), the layered-architecture & dependency rules, SQL/append-only laws, go-git rules, the security-audit remediations (SEC-01..SEC-12, F-01..F-12), function/file size limits, and anti-stub verification. Findings are logged and resolved before closure. Use the security-review skill for the security pass. The reviewer must be independent of the implementer. COMMIT MESSAGE: follow CLAUDE.md format {type}({scope}): {desc} + 'Refs: MGIT-11.x'. Do NOT add a 'Co-authored-by' trailer, an agent name, an assistant signature, or any 'Generated with' line. Rationale: commit metadata is an audit artifact and must not disclose the internal agent/tooling used to produce the change (information-exposure control).

nodes.title: Guest→host land-ready notification channel (auto-land trigger)

CONTEXT: MGIT-11.10.10 shipped the host-initiated land DATA path: `mgit sandbox land --task <id>` → daemon → service.LandService → verified LandOrchestrator → host dials the guest land vsock port (1025) and pulls the object pool (single peer-authorized read, replayed to the orchestrator; SEC-06/SEC-10). The notify channel carries NO land data and asserts NO provenance — it is only a trigger; the verified host pull does all the work. Two viable shapes (decide + justify):

nodes.title: Guest-side vsock↔TCP publish bridge (complete SEC-09 reachability)
nodes.prompt:
Complete one-way port publishing (SEC-09): the host-side publisher + model + CLI + the SEC-09 one-way isolation are done (MGIT-11.10.12) and the guest-cannot-reach-host-loopback e2e PASSES, but the host→guest REACHABILITY does not work end to end. Live KVM run of TestE2E_PortPublish_GuestServiceReachableOnHost FAILED: the publisher's firecracker.portDialer.DialGuestPort does fcvsock.Dial(vsockPath, guestPort) — a host→guest VSOCK connect — but a real guest dev server (and the e2e's busybox `nc -ll`) listens on TCP, not AF_VSOCK. Then the host publisher's host→guest vsock connect (DialGuestPort) reaches the guest bridge → the TCP dev server → response flows back to host 127.0.0.1:<hostport>.

nodes.title: mgit run — task-bound sandbox command routing (foundation)
nodes.prompt:
Build `mgit run [--] <command...>`, the host-side routing primitive the rest of MGIT-11.11 rests on (the Claude PreToolUse hook in 11.11.1 rewrites Bash to `mgit run -- bash -lc <orig>`; the 11.11.3 shims call `mgit run`). It auto-routes a task command into that task's bound sandbox, FAIL-CLOSED: if no sandbox is bound for the cwd or the daemon is unavailable, it errors with a non-zero exit and NEVER runs the command on the host.

DESIGN (decided in scout): `mgit run` is a PURE daemon client — it never touches Store/Manager (CLI-is-thin-client rule). Resolution: connect via the same productionSandboxConnect as `mgit sandbox`; call List(); pick the sandbox whose WorktreePath is the nearest ancestor of (or equals) the cwd; Exec into it with ExecRequest{Command: args, Dir: cwd}. Identical-path mount => guest Dir == host cwd. Host environment is NEVER forwarded (FR-17.3); only explicit --env KEY=VALUE injections pass, mirroring `mgit sandbox exec`. SEC-05: surface only host-observed identity in errors. Propagate the guest exit code verbatim via exitError (like sandbox exec). There is NO host-exec code path in this command at all — fail-closed is structural.

Add a hidden/health surface the 11.11.1 hook uses to decide allow-vs-ask: a way to answer "is a sandbox available for this cwd?" without running anything (resolve cwd->sandbox via List + check State is created/running/suspended; not-found or daemon-unreachable => unavailable).

ARCH: cmd/mgit/run.go, registered in rootCmd; reuse the sandboxClient interface + connectFunc injection from cmd/mgit/sandbox.go so it is unit-testable with the existing fakeSandboxClient. No new service/store layers.

nodes.title: Harden ADR-002 content_hash (omitted fields + sub-second time)
nodes.description: The ADR-002 content_hash formula (SHA-256 over message+file_diffs+task_id+parent+created_at) omits AgentID/CreatedBy/SessionID/CommitType/Branch and truncates created_at to second precision. Two distinct audit records can therefore collide on content_hash. Found by the MGIT-11.8 closure security pass (F3); pre-existing, not introduced by 11.8.
nodes.prompt:
The authoritative ADR-002 content_hash is model.Commit.ComputeContentHash = SHA-256(message + file_diffs_json + task_id + parent_id + created_at), with created_at formatted to SECOND precision ("2006-01-02T15:04:05Z"). The MGIT-11.8 closure security pass (F3, MEDIUM) found:
1. The hash OMITS AgentID, CreatedBy, SessionID, CommitType, Branch — two commits differing only in (e.g.) AgentID produce the SAME content_hash, so the "authoritative compliance identifier" does not uniquely identify the audited record, weakening "if hashes diverge, the commit was tampered with".
2. created_at is truncated to second precision — sub-second differences collide.
3. The formula uses parent_id (parent SHA-1) where ADR-002's prose says parent_content_hash.

This is a PRE-EXISTING design issue (predates FR-17; 11.8 only extracted the function to model and single-sourced it). It was NOT changed in 11.8 because changing content_hash REWRITES every existing commit's hash — a breaking, migration-bearing change to ADR-002 that needs its own ADR revision + data-migration plan.

SCOPE: revise ADR-002 to define a complete, collision-resistant content_hash (include the identity-bearing fields; full-precision UTC time; resolve the parent_id-vs-parent_content_hash wording), with a migration/versioning strategy (e.g. a content_hash version tag) so existing task_commits remain verifiable. Coordinate with FR-3.1, FR-12.3, and the sandbox land re-verification (FR-17.24) which recomputes via the same function. Owner decision: whether to version the hash or accept the documented limitation for v1.

Refs: ADR-002, FR-3.1, FR-12.3, FR-17.24; found in MGIT-11.8 closure (F3).
nodes.acceptance: A decision (revise vs. accept-documented) recorded; if revised, ADR-002 updated with a complete content_hash definition + a migration/versioning plan that keeps existing commits verifiable, and model.Commit.ComputeContentHash updated accordingly with tests.

nodes.title: FR-17 closure-review medium/low findings (hardening + correctness)
nodes.prompt:

MEDIUM:
- F-B (SEC-04 IPv6): allowlist firewall is iptables-only; guest eth0 auto-gets a link-local IPv6 and there is no ip6tables DROP chain — SEC-04 flow-layer default-deny is realized for v4 only. Not exploitable in v1 (no host v6 routing/forwarding for the tap, per-VM /30), but relies on absence-of-routing. Fix: add `ipv6.disable=1` to the guest kernel cmdline (and/or mirror an ip6tables chain) + a test that the guest has no usable v6 route in allowlist mode.
- F-C (DeriveState bug, CONFIRMED w/ PoC): internal/store/index/sandbox_events.go DeriveState excludes only `policy_granted`; a running T2 sandbox whose latest event is `credentials_injected` is mis-read as ErrIndexCorrupted. Fix: exclude ALL non-state-bearing events (single-source the set from the model via StateForEvent ok) + regression test TestDeriveState_LatestIsCredentialsInjected.
- F-D (suspend/resume grants): suspendLocked calls StopEgress not Revoke; resume's StartEgress rebuilds an empty allowlist and never replays LiveGrants, while RecordDenial still sees s.live and suppresses re-prompting — a granted dest is permanently denied post-resume. Fix: replay LiveGrants on resume (grants are sandbox-lifetime scoped, spanning suspend) + suspend->resume->grant-honored test. (Matches the interaction flagged on MGIT-11.9.4.)
- F-E (SEC-10 latent): fcVM.PeerIdentity() returns constant "cid:3"; Authorize is currently a tautology. v1 isolation is via per-VM socket path (sound), but the guest->host inbound channel (pairs with MGIT-11.10.11) must feed a per-VM-distinct host-observed source identity into Authorize, never the constant CID. Add an inbound-direction two-guest isolation test when that channel ships.

LOW / hardening:
- DNS server returns denied-range IPs to the guest + over-wide pin set (filter IsUnconditionallyDenied from answer + pin).
- DNS rate limiter is fixed-window (2x boundary burst) — consider sliding window/token bucket.
- daemon dialOK accepts a 3-byte greeting prefix (compare full greeting for symmetry).

- F-06: confirm `mgit verify --independent` (independent re-verification) is scheduled outside MGIT-11 per its original P2 disposition, or implement it.

nodes.title: Land path concurrency + buffered-memory budget cap
nodes.prompt:
Bound the land path's worst-case host memory. CROSS item carried over from the MGIT-11.10.10 security annotation: \"max concurrent land ops; stream-to-store (bounded memory) — DefaultLimits 4GiB x concurrency must fit a documented host budget.\"

CURRENT STATE (MGIT-11.10.10): sandboxd.LandChannel reads each guest pool ONCE into an in-memory buffer bounded per-pool by land.DefaultLimits().MaxTotalBytes (4 GiB), keyed by sandbox id, replayed to the orchestrator and dropped after (Discard on every abandoned-land path). There is NO cap on CONCURRENT in-flight lands: the daemon's MaxConns (default 64) bounds connections, not land memory — so the theoretical worst case is MaxConns × 4 GiB buffered at once. In practice lands are single-client/serialized today, so this is latent, not live.

WHAT TO DO:
- Add an explicit concurrent-land cap (a small semaphore around the land path, separate from MaxConns) and a documented host memory budget = cap × MaxTotalBytes; surface both as daemon config with safe defaults.
- Consider streaming the pool to a temp object store instead of a full in-RAM buffer if a larger pool ceiling is ever needed (keeps the single-read SEC-06 property — verify the bytes you import — while bounding RAM). Document the tradeoff if kept in-RAM.
- log() what is bounded/rejected (no silent truncation).
- Reconcile with land.DefaultLimits (per-object/count/total ceilings already enforced in DecodeObjects).
nodes.acceptance: The daemon enforces a documented maximum concurrent-land count and a derived host memory budget (cap × per-pool ceiling); exceeding the concurrency cap rejects/queues rather than over-allocating. The per-pool ceiling and the concurrency cap are config with safe defaults and are logged. A test demonstrates the cap rejects/queues beyond the limit and that buffered memory is bounded.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: MGIT-11.7 network enforcement: KVM e2e round-trip + open-mode extIface
nodes.prompt:
Validate the MGIT-11.7 network policy enforcement end-to-end on a real guest (the KVM box at the dev runner), and close the two non-portable gaps. The host-side engine + firecracker tap/NIC/firewall + daemon->service->egress.Runner wiring are all implemented, unit-tested, cross-compiled and linux-lint-clean (commits 6b6aeb0..4a06420); what remains is the live round-trip that can only run on KVM with a guest image, plus open-mode external-interface plumbing.

DO (gate like the exec/land e2e — MGIT_E2E_GUEST_ROOTFS + /dev/kvm + root):
1. allowlist round-trip: launch an allowlist sandbox; from the guest, a TCP connect + DNS resolve to an allowlisted host (e.g. registry.npmjs.org) SUCCEEDS through the host proxy/DNS on the tap gateway; a connect to a non-allowlisted host, a raw-IP connect to a non-allowlisted IP, a QUIC/UDP attempt, and any RFC1918/link-local/metadata (169.254.169.254) destination are DENIED; every allow/deny lands in sandbox_egress_log. Verify the guest has no direct route (tap firewall default-deny) and DNS resolves only allowlisted names (rate-limited; NXDOMAIN burst flagged).
2. none round-trip: the guest has no NIC and cannot egress at all.
3. open-mode extIface: the firecracker backend's fcHypervisor.extIface is currently always "" so open mode fails closed (TapPlan.validate needs an external interface to MASQUERADE through). Wire it: either auto-detect the host default-route interface on Linux, or expose it via firecracker.Config / a daemon flag, then prove an open-mode guest reaches an arbitrary host (NAT) and the open risk note is recorded.
4. one-way port publish (SEC-09): a guest dev server is reachable at host 127.0.0.1:<port>; the guest cannot reach a host loopback service.
5. DNS-server fuzz: fuzz egress.DNSServer.handleQuery against malformed/hostile packets (it parses guest input via x/net/dnsmessage) — pairs with the land-parser fuzz in 11.13.3.

Refs: FR-17.7, FR-17.8, SEC-04, SEC-07, SEC-09; memory note fr17-network-enforcement. No co-authored-by/agent/Generated-with trailer.
nodes.acceptance: On the KVM box: an allowlist guest reaches allowlisted hosts via the host proxy/DNS and is denied for non-allowlisted/raw-IP/QUIC/RFC1918/link-local/metadata destinations (all audited); none guest cannot egress; open guest reaches arbitrary hosts via host NAT with the risk note recorded (extIface wired); one-way port publish works and the guest cannot reach host loopback; DNSServer fuzz passes. Gated like the exec/land e2e.

nodes.title: Guest writable root (overlay) for arbitrary identical-path worktree mounts
nodes.prompt:
DISCOVERED in MGIT-11.13.4 (real exec round-trip, 2026-06-20). The guest rootfs is mounted READ-ONLY (FR-17.17 immutable pinned image), so mgit-guest (PID 1) can only mount the worktree over a PRE-EXISTING mount point — it cannot os.MkdirAll an arbitrary host worktree path (e.g. /home/user/repo/worktrees/task) on a read-only root (the mkdir fails). The cached CI image sidesteps this with an external /sbin/overlay-init that makes / writable via overlayfs(lower=squashfs RO, upper=overlay COW drive vdb) then switch_roots. mgit-guest needs the equivalent so the identical-path worktree mount (FR-17.3, MGIT-11.6.5) works for ANY host path, not just a baked one.

SCOPE: make the guest root writable before mounting the worktree. Option A (preferred): mgit-guest, as PID 1, mounts an overlayfs (lowerdir = the RO image root, upperdir/workdir on the backend's overlay drive vdb or a tmpfs) and switch_root/pivot_root into it, then continues (mount /proc already done, /dev, worktree at its now-creatable identical path, /tmp). Option B: ship overlay-init in the guest image and chain init -> mgit-guest after it sets up the writable root. The backend already attaches the overlay drive (vdb); wiring mgit-guest to consume it as the upper is the natural fit. This also removes the os.MkdirAll-on-RO-root limitation noted in MGIT-11.6.5 and lets MGIT-11.13.4's e2e use a t.TempDir() worktree (drop the baked-mountpoint requirement, MGIT_E2E_WORKTREE).

nodes.title: Guest writable root: disk-backed COW upper (vdb) instead of tmpfs
nodes.prompt:
Follow-on from MGIT-11.6.6. mgit-guest's makeRootWritable currently uses a TMPFS upper for the writable overlay root (RAM-backed, ephemeral) — chosen for v1 simplicity (no in-guest mkfs). But FR-17.17/NFR-17.7 mandate a per-VM DISK-BACKED COW overlay that 'grows only with what the task installs', and the firecracker backend ALREADY attaches one as the overlay drive vdb (microvm createOverlay -> a sparse file, attached IsReadOnly=false). The cached image's /sbin/overlay-init overlays onto vdb, not tmpfs. With a tmpfs upper, every byte written outside the worktree (npm/pip/apt installs, build artifacts that escape the worktree) consumes guest RAM and can OOM the guest on large installs, and is invisible to the disk quota the overlay drive is sized to.

SCOPE: make mgit-guest use the backend's overlay drive (vdb) as the overlayfs upperdir when present, falling back to tmpfs when no overlay drive is attached (e.g. vzf/virtiofs). The drive is a raw sparse file, so the guest must mkfs it on first boot (busybox mkfs.ext4 or e2fsprogs in the image) then mount it for upper/work. Mind drive ordering (rootfs=vda, overlay=vdb, worktree=vdc) and that the worktree is mounted AFTER switch_root. Host-supply the overlay device the same way the worktree descriptor is supplied (guestboot cmdline) rather than hardcoding /dev/vdb.

nodes.title: SEC-03: wire quarantine into the launch path (private store + worktree delivery)
nodes.prompt:
HIGH finding from the FR-17 story-closure security review (AUDIT-FR17-SANDBOX-CLOSURE-V2.md, finding F-A). The SEC-03 quarantine control is NOT realized: internal/sandboxd/quarantine/ (BuildPlan/BindPrivateStore) is implemented and correct in isolation (tested) but has ZERO production importers. Every backend delivers the raw worktree to the guest with no private-store rebind and no symlink canonicalization: firecracker `mke2fs -d <worktree>` packs the subtree wholesale (worktree_image.go), vzf shares the live dir (hypervisor_darwin.go), microvm/container pass WorktreePath through.

CALIBRATION: the shared .mgit store is a SIBLING of the worktree, so it is NOT packed today — there is no constructible shared-store read/write in the current layout (hence High, not Critical). But (a) nothing enforces shared-store non-reachability, and (b) any .git inside a worktree (e.g. a clone, as internal/guest/land.go's PlainOpen expects) is packed verbatim, exposing that clone's reachable history to a compromised guest (T6 cross-task exposure). SEC-03's "guest mount is working-tree files only; .git rebound to a private sandbox-local store" is unmet.

DO:
1. Wire quarantine.BuildPlan + BindPrivateStore into the microvm CreateVM path (both firecracker + vzf) and the container backend. Exclude/rebind .git/.mgit; mount a fresh private object store at the guest .mgit; fail the launch (ErrSharedStoreReachable) if non-reachability cannot be guaranteed.
2. Canonicalize worktree symlinks on delivery and reject any whose resolved target escapes the worktree (finding F-A / NEW-2): firecracker pack and vzf share both need this; the land/commit side already defends symlinks but the mount-delivery side has none.
3. Add a hostile-guest test: a guest cannot read the shared store, other tasks' objects, or follow an escaping symlink; land remains the only private->shared path.

Blocks MGIT-11 closure on SEC-03. Refs: SEC-03, AUDIT-FR17-SANDBOX-CLOSURE-V2.md F-A. No co-authored-by/agent/Generated-with trailer.
nodes.acceptance: quarantine.BuildPlan/BindPrivateStore are invoked by the microvm (firecracker+vzf) and container launch paths; the guest mount is working-tree files only with a private sandbox-local object store, the host shared store/refs/index/parent .mgit are not resolvable from the guest, escaping worktree symlinks are rejected on delivery, launch fails closed (ErrSharedStoreReachable) otherwise, and a hostile-guest test proves it.

nodes.title: Extend SEC-03 quarantine delivery to vzf (macOS) + container
nodes.prompt:

The SEC-03 quarantine (private-store provisioning + plan + fail-closed wiring) is realized and live-validated on the firecracker/KVM backend (the host-side provision package, BuildPlan/BindPrivateStore, and the firecracker copy-and-land staging that drops in-worktree stores, rejects escaping symlinks, and lays in the private .mgit). Refs: SEC-03, AUDIT-FR17-SANDBOX-CLOSURE-V2.md F-A, split from MGIT-11.6.8. No co-authored-by/agent/Generated-with trailer.

nodes.title: Sub-agents do not checkpoint: every task's commits are a burst at the END of the run, so an interrupted agent loses everything
nodes.description:
MEASURED 2026-08-12/13 across five real sub-agent runs on this repo. This is evidence bearing directly on MGIT-28's open question, and it is negative evidence about our own product.

WHAT PROMPTED IT
An agent working MGIT-109 was killed by an accidental ctrl-c roughly 30 minutes in. Recovering its work was the natural test of mgit's central claim — "every coherent step is a task-tagged micro-commit ... so the agent can orient, course-correct, and land only the reviewed result".

mgit contributed NOTHING to that recovery, because the agent had made ZERO commits. What survived was uncommitted files in a directory. A plain directory would have done exactly as well.

THE MEASUREMENT (mgit log --task-id <T> --json, timestamps vs each agent's wall-clock run)

  task       commits   commit window   agent run   checkpointing?
  MGIT-102       7        6.5 min        ~40 min      no - burst at end
  MGIT-103       2        2.0 min        ~34 min      no - burst at end
  MGIT-105       2        1.0 min        ~16 min      no - burst at end
  MGIT-095       2          -            ~33 min      no - burst at end
  MGIT-109       0          -            ~30 min      none at all

Every agent treats `mgit commit` as a FINAL PACKAGING STEP, not a checkpoint. MGIT-102's seven commits look like a healthy micro-commit trail until you notice they were all written in the last 6 minutes of a 40-minute run, 13 seconds apart. The trail is manufactured at the end to look like a history that never happened.

WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE LOST WORK
1. The checkpoint substrate is the product. If agents only commit at the end, mgit is functioning as a fancy `git add && git commit` at hand-off time, and the "orient and course-correct from a checkpoint" loop has no checkpoints to work from.
2. It makes the reviewer's record thinner than it looks. A reviewer reading seven commits believes they are seeing seven coherent steps; they are seeing one step split seven ways after the fact. That is a provenance claim the record does not support.
3. It is direct evidence for MGIT-28 (whether agents use the backtrack/fork/cherry-pick loop autonomously). At least the checkpoint half: they do not. Not because they refuse, but because nothing asks them to, and no failure mode punishes them until an interruption does.
4. CLAUDE.md's spawning section tells agents to "commit a step" with `mgit commit -a`, but says nothing about CADENCE, and nothing in the loop prompts a checkpoint. The instruction reads as "how to commit", not "when".

NOT A CODE DEFECT. mgit works as built. This is a gap between the discipline the product assumes and the behaviour it actually gets, which is exactly the kind of thing only dogfooding surfaces.</description>
<prompt>Make checkpointing actually happen, then measure whether it did.

FIRST, DECIDE WHAT THE RIGHT CADENCE IS — do not assume "more commits is better". A checkpoint is worth making when there is something a later agent or reviewer would want to return to: a passing test after a red one, a working increment, a decision taken. Commits per elapsed minute is the wrong target and would produce noise that makes the record worse, not better.

CANDIDATE MECHANISMS, in rough order of cheapness:
1. Instruction: state the cadence explicitly in the spawning brief and in the generated agent discipline (internal/agentadapter/claudemd.go) — the generated block is how agents learn the verbs, and it currently teaches HOW to commit but not WHEN.
2. Prompt: have `mgit` itself notice a long gap since the last task commit with a dirty worktree, and say so on the next command. A nudge at the moment of use beats a rule read once at the start.
3. Enforcement: something stronger (a pre-exec hook, a `mgit run` reminder). Weigh carefully — an agent that commits to satisfy a checker produces exactly the manufactured trail this ticket complains about.

THEN MEASURE IT THE SAME WAY. The measurement above is repeatable: `mgit log --task-id <T> --json` gives created_at per commit; compare the spread against the agent's run duration. A fix is proven when a real task's commits are spread across the run, not when the instruction exists. Re-measure on the next few real tasks and report the same table.

ALSO CONSIDER: is there a cheap `mgit` verb that would make an interrupted agent's state recoverable even without a deliberate commit (a WIP checkpoint, an autosave)? Only propose it if it does not muddy the audit trail — an autosaved blob presented alongside deliberate task commits would be a worse lie than no autosave. Filing a separate ticket for that is fine.

Refs: MGIT-110, MGIT-28, MGIT-109, FR-1.1</prompt>
<acceptance>The cadence is stated where agents actually read it, and a re-measurement across at least three subsequent real sub-agent runs shows task commits spread through the run rather than bursting at the end — reported as the same commits/window/run-duration table. Any enforcement mechanism is assessed against the risk that it manufactures a trail rather than recording one.</acceptance>

nodes.title: vzf backend serves no egress-policy verbs at all — `policy set/show/revoke` report "not served by this daemon"
nodes.description:
Found while fixing MGIT-109 (item 5: "check the other backends; fix what is the same defect, file what is not"). This is NOT the same defect and was deliberately not fixed there.

WHAT WAS CHECKED

- libkrun (macOS default, and linux+libkrun): had the MGIT-109 defect — `policy_wiring_libkrun.go` dialed `libkrun.NewPolicyClient(workDir, sandboxID)` with no consultation of sandbox state. FIXED in MGIT-109 by routing the decision through the service layer, above the controller.

- firecracker (Linux/KVM): SAME defect shape, one layer down. `runnerPolicyController.SetEgressPolicy` calls `egress.Runner.SetPolicy(sandboxID, ...)`, and the runner returns `sandbox %q has no running egress stack` for any sandbox whose VM has not booted — because `Start` is only called from `EnsureRunning`. FIXED by the same MGIT-109 change: the service now stages onto the pending launch and never reaches the controller for a `created`/`suspended` sandbox, so the fix is backend-independent by construction. Code-verified and covered by the service unit tests (the fake controller stands for both backends); NOT live-verified — no Linux/KVM box was available in that session.

- vzf (macOS, `-tags vzf`): DIFFERENT problem, described below.

THE vzf GAP

With `-tags vzf` on darwin:
  - `policy_wiring_libkrun.go` is excluded (its tag is `cgo && !vzf && ...`), so `platformPolicyController` comes from `policy_wiring_other.go` and returns nil;
  - `wireEgress` comes from `egress_wiring_other.go` (`!linux`) and returns an empty `egressWiring`, so `wired.Policy` is nil too.

`selectPolicyController` therefore yields nil, `dcfg.Policy` is never set, and all three verbs reply `controlproto kind 0x50/0x51 not served by this daemon`.

That is CORRECT behaviour given the state of the backend — the daemon fails closed rather than answering a revoke with a silent success — and it is the reason MGIT-109 did not extend staging to vzf: staging a policy for a backend with no enforcer would report "this will be enforced when the VM boots" when nothing would enforce it, which is exactly the lie MGIT-109 removed.

The real gap is upstream: vzf has no allowlist egress enforcement at all. `egress_wiring_other.go` says so — the host-tap proxy/DNS enforcement is the firecracker backend's, and vzf uses a NAT attachment rather than a host tap + firewall.

WHY IT MATTERS ANYWAY

The message an operator gets ("not served by this daemon") describes the daemon's wiring, not the containment reality. An operator on a vzf build who runs `sandbox policy set` learns their command was not served; they do not learn that their `--network allowlist` sandbox has no live egress enforcement to change. Those are different facts, and the second one is the one that matters before running untrusted code. That is the MGIT-104 class of problem again, in a place MGIT-109 did not touch.
nodes.prompt:
Decide and implement vzf's egress-policy posture, and make the operator-facing answer describe containment rather than wiring.

1. ESTABLISH THE GROUND TRUTH FIRST. Determine what a vzf sandbox launched with `--network allowlist` actually enforces today. If the answer is "nothing", that is a containment finding in its own right and outranks this ticket's title — file it and escalate rather than proceeding.

2. THEN CHOOSE ONE:
   (a) Implement live egress policy for vzf (a NAT-attachment equivalent of the firecracker runner's authorizer), so the verbs are served for real; or
   (b) Keep them unserved, but change the refusal so it names the CONTAINMENT fact: this build's vzf backend does not enforce a live allowlist, so there is no policy to change — and say what the operator should use instead (the libkrun default on macOS).

   Option (b) is cheap and honest and should ship regardless of whether (a) is scheduled; do not let (a)'s cost delay the message fix.

3. DO NOT extend MGIT-109's pending-launch staging to vzf until (a) lands. Staging implies enforcement at boot; on a backend that enforces nothing, `PENDING` would be a false promise, which is the exact failure mode MGIT-109 exists to remove.

4. While here, live-verify the MGIT-109 fix on firecracker/KVM. It is code-verified only: `policy set` against a `created` firecracker sandbox should stage and the booted VM should enforce the staged allowlist, asserted by reading it back — the same bar MGIT-109 met on libkrun.

Refs: MGIT-109, MGIT-104, MGIT-72, FR-17.7, FR-17.8, SEC-04
nodes.acceptance: A vzf build either serves the egress-policy verbs against a real enforcer, or refuses them with a message that names the containment fact (no live allowlist enforcement on this backend) and points at the alternative — never with a message that only describes daemon wiring. Pending-launch staging is not offered on a backend that would not enforce it. The MGIT-109 fix is live-verified on firecracker/KVM: a policy set against a `created` sandbox stages, and the booted VM is observed enforcing it.

nodes.title: `export --format git` emits a header-only patch: the git rendering depends on state only the non-dry-run squash creates
nodes.description:
Reported upstream by the integrating lane during a work-item recovery (found, reported, NOT worked around). Their receipts reference a commit-and-revert pair, which invited the benign reading — a net-zero change legitimately produces no hunks. REPRODUCED AND ROOT-CAUSED HERE 2026-08-15, and that reading is WRONG: it fails on a plain additive change with no revert anywhere.

REPRODUCTION (main @ 7b0c020, scratch repo, two ordinary commits)

    echo "line one" > f.txt ; mgit commit -a --task-id EXP-1 -m "add f.txt"
    printf 'line one\nline two\n' > f.txt ; mgit commit -a --task-id EXP-1 -m "add second line"

    mgit export --task-id EXP-1 --format git      -> 0 hunks, header only.
                                                     No `diff --git`, no ---/+++, no @@.
                                                     f.txt does not appear at all.

    mgit squash --task-id EXP-1 --to-git          -> 1 hunk, correct:
        diff --git a/f.txt b/f.txt
        @@ -0,0 +1,2 @@
        +line one
        +line two

Same task, same commits, two verbs, opposite results.

ROOT CAUSE
`cmd/mgit/export.go` case "git" calls SquashTask with **DryRun: true**, explicitly so the export does not mutate state, then hands the result to `SquashService.ExportToGitPatch`.

But `ExportToGitPatch` renders from `c.FileDiffs`, and those are only populated on the NON-dry-run path. `squash.go` binds the identity the diff needs only after the commit is really created:

    hash, err := s.commitStore.CreateSquashCommit(...)
    // Bind the created commit's identity so GitFormatPatch can compute the net
    // base->squash tree diff for the git-am-compatible export. Refs: MGIT-33
    squashCommit.CommitID = hash
    squashCommit.ParentID = base

In dry-run none of that happens, so there is no tree to diff, `FileDiffs` is empty, and the renderer's per-file loop iterates zero times — emitting the mbox header, the `---` separator and the trailer, and nothing else.

WHY THIS IS THE WORST FAILURE SHAPE
The output is SYNTACTICALLY VALID. `git apply` and `git am` accept it and apply nothing, exit 0. A user piping `mgit export --format git | git apply` gets a clean success and an unchanged tree — the loss is silent, on the verb whose entire purpose is getting work OUT of mgit. Compare MGIT-77, where `mgit commit` reported success for work it never recorded; this is the same class on the landing path.

The lane found it during a RECOVERY, which is the worst possible moment: the export is what you reach for when you are already trying to rescue work.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT A REGRESSION. `git log v0.4.5..HEAD -- cmd/mgit/export.go internal/service/squash.go` is empty, so v0.4.5 has it too. Shipping the current release does not worsen it; NOT disclosing it would.

NOTE THE ASYMMETRY THAT HID IT: `squash --to-git` is correct, and that is the path CLAUDE.md documents and that this project has used to land every change this cycle. So our own dogfooding exercised the working verb and never the broken one. The documented path being right is exactly why nobody noticed the other.</description>
<prompt>Make `export --format git` produce the same patch as `squash --to-git`, without mutating state.

1. The export must compute a REAL base->tree diff. Two shapes are defensible:
   (a) compute the net diff directly from the task's commits against the base, with no squash commit created at all — the cleanest, since export is a read;
   (b) build the squash tree in memory (or in a temp ref that is not indexed, not audited, and cleaned up) purely to diff it.
   Prefer (a) if the store can diff two trees without materialising a commit. Whichever you choose, `export` MUST NOT create an indexed or audited squash commit — it is a read verb and its current dry-run intent is correct.

2. NEVER EMIT A SYNTACTICALLY VALID EMPTY PATCH FOR A NON-EMPTY TASK. This is the core of the defect. If the diff cannot be computed, fail loudly and exit non-zero — a patch that applies cleanly and changes nothing is worse than an error, because the caller has already moved on.

3. A genuinely empty net diff (the commit-and-revert case that prompted the report) is legitimate and must be DISTINGUISHABLE from a failure. Say so explicitly — e.g. an informational line on stderr that the task's net change is empty — so a reviewer reading a recovery never has to guess whether the tool failed or the work cancelled out. Do not print an empty patch silently in either case.

REQUIRED TESTS
- `export --format git` and `squash --to-git` produce EQUIVALENT diffs for the same task: added, modified, deleted, and multi-file. Assert on hunks, not on the header — a header-only patch passes any header assertion, which is presumably how this survived.
- The round trip is what actually matters: `export --format git | git apply` in a real git repo reproduces the task's files. Assert the FILE CONTENT afterwards, not the exit code of git apply — apply succeeds on the broken output today.
- A task whose net change is genuinely empty is reported as such and is distinguishable from a failure.
- Export leaves no squash commit indexed and no audit record written.

Check `--format json` and `--format audit-log` for the same dry-run-state-dependency while you are here, and report what you find.

Refs: MGIT-112, MGIT-33, MGIT-77, FR-7</prompt>
<acceptance>For any task, `mgit export --format git` yields a patch whose hunks match `mgit squash --to-git` for that task, and piping it into `git apply` in a real repo reproduces the task's file contents (asserted on content, not exit code). A task with a genuinely empty net change says so distinguishably from a failure, and an uncomputable diff fails loudly rather than emitting an applyable empty patch. Export still creates no indexed squash commit and writes no audit record.</acceptance>
