nodes.title: Fleet soak + chaos gate: N concurrent sandboxes under churn with daemon SIGKILL, continuously gated
nodes.description:
Requested by the integrating lane (2026-08-15) as roadmap input: their worker pools drive N concurrent task sandboxes under churn, and they want the registry/reaping class kept dead UNDER LOAD, not merely under tests.

WHY THIS IS WORTH BUILDING, stated precisely. Everything we fixed this cycle in that class was found and verified SEQUENTIALLY, one sandbox at a time, by hand:
  - MGIT-102 (registry lost when the daemon exits) — one sandbox, one daemon, one restart.
  - MGIT-103 (VM orphaned by SIGKILL) — one daemon, one VM, one kill.
  - MGIT-109 (policy staged onto an unbooted sandbox) — one sandbox.
  - MGIT-98 (fleet memory ceiling) — the AGGREGATE path, and its aggregate refusal is proven BY TEST ONLY, because reaching it needs 8 concurrent VMs. That is the clearest admission that our concurrent behaviour is unmeasured.
Each fix is correct for the case it was tested against. None has been exercised with sandboxes being created, executed, synced, landed and killed simultaneously, which is exactly the shape a worker pool produces.

THE SPECIFIC RISKS THIS WOULD COVER, none currently gated:
  1. Registry rehydration racing concurrent registrations at daemon start.
  2. The aggregate ceiling under genuine concurrency rather than a unit test's sequence — including admission/release accounting drift, where a leak in the released-capacity path would slowly wedge the fleet.
  3. Reaping N VMs on one SIGKILL, not one. The lifeline is per-child; N children closing at once is a different load.
  4. Policy staging racing a boot (ErrSandboxBooted) when many sandboxes boot at once — currently proven by a targeted unit test.
  5. Per-sandbox state directory and socket collisions under rapid create/destroy cycling.
  6. Audit-trail coherence under concurrency: every sandbox that ends must still leave a terminal event, and events must not interleave into an unreadable trail.

SHAPE
A soak script driving parallel create/exec/sync/land across N sandboxes with churn (create and destroy while others run), mixing in daemon SIGKILL at intervals, then asserting invariants rather than absence of crashes:
  - no orphaned VM processes after any kill;
  - every registration either present-and-usable or absent-with-a-terminal-audit-event, never present-and-dead;
  - accounted fleet capacity returns to its floor when the fleet drains (no accounting leak);
  - no state-dir or socket collisions;
  - the audit trail reconstructs a coherent per-sandbox history.

CONTINUOUSLY GATED, per the lane's ask and R-H234's standard: it runs on every change, and a SKIP is visibly not a pass, following scripts/e2e/sandbox_cli_surface.sh and sandbox_registry_durability.sh. Runtime must be bounded so it can gate every push; if the full soak is too slow, gate a short profile on every push and run the long one nightly, and SAY which ran rather than letting a short run imply the long one passed.</description>
<prompt>Build a bounded, continuously-gated fleet soak that asserts invariants under concurrency and churn.

1. START BY MEASURING WHAT N COSTS. Before designing, find out how many concurrent microVMs a CI runner can actually boot, and how long N create/exec/land cycles take. The gate's value depends on N being large enough to expose races and small enough to run every push. Report the measurement; do not pick N by intuition.

2. ASSERT INVARIANTS, NOT ABSENCE OF CRASHES. A soak that only checks "nothing exploded" passes while the fleet quietly leaks capacity. The invariants are listed in the description; each needs a positive assertion with its own failure message naming which invariant broke.

3. MAKE IT FAIL FOR THE RIGHT REASON. For each invariant, verify the gate goes RED against a deliberately broken build (as sandbox_registry_durability.sh was verified against a neutered watchdog). An unverified gate is a decoration — this project has now shipped two gates that were not actually running and one test that passed vacuously.

4. CHURN MUST BE REAL. Sandboxes created and destroyed WHILE others run, not a clean create-all-then-kill-all phase. The interesting races live in the overlap.

5. BOUND THE RUNTIME AND SAY WHAT RAN. If a short profile gates every push and a long soak runs nightly, the output must state which profile executed. A short run that reads as a full soak is the same lie as a SKIP that reads as a pass.

6. RESOURCE HONESTY. This interacts with MGIT-95 caps and MGIT-98's fleet ceiling; N sandboxes at the policy default is real host memory. Ensure the soak declares modest per-sandbox caps rather than trusting defaults, and that hitting the ceiling is treated as a VALID outcome to assert on, not a failure to work around.

Expect this to FIND defects — that is the point. File what it finds rather than fixing everything inline, so each defect gets its own reproduction and review.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-102, MGIT-103, MGIT-98, MGIT-109, R-H234, FR-17.26</prompt>
<acceptance>A bounded soak drives N concurrent sandboxes through create/exec/sync/land with real churn and interleaved daemon SIGKILLs, asserting each listed invariant with its own failure message; it is wired to run on every change with a SKIP visibly not a pass; each invariant is demonstrated to fail against a deliberately broken build; the chosen N and the runtime are backed by a measurement; and the output states which profile ran.</acceptance>

nodes.title: Delete SquashService.ExportToGitPatch — a patch renderer that cannot produce a valid git patch
nodes.description:
Follow-up cleanup from MGIT-112. `SquashService.ExportToGitPatch` renders model.FileDiff metadata into format-patch-shaped text. After MGIT-112 it has ZERO production callers — `mgit export --format git` now uses PreviewGitPatch and `mgit squash --to-git` uses GitFormatPatch, both of which diff real trees through go-git's own unified encoder.

It should be deleted rather than left in place, because it is not merely unused, it is INCAPABLE of emitting a correct patch:

1. It emits `--- a/<path>` for an added file where git requires `--- /dev/null`.
2. Its `@@` line numbers come from `changeHunks`, which hard-codes LineStart: 1 for display purposes, so the hunk headers are wrong for anything not starting at line 1.
3. It renders whatever is in c.FileDiffs, which is EMPTY on a dry-run squash. That is exactly how MGIT-112 shipped: a syntactically valid, hunk-free patch that `git apply --allow-empty` accepted, exited 0 on, and applied to nothing.

Leaving a public method whose output looks like a patch and applies to nothing is a footgun of precisely the class MGIT-112 and MGIT-77 came from. MGIT-112 kept it (with a loud DO-NOT-USE godoc) only to hold the P1 fix's diff to a reviewable size — deleting it means removing internal/service/squash_export_test.go (213 lines) and rewriting the two e2e usages in e2e/squash_cli_test.go and e2e/export_cli_test.go.
nodes.prompt:
Delete `SquashService.ExportToGitPatch` from internal/service/squash.go along with its test file internal/service/squash_export_test.go.

Rewrite the two e2e call sites to assert against the renderer that actually ships:
- e2e/squash_cli_test.go TestSquash_ToGit -> use `env.squash.GitFormatPatch(ctx, squashed)`.
- e2e/export_cli_test.go TestExport_Git -> use `env.squash.PreviewGitPatch(ctx, service.SquashRequest{TaskID: taskID})`.

Keep `mboxHeader`, which both surviving renderers share.

While rewriting those tests, make them assert on HUNKS and not only on mbox headers. Both currently assert `HasPrefix(patch, "From ")` / `Contains(patch, "Subject: [PATCH] ")`, which a header-only patch satisfies — that is how MGIT-112 survived its own test suite. Seed the fixtures with commits that record real content (not AllowEmpty), and assert the patch contains `diff --git`, a real `@@` hunk, and the expected +/- content.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-112, FR-7

nodes.title: TestClaudeHook_RealProcess flakes under full-suite load: a fixed 10s wall clock for one `mgit init` subprocess
nodes.description:
Observed while verifying MGIT-112 on macOS (Apple Silicon), 2026-08-15.

`go test ./... -count=1` failed once with:

    --- FAIL: TestClaudeHook_RealProcess_StdinToStdoutContract (12.82s)
        claude_hook_realprocess_test.go:34: mgit [init]: signal: killed
        Error: Received unexpected error: signal: killed

Re-running the test alone passed in 2.7s, and a second full-suite run passed clean. So it is load-sensitive, not a real regression.

ROOT CAUSE: cmd/mgit/claude_hook_realprocess_test.go:83, `runMgitTest`, gives a single `mgit init` subprocess a FIXED 10-second context timeout. Under `go test ./...` every package builds and runs in parallel — including the e2e package, which is the heaviest in the tree at ~24s — so a cold `mgit init` (which opens SQLite with `synchronous = FULL` and initialises a repo) can genuinely exceed 10s of wall clock on a loaded machine. `exec.CommandContext` then SIGKILLs it and the failure reads as "signal: killed", which names nothing useful and looks like a product bug.

`runMgitTestStdin` in the same file very likely carries the same fixed budget.

Note honestly: MGIT-112 added CLI-level tests to cmd/mgit that spawn real `git` subprocesses, so that package got slightly heavier. That may make this flake marginally more likely to be observed; it did not create it (the timeout is unconditional wall clock, and the failing subprocess is `mgit init`, which MGIT-112 does not touch).

WHY IT MATTERS: a red CI run that disappears on re-run trains people to re-run rather than read, which is how a real intermittent defect gets waved through.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Make the real-process hook tests robust to machine load without weakening what they assert.

In cmd/mgit/claude_hook_realprocess_test.go:
1. Raise the per-subprocess budget in `runMgitTest` (and `runMgitTestStdin`, if it carries the same literal) well above the 10s that a loaded machine can exceed, or better, derive it from the test deadline (`t.Deadline()`) so it scales with `-timeout` instead of being a magic number.
2. When the context expires, fail with a message that says the subprocess was KILLED BY THE TEST'S OWN TIMEOUT after N seconds, and include the partial output. "signal: killed" alone reads as a product crash and cost real debugging time.

Check whether other real-binary helpers in the tree carry the same fixed budget: e2e/coexist_e2e_test.go `gitCmd` uses 30s, which is safer, and `buildMgitTestBinary` / `buildMgitBinary` should be checked too. Prefer one shared convention over per-file literals.

Do NOT fix this by skipping the test or by dropping the real-process coverage — that coverage exists because the in-process tests with a fake connector missed the production path (see the test's own doc comment, MGIT-11.11.1).

Refs: MGIT-115, MGIT-11.11.1
nodes.acceptance: `go test ./... -count=1` passes repeatedly on a loaded machine. The subprocess timeout is either derived from the test deadline or generous enough not to trip under a full parallel suite, and a timeout failure message states that the test's own budget killed the process, with the elapsed time and any partial output.

nodes.title: index.GetWorktreeByTask reports a store failure as "worktree not found", so a broken index reads as a missing worktree
nodes.description:
Found while building the MGIT-110 cadence label.

`internal/store/index/worktrees.go` GetWorktreeByTask (and GetWorktree) collapse EVERY error into ErrWorktreeNotFound:

    err := s.ReadTx(...)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: task %s", model.ErrWorktreeNotFound, taskID)
    }

sql.ErrNoRows and "the database is closed" become the same answer, and the underlying error is not wrapped, so errors.Is/As cannot recover it either.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS. A caller that branches on ErrWorktreeNotFound — which is the documented, intended way to handle "this task was never given a worktree" — silently takes the not-found branch when the store is actually broken. In service.TaskCadence (MGIT-110) that means a failed index read degrades to INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE / NO_DENOMINATOR rather than an error. That particular degradation happens to be the humble direction, so it is not a live defect there, but the next caller to make that distinction load-bearing will get a confident wrong answer from a dead database.

The fix is the same shape as GetCommitProvenance in task_commits.go, which already gets this right: match sql.ErrNoRows explicitly for the not-found case and wrap anything else as its own failure.

Refs: MGIT-110, FR-16</description>
<parameter name="acceptance">GetWorktree and GetWorktreeByTask return ErrWorktreeNotFound only for sql.ErrNoRows, and wrap any other failure as a distinct error that errors.Is can tell apart. A test asserts that a closed/failing index yields a non-not-found error.

nodes.title: Commits from a task-bound worktree record agent_id "cli", not the agent bound to it — the provenance column is dead
nodes.description:
Found while building the MGIT-110 cadence label, from the live index on this repo.

    sqlite3 .mgit/index.db "SELECT agent_id, count(*) FROM task_commits GROUP BY agent_id"
    cli          70
    mgit-squash  42

Every human/agent-authored commit in this repo's entire history says "cli". Not one says which agent made it.

WHY. `mgit commit --agent-id` defaults to "cli" (cmd/mgit/commit.go). `mgit work` DOES record an agent_id in the worktrees registry (claude-mgit-102, claude-mgit-112, ...) and a worktree commit already auto-inherits the bound TASK id — but not the bound AGENT id. So the one place the agent's identity is known is not consulted by the one place it would be recorded.

WHAT IT COSTS. task_commits.agent_id is indexed, exposed in `mgit log --json`, and `mgit log --author <id>` filters on it — that filter can currently only ever match "cli". README states "every commit carries its task and agent identity"; the task half is true and the agent half is not. With parallel agents on one store, which is the case this project is built for, there is no way to attribute a commit to the agent that made it.

It also matters to MGIT-110's second half: R-H234 separates what the SYSTEM knows from what the AGENT claims. An authored commit whose author is literally "cli" cannot carry an agent's claim at all.

FIX SHAPE: a commit from inside a linked worktree should inherit the worktree's agent_id the same way it inherits its task ID, with an explicit --agent-id still overriding. "cli" should remain the default only outside a worktree, where nothing better is known.

Refs: MGIT-110, R-H234, FR-4, FR-16</description>
<parameter name="acceptance">A commit made from inside a task-bound worktree records the worktree's agent_id in task_commits; an explicit --agent-id still wins; outside a worktree the default is unchanged. A test asserts the inherited value, and `mgit log --author <agent>` returns that commit.

nodes.title: Fleet-ceiling refusal is rendered as an in-guest OOM diagnosis advising a LARGER --memory-mb
nodes.description:
Found by the MGIT-113 fleet soak, live on macOS/libkrun. Reproducible once the fleet is at its ceiling.

WHAT HAPPENS. When a launch is refused by the aggregate fleet ceiling, `mgit sandbox exec` prints the correct refusal AND THEN a second, contradictory diagnosis:

    mgit sandbox: sandbox exec: sandbox ensure-running: global sandbox ceiling exceeded: the host is already running or admitting 8 sandboxes (host-wide cap 8); this launch is not too big — free capacity with `mgit sandbox remove <task>` or wait for one to expire

    mgit: the guest stopped answering mid-command.
    This sandbox (task P-9) is capped at 512 MB of memory and 1 vCPU. Memory exhaustion inside the guest presents exactly like this, and the cap is a property of THIS SANDBOX, not of your project.
    If the workload needs more, declare it — do not reshape the build to fit the sandbox:
      mgit sandbox remove P-9 && mgit sandbox launch --task-id P-9 --worktree ... --memory-mb 1024

The first message is right; the second is wrong in every particular. No VM was ever attempted, so the guest cannot have "stopped answering mid-command", and there was no in-guest memory exhaustion. Worse, the advice INVERTS the fix: raising this sandbox's --memory-mb makes a host-wide capacity refusal MORE likely, not less. The ceiling message even says "this launch is not too big" two lines above the advice to make it bigger.

WHY IT MATTERS. An agent under progress pressure reads the last, most actionable-looking paragraph and follows it. The remediation printed (`sandbox remove` then `launch --memory-mb 1024`) frees one sandbox's worth of capacity and then asks for double, so the loop can oscillate instead of converging. This is a diagnosis-quality defect, not a containment breach — the refusal itself is correct and fails closed.

ROOT CAUSE (read, not inferred). cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure.go, classifyGuestFailure lines 77-90. Two signals put a failure in phaseNeverStarted: a VM-start marker in the console tail, or ErrGuestNotServing. EVERYTHING ELSE falls through to the default:

    if !neverStarted {
        return guestFailure{phase: phaseLostServing}
    }

phaseLostServing unconditionally prints the MGIT-95 memory-cap advisory (writeGuestFailure lines 163-165). A ceiling refusal (model.ErrSandboxCeilingExceeded) matches neither signal, so it is classified as a guest that was serving and was lost.

This is MGIT-104's exact defect class recurring in a third phase. MGIT-104 split "never started" from "lost serving" and stopped the advisory leaking into the former; the admission-refused phase — where no VM was ever attempted — was not modelled, and the classifier's default sweeps it into the OOM bucket. It is concurrency-only, which is why sequential testing never saw it: reaching the ceiling needs a real fleet.

A SECOND CAUSE HAS SINCE BEEN OBSERVED LANDING IN THE SAME DEFAULT: a client-side control-socket timeout (MGIT-122) is also rendered as in-guest memory exhaustion. Two distinct wrong diagnoses from one default branch is the argument for changing the default itself, not just adding a third case.

REPRODUCTION. Boot sandboxes until the ceiling refuses (default cap is 8 concurrent; or lower the memory ceiling with `{"max_total_memory_percent":N}` in <repo>/.mgit/sandbox/policy.json), then exec into one more. Automated: scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh phase 3, which currently records this as a KNOWN DEFECT rather than a hard failure.

ACCEPTANCE. A launch refused by the aggregate fleet ceiling prints the ceiling refusal and NOTHING that attributes the failure to in-guest memory exhaustion or advises a larger --memory-mb. classifyGuestFailure models the admission-refused phase explicitly rather than defaulting it to phaseLostServing, with table-driven tests covering ErrSandboxCeilingExceeded alongside the existing never-started/lost-serving cases. The known_defect call for this ticket is removed from scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh so the assertion beside it becomes hard, and the soak then reports a clean PASS.

PROMPT. Fix the classifier so a fleet-ceiling refusal is not diagnosed as in-guest memory exhaustion. Start at cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure.go:77-90. An admission refusal is a THIRD phase: no VM was attempted, so neither the workload nor in-guest memory is implicated, and the correct advice is to free host capacity — the opposite of raising --memory-mb. Follow MGIT-104's precedent: exactly one diagnosis per failure, and only the phase the evidence supports. The sentinel must be matched by TEXT as well as errors.Is, because the error crosses the daemon control protocol as a string (the same reason MGIT-104 matches ErrGuestNotServing both ways) — model.ErrSandboxCeilingExceeded is "global sandbox ceiling exceeded". Strongly consider making the default branch "unidentified, here is the evidence" rather than a specific diagnosis, given two unmodelled causes have now landed in it. Add the phase to cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure_test.go, then delete the known_defect call in the soak's phase 3 and confirm a clean PASS.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-104, MGIT-122, MGIT-98, MGIT-95, R-H212
nodes.prompt:
Fix the guest-failure classifier so a fleet-ceiling refusal is not diagnosed as in-guest memory exhaustion.

Start from cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure.go:77-90. The classifier has two phases (phaseNeverStarted, phaseLostServing) and defaults everything unrecognized to phaseLostServing, which carries the MGIT-95 memory-cap advisory. An admission refusal is a THIRD phase: no VM was attempted, so neither the workload nor in-guest memory is implicated, and the correct advice is to free host capacity — the opposite of raising --memory-mb.

Follow MGIT-104's precedent: exactly one diagnosis per failure, and only the phase the evidence supports. Note the sentinel must be matched by TEXT as well as errors.Is, because the error crosses the daemon control protocol as a string (the same reason MGIT-104 matches ErrGuestNotServing both ways) — model.ErrSandboxCeilingExceeded is "global sandbox ceiling exceeded".

Consider whether the default branch should be phaseLostServing at all, given this is the second time an unmodelled cause has landed in it by default. A classifier that defaults to "unidentified, here is the evidence" is harder to be wrong with than one that defaults to a specific diagnosis.

Add the phase to the table-driven tests in cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure_test.go, then delete the known_defect call for this ticket in scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh phase 3 and confirm the soak reports a clean PASS.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-104, MGIT-98, MGIT-95</prompt>
</invoke>

nodes.title: max_concurrent_sandboxes in host policy is dead config: the count ceiling comes only from a daemon flag the CLI never sets
nodes.description:
Found by the MGIT-113 fleet soak work, live on macOS/libkrun, verified both by experiment and by reading the wiring.

WHAT HAPPENS. An operator who lowers the fleet's concurrent-sandbox cap in host policy gets no enforcement at all, silently.

    $ printf '{"memory_mb":333,"max_concurrent_sandboxes":2}' > <repo>/.mgit/sandbox/policy.json
    # memory_mb IS honoured: sandbox status --json reports "memory_mb":333
    # max_concurrent_sandboxes is NOT: a third, fourth ... eighth sandbox boots

The same file, read by the same loader, in the same run: one field takes effect and the other is ignored. There is no warning, no log line, and no way to observe the cap in force — so the only way to discover it is to boot past it, which needs a real concurrent fleet.

ROOT CAUSE (read, not inferred). cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go:183:

    manager := sandboxd.NewCeilingManager(selected, opts.maxSandboxes,
        ceiling.maxTotalMemoryMB, ceiling.defaultMemoryMB)

The MEMORY dimension is resolved from host policy (resolveFleetCeiling in cmd/mgit-sandboxd/ceiling_wiring.go:82, honouring max_total_memory_percent — this is the MGIT-98 fix and it works). The COUNT dimension is taken from opts.maxSandboxes, the --max-sandboxes flag, whose default is 8 (main.go:77). model.SandboxPolicy.MaxConcurrentSandboxes (sandbox_policy.go:47, default 8, validated at :105) is never read into the ceiling by anything.

The asymmetry is even acknowledged in the comment directly above the call — "Both dimensions are live in a default install — the memory one resolved from host policy above rather than from an off-by-default flag (MGIT-98)" — which describes the memory dimension being rescued from a flag while leaving the count dimension on exactly such a flag.

It compounds: the CLI auto-spawns mgit-sandboxd and does not pass --max-sandboxes, so in normal use the count cap is ALWAYS the hard-coded 8, regardless of policy. The field is settable, validated, documented by its own JSON name, and inert.

WHY IT MATTERS. It is a resource control that reports nothing and does nothing. An operator sizing a runner for parallel agents — the integrating lane's worker pools — sets it, sees sandboxes boot, and concludes it is enforced. The fleet then runs to a cap they did not choose. It also blocks cheap testing of the aggregate refusal: the MGIT-113 soak wanted to bind the ceiling at a low count and had to lower the MEMORY percentage instead, because the count knob does nothing.

Note the two dimensions are NOT interchangeable for an operator: memory percent caps total RAM, count caps how many VMs contend for CPU and I/O. A host with plenty of RAM and few cores is exactly where the count cap is the one you want.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-98, MGIT-95, FR-17.26</description>
<parameter name="acceptance">max_concurrent_sandboxes set in host policy is enforced: with the field set to N, the (N+1)th concurrent sandbox is refused with the aggregate ceiling error naming the count cap. Precedence between the policy field and the --max-sandboxes flag is explicit and documented in the same shape as the memory dimension's (flag overrides policy overrides default), and the effective count cap is emitted in the daemon's existing fleet_memory_ceiling start-up log line alongside ceiling_mb so an operator can observe what is in force. A test covers policy-set, flag-overrides-policy, and neither-set. Verify by lowering the policy count cap in scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh phase 3 and confirming the ceiling binds where the policy says.
nodes.prompt:
Wire model.SandboxPolicy.MaxConcurrentSandboxes into the fleet admission ceiling, or remove the field.

Read cmd/mgit-sandboxd/ceiling_wiring.go first: resolveFleetCeiling already does exactly this job for the memory dimension, with a precedence chain (flag > policy percent > conservative fallback), a source label, and a start-up log line naming what is in force. The count dimension needs the same treatment; the fix is to extend that resolution rather than to add a second, differently-shaped path.

The call site is cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go:183, which currently passes opts.maxSandboxes (the --max-sandboxes flag, default 8) straight through. Note the flag's default is indistinguishable from an operator explicitly choosing 8, which is the same trap the memory dimension had — resolve "was the flag actually set" the way the memory side does rather than treating the default as an operator choice.

Extend the fleet_memory_ceiling log event (ceiling_wiring.go logFleetCeiling) so the effective COUNT cap and its source are emitted too; today nothing exports either dimension, and an operator has no way to see the cap in force.

If the conclusion is that the policy field should not exist, delete it and its validation rather than leaving settable, validated, inert config — but prefer wiring it: the count cap is the dimension that matters on a RAM-rich, core-poor host, and it is not substitutable by max_total_memory_percent.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-98, FR-17.26

nodes.title: Windows-native sandbox backend (WCOW)
nodes.description: Native Windows sandbox backend using Hyper-V-isolated Windows containers (WCOW), Windows guest, host-matching. Deferred until there is developer demand for Windows-host support; Windows hosts are served by the audited container fallback until then. Implements ADR-006 / FR-17.39.
nodes.prompt:
EPIC: Windows-native sandbox backend (WCOW) for FR-17. Build the Windows sandbox backend per ADR-006 and FR-17.39: the guest is a WINDOWS guest in a Hyper-V-isolated Windows container (WCOW), NOT a Linux guest (LCOW). Host-matching principle — a Windows developer's toolchain (npm/python/go/cargo/MSVC) runs on Windows, so the sandbox isolates a Windows execution environment; this also removes Linux<->Windows path/EOL/permission translation at the land boundary.

WHY DEFERRED: MGIT-11.5.3 reached a decision + validation but no implementation. Pick this epic up when developers request Windows-host sandbox support. Until then Windows hosts use the reduced-isolation container fallback (--backend container --acknowledge-reduced-isolation).

VALIDATED (2026-06-15 WCOW pilot, recorded on MGIT-11.5.3): on a Win10 Pro 22H2 host, docker --isolation=hyperv booted an ltsc2019 Windows container, and Go 1.23.4 / Node 20.18.1+npm (React/Angular) / Python 3.12.7 / C (gcc 14.2) / C++ (g++ 14.2 STL) / Rust 1.96 (gnu) all compiled+ran inside it. So the guest environment is proven; this epic is the productionization.

KEY CONSTRAINTS (read ADR-006, ADR-005, FR-17.* esp. FR-17.39/27/35/15/16/17/31, AUDIT-FR17-SANDBOX-*):
- Drive WCOW HEADLESSLY via the HCS API (vmcompute.dll/computecore.dll via x/sys/windows) and/or containerd — NEVER Docker Desktop (GUI/session-bound, unfit for a daemon; it was the source of all SSH-pilot flakiness).
- Do NOT vendor hcsshim internal/ (unsupported-code supply-chain hazard); prefer the documented HCS public API or containerd's public client.
- Control/land channel = HvSocket (AF_HYPERV), peer-bound to the VM identity GUID (FR-17.27); framed protocol per FR-17.35; enforce ceilings.
- Windows mgit-guest agent (the current one is //go:build linux); transport-only, no signing key (SEC-01).
- Prepared, digest-pinned Windows base image (FR-17.17/31, SANDBOX-IMAGES register, Ed25519 signing FR-17.29/38). Version matrix: ltsc2019 for a Win10 host, ltsc2022 for Win11/Server 2022 (Hyper-V isolation needs host build >= container base build).
- This backend will NOT reuse the Linux/macOS microvm.Manager seam (kernel+rootfs); it is a distinct container+UVM model, closer to a Hyper-V-isolated variant of the container backend. Still behind model.SandboxManager (FR-17.15), wired via select.go.
- All CLAUDE.md rules apply: TDD, coverage gates, pre-import vuln checks + package approval for any new dep, /simplify after green, story-closure independent review + security pass. Commit format {type}({scope}): {desc} + Refs: MGIT-12.x; NO co-authored-by / agent name / Generated-with trailer (information-exposure control).
- DEV/TEST target: Windows 11 Pro or Windows Server 2022 (for ltsc2022 + headless containerd). Win10 22H2 works only with ltsc2019.
nodes.acceptance: A Windows host launches a per-task Hyper-V-isolated Windows container (WCOW) via mgit; the developer's Windows toolchain runs inside it; the worktree is mounted at the identical path; control/land works over HvSocket with VM-GUID peer binding; quarantine-then-land enforces dual-hash + task binding + attestation identically to the Linux backend; teardown leaves no host residue; backend selectable via select.go; coverage + lint + vuln gates met; story-closure independent review + security pass completed.

nodes.description: A Windows build of mgit-guest (the current one is //go:build linux): in-guest supervisor + clean-env exec + framed IO over HvSocket, transport-only.

nodes.title: HvSocket control/land transport (AF_HYPERV)
nodes.description: Host↔guest control and land transport over Hyper-V sockets (AF_HYPERV), peer-bound to the VM identity GUID per FR-17.27.
nodes.prompt:
Implement the host-side and guest-side HvSocket (AF_HYPERV) transport for the WCOW backend — the Windows analog of the Linux vsock channel. Register the GuestCommunicationServices service GUID (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Virtualization\GuestCommunicationServices); peer-bind each guest's control/land channel to its VM identity GUID and REJECT messages from any other peer (FR-17.27); invalidate the binding at teardown so a recycled VM GUID cannot inherit a destroyed sandbox's channel. Implement the FR-17.35 framed protocol with enforced ceilings (max object 64 MiB, max objects/land 100000, max payload 4 GiB; canonicalize tree-entry paths, reject traversal/non-canonical). Pure-Go AF_HYPERV via golang.org/x/sys/windows if sufficient, else an approved lib (vuln-check first). Refs: FR-17.27, FR-17.35, ADR-006.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
- Host and guest exchange framed control/land messages over HvSocket.
- Peer binding to VM-GUID enforced; cross-guest addressing rejected and audited; binding invalidated at teardown.
- Protocol ceilings + path canonicalization enforced (fail closed).
nodes.acceptance: Framed control/land messaging over HvSocket works host↔guest; VM-GUID peer binding rejects cross-guest traffic and is invalidated on teardown; FR-17.35 ceilings and path canonicalization enforced.

nodes.title: WCOW backend manager (model.SandboxManager)
nodes.description: Implement model.SandboxManager for Windows over the chosen WCOW API; distinct from the Linux/macOS microvm.Manager (container+UVM model). Wire into select.go.

nodes.title: mgit work holds the repo-wide exclusive lock across worktree materialization AND the sandboxd round-trip, so concurrent task provisioning times out at 30s
nodes.description:
Found by the MGIT-113 fleet soak, reproduced live on macOS/libkrun, root-caused by reading the lock's critical section. This is the worker-pool shape the integrating lane actually runs, so it is filed P1.

WHAT HAPPENS. Four concurrent `mgit work <path> --task-id <T> --sandbox --image <ref> --memory-mb 512 --cpus 1` in one repo: two succeed, two die after 30 seconds with

    Error: another mgit process is running: held by PID 91170 (mgit work wt-R-4 --task-id R-4 --sandbox --image base@sha256:...) after 30s

followed by the full `mgit work` usage block, which buries the error. One `mgit work` held the repo lock for more than THIRTY SECONDS. The same four-wide shape succeeds when the repo is fresh and the daemon idle, and fails once the repo carries several materialized worktrees and the daemon is busy booting — so it degrades exactly as a worker pool warms up.

ROOT CAUSE (read, not inferred). The lock is `.mgit/locks/mgit.lock`, acquired in cmd/mgit/app.go:76 via `lock.Acquire(storeDir, lock.DefaultTimeout)` and released only by `defer app.Close()` — i.e. held for the WHOLE command (cmd/mgit/work.go:82-87). Inside that one critical section `work` does all of:

  1. `SyncService.EnsureSynced` (internal/service/sync.go:96) -> `WorkingTreeFingerprint` (internal/store/git/sync.go:24-43), which READS AND SHA-256s THE CONTENT OF EVERY WORKING FILE, and on drift resyncs with another full walk.
  2. `MaterializeBranchTo` (internal/store/git/worktree.go:377-411), which inflates and writes EVERY BLOB of the branch tree to disk, serially, with ctx explicitly discarded.
  3. With --sandbox, the daemon round-trip: `EnsureRunning` (up to 5s activation, internal/sandboxd/daemon.go:407) then `cl.Launch` (internal/sandboxd/client.go:131), bounded only by a 30s socket deadline.

Step 3 has head-of-line blocking of its own: the daemon serves KindLaunch through `Service.Register`, which takes the service mutex (internal/service/sandbox.go:230) — and that SAME mutex is held across a full VM boot in `EnsureRunning` (sandbox.go:353-365, spanning `manager.Launch`, `StartEgress`, `StartPublish`). So one agent's `work --sandbox` waits on another agent's VM boot WHILE HOLDING THE REPO LOCK that every other mgit command needs.

Step 1 compounds over time: `listWorkingFiles` (internal/store/git/worktree_fs.go:97-136) excludes only top-level `.mgit`/`.git`, and `MaterializeBranchTo` writes the worktree wherever the path says — so worktrees created inside the repo root are themselves walked and hashed by every LATER `mgit work`. That is quadratic growth in a worker pool that creates worktrees under the repo, and it happens under the lock. (This last point is inference from the code, well supported but not directly measured.)

THE ASSUMPTION IT VIOLATES IS WRITTEN DOWN. ADR-009 (docs/adr/009-per-operation-locking.md:10-13) justifies the lifetime lock precisely because "for a CLI command this is exactly right: the lock is held for the command's (short) lifetime", and :75 confirms "CLI is untouched. Only serve detaches". internal/store/lock/guard.go:14-15 and cmd/mgit/app.go:157 repeat it. `mgit work --sandbox` is not a short command, and it is the one every parallel agent starts with.

TWO ADJACENT DEFECTS FOUND WITH IT:

  a. REQUIREMENTS.md:270 and :1206 promise the lock timeout is "configurable via locks.timeout_seconds". That knob does not exist in the code — `lock.DefaultTimeout` (internal/store/lock/lock.go:28) is a compile-time 30s constant and every call site passes it verbatim. An operator cannot widen the timeout to work around this.

  b. The user-facing guidance attributes this error to the wrong cause. .mtix/docs/MGIT_WORKING_DISCIPLINE.md:275-279 (and CHANGELOG.md:1028) tell the reader "'another mgit process is running' means a server holds the lock ... it now takes the lock only per operation, so this error is brief and self-clears." Here it is a CLI command holding it, and it does not self-clear within the timeout.

WHY IT IS ONLY BEING FOUND NOW. Nothing tests concurrent `mgit work`. e2e/concurrent_cli_test.go spawns real processes but runs only `mgit commit --allow-empty`, and caps each child at 30s — the same order as the lock timeout, so it would mask this class. docs/E2E-MATRIX.md:43 already notes that `TestWorktreeIntegration_ConcurrentWorktrees` "is in-process and not actually concurrent despite its name".

NOTE FOR THE FIX. `mgit sandbox launch` does the same daemon registration and takes NO repo lock at all (cmd/mgit/sandbox.go opens no App). So the containment path does not inherently need the lock — `work` is holding it across a call that its sibling command performs without it. The MGIT-113 soak now provisions worktrees serially and launches sandboxes concurrently for exactly this reason.

Refs: MGIT-113, ADR-009, NFR-3.5, FR-16</description>
<parameter name="acceptance">N concurrent `mgit work --task-id <distinct> --sandbox` invocations in one repo all succeed, with N at least the fleet width the soak drives (4), and none fails with ErrLockHeld. The repo lock is not held across the sandboxd round-trip, and preferably not across worktree materialization. scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh phase 0 asserts this directly and currently records it as a KNOWN DEFECT for this ticket; that known_defect call is removed and the assertion becomes hard. Separately: either implement locks.timeout_seconds as REQUIREMENTS.md:270 promises or correct the requirement, and fix the MGIT_WORKING_DISCIPLINE.md guidance that attributes this error solely to a running server.</parameter>
<parameter name="prompt">Stop `mgit work` from holding the repo-wide exclusive lock across slow, unbounded work.

Reproduce first: scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh phase 0 drives 4 concurrent `mgit work --sandbox` and reports this as a known defect. Confirm you see ErrLockHeld before changing anything.

The critical section is cmd/mgit/app.go:76 (acquire) to app.go:179 (release via defer app.Close()), spanning all of cmd/mgit/work.go:87. Three things inside it are the problem, in descending order of value to fix:

  1. The sandboxd round-trip (work.go:205-236). `mgit sandbox launch` performs the same registration and takes no repo lock at all, which is the strongest evidence the lock is not protecting anything here. Releasing before the daemon call, or acquiring around only the store mutations, is the smallest correct change.
  2. `EnsureSynced`'s full working-tree fingerprint (internal/service/sync.go:96), which hashes the content of every working file on every invocation.
  3. `MaterializeBranchTo` (internal/store/git/worktree.go:377), which writes every blob serially with ctx discarded.

While you are in the fingerprint path, look at internal/store/git/worktree_fs.go:97-136: only top-level .mgit/.git are excluded, so worktrees materialized inside the repo root are walked and re-hashed by every later `mgit work`. Registered worktree paths should be excluded from the walk regardless of where they sit.

Do NOT fix this by widening the 30s timeout; that converts a wedge into a slower wedge. If the timeout should be configurable, implement locks.timeout_seconds as REQUIREMENTS.md:270 already promises, as a separate concern.

Add a genuinely concurrent test: e2e/concurrent_cli_test.go currently spawns processes but only runs `commit --allow-empty`, and its 30s per-child cap is the same order as the lock timeout, so it masks this. A new case must run N concurrent `work --task-id <distinct>` and assert all succeed.

Refs: MGIT-113, ADR-009, FR-16</parameter>

nodes.title: applyPragmas sets journal_mode=WAL before busy_timeout, so concurrent index opens fail with SQLITE_BUSY and the daemon dies at start-up
nodes.description:
Found by the MGIT-113 fleet soak on its first run with the repo lock taken out of the path. Intermittent by nature (it is a race), reproduced live on macOS, and the root cause is a two-line ordering bug that is decisive on reading.

WHAT HAPPENS. Four concurrent `mgit sandbox launch` in a repo with no daemon running: each spawns a daemon, and ALL FOUR died at start-up.

    Error: sandbox daemon unavailable (no fallback — task work runs only inside the sandbox):
    sandboxd activation: .../d.sock not dialable after spawn
    the daemon reported:
      sandbox fleet memory ceiling resolved
      sandbox VMM linked at build time
      sandbox VMM capabilities verified
      sandbox service wiring failed: open sandbox audit index: apply pragmas:
        write db pragma "PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL": database is locked (5) (SQLITE_BUSY)

The fleet did not come up at all. The failure is fatal to the daemon (cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go returns 2 on service wiring failure), so the CLI correctly reports the daemon as unavailable and fails closed — but every agent in a worker pool gets that answer at once.

ROOT CAUSE (read, not inferred). internal/store/index/store.go:173-190, applyPragmas:

    pragmas := []string{
        "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON",
        "PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL",     // <-- needs an exclusive lock
        "PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000",    // <-- set AFTER the pragma that needs it
        "PRAGMA synchronous = FULL",
    }

Switching a database into WAL mode takes an exclusive lock on it. busy_timeout is still at SQLite's default of ZERO when that runs, so a second opener does not wait 5 seconds — it returns SQLITE_BUSY immediately. The busy_timeout that exists precisely to absorb this contention is installed one statement too late, on every connection, on both pools.

CLAUDE.md's SQL Rule 2 mandates busy_timeout on every connection. The rule is followed and the ordering defeats it for the one statement that most needs it.

FIX. Set `PRAGMA busy_timeout` FIRST, before journal_mode. It is a per-connection setting that takes no lock, so nothing is lost by hoisting it.

    "PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000",
    "PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON",
    "PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL",
    "PRAGMA synchronous = FULL",

SCOPE IS WIDER THAN THE SANDBOX. applyPragmas is Store's, so this affects the main repo index (.mgit/index.db) as well as the sandbox audit index (.mgit/sandbox/sandbox-index.db). CLI commands mostly escape it because they serialize on the repo-wide lock before opening any store (cmd/mgit/app.go:76) — the lock has been masking this. The paths that take NO repo lock are exactly the ones exposed: `mgit sandbox *` (cmd/mgit/sandbox.go opens no App) and mgit-sandboxd itself. That is why a fleet gate found it and the existing suites did not.

WHY IT IS INTERMITTENT. The window is the moment several processes open the same index for the first time. Isolated four-wide reproduction attempts passed twice; the soak hit it when four launches raced daemon activation under load. Do not treat a passing run as a fix — the ordering is wrong whether or not a given run loses the race, and the fix should be verified by reading the pragma order, plus a test that opens one index concurrently from several goroutines/processes.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-102, CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2, NFR-17.6</description>
<parameter name="acceptance">internal/store/index/store.go applyPragmas sets busy_timeout before journal_mode (and before any other lock-taking pragma), on both the read and write pools. A test opens the same index concurrently from several openers and asserts every one succeeds, failing against the old ordering. The MGIT-113 soak's cold-start phase, which currently records this as a KNOWN DEFECT, has its known_defect call removed so the assertion becomes hard.</parameter>
<parameter name="prompt">Hoist PRAGMA busy_timeout above PRAGMA journal_mode in internal/store/index/store.go applyPragmas (lines 173-190).

Switching to WAL takes an exclusive database lock; with busy_timeout still 0 a concurrent opener gets SQLITE_BUSY instead of waiting, and for mgit-sandboxd that is fatal at start-up — the whole fleet then reports "sandbox daemon unavailable". busy_timeout is per-connection and takes no lock, so hoisting it is safe and sufficient.

Write the failing test first: open one index concurrently from N openers (goroutines over the same path, or subprocesses for the daemon shape) and assert all succeed. Confirm it fails with the current ordering before you change it — the race window is narrow, so run it with -count and -race, and do not conclude from a single green run.

While you are there, consider whether a daemon that cannot open its audit index should retry before exiting. Failing closed is right; failing closed because a sibling held a lock for a few milliseconds is a start-up race, not a policy decision. Check cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go's service-wiring failure path.

Then remove the known_defect call for this ticket from scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh and confirm the soak's cold-start phase passes.

Refs: MGIT-113, CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2</parameter>

nodes.title: Index pool connections after the first are created with NO pragmas: busy_timeout=0 and foreign_keys=0 on read connections 2..5
nodes.description:
Found while auditing connection-open sites for MGIT-121. Same defect class as that ticket — a connection that reaches the database with busy_timeout still at zero — but reached by a different route, so fixing the pragma ORDER does not fix it.

WHAT HAPPENS. internal/store/index/store.go opens two pools over one file (writeDB, MaxOpenConns=1; readDB, MaxOpenConns=5) and applies pragmas with db.ExecContext. database/sql routes that Exec to ONE pooled connection. Pragmas are per-CONNECTION state, so only that one connection gets them. readDB's other four connections are created lazily, later, under concurrent read load — bare.

MEASURED (grab five *sql.Conn from readDB at once, right after New):

    read conn 0: busy_timeout=5000 foreign_keys=1 synchronous=2 journal_mode=wal
    read conn 1: busy_timeout=0    foreign_keys=0 synchronous=2 journal_mode=wal
    read conn 2: busy_timeout=0    foreign_keys=0 synchronous=2 journal_mode=wal
    read conn 3: busy_timeout=0    foreign_keys=0 synchronous=2 journal_mode=wal
    read conn 4: busy_timeout=0    foreign_keys=0 synchronous=2 journal_mode=wal

journal_mode reads back as wal on all five only because WAL is a persistent database property, not per-connection.

WHY IT MATTERS. A read that meets a writer's lock on one of those four connections fails INSTANTLY with SQLITE_BUSY instead of waiting up to 5s — exactly the failure MGIT-121 was about, on the path that carries concurrent readers. It shows up only when several readers are in flight at once, i.e. under fleet load, which is where it is least welcome and hardest to reproduce. The write pool is exposed too, if more rarely: MaxOpenConns(1) bounds concurrency but does not pin identity, so a connection discarded after a driver error is replaced by a bare one.

foreign_keys=0 on read connections is not a data-integrity risk today (ReadTx opens read-only transactions), but it is the same silent divergence from what CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2 promises.

FIX. Pragmas must be applied per CONNECTION, not per pool. The clean way is a connect hook: wrap modernc's driver in a driver.Connector whose Connect applies the pragma sequence (including MGIT-121's ordering and the WAL retry) before handing the connection back, then sql.OpenDB(connector) instead of sql.Open. Note the DSN-query alternative (`file:...?_pragma=...`) requires URI-escaping arbitrary host paths, which is its own hazard on Windows — prefer the connector.

Deliberately NOT half-fixed under MGIT-121: pre-warming the five connections at open would set the pragmas on them today but leave any later-replaced connection bare, making the remaining case rarer and correspondingly harder to find.

Refs: MGIT-121, CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2
nodes.prompt:
Replace the per-pool pragma application in internal/store/index/store.go with a per-connection one.

Build a driver.Connector that wraps modernc.org/sqlite's driver: Connect opens the underlying connection, applies pragmaStatements() in order (busy_timeout first — see MGIT-121) and routes journal_mode through setJournalModeWAL's retry, then returns it. Open both pools with sql.OpenDB(connector). Keep pragmaStatements/setJournalModeWAL as the single source of truth for what and in what order; this ticket changes WHERE they are applied, not what they say.

Write the failing test first: open a Store, take MaxOpenConns distinct *sql.Conn from readDB simultaneously, and assert busy_timeout and foreign_keys on each. It goes red today on connections 1..4.

Do not use DSN _pragma= query parameters: dbPath is an arbitrary host path and would need URI escaping.

Refs: MGIT-121, CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2
nodes.acceptance: Every connection either pool hands out has busy_timeout=5000 and foreign_keys=ON, including connections created after open. A test grabs MaxOpenConns distinct *sql.Conn from each pool, plus at least one connection created after a forced replacement, and asserts the pragmas on each; it fails against the current per-pool application.

nodes.title: One VM boot blocks every other sandbox operation on the daemon: the service mutex is held across Launch, so concurrent execs time out at 30s
nodes.description:
Found by the MGIT-113 fleet soak, observed live on macOS/libkrun and root-caused by reading the service and client.

WHAT HAPPENS. With a fleet of five sandboxes running and a sixth booting, an exec against a DIFFERENT, already-healthy sandbox failed:

    mgit sandbox: sandbox client: read exec stream: read unix ->/.../d.sock: i/o timeout

    mgit: the guest stopped answering mid-command.
    This sandbox (task X-6) is capped at 512 MB of memory and 1 vCPU. ...

Nothing was wrong with that sandbox or its guest. The daemon was busy booting another VM and could not answer within the client's deadline.

ROOT CAUSE (read, not inferred), two parts that compound.

1. THE DAEMON SERIALIZES ON A BOOT. `SandboxService.EnsureRunning` takes the service mutex (internal/service/sandbox.go:353-354) and holds it across `manager.Launch` — a FULL VM boot — plus `StartEgress` and `StartPublish` (sandbox.go:365 onward). `Register` takes the same mutex (sandbox.go:230). So while any one sandbox boots, every registration and every operation needing that mutex waits, however healthy their own sandboxes are.

2. THE CLIENT DEADLINE IS SET AT DIAL AND NEVER RE-ARMED. internal/sandboxd/client.go:47 sets a read deadline of `now + controlproto.DefaultRequestTimeout` when the connection is dialled; `roundTripRaw` (client.go:92-108) does not re-arm it before `ReadResponse` at line 103. The response read is therefore bounded by a deadline set BEFORE the request was even written, and `DefaultRequestTimeout` is 30s (internal/controlproto/controlproto.go:92).

Measured boot times make the collision routine rather than exotic: concurrent create+first-exec took 16.5s for 4 sandboxes and 41-59s for 8 on a 10 vCPU / 16 GB host (see docs/E2E-MATRIX.md). A boot that takes longer than 30s guarantees that anything queued behind it fails, and boots pass 30s at fleet widths this product is explicitly built for.

WHY IT MATTERS. This is the failure mode a worker pool sees most often: random, unattributable "the guest stopped answering" errors on sandboxes that are fine, whenever a sibling happens to be booting. An agent cannot distinguish it from a real guest failure, and the advice it is given (raise --memory-mb) is unrelated to the cause.

THE DIAGNOSIS IS ALSO WRONG, and it is the same defect as MGIT-118 reached by a different route: a client-side socket timeout falls into `classifyGuestFailure`'s default branch (cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure.go:86-88) and is rendered as in-guest memory exhaustion. This is the second distinct cause observed landing in that default, which strengthens MGIT-118's recommendation that the default become "unidentified, here is the evidence" rather than a specific diagnosis.

SUGGESTED DIRECTION (not prescriptive). The mutex is doing two jobs: protecting the registry map, and serializing launches. A boot does not need the registry lock for its whole duration — reserve the slot under the lock, release it, boot, then re-take it to record the result. If launches must be serialized, that is a separate, narrower lock, and the client should be told to wait rather than left to time out. Separately, the read deadline should be re-armed per request rather than inherited from dial time.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-118, MGIT-98, NFR-17.6</description>
<parameter name="acceptance">An exec against a healthy sandbox succeeds while another sandbox on the same daemon is booting, at the fleet widths the soak drives. The service mutex is not held across manager.Launch, or launch serialization is explicit and bounded such that waiting clients are not left to hit a socket deadline. The control client re-arms its read deadline per request rather than inheriting the one set at dial. A test drives a slow/blocking backend Launch and asserts an unrelated exec still completes.</parameter>
<parameter name="prompt">Stop one VM boot from blocking every other operation on the daemon.

Read internal/service/sandbox.go:353-365 first: EnsureRunning holds s.mu across manager.Launch (a full VM boot), StartEgress and StartPublish, and Register takes the same mutex at :230. The mutex is protecting the registry map, but it is also — incidentally — serializing boots, and boots take 16-59s at the fleet widths measured in docs/E2E-MATRIX.md.

The shape of the fix is to hold the lock for the map mutation, not for the boot: mark the sandbox as launching under the lock, release, boot, re-take to record the outcome. Watch for the races that opens — a second EnsureRunning for the SAME task must wait for the first rather than launching a second VM, and a remove arriving mid-boot must not lose the VM. Those are the cases to write tests for first.

Also fix the client deadline: internal/sandboxd/client.go:47 sets the read deadline at dial and roundTripRaw (client.go:92-108) never re-arms it before ReadResponse, so a request's budget is consumed by anything that happened before it was written. Re-arm per request.

Test with a backend whose Launch blocks on a channel the test controls: assert an exec against an already-running sandbox completes while a launch is in flight. That test should fail against the current code.

Refs: MGIT-113, MGIT-98</parameter>

nodes.title: `mgit status` swallows uncommitted work into the base via auto-sync, making it uncommittable and untraceable
nodes.description:
Reported from a live pilot run as a case-sensitivity defect (files under case-mixed directories staging paths but not content). REPRODUCED AND ROOT-CAUSED 2026-08-16: it has NOTHING TO DO WITH CASE. The trigger is `mgit status`, and the same failure occurs with a single lowercase file at the repo root.

MINIMAL REPRODUCTION — two lines apart

    add -> commit             : WORKS      [6c14c8ad] [MGIT:I-1] x
    status -> add -> commit   : FAILS      Error: nothing to commit: no staged changes
                                           (the commit tree would be identical to its parent)

One plain file, `only.txt`, no directories, no mixed case, no collisions. The ONLY difference is a prior `mgit status`.

ROOT CAUSE — status is not a read

cmd/mgit/status.go calls `app.Sync.EnsureSynced(ctx)` before reading, commented as "Auto-housekeep: keep the .mgit base coherent with the current local working state before reading status (ADR-008 §3)". That resync ABSORBS THE UNCOMMITTED WORKING TREE INTO THE BASE. Measured directly:

    base BEFORE status:  3fef1561 mgit: initial commit
    run mgit status
    base AFTER status:   c88d83eb [mgit-sync] resync base to local working state (git b37ae8ec7548)
                         3fef1561 mgit: initial commit

The user's edits are now IN the base. Every reported symptom follows from that one fact:
  - `status` reports "working tree clean" -- it is, because status just made it so;
  - `add` reports "Staged: <path>" truthfully, but the content already matches the base;
  - `commit` refuses "the commit tree would be identical to its parent" -- it genuinely is;
  - `commit -a` is NOT immune; it fails the same way.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A BLOCKED COMMIT
The work is not lost from disk, but it is:
  1. absorbed into an UNTAGGED housekeeping commit attributed to no task;
  2. made uncommittable to the task the agent is actually working;
  3. hidden from `status`, which reports clean.
That defeats the core premise of the product. mgit exists so every coherent step is a TASK-TAGGED micro-commit a reviewer can trace; here a user's work silently lands in `[mgit-sync]` instead of `[MGIT:TASK-N]`, with no diagnostic anywhere. A reviewer reading the trail sees housekeeping, not the change.

It is also a first-hour path: `status` is the most natural command a new user runs before committing.

WHAT WAS RULED OUT, by measurement
  - Mixed-case directory alone: `src/CapacityCalculator/index.ts`, add + commit, WORKS.
  - Lowercase directory: WORKS.
  - GENUINE case collision (`src/auth.tsx` and `src/Auth.tsx` both in the git tree, checked out on case-insensitive macOS, colliding file edited): add + commit WORKS, provided `status` was not called first.
  - The reported LOWERCASING of paths could NOT be reproduced: `mgit show` and `--stat` echo `src/CapacityCalculator/index.ts` with case intact. Either it needs a condition not yet identified, or it was a downstream artifact of the swallowed content. The pilot's wi-23 receipts should be re-read against this root cause before treating lowercasing as a separate defect.

RELATIONSHIP TO ADR-008
ADR-008 auto-housekeeping exists for a real reason: keeping the .mgit base coherent with the user's real git so mgit does not diff against a stale base. The defect is not that it syncs, but WHAT it syncs -- it takes the working tree, including uncommitted user edits, rather than the committed git state. Do not delete the mechanism; correct what it absorbs.</description>
<prompt>Stop `mgit status` (and any other read verb) from absorbing uncommitted user work into the mgit base.

1. REPRODUCE FIRST and capture it, using the two-line case in the description. A fix without a captured before-state is a hypothesis.

2. FIND EVERY CALLER of the auto-sync, not just status. `EnsureSynced` is called from more than one place; any READ verb that calls it has this defect. Enumerate them and report the list — a fix that repairs `status` and leaves `log`, `show`, `diff` or `verify` doing the same thing has moved the bug rather than fixed it.

3. THE FIX BOUNDARY, and think about this carefully rather than taking my framing on faith. ADR-008 exists so mgit does not diff against a stale base when the user's real git has moved. That is legitimate. What is not legitimate is absorbing the working tree's UNCOMMITTED content. The base should track what the user's git has COMMITTED, and uncommitted work must stay uncommitted and visible so the user can attribute it to a task. If you conclude the boundary is somewhere else, say so with evidence and follow ADR-008's actual text — and if the ADR itself specifies the current behaviour, the ADR needs amending and that is part of this task.

4. `status` MUST REPORT UNCOMMITTED WORK. After the fix, the two-line reproduction must show the file as uncommitted/untracked and then commit it to the task with its content.

REQUIRED TESTS
- `status -> add -> commit` records the content, with the commit attributed to the task; assert on the COMMITTED CONTENT, not on the command's exit code.
- The same for `status -> commit -a`.
- Repeated `status` calls do not create `[mgit-sync]` commits that absorb user content; assert the base does not gain a commit for an uncommitted edit.
- The legitimate ADR-008 case still works: when the user's real git HEAD has genuinely moved, the base still resyncs and mgit does not diff against a stale base. Do not fix this by disabling housekeeping.
- A genuine case collision (`src/auth.tsx` + `src/Auth.tsx` in the tree, checked out on a case-insensitive host) still commits correctly — it does today, and must keep doing so.

VERIFY LIVE, not only by unit test: run the real binary through the two-line sequence in a scratch repo and show the content landing in a task-tagged commit.

Export PKG_CONFIG_PATH=/opt/homebrew/lib/pkgconfig:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH first. Run `make lint` (GOOS=linux, what CI runs) plus native golangci-lint.

Refs: MGIT-123, ADR-008, MGIT-77, FR-1.1</prompt>
<acceptance>`mgit status` never absorbs uncommitted working-tree content into the mgit base; after any sequence of read verbs, an uncommitted edit is still reported by `status` and still commits to its task with its content intact, asserted on committed content rather than exit codes. Every caller of the auto-sync is enumerated and audited, not just `status`. The legitimate ADR-008 resync — when the user's real git HEAD has moved — still works, and a genuine case collision still commits correctly. The original two-line reproduction is captured before and shown resolved after.</acceptance>
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Case-colliding git paths: mgit reports the on-disk casing with no diagnostic (explains the "lowercasing" field report)
nodes.description:
Follow-up from MGIT-123. The pilot reported `mgit show` echoing paths lowercased (`CapacityCalculator` -> `capacitycalculator`). MGIT-123 could not reproduce it, and after the MGIT-123 fix it still does not reproduce in the normal case: `status`, `show`, `show --stat`, `show --json` and `diff` all round-trip `src/CapacityCalculator/index.ts` and `lib/MixedCase/FooBar.TSX` with case intact.

REPRODUCED MECHANISM (2026-08-16), and it is not mgit lowercasing anything:

    git hash-object -w blob.tmp
    git update-index --add --cacheinfo 100644,$B,src/CapacityCalculator.ts
    git update-index --add --cacheinfo 100644,$B,src/capacitycalculator.ts
    git commit -m collide ; git checkout -- .

    git ls-tree -r HEAD --name-only  ->  BOTH src/CapacityCalculator.ts
                                              src/capacitycalculator.ts
    find src -type f                 ->  ONLY src/capacitycalculator.ts

On a case-insensitive filesystem `git checkout` materializes only ONE of the two colliding entries, and here it is the all-lowercase one. An editor writing `src/CapacityCalculator.ts` then writes into that SAME inode. mgit walks the working tree and faithfully records/reports the on-disk name, so the commit and `show --stat` read `src/capacitycalculator.ts` while the user is thinking of `CapacityCalculator.ts`. That looks exactly like "mgit lowercased my path".

mgit's behaviour is correct (report on-disk truth), but it is silently confusing: the user cannot tell that git's tree holds two entries and that their edit landed under the other casing.

PROPOSED: a diagnostic, not a behaviour change. When the working-tree walk finds a path whose git tree has a case-colliding sibling, warn once on `status`/`commit`, e.g.

    warning: src/capacitycalculator.ts collides with src/CapacityCalculator.ts in git's tree;
             this filesystem is case-insensitive, so only one is checked out

Needs a cheap case-folded collision check over gitref.CommittedBlobs (already available since MGIT-123), gated to case-insensitive hosts.

Refs: MGIT-123, ADR-008
nodes.acceptance: A case-colliding path in the project's git tree produces a clear one-time warning naming both casings on the commands that touch it, on case-insensitive hosts; recorded paths continue to be the on-disk truth (no renaming, no case rewriting); no warning and no measurable cost on repos without collisions.

nodes.title: Fleet soak never exercises the concurrent daemon cold start it was meant to gate (MGIT-121's field shape)
nodes.description:
MGIT-121 was found by four concurrent `mgit sandbox launch` into a repo with NO daemon: each spawned a daemon and all four raced to open the shared audit index. The soak's phase 1 now brings the daemon up with ONE serialized launch first (cold_first), precisely because that race was a known defect, and then races the rest against an already-running daemon.

So with MGIT-121 fixed, the gate that found it no longer covers it. The concurrent-daemon-spawn path — the one that failed in the field — is asserted nowhere in the soak. It is unit-covered in internal/store/index (8 simultaneous opens of one index, plus a deterministic contended open), but that is in-process, not the multi-process daemon-activation shape.

Suggested: add a phase that starts from no daemon and launches N at once, asserting every launch succeeds and that exactly one daemon ends up serving. Keep the serialized cold start as a separate, earlier assertion so a plain start-up failure is still reported as one rather than as N downstream failures.

Not done under MGIT-121 because the soak needs KVM or an entitled macOS daemon plus guest images, and the change could not be validated from that ticket's environment.

Refs: MGIT-121, MGIT-113
nodes.acceptance: scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh has a phase that launches N sandboxes concurrently into a repo with no running daemon and requires all to succeed. The phase is shown to go red against a build with the MGIT-121 pragma ordering restored (fleet_soak_redteam.sh case).
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: `mgit add CLAUDE.md` stages mgit's own generated block, so a real directive edit cannot be committed without hand-stripping it
nodes.description:
Hit while fixing MGIT-121, which required editing the project directive (CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2) from inside an mgit worktree.

`mgit work` appends its own `<!-- BEGIN mgit-sandbox (generated; do not edit) -->` block to the worktree's CLAUDE.md and lists CLAUDE.md in .mgit/generated, so `mgit commit -a` skips it — good, that is MGIT-80 working. The generated block then tells the agent: "If you genuinely mean to change one of those files — a real project directive, not mgit's generated block — stage it by name: `mgit add CLAUDE.md`."

Following that instruction stages the WHOLE file, generated block included. The block is worktree- and host-specific (it says whether THIS worktree has a sandbox), so committing it puts mgit's scaffolding into the project's directive — the exact class of leak MGIT-80 fixed for bulk staging. `mgit add` does print a note warning that this is happening, which is how it was caught, but the note is the only defence: the correct sequence is left entirely to the agent, and the instruction one paragraph earlier tells it to do the wrong thing.

Worked around by deleting the block from the file before `mgit add CLAUDE.md`, then committing.

Suggested fix: when staging a file listed in .mgit/generated, stage it with mgit's own generated block removed — the block is delimited by BEGIN/END markers, so this is mechanical — and keep the working copy intact. Then the instruction in the generated block becomes true as written.

Refs: MGIT-121, MGIT-80
nodes.acceptance: `mgit add CLAUDE.md` on a worktree whose CLAUDE.md carries a generated block stages the file WITHOUT that block; the working copy keeps it. A test edits the non-generated part, stages by name, and asserts the committed blob contains the edit and no BEGIN/END mgit-sandbox markers.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: mgit work --branch <name> is ignored when the branch does not exist: the task branch is created as task/<id> and materialization then fails with "branch not found"
nodes.description:
Found while writing MGIT-120's same-branch race test (the test had to pre-create the contested branch to work around this).

REPRODUCE, in any mgit repo with content:

    mgit work wt-x --task-id NEWBR-1 --branch feature/custom
    Error: work: create worktree: worktree add: materialize source: branch not found: feature/custom

    mgit branch | grep NEWBR
      task/NEWBR-1   afbbd882      <-- created, and orphaned

ROOT CAUSE (read, not inferred). internal/service/worktree.go resolveForkBase derives branchName from --branch, but when the branch does not already exist it calls s.branch.CreateBranch(ctx, opts.TaskID), and BranchService.CreateBranch (internal/service/branch.go:33) ALWAYS names the branch model.TaskBranchName(taskID) — i.e. `task/<taskID>` — ignoring the caller's branch name entirely. The claim then registers the worktree with branch_name = the REQUESTED name, and MaterializeBranchTo looks up that name and fails.

CONSEQUENCE. The worktree registration is rolled back (correctly), but the wrongly-named branch `task/<taskID>` is left behind in refs and in the branches index. So the failure is not clean: a retry with the default branch name now finds an existing branch and silently pins its tip as the fork-base.

`--branch` works only in the one case where the branch already exists (that is how MGIT-120's e2e same-branch race test exercises it).

FIX SHAPE. Either give BranchService a create-at-name entry point that honors the requested branch (CreateBranchAt already takes an explicit commit; it needs an explicit NAME too), or reject --branch for a non-existent branch with a clear message instead of creating a differently-named one. Whichever is chosen, a failed provision must not leave the branch behind.

Refs: MGIT-120, FR-16
nodes.acceptance: `mgit work <path> --task-id T --branch feature/custom` either creates and binds `feature/custom` (and materializes it), or is refused up front with a message naming the problem — never creates `task/T` instead. A failed provision leaves no branch behind. Covered by a test that asserts the created branch's name equals the requested one.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A failing mgit command prints the full cobra usage block after the error, burying the diagnosis the error just gave
nodes.description:
Noted in MGIT-120's own report ("followed by the full `mgit work` usage block, which buries the error") and hit repeatedly while testing it.

WHAT HAPPENS. Any RunE error causes cobra to print the command's whole usage block after the error line, because SilenceUsage is not set on the root command. A real diagnosis is then followed by ~15 lines of flag documentation:

    Error: work: create worktree: worktree add: materialize source: branch not found: feature/custom
    Usage:
      mgit work [path] [flags]

    Flags:
          --agent-id string     agent ID recorded with the worktree
          ... 12 more lines ...

WHY IT MATTERS HERE. The consumers are agents and scripts that capture combined output and show the first line or two. In the fleet soak the useful text ("another mgit process is running: held by PID ...") had to be cut to 200 characters to keep the usage block out of the log; a reader who sees only the tail sees flag help and no cause.

Usage is the right output for a USAGE error (unknown flag, wrong arg count) and the wrong output for a RUNTIME error (lock contention, branch not found, nothing to commit). cobra separates these: set SilenceUsage on the root and let argument/flag validation still print it (cobra prints usage for arg-validation errors before RunE runs, or the command can call cmd.Usage() explicitly for the cases that deserve it).

Refs: MGIT-120
nodes.acceptance: A runtime failure (e.g. lock contention, `branch not found`, `nothing to commit`) prints the error and nothing else. A usage failure (unknown flag, wrong number of args, missing required flag) still prints the usage block. Covered by a CLI test asserting both shapes.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: squash --to-git --dry-run fails with "commit not found: to commit", so previewing the export requires recording a squash artifact
nodes.description:
Hit while working MGIT-121.1, checking what my branch would hand a reviewer.

REPRODUCE, on any branch with commits for a task:

    $ mgit squash --task-id MGIT-121.1 --to-git --dry-run
    Error: squash --to-git: squash git patch: commit not found: to commit
    (then the usage block)

Note the trailing empty ref in the message: "to commit " with nothing after it. --dry-run skips creating the squash commit, and the --to-git export then asks git-patch for a range whose "to" end is the empty string, so it fails instead of previewing.

Both flags are documented and neither warns about the other:

      --dry-run                Preview without making changes
      --to-git                 Export squashed commit as git format-patch

WHY IT MATTERS. Squash is append-only by design (MGIT-22): every `mgit squash --task-id X --to-git` appends a squash artifact commit to task/X. That is correct for landing. But the ONLY way to see the patch a reviewer will get is to run it for real, which means a preview permanently adds a commit to the task trail — I did exactly this twice on task/MGIT-121.1, and the trail now carries two squash artifacts interleaved with the work. --dry-run is the flag that exists to avoid that, and it is the one combination that does not work.

EXPECTED. `--to-git --dry-run` prints the patch it would export (to stdout, or --to-git-output) and records nothing. Failing that, it should refuse the combination up front with a message that says so, rather than dying inside the patch formatter on an empty ref.

Refs: MGIT-121.1, MGIT-22
nodes.prompt:
Fix `mgit squash --to-git --dry-run`. Today the dry-run path skips creating the squash commit and the --to-git export then formats a patch against an empty "to" ref, producing `commit not found: to commit ` (note the empty ref).

Make dry-run compute the tree/patch it would export and print it without recording anything, so a preview does not append a squash artifact to the task branch. Squash is append-only (MGIT-22), so a preview that records is not a preview.

Write the failing test first: run --to-git --dry-run on a task with commits, assert the patch bytes match the non-dry-run export and that the task's commit count is unchanged.

Refs: MGIT-121.1, MGIT-22
nodes.acceptance: `mgit squash --task-id X --to-git --dry-run` writes the same patch bytes that `--to-git` would export, and `mgit log --task-id X` shows no new commit afterwards. A test asserts both: patch content equal to the non-dry-run export, and commit count unchanged. If the combination is instead rejected, it is rejected before any patch formatting with a message naming both flags.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Host-side guest vsock dialer (real GuestDialer)
nodes.prompt:
DISCOVERED GAP (2026-06-17, backend-boot track): both microVM backends really boot (vzf real VZVirtualMachine; firecracker real firecracker-go-sdk) and wire a vsock device, but there is NO concrete host-side GuestDialer (microvm.Manager.GuestDialer is the interface; only a test pipeDialer exists). So microvm.Manager.Exec returns ErrSandboxBackendUnavailable and exec/land cannot reach the guest's vsock :1024 listener (cmd/mgit-guest). This blocks the exec/land e2e that 11.6/11.7/11.9 defer to.

Implement the real host-side guest dialer that the daemon injects into microvm.Config.GuestDialer.

PORTABLE CORE (build-tag-free, unit-testable on any OS — DO FIRST): firecracker exposes vsock via a per-VM unix socket with host-initiated connections: the host dials the uds, sends "CONNECT <port>\n", firecracker replies "OK <hostport>\n" on success, then proxies the stream to the guest's vsock port. This handshake is plain I/O over a unix socket and is OS-portable (unix sockets work on macOS+Linux), so the firecracker dialer + handshake is fully unit-testable against a fake firecracker uds server WITHOUT /dev/kvm.

PLATFORM WIRING (needs the hardware, defer): (a) firecracker (linux): the firecracker manager must expose each sandbox's vsock.sock path, and a GuestDialer maps sandboxID -> that path -> the portable Dial; wire PeerBinder.Bind(sandboxID, peer) at launch (SEC-10). (b) vzf (macOS, CGO): VZVirtioSocketDevice.Connect(port) on the running VM returns a VZVirtioSocketConnection — a thin GuestDialer wrapper; needs the VZ virtualization entitlement + a real guest image to test. Real-VM round-trips (exec/land) are e2e (MGIT-11.13), needing the Linux KVM box / entitled Mac.

DEFINITION OF DONE per issue: TDD red->green->refactor; REQUIRED TESTS pass; coverage gates met (other 90%/85%); zero linter/vet/race/vuln findings; /simplify after green; full Verification Checklist. Commit format {type}({scope}): {desc} + 'Refs: MGIT-11.5.x'. NO co-authored-by/agent/Generated-with trailer (information-exposure control).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA:
The portable firecracker vsock dialer connects to a uds and completes the CONNECT handshake to a guest port, returning a stream; a rejected/garbled handshake and an absent socket fail closed; the dialer satisfies a host-side dial contract the microvm.Manager.GuestDialer can adopt. (Platform manager wiring + real-VM exec/land round-trip are tracked for the e2e step on real hardware.)

REQUIRED TESTS:
  - TestFCVsock_Dial_HandshakeSucceeds
  - TestFCVsock_Dial_HandshakeRejected
  - TestFCVsock_Dial_SocketAbsent
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: vzf (macOS) GuestDialer via VZVirtioSocketDevice.Connect
nodes.prompt: The macOS half of the host-side guest dialer (MGIT-13 delivered firecracker via fcvsock + firecracker.guestDialer). Implement a microvm.GuestDialer for the vzf backend wrapping VZVirtioSocketDevice.Connect(port) on the running VZVirtualMachine, returning the VZVirtioSocketConnection as a net.Conn. CGO/darwin-tagged (the vz binding lives in internal/sandboxd/backend/vzf); inject into the vzf manager's microvm.Config.GuestDialer (mirror firecracker.NewManager). Needs the com.apple.security.virtualization entitlement + a guest image to test the real round-trip (e2e). Unlike firecracker (host-initiated CONNECT over a unix socket), vzf connects via the framework API on the live VM handle, so design how the dialer resolves sandboxID -> live VZVirtualMachine. No co-authored-by/agent/Generated-with trailer.
nodes.acceptance: The vzf backend exposes a GuestDialer that connects to a running guest's vsock port via VZVirtioSocketDevice.Connect; microvm.Manager.Exec routes through it on macOS; fail-closed when the VM or socket device is absent.
