nodes.title: vzf (macOS) land-channel dialer
nodes.prompt:
Provide the macOS (vzf / Virtualization.framework) land-channel dialer so `mgit sandbox land` works on macOS, not just Linux KVM.

CONTEXT: MGIT-11.10.10 shipped the host-initiated land path with a firecracker-specific dialer: firecracker.NewLandDialer(workDir) dials the guest land vsock port (1025) over the per-VM firecracker unix socket. sandboxd.LandChannel takes any dialer satisfying microvm.GuestDialer (DialGuest). cmd/mgit-sandboxd/land_wiring.go currently wires firecracker.NewLandDialer unconditionally, so v1 land transport is Linux-KVM only. The guest land server (mgit-guest, internal/guest.ServeLandHead) is platform-agnostic and already serves port 1025.

WHAT TO DO: add a vzf land dialer analogous to MGIT-13.1's exec GuestDialer (VZVirtioSocketDevice.Connect to port 1025) and select it in the daemon land wiring based on the active backend (firecracker vs vzf), instead of hardcoding firecracker. Keep the dialer behind the microvm.GuestDialer seam so LandChannel is unchanged. Pairs with MGIT-13.1 (exec dialer) — share the connect mechanism; only the port differs.

Refs: FR-17 v1 platform scope (Linux+macOS); see memory note fr17-land-transport-directions.
nodes.acceptance: On macOS (vzf backend) `mgit sandbox land --task <id>` pulls the guest land pool over the Virtualization.framework vsock land port and runs the same verified land path as on KVM. The daemon land wiring selects the dialer by active backend rather than hardcoding firecracker. Unit-tested against a fake vsock; gated real-VM e2e on macOS.

nodes.title: internal/testutil.NewTestStore carries the MGIT-121.1 defect (per-pool pragmas, unbounded pool) and has zero callers
nodes.description:
Found while auditing connection-open sites for MGIT-121.1.

internal/testutil/sqlite.go NewTestStore opens one *sql.DB and applies the four safety-critical pragmas with db.ExecContext, exactly as internal/store/index did before MGIT-121.1. database/sql routes that Exec to ONE pooled connection and pragmas are per-CONNECTION state, so only that connection gets them.

It is worse here in one respect and harmless in another:

- WORSE: it never calls SetMaxOpenConns, so the pool is unbounded (default 0 = unlimited). Every connection past the first is bare, with busy_timeout back at zero.
- HARMLESS TODAY: `grep -rl testutil.NewTestStore` returns nothing. The helper has no callers at all.

So this is not a live bug; it is a loaded gun for the next person who reaches for the obvious-looking test helper, and its comment currently claims "The database is configured with safety-critical PRAGMAs per CLAUDE.md" — which is true of one connection and false of the pool.

It even carries the MGIT-121 fix (busy_timeout hoisted first, with the comment explaining why), which makes it read as considered and correct.

TWO HONEST OPTIONS, in preference order:
1. DELETE it. Nothing uses it, index.New is the real thing, and dead test infrastructure that looks authoritative is a trap.
2. If it is to be kept, route it through the same pragmaConnector index.New uses (internal/store/index/connector.go) and bound the pool, so there is one answer to "how is a mgit SQLite connection configured".

Refs: MGIT-121.1, MGIT-121, CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2
nodes.prompt:
internal/testutil/sqlite.go NewTestStore applies SQLite pragmas with db.ExecContext on an unbounded pool, so only one connection ever gets them — the defect MGIT-121.1 fixed in internal/store/index. It currently has zero callers.

Prefer deleting it: confirm with `grep -rn 'testutil.NewTestStore' --include='*.go'` that nothing uses it, remove it, and run the full suite. If it must be kept instead, open its pool through the pragmaConnector in internal/store/index/connector.go (exporting what is needed, or moving the connector somewhere both can reach) and bound the pool, then pin it with a test that takes MaxOpenConns distinct *sql.Conn and asserts busy_timeout and foreign_keys on each.

Refs: MGIT-121.1, CLAUDE.md SQL Rule 2
nodes.acceptance: Either internal/testutil/sqlite.go's NewTestStore is deleted (with the file removed if it becomes empty and the suite still green), or every connection it hands out has busy_timeout=5000 and foreign_keys=ON with a bounded pool, proven by a test that holds MaxOpenConns distinct *sql.Conn and asserts the pragmas on each. Its doc comment must match whichever is true.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: build/ is not ignored, so `mgit commit -a` sweeps locally built binaries into the task branch
nodes.description:
Hit while running the MGIT-121.1 verification checklist. Step 6 of that checklist is `go build -o mgit ./cmd/mgit/`, and the natural place to put the binary is build/. The very next `mgit commit -a -m "..."` recorded a 40MB Mach-O binary into task/MGIT-121.1 alongside the source change.

`-a` is the correct and instructed way to commit (CLAUDE.md, MGIT-77: a bare `mgit commit` with nothing staged is refused), so "stage more carefully" is not the fix — the repo should not have an unignored directory whose whole purpose is build output.

CURRENT STATE: .gitignore has no `build` entry. build/darwin is tracked, which is presumably why the directory was never ignored wholesale.

This is the MGIT-80 shape again (scaffolding landing in user patches), one level out: not mgit's own files this time, but the repo's build output.

The damage is contained — squash exports a base-to-tip diff, so adding then deleting the binary nets to nothing in the landed patch — but it sits in the branch's object store and in the trail a reviewer reads.

FIX: ignore build output while keeping whatever under build/ is genuinely tracked. Either ignore `build/` and un-ignore the tracked paths, or move build output somewhere already ignored and say so in the CLAUDE.md verification checklist, which currently tells the agent to build a binary and does not say where to put it.

Refs: MGIT-121.1, MGIT-80, MGIT-77
nodes.prompt:
Stop locally built binaries from being swept into task branches by `mgit commit -a`.

nodes.title: A plain `mgit` on PATH can be days behind main, so dogfooding agents test fixed bugs against stale binaries and re-file them
nodes.description:
Concrete cost, 2026-08-16/17: I filed MGIT-129 against `mgit squash --to-git --dry-run` and it cost a reviewer three separate reproduction attempts before the cause was found. The defect was real, was MGIT-112, and had been fixed in #24 (406a769) the day before I filed. I ran a binary from fa278f5 (#23) — the commit that DISCLOSED the defect, built about five hours before the fix landed.

    $ which -a mgit
    /Users/vimal/.local/bin/mgit
    $ mgit --version
    mgit version 0.5.0 (commit: fa278f5, built: 2026-08-15T10:13:50Z)
    $ git merge-base --is-ancestor 406a769 fa278f5 ; echo $?
    1

WHY THIS IS STRUCTURAL, NOT JUST MY MISTAKE. CLAUDE.md's dogfooding section instructs every parallel task to drive `mgit work`, `mgit run`, `mgit commit`, `mgit sandbox …`, `mgit squash` — all unqualified, i.e. whatever is on PATH. It is emphatic that using the tool is where the defects come from, and it is right: nearly every recent ticket came from that. But the same instructions never mention that the PATH binary and the worktree source are two different programs. So an agent works IN current source and reports bugs FROM a stale binary, which quietly inverts dogfooding's value — instead of finding new defects it manufactures reports of already-fixed ones, and every such report burns reviewer time in the most expensive way (they cannot reproduce it, so they must disprove it).

It is undetectable from inside the loop as things stand. `mgit --version` prints a commit hash that means nothing without a `git merge-base` against the repo, and nothing prompts an agent to run either. My worktree even passed the obvious sanity check — the MGIT-112 fix WAS present in its source.

This is adjacent to the release-gap problem but not the same one: that was about published releases lagging main; this is about a developer's own PATH binary lagging the tree they are actively editing, inside the repo, while dogfooding it.

OPTIONS, cheapest first:
1. Have mgit tell the agent. When cwd is inside an mgit-managed repo whose source builds a different commit than the running binary, print a one-line warning naming both commits, e.g. `mgit: running 0.5.0 (fa278f5); this tree is at 55b0c4b — rebuild before trusting a bug report`. Cheap, and it fires exactly when it matters.
2. Say it in CLAUDE.md. The dogfood section should state plainly that `mgit` on PATH is not the tree, and require `mgit --version` in any bug report filed from a dogfood session — the reviewer asked me for exactly that field, which is evidence it belongs in the template.
3. Make `mgit work` do it. Provisioning a task worktree is the natural moment to check binary-vs-tree and either warn or build a task-local binary.

Refs: MGIT-129, MGIT-112, MGIT-121.1
nodes.prompt:
Make the gap between the `mgit` binary on PATH and the mgit source tree visible to a dogfooding agent.

Background: MGIT-129 was filed against an already-fixed defect (MGIT-112, fixed in #24/406a769) because the reporting agent ran a PATH binary built from fa278f5, five hours before the fix landed, while editing a tree that contained it. Nothing in the loop surfaced the mismatch, and disproving the report cost the reviewer three reproduction attempts.

Preferred fix: when mgit runs with cwd inside an mgit-managed repo, compare the binary's build commit against the tree and print a one-line warning to stderr on mismatch, naming both commits. Keep it to one line and do not fail the command. Take care that it stays silent for users running a released binary against an unrelated project — the check is only meaningful when the tree IS mgit's own source.

Also update CLAUDE.md's dogfood section to say that `mgit` on PATH is not the tree, and to require `mgit --version` in any bug filed from a dogfood session.

Refs: MGIT-129, MGIT-112
nodes.acceptance: An agent dogfooding mgit from inside the repo learns, without being told to look, that its `mgit` binary is built from a different commit than the tree it is editing. Either mgit warns on that mismatch (naming both commits), or CLAUDE.md's dogfood section states it and requires `mgit --version` in bug reports — verified by reproducing the MGIT-129 situation: a stale binary plus a current tree must produce a visible signal before a report is filed.

nodes.title: The exec stream has no liveness signal, so a client cannot tell a working guest from a wedged daemon
nodes.description:
Found while fixing MGIT-122, and created by its fix — filed rather than hidden.

CONTEXT. The daemon does not stream a command's output: `serveExec` calls the service, waits for the whole ExecResult, and only then relays stdout/stderr frames (internal/sandboxd/dispatch.go). So between the exec request and the command finishing, the control socket carries NOTHING.

MGIT-122 removed the client's read deadline from that stream, because it was not a liveness check at all — it was a cap on how long a build may take, and it capped every exec at 30s (measured: `sandbox exec -- sleep 45` failed at exactly 30s on a warm, idle, single-VM sandbox). What bounds the wait now: the per-exec timeout and the sandbox TTL (daemon-enforced), a dead daemon (its socket closes and the read ends at once), and the caller's context (now wired to the connection).

THE RESIDUAL GAP. A daemon that is alive but wedged — deadlocked, or blocked in a backend call that never returns — is indistinguishable from a guest doing slow work. The client waits until the operator cancels. That is strictly better than the previous behaviour (which killed healthy long commands) but it is not the same as bounded.

TWO PIECES, either of which helps:

1. A liveness frame on the exec stream. Add an execwire frame kind the daemon emits periodically while an exec is outstanding, and have the client treat the gap between frames — not the command's duration — as its deadline. Note the wire-tag hazard: two parallel branches once collided on a frame tag (MGIT-73), so pick the tag in one place and assert it in a test. Old clients would see an unknown frame kind and error, so this needs the same-release reasoning the greeting has, or a negotiated capability.

2. `mgit sandbox exec` / `mgit run` expose no --timeout, so model.ExecRequest.Timeout is always zero and the sandbox TTL is the only bound. A caller who wants a bounded command cannot ask for one.

Refs: MGIT-122, MGIT-118, MGIT-73, FR-17.11
nodes.acceptance: A client blocked on an exec stream can distinguish "the guest is working" from "the daemon stopped answering", and reports the second as such rather than waiting indefinitely. Either the daemon emits a periodic liveness frame the client uses as an idle deadline, or an equivalent mechanism is chosen and its rationale recorded. `mgit sandbox exec` and `mgit run` accept a --timeout that populates ExecRequest.Timeout. A test drives a daemon that accepts an exec and then never answers, and asserts the client reports a daemon-side stall — not a guest failure, and not an in-guest memory diagnosis (MGIT-118).
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: `mgit add <path>` only warns when a file carries mgit's generated block — the block still lands in the patch
nodes.description:
Hit while doing MGIT-131, from the same direction MGIT-131 was fixing.

MGIT-131's work required editing the project's real CLAUDE.md (the verification checklist step 6 now names build/ as the output path). CLAUDE.md is a real project directive, so it must be committable — and `mgit commit -a` deliberately SKIPS it as generated (MGIT-80), so the ONLY way to commit that edit is `mgit add CLAUDE.md` by name.

But the worktree's CLAUDE.md is the project file PLUS mgit's appended BEGIN/END mgit-sandbox block. Staging it by name stages the whole file, so the generated block went into the task branch, where `squash --to-git | git apply` would have appended a worktree- and host-specific block ("No sandbox was requested for this worktree...") to the project's CLAUDE.md.

`mgit add` DOES warn (warnIfGenerated, cmd/mgit/add.go) — and the warning is easy to walk past: it arrives on stderr in the middle of a multi-file stage that otherwise succeeded, and it describes the consequence rather than blocking it. It was caught here only by later grepping `mgit diff --task-id` for the marker; the fix was a manual strip plus a second commit.

This is MGIT-80's defect one level out. MGIT-80 stopped the BULK path from sweeping generated scaffolding in; the by-name path is still open, and by-name is the ONLY path available for a legitimate edit to a file that also carries a block.

FIX DIRECTION: the block is delimited by unambiguous BEGIN/END markers and internal/store/git/worktree_generated.go already records which paths carry one, so the content is separable without heuristics. Decide deliberately between staging the file with the block STRIPPED (matches what the agent means, but makes staged content differ from disk, which no other path does) and refusing with a named flag. Whatever is chosen, the outcome that must not survive is: the block lands in the patch and nobody notices until a reviewer reads the diff.

REQUIRED TESTS: a worktree CLAUDE.md with a block, edited above the block and staged by name, records the edit and NOT the block; `squash --to-git` for that task emits a patch with no BEGIN/END marker; a project tracking its own CLAUDE.md with no mgit block is unaffected; the fully-generated .claude/settings.json case behaves as it does today. Verify live in a real worktree.

Refs: MGIT-80, MGIT-131
nodes.acceptance: Staging a generated-block-carrying file by name never puts the block into a task branch; `mgit diff --task-id <ID>` and `mgit squash --to-git` for such a task contain no `BEGIN mgit-sandbox` marker. A genuine user edit to the same file still commits. A project file with no generated block is untouched by the new behavior.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A daemon's per-repo runtime directory outlives it: per-sandbox state dirs are left on disk after the fleet is gone
nodes.description:
Observed while verifying MGIT-122 on macOS/libkrun, by looking at the host after the runs rather than by reading code — so the root cause below is where to START, not a finding.

WHAT WAS OBSERVED. After a full `MGIT_SOAK_PROFILE=long make soak` — which drains its fleet in phase 6, removes every sandbox, kills the daemon and `rm -rf`s its scratch repo — the daemon's runtime work directory is still there, with per-sandbox state directories inside it:

    $ ls /var/folders/.../T/mgit-501/626efae543b9/
    d.sock  d.sock.lock  daemon.log  w/
    $ ls /var/folders/.../T/mgit-501/626efae543b9/w/
    VQ6MVMPJ  HM7KVPF0  3646HZ4H  ...

The repo those belonged to no longer exists. Nothing can address them, and nothing will clean them.

ON THIS HOST it has accumulated: 399 per-repo runtime directories dating back to 2026-08-12, of which 33 still hold per-sandbox state, ~300 MB excluding the one live daemon's. Each state dir holds a sandbox's overlay, its copy of the worktree and its sockets, so the cost scales with the worktrees involved, not with the count.

WHY THE SOAK DOES NOT CATCH IT. Invariant I4 asserts no state dir leaks after destroy, and it passes — because it runs after the CHURN phase, against a live daemon, and that path is correct. What is not asserted is the state after the daemon is gone, which is exactly where phase 4's SIGKILL leaves sandboxes: the replacement daemon reconciles the REGISTRY (MGIT-102) and reaps the VM PROCESSES (MGIT-103), and the on-disk state of the sandboxes it inherited appears to be nobody's job.

WHERE TO LOOK. The work dir is derived per repo root in cmd/mgit/sandbox_connect.go and passed as --work-dir; the daemon creates per-sandbox subdirectories under it. Candidates: teardown removes the state dir only on the graceful path; rehydration of a predecessor's sandboxes drops the registry row without removing what is on disk; nothing ever removes the per-repo dir itself, even when the repo is gone.

FR-17.19 says a sandbox leaves no residue. This is residue, just one level up from where the invariant looks.

Refs: MGIT-122, MGIT-113, MGIT-102, MGIT-103, FR-17.19
nodes.acceptance: After a sandbox is destroyed by any path — graceful remove, land, TTL reap, or inherited by a replacement daemon after its own daemon was SIGKILLed — its per-sandbox state directory is gone from the daemon's work dir. A per-repo runtime directory whose repo no longer exists is not left behind indefinitely (removed on the daemon's idle exit, or swept). The fleet soak asserts the post-daemon state, not only the mid-run state, so this class cannot pass I4 again: after phase 5's replacement daemon has accounted for the fleet it inherited, no state directory remains for a sandbox that is gone.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The CLI↔daemon control plane cannot add a wire feature without breaking one version direction
nodes.description:
Found while implementing MGIT-133's liveness beat, and verified live on this host rather than reasoned about.

THE CONSTRAINT. internal/controlproto decodes BOTH requests and responses with json.DisallowUnknownFields, and the greeting is a fixed 17-byte constant an old client reads with io.ReadFull + exact compare. Together these freeze the wire in both directions:

- a new REQUEST field makes an old daemon reject the request ("invalid request"), and the reply is not even the right shape for a client waiting on exec frames;
- a new RESPONSE field makes an old client fail to decode (this is how MGIT-109's PolicyResult.Pending, MGIT-76's Synced and the ErrorCode field each broke old clients when they landed);
- extending the greeting leaves unread bytes in an old client's socket, which it then misparses as its response length;
- a new exec FRAME kind is an "unexpected exec frame" to an old client.

So there is no capability negotiation available at all, and any addition must pick a direction to break. MGIT-133 picked deliberately: new-client/old-daemon (the COMMON pair — an upgraded CLI against the long-lived daemon the previous release left running) keeps working via first-beat detection and an honest notice; old-client/new-daemon breaks.

MEASURED, on this host, mgit v0.5.0 CLI against an MGIT-133 daemon:
- `sandbox list`, `sandbox status`, `run --check` — all still work;
- `mgit run -- echo hi` — fails, AND the old binary's classifier lands the "unexpected exec frame 0x48" error in phaseLostServing, so it prints the memory-cap advisory. A wire-version mismatch is reported to the user as in-guest memory exhaustion: MGIT-118's misdiagnosis, reached from a new direction, in a binary we can no longer change.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT (for the NEXT addition, not this one). Some forward-compatible seam in controlproto, chosen once:
- relax DisallowUnknownFields to a decode that ignores unknown fields it does not need, keeping the strict path for the fields it does (the ceiling checks that motivated strictness are on size, not on field names); and/or
- a version/capability exchange that an old peer tolerates — e.g. the client stating its protocol version in the first request, which requires the above to land first.

Until then the rule should be written down where a future author meets it: adding anything to this wire is a same-release change, and the release notes have to say so.

Refs: MGIT-133, MGIT-109, MGIT-118, MGIT-76, FR-17.34
nodes.acceptance: controlproto can gain a request field, a response field, or an exec frame kind without an older peer on either side failing — or, if that is judged not worth the complexity, the same-release constraint is recorded in the IDD and in CONTRIBUTING with the measured evidence above, and the old-client failure is at minimum not rendered as a guest memory diagnosis in the next release.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: go-git v5.19.1 carries two called vulnerabilities, so govulncheck fails the verification bar on every branch
nodes.description:
Found while running the MGIT-136 verification checklist (step 5). `govulncheck ./...` exits 3 on a clean tree — this is not caused by MGIT-136 and reproduces on any branch.

    Vulnerability #1: GO-2026-6214
      Module: github.com/go-git/go-git/v5
        Found in: github.com/go-git/go-git/v5@v5.19.1
        Fixed in: github.com/go-git/go-git/v5@v5.19.2
    Vulnerability #2: GO-2026-6213
      (same module, same fixed version)

    Your code is affected by 2 vulnerabilities from 1 module.

Both are REACHED, not merely present: the trace names our own call path, e.g.
`internal/store/git/diff.go:51 DiffStore.DiffCommits -> object.Tree.Diff -> git.worktreeFilesystem.Readlink`.

Two reasons this matters beyond hygiene:

1. CLAUDE.md's verification checklist has a zero-tolerance line — "Zero known vulnerabilities — govulncheck passes". Right now no branch can satisfy it, so every agent either reports a failing bar it did not cause or quietly stops running the step. A gate that cannot be met stops being a gate.
2. go-git is the storage engine, not a leaf dependency (ADR-001), and the calls are in the diff path.

The fix looks like a patch bump within the approved major (APPROVED-PACKAGES.md pins `go-git/go-git/v5 >= 5.13.0`; v6 is explicitly not approved, ADR-004), so this should be `go get github.com/go-git/go-git/v5@v5.19.2 && go mod tidy` plus a full test + e2e pass to confirm no behaviour change in the diff/worktree paths.

Refs: MGIT-136 (found during its verification), ADR-001, ADR-004, APPROVED-PACKAGES.md
nodes.acceptance: `govulncheck ./...` exits 0 on main with no suppressions, go.mod pins go-git v5.19.2 or later within the approved v5 major, and the full test suite plus the store/git diff tests pass unchanged.

nodes.title: MGIT-133's "this daemon predates MGIT-133" notice is unreachable once the version handshake lands — decide whether it stays
nodes.description:
Filed from MGIT-136, to be settled when PR #35 (MGIT-133) merges. It is a reconciliation item, not a defect.

MGIT-133 added a client-side fallback for the mixed pair it deliberately kept working: a daemon that never emits a liveness beat is treated as an older build, the stall deadline is dropped, MGIT-122's unbounded wait is restored, and `writeNoLivenessNotice` tells the caller once that nothing bounds the wait ("this mgit-sandboxd sends no liveness beats (it predates MGIT-133) ..."). It is pinned by `TestClient_Exec_OlderDaemonNeverBeats_WaitsAndSaysWhy`.

MGIT-136 makes that state unreachable in production. A daemon that predates MGIT-133 also predates the version handshake, so it is refused at `dialGreeted` — before the exec request is written and long before the frame loop — with an explicit skew message. The only way to reach `writeNoLivenessNotice` now is a daemon that speaks control protocol 2 (so it is current) and yet does not beat, which no shipped build is.

Neither outcome is obviously right, so it should be a decision rather than a drift:

- KEEP it as defense-in-depth. It costs one branch and one notice, it is the honest behaviour if a future daemon ever suppresses beats (a build tag, a backend that cannot beat), and deleting a "we could not tell" path in favour of an assumption is how the MGIT-118 class of misdiagnosis gets built.
- REMOVE it and simplify the frame loop to "beats are guaranteed by the protocol version", deleting the `beating` flag and the stall==0 escape hatch. Cheaper to read, but it makes protocol 2 a promise the daemon must keep forever.

Whichever is chosen, the test's doc comment needs updating: it currently frames the case as "the ordinary one — an upgraded CLI talking to the long-lived daemon the previous release left running", and after MGIT-136 that pair is refused at the handshake instead.

Refs: MGIT-133 (PR #35), MGIT-136, MGIT-122, MGIT-118
nodes.acceptance: After PR #35 merges, a decision is recorded in code (either the no-liveness fallback is kept with a comment saying why it is now unreachable in production, or it is removed along with the `beating` flag), and `TestClient_Exec_OlderDaemonNeverBeats_WaitsAndSaysWhy`'s rationale matches the post-MGIT-136 reality rather than describing a pair that is now refused earlier.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Optional: restart the daemon automatically on a version-skew refusal, instead of naming pkill
nodes.description:
Filed as an OPTIONAL follow-up to MGIT-136 by founder invitation (R-H273). MGIT-136 is complete without it and should not wait for this.

CONTEXT. MGIT-136 gives the control plane a version handshake and refuses a mismatched pair outright (exact equality — a range this codec cannot honor would convert a clean refusal into a pair that works until it silently does not). The refusal names the remedy, including `pkill -f mgit-sandboxd`, because a daemon left running across an upgrade is the realistic way to end up mixed: the CLI is replaced on disk while the old daemon keeps holding the socket.

THE IDEA. That specific case is mechanically recoverable. The CLI already spawns a daemon when none is dialable, so on a skew refusal it could stop the stale daemon and respawn from its own build rather than asking a human to run pkill.

WHY IT IS FILED RATHER THAN BUILT, and why the bar is high:

1. Killing another process is not a step to take on inference. This session has already had two incidents of exactly that shape — an agent nearly killing daemons by name alone, and a wrong-pid freeze that produced a false negative before it was caught. Whatever a skew handler kills must be established as OUR daemon for THIS repo (its socket, its repo-root, a pid whose liveness is checked), never matched by name. A daemon belonging to another repository must be untouchable; this host routinely runs several.

2. It must not become a retry loop. If the respawned daemon also mismatches — a stale binary earlier on PATH, a packaging error — the second refusal must be terminal and say so. An auto-restart that silently retries turns a clear diagnosis into a hang, which is the failure MGIT-133 exists to prevent.

3. It removes a reader's chance to notice. The refusal currently tells someone their CLI and daemon disagree, which is information about their install (see MGIT-132: a PATH binary days behind the tree invalidated a real bug report). Fixing it silently means nobody learns their environment is mixed. If this is built, it should still SAY what it did and why.

4. The daemon may be serving other tasks. Restarting it is not free for a fleet mid-run — MGIT-102 made registrations durable, so they survive, but in-flight execs on other tasks do not.

SCOPE IF TAKEN: the auto-restart applies only to the CLI-newer-than-daemon direction, where the CLI's own build is authoritative and can supply the replacement. The reverse (old CLI, new daemon) cannot be fixed by the CLI at all and must keep refusing.

Refs: MGIT-136, MGIT-132, MGIT-133, MGIT-102</description>
<prompt>Decide first whether this should exist at all; implement only if the answer is yes.

If implemented:
1. Trigger ONLY on a version-skew refusal where the CLI is newer, and only for a daemon proven to be this repo's own — established from its socket path and repo-root, with a liveness-checked pid. Never match by process name. A daemon belonging to another repository must be untouchable.
2. Stop the stale daemon, respawn from the CLI's own build, retry the verb ONCE. A second skew is terminal and says so plainly.
3. Say what happened. The user should still learn their environment was mixed and what was replaced, per MGIT-132's finding that a stale binary silently invalidates bug reports.
4. Warn if the daemon was serving other tasks, since in-flight execs on them are lost even though registrations survive (MGIT-102).

TESTS: skew triggers exactly one restart; a second skew after restart is terminal; a foreign repo's daemon is never targeted (assert the negative); the reverse direction still refuses without restarting.

Refs: MGIT-136, MGIT-132, MGIT-133, MGIT-102</prompt>
<acceptance>Either a recorded decision not to build it with the reasoning, or: a version-skew refusal in the CLI-newer direction restarts only this repo's own daemon, identified by socket and repo-root rather than by name, retries once, reports what it did, and treats a second skew as terminal. A foreign repo's daemon is provably never targeted, and the old-CLI direction still refuses.</acceptance>

nodes.title: mgit must operate over an existing git repository (.mgit self-contained; never touch project .git)
nodes.prompt:
FOUNDATIONAL / RELEASE-BLOCKER. mgit's first-level requirement is that it runs INSIDE a git-managed project and works OVER AND ABOVE the existing git repo — adding task-tagged micro-commits without owning, replacing, reading, or mutating the project's normal git history. Today it does NOT: mgit cannot initialize or run in any existing git project.

ROOT CAUSE (verified, reproducible 2026-06-22): internal/store/git/repository.go Init/Open open the go-git repo with storage=.mgit/ but pass the PROJECT ROOT as the go-git worktree; and commit/staging/merge/checkout are built on go-git's Worktree+index (wt.Add/wt.Commit/wt.Checkout/wt.Status/wt.Clean — 7 sites: repository.go:191, commit.go:47, worktree.go:60/85/102/121, merge.go:98). go-git writes a `.git` gitfile at any worktree root, so mgit (a) in an empty dir writes `.git -> .mgit` (hijacks the .git slot), and (b) in a REAL project FAILS at init: `init go-git repo: open <root>/.git: is a directory`, then `resolve HEAD: reference not found` on every later command. mgit only works in an empty directory.

WHY MISSED: every test inits in a fresh EMPTY t.TempDir() (only greenfield ran; line coverage can't detect a missing scenario); mgit never dogfooded on a real repo (mgit-dev has no .mgit); FR-17 audits were scoped to the sandbox guest threat model, not core git coexistence; the requirement was never an encoded acceptance criterion.

DESIGN (ADR-001 amendment 2026-06-22): .mgit/ is a self-contained go-git store mgit drives PURELY via plumbing, COEXISTING with — never touching — the project .git. (1) never create/open/read/mutate project .git or write a root .git gitfile; project history is sacrosanct. (2) .mgit/ opened bare/storer-only (worktree=nil). (3) read project files via Repository.Root()+osfs, build blob/tree/commit via plumbing, manage refs (HEAD, task/<id>) directly. (4) mgit-owned staging (stateless build-from-FileDiffs + file content, or SQLite index) replacing .git/index. (5) FR-16 checkout writes files via plumbing/osfs, not wt.Checkout(). TreeStore.BuildTree already does plumbing tree-building (migration target).

BLAST RADIUS: repository.go, commit.go, worktree.go, merge.go; ~28 test files; the sandbox quarantine bind-mount of worktreePath/.git.

SEQUENCING (owner-approved): spec now (ADR amendment done; skipped spec test landed; this epic). Implementation = dedicated, ISOLATED, INDEPENDENTLY-REVIEWED effort (sits under everything in internal/store/git); do NOT interleave with other feature work.

CLOSURE GATES: skipped spec test TestInit_OverExistingGitRepo_* green; a dogfooding e2e (full lifecycle init/add/commit/squash/rollback/worktree over a REAL git repo, project .git + history byte-for-byte intact) in CI; independent story-closure + security review of the never-mutate-project-git invariant. Commit Refs: MGIT-<id>; NO co-authored-by/agent/Generated-with trailer.

nodes.title: Init/Open/createInitialCommit: self-contained .mgit store (no root .git)

nodes.title: Core review remediation: symlink/mode fidelity, checkout guard, ref CAS, partial-checkout
nodes.prompt:
Remediate the findings from the independent security/correctness review of the MGIT-14.2-14.4 core (merged at main 4471443). The `.git`-never-touched invariant was verified SOUND; these are data-fidelity/safety defects in the new plumbing checkout/commit path (all in internal/store/git/). Fix with TDD; the behavioral tests are the point (CLAUDE.md rule 12 — test real behavior, not metrics).

[HIGH] #2 SYMLINKS dereferenced + committed as out-of-tree content. worktree_fs.go readWorkingFile/listWorkingFile use os.ReadFile which follows symlinks: a working-tree symlink (e.g. link->/etc/passwd or ->../../secret) is staged + committed as a regular blob holding the TARGET's content (exfiltration into the audited history + git divergence). FIX: detect symlinks via os.Lstat / d.Type()&fs.ModeSymlink; store them as git symlink entries (mode 120000, blob = link text) like git does — do NOT silently dereference. (Refusing with a clear error is an acceptable v1 alternative if symlink-entry support is too large, but git-faithful is preferred.)

[HIGH] #3 FILE MODES dropped on commit + checkout. plumbing.go writeNestedTree hardcodes filemode.Regular; worktree_fs.go writeBlobToDisk hardcodes 0o600; the staging->tree->disk model carries no mode. So a 0o755 script commits as 100644 and restores as 0o600 (exec bit lost) — mgit's tree hash can never equal git's, breaking the reproducible-provenance claim. FIX: make the pipeline mode-aware — carry (hash, filemode) per path; read mode via os.Lstat at stage/commit; emit correct filemode in writeNestedTree (100644/100755/120000); restore mode on checkout (chmod / recreate symlink). Preserve at least git's regular/executable/symlink distinction. (This and #2 share the mode-aware refactor.)

[MED] #4 WorktreeStore.Checkout (worktree.go materializeCommit) overwrites/removes disk files with NO clean check — safe today only because service/checkout.go guards with IsClean first. Move a clean-or-fail guard into the store method (defense in depth) + a test that a direct Checkout on a dirty worktree refuses rather than clobbering uncommitted work.

[MED] #5 Branch-ref advance is read-modify-write with no CAS (commit.go CreateCommit, merge.go): two concurrent commits parent off the same H; the later SetReference wins and the earlier commit is orphaned (lost from the branch/audit). FIX: use go-git CheckAndSetReference(new, old) for branch advancement so a concurrent move fails loudly. Add a concurrent-commit/lost-update test.

[LOW] #7 materializeCommit writes blobs in map order and aborts on first bad path — a crafted imported tree with a `../escape` entry is correctly rejected (no out-of-root write) but legitimate files may already be written, leaving a partial checkout. FIX: validate ALL target paths up front before writing any file (or stage-to-temp + rename).

COVERAGE: do NOT add a fault-injecting storer. Add behavioral tests: checkout removing a tracked-but-absent-in-target file; checkout overwrite semantics; executable-bit preservation round-trip; symlink handling; concurrent-ref/CAS.

ACCEPTANCE: symlinks no longer dereferenced (stored as git symlink entries or refused); exec/symlink modes preserved commit->tree->checkout (mgit tree hash matches git's for a mode-varied tree); direct Checkout refuses on a dirty worktree; concurrent ref advance is CAS-guarded; partial-checkout closed; behavioral tests added. Full suite green; -race/lint/vet clean; /simplify. Scope: internal/store/git/* only. Commit Refs: MGIT-14.7; no trailers.

nodes.title: DECIDED (declined): no aggregate memory bound for concurrent go-test VM boots — build tags already prevent the case
nodes.description:
RECORDED DECISION, not open work. Filed so the reasoning is durable and the revisit trigger is dated rather than remembered. Accepted by the founder as R-H278.

THE CONCERN, raised 2026-08-18: `go test ./...` runs packages in parallel, several packages contain tests that boot real microVMs, and each declares 512-1024 MB with nothing bounding their sum. A test run could in principle consume the host.

MEASURED 2026-08-19 on main, rather than reasoned about:

1. ONLY ONE VM-BOOTING PACKAGE CAN COMPILE PER PLATFORM-AND-TAGSET. The build tags are mutually exclusive, not merely different:
     internal/sandboxd/backend/libkrun   //go:build cgo && !vzf && (darwin || (linux && libkrun))
     internal/sandboxd/backend/vzf       //go:build darwin && cgo   [needs -tags vzf]
     internal/sandboxd/backend/firecracker            [linux]
   macOS default -> libkrun only, because vzf requires -tags vzf and libkrun's own
   !vzf constraint then excludes it. macOS -tags vzf -> vzf only. Linux default ->
   firecracker only, since libkrun there requires -tags libkrun.
   Go's package-level parallelism cannot multiply these: the others are excluded at
   COMPILE time, not skipped at runtime.

2. NO REAL-VM TEST CALLS t.Parallel(). Within the one package that does compile, they run sequentially.

3. EVERY ONE IS ENV-GATED (MGIT_E2E_LIBKRUN=1 and equivalents), so a plain `go test ./...` boots nothing at all.

So the worst case is ONE VM at a time at a declared 512-1024 MB — a bounded case, not an unbounded sum.

WHY NOT BUILD THE BOUND ANYWAY. It would be a mechanism guarding a case the build tags already prevent, carrying its own maintenance and its own ways of being wrong. The place a fleet genuinely runs is the soak, and the bound is already there: scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh declares 512 MB per sandbox rather than trusting the 2048 MB policy default, and fleet_set_ceiling derives an aggregate ceiling from actual host memory. A second bound elsewhere would not make that one truer.

WHERE THE REAL COST WAS. The accumulation that actually bit this host was MGIT-135: 399 orphaned per-repo daemon runtime directories, 33 still holding per-sandbox state, roughly 300 MB. That is folded into the MGIT-103 reaper, which is the correct owner, since cleanup belonging to a dying daemon cannot be performed by that daemon.

REVISIT TRIGGER — reopen this decision if ANY of the following becomes true:
  a) the backend build tags stop being mutually exclusive, so two VM-booting packages can compile together (e.g. libkrun and vzf become co-installable, or a backend loses its tag);
  b) any real-VM test gains t.Parallel(), or a package starts booting more than one VM at a time;
  c) the env gates are removed or defaulted on, so an ordinary `go test ./...` boots a VM;
  d) a new VM-booting package appears outside internal/sandboxd/backend/.

Refs: MGIT-135, MGIT-103, MGIT-113, MGIT-95, MGIT-98, R-H278</description>
<prompt>No work is requested. This node records a decision and its revisit trigger.

If you are reading this because one of the trigger conditions (a)-(d) in the description now holds, do NOT simply implement a bound: re-measure first, exactly as the original decision did, and record the new measurement here before deciding. The value of this record is the measurement, not the conclusion.</prompt>
<acceptance>Not applicable — this is a decision record. It is correct while the four measured facts in the description hold; the revisit trigger names precisely what would falsify them.</acceptance>

nodes.title: Skew remedy's `pkill -f mgit-sandboxd` kills every repo's daemon, not the stale one
nodes.description:
Found while verifying MGIT-138 live (both skew directions on a scratch repo).

The daemon-stale branch of `controlproto.SkewMessage` now correctly renders only when the DAEMON is the old half, and the command it names is `pkill -f mgit-sandboxd`. That command is broader than the fault: `mgit-sandboxd` is PER REPO — `cmd/mgit/sandbox_connect.go:resolveSandboxPaths` keys the socket on a sha256 of the repo root, so a developer with three mgit repos open has three daemons, each supervising its own running microVMs. `pkill -f mgit-sandboxd` kills all of them, tearing down VMs and in-flight execs belonging to repos that were never mismatched.

The stale one is precisely identifiable: its socket path is the repo's own (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR|$TMPDIR/mgit-<uid>/<key>/d.sock`), and it is the process whose `--socket` argument is that path. So the remedy could name the repo-scoped action instead of the host-wide one.

Options, roughly in order of cost:
1. Render the socket path the peer is actually talking on into the message and tell the reader to kill the process holding it (`pkill -f 'mgit-sandboxd --socket <path>'`). The daemon knows its own socket; the client knows the one it dialed. Both already have the string.
2. A verb: `mgit sandbox daemon stop` (this repo's daemon only), which is also the thing an agent can be told to run without a process-name pattern.
3. Leave it, and say explicitly that the command stops EVERY mgit daemon on the host.

Note this is the same hazard the sub-agent working rules already encode ("other repos' daemons run on this host and must never be killed by name alone") — the message currently instructs the reader to do the thing the working rules forbid.

Refs: MGIT-138, MGIT-136, MGIT-132
nodes.acceptance: The skew message's daemon-stale remedy either names an action scoped to the mismatched repo's daemon (its socket path, or a repo-scoped stop verb), or states plainly that `pkill -f mgit-sandboxd` stops every mgit daemon on the host. Asserted in the controlproto skew tests, in the daemon-stale direction only.

nodes.title: Scope tripwire: check a branch's files-touched against its ticket's named scope before a PR opens
nodes.description:
Ordered by the founder (R-H286) after a real incident, with the bar set by that incident (R-H285 addendum): a branch cut for a ONE-FILE CI change carried 531 lines across six files, and nothing noticed until a filename appeared in merge output.

THE INCIDENT, in full, because the ticket's value is the mechanism not the moral. The branch `fix/ci-kernel-tarball-retry` was created with `git checkout -b` while standing on `fix/mgit-118-humble-default` rather than on main. It therefore inherited the entire MGIT-118 classifier rewrite. Its PR was reviewed and merged as a CI retry, and 9abf4ce landed on main claiming to be a 24-line change to one shell script while actually carrying:

    cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure.go        287 +++++----
    cmd/mgit/sandbox_entitlement.go           74 ++++
    cmd/mgit/sandbox_guest_failure_test.go   164 ++++
    docs/adr/014-...                          42 ++++
    scripts/e2e/sandbox_fleet_soak.sh         11 +-
    scripts/sandbox-image/build-libkrun.sh    25 +-     <- the only intended file

Only 25 of 531 added lines were the change the message described. Nothing unsafe shipped and CI was green on every gate, but `git blame` on the classifier answered "ci: retry the libkrunfw build" until 9abf4ce was reverted and re-landed as two honestly-described commits (#41).

WHY A TRIPWIRE RATHER THAN CARE. The error is not one of attention; it is that `git checkout -b` silently inherits whatever branch you happen to be standing on, and a diffstat is only read when something already looks wrong. Every other guard this project has added works the same way: the safe state is checked mechanically, not remembered.

WHERE IT MUST FIRE: at BRANCH TIME or at least before a PR opens — not in merge output, which is where this one surfaced by luck.

DESIGN LATITUDE IS DELIBERATE; the requirement is the catch, not the shape. Candidate shapes, to be weighed rather than assumed:
  - a check invoked before `gh pr create` (a script, a make target, or a wrapper) comparing `git diff --name-only <base>...HEAD` against the ticket's declared scope;
  - `mgit work` recording the intended scope when a task worktree is provisioned, so the comparison has something to compare against;
  - a warning at branch-creation time when the new branch's base is not main and not an explicitly named parent.

WHAT "SCOPE" MEANS is the hard part and must be answered, not skipped. A ticket does not carry a file list today. Options include: files named in the ticket's own text, a scope declared when the branch is created, or simply "files that differ from main's merge-base" with the branch's OWN base asserted to be main unless stated otherwise. That last one would have caught this incident on its own and needs no ticket metadata at all -- prefer the cheapest thing that catches the real case.

MUST NOT become noise. A tripwire that fires on legitimate multi-file work will be disabled within a week -- the same reasoning that set MGIT-131's 5 MiB threshold by bracketing real data rather than by feel. Legitimate wide changes exist (this repo has several) and must pass without ceremony or with a one-word override that is recorded.</description>
<prompt>Build a check that catches an out-of-scope branch before its PR opens.

1. DECIDE WHAT SCOPE MEANS and justify it. The cheapest candidate that catches the real incident is asserting the branch's merge-base is main (or an explicitly declared parent) and printing the diffstat when it is not — no ticket metadata required. Weigh that against richer definitions before choosing; prefer the cheapest thing that catches the case.

2. FIRE BEFORE THE PR EXISTS. Merge output is too late; that is where the incident surfaced by luck. Branch creation or a pre-PR check are both acceptable.

3. BLOCK WITH THE LIST PRINTED. The founder's requirement is that an out-of-scope diffstat blocks and names what is out of scope — a warning that scrolls past is not a tripwire.

4. AN OVERRIDE THAT IS RECORDED. Legitimate wide changes exist. Provide one, name it in the refusal, and make using it visible rather than silent — same contract as MGIT-131's --allow-large.

5. DO NOT MAKE IT NOISE. Verify against this repository's real branch history: run it over recent merged branches and report how many would have fired. If it fires on legitimate work, the rule is wrong. This is MGIT-131's threshold discipline applied to a different guard.

REQUIRED TESTS
- The exact incident is caught: a branch cut from another task branch, carrying that task's files, is refused with the out-of-scope files listed.
- A legitimate branch cut from main is not.
- The override works and is discoverable from the refusal.
- Run it against real recent branches and report the false-positive count.

Refs: MGIT-131, MGIT-118, MGIT-119, R-H286, R-H285</prompt>
<acceptance>A branch whose changes fall outside its declared or inferred scope is refused before its PR opens, with the out-of-scope files listed; the refusal names an override that is recorded when used; a branch cut from main doing ordinary work passes without ceremony; and the check is demonstrated against this repository's real recent branches with the false-positive count reported. The specific incident — a one-file CI branch carrying 531 lines across six files from another task — is caught.</acceptance>

nodes.title: Nothing installs the pre-push hooks, so the MGIT-142 tripwire is off in a fresh clone
nodes.description:
MGIT-142 put the branch-scope tripwire in `scripts/hooks/pre-push`, which only runs after someone types `make install-hooks` once per clone (git's `core.hooksPath` is per-clone local config and cannot be committed). Nothing reminds anyone, and the person most likely to skip it is a freshly-spawned agent in a freshly-cloned worktree — the exact population that produced the 9abf4ce incident.

The CI job "Branch scope" is the backstop for this, so nothing reaches main unnoticed. But the backstop fires AFTER the pull request exists, which is precisely the position the ticket rejected: the founder's bar was that the branch is caught before the PR opens.

Cheapest candidate fixes, in order of cost:
  - `make build` / `make test` print a one-line warning when `git config core.hooksPath` is not `scripts/hooks`;
  - a `make setup` that new contributors are pointed at, which runs install-hooks (CONTRIBUTING.md already tells them to run it in Setup);
  - nothing at all, if the CI backstop is judged sufficient — a defensible answer, but it should be a recorded decision rather than an unexamined gap.

Do not build a hook auto-installer that runs implicitly from a Go build: silently rewriting a developer's git config is worse than the problem.

ACCEPTANCE: either a fresh clone gets a visible, cheap reminder that the pre-push branch-scope hook is not installed, or the decision to rely on the CI backstop alone is recorded with its reasoning. No implicit rewriting of a developer's git config.
nodes.prompt: Read internal/branchguard's package doc and CONTRIBUTING.md's "Branch scope" section first — the guard, its wiring and its backstop are all already there; this ticket is only about whether the local half is actually switched on in a fresh clone. Prefer the cheapest visible reminder over any automation that touches git config without being asked. Refs: MGIT-142

nodes.title: Every third-party fetch in CI is retried, timed out, and restores its preconditions — an unguarded fetch is a declared exception
nodes.description:
Ordered by the founder (R-H288, refined in R-H285-addendum). The safe state becomes the default: a fetch without a guard is a DECLARED EXCEPTION carrying its reason, not something nobody got to yet. Same inversion as "a default is not a diagnosis" (MGIT-118) and "the registry, not the lock, enforces exclusivity" (MGIT-120) — the guarantee is structural rather than remembered.

FOUR INCIDENTS, all in one week, all reddening CI for reasons outside this repository:

  1. Homebrew bottle CDN — `Failed to download resource "virglrenderer"`, three consecutive failures. Diagnosed as a flake, then correctly re-diagnosed as a gitlab.freedesktop.org 504 outage. Fixed with retry + a downloads cache (MGIT-119).
  2. apt-get host tooling — HUNG, not failed. Six hours on one run, 145 minutes on another, on a step that normally takes ~1 minute. A re-run cleared it in 3m11s both times.
  3. libkrunfw kernel tarball — `curl: (18) transfer closed`, twice in a row, the second worse than the first. Fixed with retry.
  4. The retry from (3) then failed three times deterministically at the EXTRACT step, because a truncated tarball satisfied make's existence check and every attempt re-extracted the same corrupt file.

THREE CLAUSES, and each exists because one of the above proved it necessary:

CLAUSE 1 — RETRY ERRORS. A fetch that fails is retried with bounded attempts and widening backoff. Every retry is surfaced (a run that only succeeded on the third says so), and exhausting the attempts fails LOUDLY and says to read it as an outage rather than a flake. Proven by (1) and (3).

CLAUSE 2 — TIMEOUT HANGS. A hang is NOT a failure and retry alone catches neither apt incident: apt never returned an error to retry, it simply sat there while a six-hour job timeout was the only thing that eventually noticed. Every fetch needs a per-step timeout that converts a hang into a failure fast enough for clause 1 to act on. Proven by (2), twice.

CLAUSE 3 — RESTORE PRECONDITIONS. Every retry clears the failed artifact so each attempt is genuinely fresh. Proven by (4), which is the worked example this brief should cite: the retry's own refusal message was loud, well-worded, and honest about the wrong thing. It reported "treat this as a real outage, not a flake" in good faith while actually repeating a deterministic failure three times. DIAGNOSTIC HONESTY DEPENDS ON THE ATTEMPT BEING REAL, NOT JUST THE MESSAGE BEING PLAIN. A retry that does not restore its preconditions is not a retry; it is the same attempt repeated, and it costs three times as long to reach the same answer while teaching readers that retries do not help.

SCOPE: every third-party fetch reachable from CI. Known sites include the Homebrew install and bottle downloads, apt-get invocations, the libkrunfw/libkrun git clones and their kernel tarball, the firecracker VMM fetch, the guest kernel and rootfs builds, rustup, and Go module downloads. Enumerate them from the workflows and scripts rather than from this list — the list is a starting point, not an inventory.

WHAT "DECLARED EXCEPTION" MEANS: a fetch may be left unguarded, but the reason is written at the call site. An unguarded fetch with no stated reason is the defect this ticket closes.</description>
<prompt>Make every third-party fetch in CI guarded by default, with all three clauses, and an unguarded fetch a declared exception carrying its reason.

1. ENUMERATE FIRST, from .github/workflows/ and scripts/, not from the ticket's list. Report the inventory: every fetch, whether it is currently retried, whether it can hang unbounded, and whether a failed attempt leaves an artifact behind. The inventory is a deliverable in its own right — it is the thing that makes "declared exception" checkable.

2. BUILD ONE MECHANISM, not per-site copies. Four near-identical retry loops already exist or are about to; a shared helper (a script function, a composite action, or a make macro) keeps the three clauses in one place so a fix to one is a fix to all. Weigh the shapes and justify the choice.

3. THE THREE CLAUSES, each verifiable:
   - retry with bounded attempts and widening backoff; every retry surfaced; exhaustion fails loudly as an outage;
   - a per-step timeout so a HANG becomes a failure the retry can act on — pick the bound from measurement (what do these steps actually take?), not from feel;
   - clear the failed artifact before each attempt so it is genuinely fresh.

4. DO NOT MAKE IT NOISE OR CEREMONY. A guard that makes every workflow step twice as long to read will be worked around. Prefer one call per fetch.

TESTS / VERIFICATION
- Each clause demonstrated against a deliberately broken case: a fetch that errors, a fetch that hangs, and a fetch that leaves a corrupt artifact. The third is the one most likely to be skipped — it is the clause that was learned the hard way.
- The timeout bound is justified by a measurement of what these steps really take, in the manner of MGIT-131's threshold and MGIT-113's fleet size.
- Any fetch left unguarded has its reason written at the call site.

Refs: MGIT-119, MGIT-113, MGIT-131, R-H288, R-H285</prompt>
<acceptance>Every third-party fetch reachable from CI is either guarded by the shared mechanism — bounded retry, per-step timeout, precondition restore — or carries a written reason for being unguarded. The inventory is reported. Each of the three clauses is demonstrated against a deliberately broken case, including the corrupt-artifact one. The timeout bound is backed by a measurement rather than chosen by feel.</acceptance>

nodes.title: Guard the two pre-checkout apt steps and the in-container apt, the three fetches MGIT-143 could only declare
nodes.description:
MGIT-143 made every third-party fetch reachable from CI either guarded by scripts/ci/guard-fetch.sh or a declared exception carrying its reason. Four sites are declared for the SAME structural reason and are worth closing properly:

1. ci.yml `libkrun-linux` / "Install build prerequisites" (apt-get update + install)
2. e2e.yml `sandbox-live-linux-libkrun` / "Install build prerequisites" (same)
   -- both run BEFORE actions/checkout, so scripts/ci/guard-fetch.sh is not on disk yet. They currently carry clause 2 only, via `timeout-minutes: 5` (4x their 56s worst success across n=256). Clauses 1 (retry) and 3 (restore) are not served.
3. scripts/sandbox-image/build-rootfs.sh and build-kernel-vz.sh: the apt-get inside the pinned builder CONTAINER, where the guard script does not exist and cannot be bind-mounted without perturbing a build whose whole purpose is byte-reproducibility.

For (1) and (2) the obvious fix is to move `actions/checkout@v4` to the first step. By inspection it is safe -- a bare ubuntu:20.04 has no git, so checkout would fall back to the REST tarball path, and neither job needs a .git directory (every build already passes -buildvcs=false, and the one `git config --global --add safe.directory` call is `|| true`). But that is a change to how the repo is obtained, and MGIT-143 was not the place to validate it blind. Measure it on a branch, confirm the checkout still costs seconds and the jobs still pass, then guard the apt steps normally.

For (3) the candidate is a read-only bind mount of scripts/ci/ into the container, weighed against the reproducibility guarantee.

Refs: MGIT-143, MGIT-119
nodes.prompt: Close the four fetches MGIT-143 could only declare. Start by measuring, on a branch, whether moving actions/checkout ahead of the apt prerequisites step in ci.yml's libkrun-linux job and e2e.yml's sandbox-live-linux-libkrun job is safe and cheap: a bare ubuntu:20.04 has no git so checkout takes its REST tarball path. If it is, guard the apt steps with scripts/ci/guard-fetch.sh (-t 300 is the MGIT-143 rule on their 56s worst success) and let scripts/ci/fetch-inventory.sh report them GUARDED. If it is not, record the measurement that says so and keep the declaration. Then decide the in-container apt case on its own merits.
nodes.acceptance: The two pre-checkout apt steps go through scripts/ci/guard-fetch.sh with all three clauses, or the reordering is measured and rejected with the measurement recorded. scripts/ci/fetch-inventory.sh reports them GUARDED rather than DECLARED. The in-container apt is either guarded or its declaration is confirmed as permanent with the reproducibility trade-off written down.

nodes.title: The OCI guest-base pull has a timeout but no retry and no precondition restore
nodes.description:
internal/sandboxd/guestbase/pull.go bounds a whole pull at 15 minutes (pullTimeout), so MGIT-143's clause 2 is already served in Go. Clauses 1 and 3 are not:

- No retry. A registry 5xx or a reset connection fails the pull outright, and `mgit sandbox base from debian:12` is on the live libkrun e2e path in CI as well as in every agent's first-hour loop.
- No precondition restore. A blob written part-way into the local cache is the exact shape MGIT-143 clause 3 exists for: if any later code path treats "the blob file exists" as "the blob is complete", a retry becomes the same attempt repeated. This needs checking rather than assuming -- whether the cache writes to a temp path and renames, and whether the digest is verified before the file is adopted.

The e2e call sites (scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh, scripts/e2e/sandbox_cli_surface.sh) currently carry a declared exception pointing here. Wrapping the CLI from the shell would guard the wrong layer: a retry outside the client cannot clear a half-written blob inside it. The guard belongs in the Go client.

Refs: MGIT-143, MGIT-119
nodes.prompt: Bring internal/sandboxd/guestbase/pull.go up to MGIT-143's three clauses. It already has clause 2 (pullTimeout, 15 minutes). Add clause 1 in the Go client, and settle clause 3 by reading how a blob is written to the local cache: prove by test whether a failed download can leave a file a later run would accept as complete. Do not wrap the CLI from the shell -- that guards the wrong layer. Update the declared exceptions in scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh and scripts/e2e/sandbox_cli_surface.sh once it is done.
nodes.acceptance: The OCI pull retries with bounded attempts and widening backoff, surfaces every retry, and fails loudly as an outage on exhaustion. Whether a failed blob download can leave an artifact a later existence check would accept is established by reading the code and proven by a test -- if it can, the retry clears it first; if it cannot, the reason is a comment at the call site. The e2e declarations are updated to match.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: `mgit show HEAD` is refused: only hex hashes resolve, so the git-familiar spelling fails
nodes.description:
Found while live-verifying MGIT-106 against a freshly built binary.

`mgit show HEAD --json` exits 1 with `Error: show: commit not found: head` and dumps the flag table. `resolveCommitHash` (internal/store/git/commit.go) rejects anything that is not a 7..40-char hex string, so symbolic refs never reach it — the reference is lowercased and then fails `hexPrefixPattern`.

Every other mgit verb is deliberately git-shaped so an agent trained on git can use it without friction (checkout -b, merge --no-ff, commit -a). `HEAD` is the single most reflexive thing to type at a `show`, and the refusal reads like the commit is missing rather than like the spelling is unsupported.

WHAT TO DO
Decide whether `mgit show` should resolve symbolic refs at all. Two honest options:

1. Resolve them: teach the resolver `HEAD` (and plausibly a branch name, which `mgit show task/MGIT-106` also refuses today) by going through the same currentRef()/branch lookup the rest of the store uses. This is the git-shaped answer and is small.
2. Refuse them well: if only hashes are ever going to resolve, say so — `show: HEAD is not a commit hash; pass a hash from `mgit log --oneline`` — instead of `commit not found: head`, which sends the reader looking for a missing commit.

Whichever is chosen, `mgit rollback --commit` and `mgit export` share the same resolver, so the answer should be applied once at the resolver rather than per command.

Refs: MGIT-106
