nodes.title: The guest base unpacks in-tree, ~900 MB and MUTABLE: move it to a content-addressed machine-wide cache
nodes.description:
Reported by go-agent from R-H296's FIRST provisioning attempt (their FEAT-3.67), and it is the sharper of the two findings that walk arrived with.

WHAT THEY HIT. Provisioning unpacks a 906 MB guest base into `.mgit/sandbox/base/` INSIDE the repository. It is gitignored, so there is no commit risk, but any repo whose declared test command walks the tree sees it: `gofmt -l .` red-lit on 757 files that are mgit's artifact, not theirs. A containment tool that breaks the host repository's own test command fails quietly at the worst possible moment — the first thing a newly-sandboxed lane runs.

THE HALF THEY DID NOT SEE, AND IT IS WORSE. The in-tree base is MUTABLE. `mgit sandbox base from <image>` rewrites that directory in place, so an agent recomposing it in one worktree silently invalidates the pinned digest for every other worktree on the machine. This lane lost two live verification runs to exactly that during MGIT-122 and MGIT-133 work:

    resolve image "base@sha256:974b1b1e...": verification failed:
    .../.mgit/sandbox/base hashes to sha256:3bb5c3c2..., pinned sha256:974b1b1e...

Both times the base had been recomposed by a different agent between provisioning and use. Verification failed CLOSED, which is correct and is why nothing unsafe happened — but the drift should not be possible, not merely detected.

THE UNIFYING FRAME (founder, R-H297 thread). This and the libkrunfw kernel tarball are the same defect wearing two sizes: a LARGE ARTIFACT, FETCHED REPEATEDLY, STORED MUTABLY, WITH NO CONTENT-ADDRESSED IDENTITY. The kernel tarball's version of it truncated mid-download, satisfied make's existence check, and made three retries re-extract the same corrupt file. The guest base's version of it lets one worktree invalidate another's pin. The fix shape is the same for both, and MGIT-143's Homebrew downloads cache is the named pattern.

FIX SHAPE, ENDORSED: one base per DIGEST, machine-wide, out of tree, immutable by construction. This is the identical-bytes law (MGIT-105/106) applied to our own base image: a digest names exactly one byte sequence, so a recompose produces a NEW entry rather than overwriting an old one, and drift becomes impossible rather than detected. A repo then holds a reference, not a copy.

SECOND-ORDER BENEFITS, worth stating so they are not lost: N repos on one machine stop paying N x 906 MB; provisioning after the first is a link rather than an unpack; and MGIT-135's orphaned-runtime-directory accounting gets simpler because the base is no longer per-repo state.</description>
<prompt>Move the guest base out of the repository into a content-addressed machine-wide cache.

1. CONTENT-ADDRESSED, NOT MERELY SHARED. The cache key is the digest. One digest names one immutable entry; recomposing produces a new entry rather than rewriting one. A shared-but-mutable cache would make the drift WORSE, not better — it would give one repo the power to invalidate every repo on the machine. This is the whole point, so get it right before optimising anything.

2. THE REPO HOLDS A REFERENCE. `.mgit/sandbox/` keeps the pinned digest and no bytes. Decide and state what happens when the referenced digest is absent from the cache: re-fetch is the obvious answer, but say so rather than leaving it implicit, and make sure the failure when it cannot be re-fetched is legible.

3. WHERE THE CACHE LIVES needs an answer that works for the real population: several repos, several agents, one machine. Respect XDG/OS conventions, and consider what happens when two agents populate the same digest concurrently — the fleet soak exists because concurrent access is where this project's defects live.

4. MIGRATION. Existing checkouts have an in-tree base. Decide whether it is migrated, ignored, or garbage-collected, and make the transition legible rather than surprising.

5. DO NOT BREAK VERIFICATION. The digest check that caught the drift twice must keep working; it becomes cheaper (identity is the path) rather than unnecessary.

TESTS
- Two worktrees sharing a machine: recomposing in one does not invalidate the other's pin. This is the regression that motivated the ticket — assert it directly.
- A repo holds no base bytes after provisioning.
- Concurrent population of the same digest by two processes yields one valid entry, not a corrupt one.
- A test command that walks the host repo tree sees no mgit artifact (this is go-agent's actual symptom — assert their case, not an approximation).

Refs: MGIT-143, MGIT-135, MGIT-105, R-H296, R-H297</prompt>
<acceptance>The guest base lives outside the repository in a machine-wide store keyed by digest; a repo holds a reference and no base bytes; recomposing in one worktree cannot invalidate another's pinned digest; concurrent population by two processes yields one valid entry; a host test command walking the tree sees no mgit artifact; and digest verification still fails closed when an entry does not match its name.</acceptance>
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The guest-base cache has no GC: a superseded base is kept forever
nodes.description:
Fallout of MGIT-147, and the deliberate half of its trade.

MGIT-147 makes a recompose publish a NEW cache entry rather than overwriting the old one — that is the whole point, and it is why one lane can no longer invalidate another's pin. The consequence is that superseded bases accumulate: composing debian:12 then alpine:3.20 leaves ~175 MB + ~10 MB in ~/Library/Caches/mgit/bases, and nothing ever removes the first. A lane that iterates on its base image half a dozen times can leave a gigabyte behind.

This is NOT a defect in the cache — deleting an entry the moment it stops being the newest is exactly what would break the property MGIT-147 exists to guarantee, because another repo or a running sandbox may still be pinned to it. What is missing is a SAFE collector.

WHAT SAFE MEANS HERE. An entry is collectable only when nothing pins it. "Nothing" spans every repo on the machine, which the cache cannot enumerate — it knows digests, not who wants them. So the collector needs either a reachability pass (walk the known repos' images.lock files) or a conservative age/LRU policy with an explicit opt-in, and it must never collect an entry a live sandbox is booted from.

The staging half is already handled: PruneStaging collects abandoned compose trees older than 24h at the start of the next compose.

Refs: MGIT-147, MGIT-135
nodes.prompt:
Add a safe collector for superseded guest-base cache entries.

1. DECIDE THE REACHABILITY MODEL FIRST, and state it. The cache is machine-wide and keyed by digest; it does not know which repositories exist. Either the cache learns who references an entry (a reference record written at pin time, which then has to be kept honest when a repo is deleted), or collection is driven from the repo side (`mgit sandbox base gc` walking this repo's lock plus a conservative age policy). Both are defensible; picking one silently is not.

2. NEVER COLLECT A LIVE BASE. A sandbox booted from an entry is holding those bytes open through virtio-fs. Collection must consult the running sandboxes, not just the locks.

3. DEFAULT TO NOT DELETING. A wrong deletion costs a multi-gigabyte re-pull and, when the source tag has moved since, may be unrecoverable at the pinned digest — see MGIT-147's provenance finding. Report first, delete on request; `--dry-run` should be the shape of the default, not an extra.

4. SIZE IS THE USER-VISIBLE PART. Whatever the command is, it should be able to say what the cache holds, what is reachable, and what is not, in bytes — that is the question a user asks before they ask for a deletion.

TESTS
- An entry a repo's images.lock pins is never collected.
- An entry a running sandbox booted from is never collected, even when no lock names it.
- A superseded entry with no reference is reported, and only deleted when asked.
- Collection is idempotent and safe to run concurrently with a compose.

Refs: MGIT-147, MGIT-135
nodes.acceptance: The cache can report what it holds and what is reachable, in bytes; an unreferenced superseded entry can be collected on request; an entry pinned by any repo's images.lock or booted by a running sandbox is never collected; and collection defaults to reporting rather than deleting.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Standing check for environment-assumption tests: green where written, red where not
nodes.description:
Ordered by the founder (R-H298) after the FIFTH instance in one cycle. Five individual catches is a class; a sixth would be banking the same lesson again instead of installing it.

THE CLASS: a test that asserts a property of the ENVIRONMENT IT WAS WRITTEN IN rather than a property of the code. It passes on the author's machine and fails somewhere else — or, worse, passes everywhere while proving nothing.

THE FIVE, each with the assumption it encoded and where it broke:

1. `TestStatus_GenuineCaseCollision_StillCommits` required exactly ONE file in src/ after checkout. True on case-INSENSITIVE macOS, false on Linux where both entries materialise. Red on CI, green on every developer machine. The property under test — a collision still commits its content — held on both.

2. The fleet soak's cold-start probe ran `/bin/true`. Present in the macOS debian base, ABSENT from the firecracker rootfs that scripts/sandbox-image/build-rootfs.sh builds. Green on the platform the author could run, red on the one they could not.

3. Cobra-driven CLI tests depending on cwd being inside an mgit repo. `openAppFromCwd()` runs before the injected callback, so with no .mgit the callback never fires and the assertion reads a ZERO STRUCT — the dangerous variant: it passed for the wrong reason wherever the developer happened to be standing inside a repo, and would have failed for any fresh clone.

4. `TestSurvey_ThisRepositoryRealBranches_RefusesOnlyKnownIncidents` required a non-empty branch corpus. `actions/checkout` fetches a single ref, so CI surveys a checkout with NO branches. The invariant it pins is vacuously true over zero branches, so the non-empty requirement added no coverage and one way to be wrong.

5. `TestE2E_FullLifecycle_OverRealGitRepo_HistoryIntact` compared every file under .git byte-for-byte. Git's own background maintenance wrote `objects/maintenance.lock` between the before and after snapshots, so the test reported GIT's write as MGIT's — and failed the coexistence guarantee, the assertion in this repository that most needs to be believed when it fires.

WHY A STANDING CHECK AND NOT MORE CARE. Every one of these was written by someone who understood the property they were testing. The failure is that a test cannot see the difference between "this is true of the code" and "this is true of my machine" — nothing in the tooling distinguishes them, so the distinction survives only as long as someone remembers to make it. Every other guard this project added this cycle followed the same reasoning: the safe state is checked mechanically (MGIT-142's scope tripwire, MGIT-143's fetch guard, MGIT-131's size guard).

CANDIDATE SHAPES, to be weighed and NOT assumed — the requirement is that the class gets caught, not that any particular mechanism is built:
  - run the suite in a deliberately hostile environment in CI (fresh single-ref clone, cwd outside any repo, a rootfs missing common binaries) and treat a diff in outcomes as the signal;
  - a lint or review checklist for the shapes that recur: file COUNTS from a filesystem, presence of a binary in a guest, cwd assumptions, branch/ref existence, byte-equality over a directory a third party writes into;
  - make the expensive-but-decisive move cheap: this repo already runs Linux and macOS CI, so the cross-platform half is nearly free; what is missing is the hostile-CLONE half.

THE FALSE-POSITIVE ASYMMETRY MATTERS HERE, and instance 5 is why: a test that reports someone else's write as ours spends the credibility of the assertion that most needs believing. Catching these is not tidiness — an assertion nobody trusts is one that gets waved through the time it is right.</description>
<prompt>Install a mechanical check for tests that assert properties of their environment rather than of the code.

1. START FROM THE FIVE. They are in the description with file names. Work out what they share MECHANICALLY, not thematically — a shape a check can look for beats a principle a reviewer must remember.

2. PREFER THE CHEAPEST THING THAT CATCHES THE REAL CASES, per MGIT-140 and MGIT-142's precedent. Running the existing suite once in a hostile environment (single-ref clone, cwd outside a repo) may catch instances 3 and 4 with no new code at all. Measure what each candidate would have caught before building anything, and say which of the five it catches.

3. DO NOT BUILD FOR CASES THAT HAVE NOT OCCURRED. Five real instances are the corpus. A general-purpose environment-dependency analyser is not the ask.

4. NOISE IS THE FAILURE MODE, as with every guard this cycle. If it fires on legitimate tests it will be disabled. Bracket against the real suite and report the false-positive count as a number (MGIT-131, MGIT-142).

VERIFICATION: demonstrate the check against the five historical instances — each is recoverable from git history. Report which it catches and which it does not, honestly; a check that catches three of five and says so is worth more than one that claims all five.

Refs: MGIT-142, MGIT-143, MGIT-131, MGIT-140, MGIT-14, R-H298</prompt>
<acceptance>A mechanical check catches environment-assumption tests, demonstrated against the five historical instances with an honest account of which it catches and which it does not; its false-positive count against the real suite is reported as a number; and the cheapest option that covers the real cases is preferred over a general analyser.</acceptance>
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Containment is ENFORCED only for Claude Code; every other agent family can escape it silently — measured
nodes.description:
go-agent asked whether an agent following the cross-vendor AGENTS.md convention escapes containment or is refused (FEAT-3.71's sharpened half). ANSWERED BY EXPERIMENT, not by reading intent. It escapes, silently, and is not refused.

THE EXPERIMENT, on a worktree provisioned with `mgit work --sandbox` and a live guest:

    # a command run WITHOUT the shim dir on PATH -- what an agent that does not
    # read (or does not obey) the PATH instruction does
    $ env PATH="/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin" sh -c 'whoami; hostname -s; touch /tmp/PROOF'
    vimal
    M5-Macbook
    -> wrote to the HOST filesystem

    # the same command WITH the shim dir first
    $ env PATH="<wt>/.mgit/shims:/usr/bin:/bin" sh -c 'whoami'
    root            <- inside the guest

The shims WORK. Nothing makes an agent use them.

WHAT EACH FAMILY ACTUALLY GETS, verified on the worktree:

  Claude Code   .claude/settings.json installs a PreToolUse hook on Bash running
                `mgit sandbox claude-hook`. The HARNESS invokes it for every Bash
                tool call, so routing does not depend on the agent's cooperation.
                This is ENFORCEMENT.

  everyone else PATH shims at .mgit/shims (bash, cargo, cc, clang, gcc, ...) plus
                an instruction in AGENTS.md / .cursor rules / .envrc telling the
                agent to prepend that directory. This is ADVICE. An agent that
                types a bare command, or resets PATH, or never reads the file,
                runs on the host.

  .envrc        would prepend the shim dir automatically -- but only if direnv is
                installed AND the directory is `direnv allow`ed. Not installed on
                this host, so inert. Its own generated comment says so:
                "cooperative; the enforced guarantee is the require_sandbox land
                attestation gate."

WHY THIS IS NOW P1 RATHER THAN A DOCUMENTED POSITION. CLAUDE.md has always said
containment for a sub-agent is "a discipline the agent must apply, not something
enforced on it", and that was an honest statement of a known limit while Claude
Code was the only lane. R-H296 made sandbox execution MANDATORY FOR ALL AGENT
LANES. A mandate that a whole family of agents can silently not comply with is
not a mandate; and the failure is silent in the worst direction -- the agent
believes it is contained (AGENTS.md now tells it so, MGIT-50), the operator
believes it is contained, and untrusted code runs on the host.

Note the asymmetry with the land gate: `require_sandbox` attestation catches
uncontained work at LAND time, which protects the artifact. It does not protect
the HOST, which is what containment is for. A poisoned dependency has already
run by then.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED HERE. This is not a sandbox escape: the guest is not broken
out of. It is a ROUTING gap -- commands never enter the guest at all. And the
Claude path is genuinely enforced, so the mandate holds for that lane today.</description>
<prompt>Close the gap between "containment is enforced" and "containment is advised", for agent families that have no harness hook.

1. ESTABLISH WHAT IS ACTUALLY POSSIBLE before designing. A PATH shim cannot be enforcement: any process can reset PATH or call an absolute path. Enumerate the mechanisms that could enforce routing for a process mgit does not control, and be honest about which are available on macOS and Linux respectively. Candidates worth weighing: running the agent process itself inside the guest (the real fix, and the one CLAUDE.md already names as the missing piece); a wrapper shell the agent is launched under; per-family harness hooks where the family offers one (Codex, Cursor); refusing to provision at all when no enforcement path exists for the declared family.

2. IF ENFORCEMENT IS NOT AVAILABLE FOR A FAMILY, SAY SO LOUDLY AND SPECIFICALLY, at provisioning time, naming that family. The present failure is that everything looks identical whether routing is enforced or merely suggested. An operator told "this lane is advisory" can make a decision; one told nothing cannot. This is the same law as the daemon-stall diagnosis and the SKIP-is-not-a-pass convention: state what is NOT established rather than letting silence read as a guarantee.

3. DO NOT WEAKEN THE CLAUDE PATH while generalising. It is enforced today and must stay enforced.

4. Consider whether `mgit work` should refuse `--sandbox` without an enforcement mechanism, or provision with a prominent advisory. Argue the choice rather than assuming it; a refusal that blocks a working lane is its own defect.

TESTS
- The experiment in the description is the acceptance test: a command run with a PATH that omits the shim dir must not silently execute on the host under whatever design you choose.
- The Claude hook path still routes every Bash call.
- Whatever advisory or refusal you add is asserted by its own words, and names the family.

Refs: FEAT-3.71, MGIT-50, R-H296, FR-17</prompt>
<acceptance>An agent family without a harness hook either has its commands genuinely routed into the guest, or is told at provisioning time — specifically, naming the family — that routing is advisory for it and why. The experiment in the description no longer ends with an unannounced host execution. The Claude Code path remains enforced.</acceptance>

nodes.title: Merge does not materialize working tree / reuses HEAD's tree (pre-existing)
nodes.prompt:
PRE-EXISTING (not an MGIT-14 regression — faithfully migrated to plumbing in MGIT-14.4; surfaced by the MGIT-14 core review, finding #6). Standalone so it does NOT gate the coexistence epic MGIT-14.

internal/service/merge.go + internal/store/git/merge.go CreateMergeCommit: a fast-forward only advances the ref (disk left stale), and a no-ff merge commit REUSES HEAD's tree — so the source branch's content is not actually incorporated into the merge commit's tree, and the working tree is never updated. The new CreateMergeCommit godoc ("useful for --no-ff merges where the materialized working state already reflects the desired result") describes materialization that nothing performs. FIX: build a real merged tree and materialize it (call the plumbing checkout/materializeCommit), or document the limitation precisely; add a test that a no-ff merge commit's tree contains the source branch's changes. ACCEPTANCE: merge commit tree reflects the merge (not just HEAD's tree) OR the limitation is explicitly documented + tested; godoc matches behavior. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Tests resolved the DEVELOPER'S OWN repository from the working directory, and mutated it
nodes.description:
Found while building MGIT-147, by having it happen.

`go test` starts every test in its PACKAGE directory, which for cmd/mgit is inside the mgit checkout. Sandbox commands resolve a repo's host root by walking UPWARDS from the working directory (MGIT-57), and a linked worktree's marker resolves further, to the PARENT repo. So a test that touched the sandbox leg found the developer's real repository — read its images.lock, and, once MGIT-147 added the in-tree-base migration, MOVED ITS 175 MB GUEST BASE out of the tree. A test run mutated the machine's real repo state.

It failed benignly this time (the migration is digest-preserving, so the pin still resolved, and another lane's older binary simply recomposed in-tree afterwards). The class of hazard is not benign: any test reaching a repo-root-relative path can read or write the developer's own store, and in CI it would reach the checkout being tested.

Two prior symptoms of the same ambient dependency, both mistaken for unrelated flakiness at the time: a work-flow test panicked on a nil connector because repoGuestBaseRef unexpectedly SUCCEEDED (it had found the real repo's registered base where a test repo had none), and the same test passed or failed depending on which directory the suite was started from.

MGIT-147 closed it for cmd/mgit with a TestMain that chdirs to a scratch directory and points the guest-base cache at a scratch root before any test runs. That fix is package-local. The audit is not done.

Refs: MGIT-147, MGIT-57
nodes.prompt:
Audit the test suite for ambient dependence on the working directory, and close it.

1. FIND THE REACH. Every test package that can resolve a repo root, a host root, a cache, or a daemon socket from the working directory is a candidate: findRepoRoot / sandboxRepoRoot / sandboxHostRoot callers, anything reading $HOME or an OS cache dir, anything that spawns the CLI without chdir'ing first. Grep is the start, not the answer — the dangerous cases are indirect, reached through a command's RunE.

2. MAKE HERMETICITY THE DEFAULT, not a per-test discipline. cmd/mgit now does it in TestMain (chdir to a scratch dir + scratch MGIT_BASE_CACHE); apply the same shape wherever the reach exists. A test that WANTS a repository should chdir into one it made.

3. ASSERT THE GUARD, do not just install it. A test that fails when run from inside an mgit checkout and passes elsewhere is exactly what nobody notices. Add a test that would catch the regression: e.g. one that asserts no repo root is resolvable from the default test working directory.

4. WHILE THERE: check the same hazard in e2e, which legitimately uses real paths — the question is whether it can ever touch a path the developer owns rather than one it created.

TESTS
- Run the full suite from inside an mgit checkout AND from outside one; both must pass identically.
- A test asserting the default test working directory has no mgit repository above it.
- No test writes to the real user cache directory (assert against a scratch root).

Refs: MGIT-147, MGIT-57
nodes.acceptance: No test reads or writes state belonging to the developer's own repository, store, or caches; the suite produces identical results run from inside and outside an mgit checkout; and a test exists that fails if that guarantee regresses.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Guest execs run as root — give the sandbox an unprivileged user
nodes.description:
Reported by go-agent from its first in-guest run. Every command `mgit run` sends into the guest executes as uid 0. `whoami` returns `root`.

The blast radius is bounded by the microVM — that is the containment story and it still holds. But running as root inside it costs us three real things:

1. **Fidelity.** A build that only works as root passes in the guest and fails on the user's machine or in their CI. The sandbox should be at least as strict as the destination, not more permissive.
2. **Defence in depth.** A guest-kernel escape is one boundary away from the host; an unprivileged process facing it is strictly better than a root one. FR-17's threat model does not assume the guest kernel is perfect.
3. **Artifact ownership.** Files a root exec creates land in the worktree owned by uid 0. On copy-out and on any host-side read they carry ownership the host user did not choose.

Discovered by USING it, which is where nearly every serious defect in this codebase has come from.
nodes.acceptance:
- Guest execs run as a non-root user by default, with a home directory that exists and is writable.
- The user's uid/gid maps to something sane for files written into the worktree — a host-side read after copy-out does not show root-owned files.
- Privilege is still reachable when a task genuinely needs it (package installs during provisioning, for example), by an explicit and documented path — not by defaulting everything to root.
- Applies across the backends that support in-guest exec, or the ones that do not are explicitly named as not-yet.
- Tests cover: default exec is unprivileged; a file written by an exec is owned by the mapped user; the escalation path works where it is offered.
- README / INSTALL-SANDBOX state which user commands run as, since a build script that assumes root will now notice.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A guest exec starts in / with a PATH that omits the toolchain
nodes.description:
Two frictions reported by go-agent from daily in-guest use. Separately small; together they are the reason a first `mgit run` fails for a reason that has nothing to do with the user's code.

1. **The guest PATH omits `/usr/local/go/bin`.** The base image installs the Go toolchain there — the canonical location, the one the official tarball instructions use — and then `go` is not on PATH. Every command becomes `export PATH=... && go test ./...`, or it fails with `go: command not found` inside a sandbox that does in fact contain Go. The same will be true of any toolchain a base installs outside the default PATH.

2. **An exec starts in `/`, not the worktree.** The task's worktree is mounted and is the entire point of the guest, and the shell lands somewhere else. Every command needs a `cd` prefix the user has to know to write.

Both are the first thing a newly-sandboxed lane meets, which is the worst place to spend a user's patience. A tool that contains your build should hand you a shell where your build runs.
nodes.acceptance:
- A guest exec starts in the worktree's mount point by default, with an explicit override for a caller that wants otherwise.
- The guest PATH includes the toolchain locations a base actually installs into — `/usr/local/go/bin` at minimum — rather than only the distro defaults.
- The mechanism is general: a base that installs a toolchain elsewhere can declare it, instead of each path being special-cased in mgit.
- `mgit run -- go version` and `mgit run -- pwd` both do the obvious thing on a freshly provisioned task, with no prefix.
- Covered by a test that runs a bare toolchain command and a bare `pwd` through the exec path — asserting the working directory and the resolved binary, not just exit 0.
- Applies to the backends that support in-guest exec; any that cannot are named.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Run the agent process itself inside the guest — the only routing that cannot be declined
nodes.description:
The real fix behind MGIT-149, split out because MGIT-149 delivered what could be delivered without it.

MGIT-149 closed the silence and moved Claude Code, Codex and Cursor to harness-hook enforcement (ADR-015). Every one of those still routes a command from OUTSIDE the guest into it. That leaves two residues:

1. **An unknown harness has no hook.** mgit can only advise it, and says so. There will always be a next harness.
2. **A hook is only as good as the harness loading it.** mgit installs the file; it cannot make a build that predates hook support honor it. Today that is mitigated by telling the agent to run `hostname; whoami` and stop if it shows the host — a check, not a guarantee.

If the agent PROCESS runs in the guest, both disappear: there is no host to reach, so routing is not a decision anything makes. CLAUDE.md has named this as the missing piece since the sandbox shipped.

Known hard parts, so the estimate is honest:
- The agent needs egress to its model API, so this collides with the default `--network none`. An allowlist for the API endpoint is the obvious answer and needs to be right rather than broad.
- Credentials must reach the guest without landing in the worktree or an image layer.
- Interactive terminal transport into the guest already exists in part (T2, MGIT-11.11.6) and should be reused rather than re-invented.
- Firecracker delivers the worktree as a launch-time image and refuses sync/export, so the edit loop differs per backend (see the backend table in README).
nodes.acceptance:
- An agent harness runs with its process inside the task's microVM, with the worktree mounted and its edits visible to the host worktree.
- Model-API egress works under an allowlist narrow enough to name, not `--network open`.
- Credentials are supplied without being written into the worktree, a commit, or an image layer — asserted by a test that greps the worktree and the composed image for the secret.
- `hostname; whoami` inside the agent reports the guest, with no hook involved.
- The routing tier for a family launched this way reports as enforced-by-location rather than by hook, and the ADR-015 table gains the row.
- Backends that cannot support it (firecracker's launch-time image) are named and refused explicitly, not silently degraded.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Daemon idle-exit asks the backend, so a registered-but-unbooted task is abandoned — and gets no passive snapshots
nodes.description:
Found while live-verifying the MGIT-110 snapshot half. Measured, not inferred.

`Daemon.hasSandboxes` (internal/sandboxd/daemon.go) asks `d.cfg.Manager.List` — the BACKEND — whether any sandboxes exist. The backend knows only BOOTED VMs. Registration is a service-layer fact.

So with lazy provisioning (FR-17.9/17.10 — the documented default of `mgit work --sandbox`), a task that is registered but has never been used has no backend VM, the daemon reports itself idle, and it exits after IdleGrace while a live task is bound to it.

MEASURED: `mgit work wt --task-id LOST-WORK --sandbox`, no exec. Daemon pid observed alive; ~200s later it was gone, with the registration still durable in the index.

This is the SAME LAYERING SHAPE as MGIT-107, which was just fixed: the daemon reaching past the service to the backend manager and getting an answer that is true of the backend but false of the system. There the question was "did this sandbox get torn down cleanly"; here it is "is anything registered with me".

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY COSMETIC. Registration is durable (MGIT-102), so a later verb rehydrates and the user sees no error — which is exactly why this has gone unnoticed. But anything the daemon does CONTINUOUSLY stops when it exits, and passive worktree snapshots (MGIT-110) are the first such thing:

  - agent registers a sandbox, starts editing, does not exec for a while
  - daemon idle-exits
  - no snapshots are taken for that window
  - the agent is interrupted, and the work is unrecoverable — the precise MGIT-109 failure the snapshots exist to prevent

In practice an agent that is working DOES exec (R-H296 makes sandbox execution mandatory), which boots the VM and resets the idle clock, so the common lane is covered — verified live: with a booted guest the snapshots appear as designed. The uncovered window is real but narrower than it first looks, and `mgit snapshot list` already states plainly that no snapshots means none were TAKEN rather than nothing changed.

NOT necessarily "make the daemon immortal". Exiting when there is genuinely nothing to supervise is a designed frugality (NFR-17.6) and should stay. The bug is asking the WRONG LAYER what "nothing" means.
nodes.acceptance:
- The idle check consults the layer that owns the registry (the service), so a registered sandbox counts as something to supervise whether or not its VM has booted.
- The frugality NFR-17.6 intends is preserved: a daemon with no registrations still exits on its idle grace.
- A test covers the lazy case directly: register without booting, advance past IdleGrace, and assert the daemon is still serving — it must fail against today's code.
- Verified live that passive snapshots continue across a window with no exec.
- If the decision is instead to KEEP exiting, then the snapshot feature's coverage gap is documented where a user reads it, rather than left to be discovered by losing work.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: `mgit log --task-id` shows `pos=N` instead of commit subjects, so a task's trail is unreadable
nodes.description:
Found by dogfooding MGIT-111 — checkpointing two real commits and then reading the trail back.

`mgit log --task-id MGIT-111` renders:

    02e9e757 [MGIT-111] pos=0
    4de61056 [MGIT-111] pos=1

The commit messages are correct and complete — `mgit show 02e9e757` prints the full subject and body. The task-scoped log simply does not have them: it reads the SQLite `task_commits` index, whose columns are commit_hash, content_hash, agent_id, position, created_at. There is no message column, so the renderer falls back to the only distinguishing field it holds, the position.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS. `mgit log --task-id` is the REVIEWER'S view of what an agent did on a task — the view the product's pitch rests on ("a reviewer can see exactly what the agent did", "makes the reviewer's record thinner than it looks" is literally MGIT-110's concern). A trail of `pos=0 pos=1 pos=2` communicates nothing about the work; the reviewer has to run `mgit show` once per commit to learn anything, which is precisely the friction the task-scoped log exists to remove.

It also undercuts the cadence label that now ships beside it (MGIT-110). The label says "packaged post-hoc" or "spread across run" about commits the reader cannot identify.

The fix is cheap and needs no schema change: the log already has each commit_hash, and the message is in the git object store. Enrich each row with the subject line read from the commit object, exactly as `mgit show` does.

NOT a data-loss bug: nothing is missing from the store, only from this view.
nodes.acceptance:
- `mgit log --task-id <ID>` prints each commit's subject line, not its index position.
- The subject comes from the commit object (the authoritative copy), not from a new index column — no schema change, and no second copy of the message that could drift from the first.
- `--json` carries the message too, so an integration reading the trail gets the same facts as a human.
- A commit whose object cannot be read degrades to the hash and says so, rather than silently printing a blank subject.
- Covered by a test that commits with a known message and asserts the log line contains it — the current code would fail it.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Live-verify MGIT-109 pending-policy staging on firecracker/KVM (code-verified only)
nodes.description:
Carved out of MGIT-111's acceptance item 4, which could not be met in the session that closed the rest of that ticket: the Linux/KVM box was unreachable (dual-boot, DHCP — `No route to host` at the address in FR17-SANDBOX-HANDOFF.md).

WHAT IS AND IS NOT ESTABLISHED. MGIT-109 moved the staging decision into the service, ABOVE the backend controller, so a `policy set` against a `created` (never-booted) sandbox stages onto the pending launch instead of dialing a control socket that does not exist. That is backend-independent by construction and is covered by service unit tests with a fake controller. It has been live-verified on libkrun. It has NOT been live-verified on firecracker.

WHY IT IS NOT JUST CEREMONY. The staged policy has to survive a path the unit tests do not exercise: it is carried on the pending launch options and applied by the firecracker egress runner when the VM actually boots. Everything between "the service stored it" and "the guest cannot reach an off-list destination" is untested on that backend.

WHY IT WAS NOT WRITTEN BLIND. The existing firecracker live-policy fixture launches through the BACKEND manager directly, so it cannot exercise a service-level staging path as-is; the test needs a service + stager wired around a created sandbox. Authoring that against a machine one cannot run is how a KVM-only gate ships red or, worse, ships green by skipping — the MGIT-148 class. Better to write it with the box in front of you.
nodes.acceptance:
- On a real KVM host: register a firecracker sandbox with `--network allowlist` and do NOT boot it; confirm the state is `created`.
- `mgit sandbox policy set` against it reports PENDING (staged, not applied) — the same bar MGIT-109 met on libkrun.
- First use boots the VM, and the booted guest is observed ENFORCING the staged allowlist: an on-list destination is reachable and an off-list one is refused, asserted from inside the guest rather than from the host's view of its own rules.
- Read the policy back after boot and confirm it matches what was staged.
- Added to the `sandbox-live-linux` gate so it is checked every release, and asserted positively there (a SKIP fails the job, per the existing convention).
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A `.git` nested below the repo root is absorbed into mgit's tree, then makes every `mgit work` fail
nodes.description:
Reported from the founder's leg-5 walk as a /tmp-vs-home failure. REPRODUCED, and the reported cause is WRONG — the path is a coincidence.

    Error: work: create worktree: worktree add: materialize source:
    materialize branch task/X: flatten tree: walk tree: invalid path component: ".git"

THE REPORTED CAUSE (falsified). The hypothesis was that /tmp is a symlink to /private/tmp, so a textual .git exclusion stops recognizing the repo's own .git. Tested directly:

  - a content-bearing git repo at /tmp/leg5-gate, `mgit init` + `mgit work`: SUCCEEDS.
  - the same repo WITH a nested .git at /tmp/leg5-nested: FAILS with the exact error.
  - THE CONTROL: the same nested-.git repo at ~/leg5-control, no symlink anywhere in the path: FAILS IDENTICALLY.

So it is not /tmp, not symlinks, and not path resolution. The two copies must have differed in whether they contained a nested .git (a vendored checkout, a test fixture, a sub-project), not in where they lived.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE. `listWorkingFiles` (internal/store/git/worktree_fs.go) excludes by TOP-LEVEL component only:

    top := strings.SplitN(rel, "/", 2)[0]
    if excludedRoots[top] { ... skip ... }

`excludedRoots` is {".mgit", ".git"}. A .git at the ROOT is excluded correctly. A .git ANYWHERE BELOW — `testdata/inner/.git/HEAD`, `vendor/x/.git/config` — has a top component of `testdata`/`vendor`, so it is walked, hashed, and ABSORBED into mgit's base tree.

The failure surfaces much later, at `mgit work`, when go-git's tree walker rejects the path: it refuses `.git` as a first OR non-final component (worktree_fs.go in go-git v5.19.2). The guard is correct and fires exactly as designed. What is wrong is upstream — the content should never have entered the tree.

Note the same top-only pattern appears in `validateRelPath` and in worktree_seed_include.go; fixing one without the others leaves the hole open on those paths.

WHY P1. It is unrecoverable without knowing the internals: once absorbed, EVERY `mgit work` on that repo fails, and the message names no cause the user can act on. Any repo containing a vendored checkout or a git fixture under test data hits it. Both mgit's own repo and any project with a nested checkout are candidates.

THREE DOOR DEFECTS ON THE SAME FAILURE (founder, same report):
1. The error is a chain of internal verbs — work / create worktree / worktree add / materialize source / materialize branch / flatten tree / walk tree — ending in a go-git string. It names no cause and no recourse.
2. cobra prints the full Usage + flag dump for a RUNTIME failure that has nothing to do with usage, burying the error above it.
3. The `--allow` flag help reportedly contains a literal "(<nil>)". NOT REPRODUCED: scanned every command's --help on both v0.6.2 (the installed binary) and current main, plus the MCP tool descriptions and the generated AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md network section (which handles a nil allowlist correctly). Needs the exact command that printed it.
nodes.acceptance:
- A `.git` (and `.mgit`) directory at ANY depth is excluded from the working-tree walk, not just at the root, so it can never enter the tree. Same treatment applied consistently to validateRelPath and the seed-include walk.
- A repo containing `testdata/inner/.git/HEAD` provisions with `mgit work` cleanly — the reproduction in this description, as a test.
- An ALREADY-POISONED repo (a tree that already contains .git from before the fix) gets a message naming the cause and a way out, rather than a chain of internal verbs.
- A runtime failure does not print the cobra usage/flag dump; a genuine usage error still does.
- The "(<nil>)" in --allow help is either reproduced and fixed, or reported back as not-reproducible with the surfaces that were checked.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Version skew between a composed base's guest and the daemon fails as EOF mid-request, and nothing anywhere records when the base was composed
nodes.description:
From the founder's leg-4 gate, walked live 2026-08-21. wi-23's submit died with:

    sync classification failed: sandbox client: read response: EOF

Six diagnostic round-trips to the cause: the repo's base was composed on Aug 15 under 0.5.0 (the old in-tree scheme), so the guest-side binaries in that base predated the 0.6.2 daemon talking to them. Nothing surfaces that fact anywhere.

MECHANISM, confirmed in code. The daemon asked the guest to serve a verb its older guest binary does not implement; the guest closed the connection and the host reported EOF. Note `execwire.ReadRequest` uses a permissive json.Unmarshal, so ExecRequest field drift is NOT the mechanism — an old guest tolerates new fields. It is missing VERBS, which is why the failure lands mid-session on a specific operation (sync) rather than at exec.

THE STRUCTURAL GAP. MGIT-136 built a Hello handshake that guards CLI<->daemon, on the principle that "a peer that sends anything else first is, by construction, a build from before the handshake existed". The daemon<->guest channel has no such guard: grep for a version exchange in internal/execwire or internal/guest returns nothing. The handshake family is half-built, and the unguarded half is the one that spans a version boundary users cannot see — a base is composed once and then used for months.

FOUR ASKS (founder), first two are the point:

1. COMPLETE THE HANDSHAKE FAMILY. A stale composed base must refuse LOUDLY at session open, naming both versions and the recompose command — never EOF mid-request. Design note: the host speaks first on the exec channel, and an old guest cannot be taught a new handshake, so detection must not depend on its cooperation. The MGIT-136 reasoning transfers: a guest that cannot answer the probe IS, by construction, pre-handshake, and that is itself the diagnosis.

2. COMPOSE PROVENANCE RECORDED AND SHOWN. images.lock gains composed_by/composed_at; `sandbox status` prints base source, digest, composed-by and age (today it prints resources only).

   THIS IS NOT A PLAIN FIELD ADDITION. images.Entry is Ed25519-signed, and Source is deliberately inside SigningPayload with the rationale "provenance an attacker can rewrite without breaking verification would be decoration, not audit". Adding composed_by/composed_at to that payload invalidates EVERY existing registration; leaving them out makes them exactly the decoration that comment rejects.

   The way through is a VERSIONED payload: sign the extended field list when the provenance fields are present, the historical list when they are absent. The honest property that buys is worth stating plainly in the code — provenance can be ERASED (an entry stripped of it verifies under the old scheme) but cannot be FORGED (fabricating it requires a new-scheme signature). Erasure degrades to "unknown", which is precisely today's state, so the scheme is never worse than the status quo and is strictly better whenever provenance survives.

3. doctor/status flags a pre-cache in-tree base and names the recompose command.

4. The EOF chain names a suspect and a next step, for every skew the handshake does not catch.

SEQUENCING. 2 before 1: the handshake's refusal message is only useful if it can say WHEN the base was composed and by WHAT — which is exactly what 2 records. 4 rides 1. 3 is cheap once 2 exists.

GOOD NEWS FROM THE SAME SESSION, worth recording: the MGIT-147 base-cache migration ran live on the founder's repo — the old in-tree base moved to the cache digest-intact, a fresh compose was clean, and the copy explained itself.
nodes.acceptance:
- A daemon that cannot complete a version exchange with a base's guest refuses at SESSION OPEN, naming the daemon version, the guest version (or "predates the handshake"), and the exact recompose command. Never an EOF mid-request.
- images.lock records composed_by and composed_at, inside a versioned signing payload so existing registrations keep verifying and fabricated provenance does not. The erase-but-not-forge property is stated in the code, not just true by accident.
- `mgit sandbox status` prints the base's source, digest, composed-by and age.
- A base composed under the pre-cache in-tree scheme is flagged by status/doctor with the recompose command.
- Any remaining EOF from the guest channel names a suspect and a next step.
- Tested across a real version boundary, not simulated by a stubbed version string alone.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The guest ships no /etc/hosts, so localhost resolution goes to DNS and dies under deny-all egress — breaking every JS project
nodes.description:
Found on the founder's leg-4 walk and PROVEN BY FIX before it was reported: two lines in their setup took vitest from EAI_AGAIN to green.

REPRODUCED here in a live guest before changing anything:

    $ mgit run -- cat /etc/hosts
    cat: /etc/hosts: No such file or directory
    $ mgit run -- getent hosts localhost
    (nothing)
    $ mgit run -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
    nameserver 1.1.1.1

The file is ABSENT ENTIRELY, not merely incomplete. So every "localhost" lookup falls through to DNS — and under the DEFAULT deny-all egress that query cannot succeed.

WHY IT IS BROAD. Anything that binds or dials a local port resolves localhost first: vitest, vite, jest, dev servers, most test harnesses that spawn a server and connect to it. In practice that is every JS project, and a large share of everything else. The sandbox looks like it cannot run tests at all.

WHY IT IS WORSE THAN IT LOOKS. The error is EAI_AGAIN — a DNS failure. It points the reader at the network policy, which is working exactly as designed, so the investigation goes to egress rules, allowlists and the proxy, and never to a missing file. It is a wrong-signpost failure, not just a missing feature.

ROOT CAUSE. mgit composes its guest userspace from an OCI image. Container images routinely ship no /etc/hosts because the container RUNTIME supplies one at start — Docker and podman both write it. mgit is the runtime here and did not. Nothing was deleted; the file was never created.
nodes.acceptance:
- Guest init writes 127.0.0.1 localhost and ::1 localhost (with the ip6-localhost/ip6-loopback aliases tools look for) in every sandbox, on every backend, before anything can attempt a lookup.
- It runs regardless of network mode: loopback resolution is not a network feature, and deny-all is exactly the mode that needs it.
- An image that ships its own hosts file keeps it — mgit adds what is missing and rewrites nothing; unrelated entries always survive.
- Idempotent: a re-init does not grow a duplicate localhost line per boot.
- World-readable, since commands do not necessarily run as whoever wrote it.
- A failure to write it is reported and never fatal: a guest that can still run commands beats one that refuses to boot over its name table.
- Verified live under the default deny-all egress: getent hosts localhost resolves with no network.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: BuildTree drops mode on diff-applied entries (squash/revert mode fidelity)
nodes.prompt: Follow-up from MGIT-14.7 (review finding #3, the diff-apply path). The MGIT-14.7 fix made the COMMIT/checkout pipeline mode-aware (exec/symlink preserved, mgit tree hash == go-git's). But TreeStore.BuildTree — used by squash/revert/merge to apply FileDiffs onto HEAD's tree — still defaults newly diff-applied entries to filemode.Regular (it preserves EXISTING HEAD entries' modes, but a file added/modified via a FileDiff loses its exec/symlink mode). So squashing or reverting changes that include an executable script or a symlink would drop the mode, diverging mgit's tree from git's for those paths. Root: model.FileDiff carries no mode. FIX: add a file-mode field to model.FileDiff (or otherwise thread the mode through the diff-apply path) so BuildTree emits 100755/120000 where appropriate; assert squash/revert of a mode-varied change preserves modes (mgit tree hash == git). Touches internal/model + internal/store/git. Standalone (does NOT gate MGIT-14 — the coexistence + commit-path mode fidelity are complete). Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A control response over 1 MiB is never sent and never refused — the client gets a bare EOF, and only the daemon log knows why
nodes.description:
The real cause of "sync classification failed: sandbox client: read response: EOF" — 4 occurrences across 3 work items on the founder's leg-4 walk, on a FRESH 0.6.2 base. (The earlier stale-base theory is withdrawn; see MGIT-158.)

MECHANISM, confirmed in code, three hops:

1. internal/controlproto/controlproto.go WriteResponse refuses any response over MaxResponseBytes (1 MiB): it returns an error and writes NOTHING to the connection.

2. internal/sandboxd/dispatch.go writeResponse logs that failure daemon-side — Warn, event "write_error" — and returns.

3. The handler's deferred conn.Close() then runs. The client is blocked in ReadResponse and gets EOF.

So an over-sized response produces: nothing on the wire, a log line only the daemon can see, and a client error that names neither the cause nor a next step. A crash where a refusal belonged.

WHY THIS EXPLAINS THE OBSERVATIONS, INCLUDING THE FALSIFIED CONTROLS. The real variable is RESPONSE SIZE, which correlates with — but is not identical to — either reported condition, which is exactly why both single-cause theories died against controls:

  - worktree containing a host-side node_modules (2x): a sync classification report enumerating tens of thousands of paths is far over 1 MiB. At roughly 60-100 bytes of JSON per path, the cap is around 12-15k paths; node_modules routinely exceeds that several times over.
  - clean two-file worktree, environment "from cache" (2x): a restored cache tree is large by the same measure, for the same reason.
  - identical worktree, environment "by running setup", synced FINE once: fewer diverged paths at that moment, so the report fitted.
  - fresh 0.6.2 base: irrelevant to this failure, which is why the version theory failed.

The founder's note that "you'll need daemon-side logs" is precisely the defect: the daemon holds the only record of what happened.

TWO LAYERS OF FIX, both wanted:

A. THE BACKSTOP, for every verb. A response that cannot be sent must become a response that CAN be: replace it with a small, legible error naming the size, the cap and the verb, rather than closing the connection. This is the founder's rule — classification must refuse legibly, never EOF; a crash is not a refusal. It is verb-agnostic and protects every over-sized reply that exists today or is added later.

B. THE REAL FIX, for sync. A classification report should be BOUNDED BY CONSTRUCTION: carry at most N paths plus honest totals, so the answer fits whatever the tree looks like. A report that can only answer for small trees is not a classification. Note the reader must be able to tell a truncated list from a complete one — a silently shortened list of diverged paths would be a worse failure than the EOF, because it would be believed.

Layer A alone converts a mystery into a diagnosis. Layer B is what makes sync work on a real project.
nodes.acceptance:
- A control response that exceeds the size cap is answered with a small legible error naming the size, the cap and the verb — never a closed connection. Covered by a test that drives a deliberately over-sized response through the real dispatch path and asserts the client reads an error rather than EOF.
- `mgit sandbox sync` (and --dry-run classification) succeeds on a worktree containing a node_modules of realistic size, live.
- The sync report is bounded by construction and states its own totals; a truncated path list is explicitly marked as truncated, with the full count, so it can never be mistaken for a complete one.
- The daemon still logs the over-size event, but the client is no longer dependent on that log to learn what happened.
- Re-verified against the founder's two observed conditions: a host-side node_modules, and an environment restored from cache.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The libkrun open-mode gate depends on a third party returning bytes on 1.1.1.1:80, and reddened main on a changelog-only commit
nodes.description:
Observed while cutting v0.6.3. `TestE2E_Libkrun_RealVM_OpenMode_ReachesRawIP` failed on main, then passed on a plain re-run with no change.

PROOF IT WAS NOT A REGRESSION, and it is the clean kind: the failing commit 232707f changed ONLY CHANGELOG.md. e2e passed on 9a4526f, the last commit that touched code. A markdown file cannot break a live network test, so the variable was outside the repository.

THE FAILURE ITSELF says the same thing:

    netprobe [dial 1.1.1.1:80] -> PROBE-RESULT DIAL = CONNECTED-NO-DATA reason="EOF"
    open mode could not reach a raw IP (1.1.1.1:80) — the ENETUNREACH HyperSwe reported

The dial CONNECTED. The property this test exists to defend — that open mode can reach a raw IP at all, rather than failing ENETUNREACH — was SATISFIED. What was missing is that the peer returned no bytes: 1.1.1.1:80 accepted and closed. Cloudflare's plain-HTTP endpoint is entitled to do that, and it varies by PoP and over time.

So the gate fails when a third party is unhelpful, and it fails LOUDLY on a release cut, which is the worst possible moment for a test to be wrong for a reason that is not ours.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY BEING TESTED. Two different claims are currently bundled into one assertion:
  1. a raw-IP dial is REACHABLE in open mode (the regression this guards — the ENETUNREACH HyperSwe reported);
  2. the destination sends application bytes back.

Only 1 is mgit's. 2 is a property of 1.1.1.1. A CONNECTED-NO-DATA result already proves 1 completely — the packet left the guest, crossed the NAT, and got a TCP handshake back from a real host on the internet.

This is the MGIT-148 class: an environment assumption embedded in a gate, green where it was written and red elsewhere or later.
nodes.acceptance:
- The open-mode raw-IP gate asserts REACHABILITY, not that a third party returns bytes: a completed TCP handshake to a raw IP passes, since that is the whole of the property being defended.
- If a byte-level check is still wanted, it targets a destination the gate controls rather than a public resolver's HTTP port.
- The distinction is stated in the test, so a future reader does not re-tighten it into the same flake.
- Re-verified by running the gate repeatedly against the live network.
- Consider the same review for any other live gate that depends on a specific public host behaving a specific way — same class, same failure mode at the same unlucky moment.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: mgit doctor: the instrument R-H300 rule 5 converts incidents into, with its first three checks
nodes.description:
R-H300 rule 5 makes the incident->doctor-check conversion mandatory at incident close, like a regression test. There is no doctor verb to convert into: `mgit doctor` does not exist.

So this builds the instrument and lands the first conversions with it, from incidents closed in v0.6.3.

WHAT A CHECK MUST DO, and these are the properties that make it worth having rather than decoration:

  - Name a REMEDY on failure, not just a verdict. A check that says "localhost does not resolve" and stops has moved the mystery, not removed it.
  - Distinguish FAILED from NOT CHECKED. A check that cannot run — no sandbox registered, no daemon, an unsupported backend — must say so and say why. Silence reading as a pass is the exact class of defect the whole standard exists for; a diagnostic that lies is worse than no diagnostic.
  - Be cheap enough to run habitually, or it will not be run.
  - Be machine-readable as well as human-readable, so a harness can gate on it.

FIRST THREE CONVERSIONS (159 and 157 endorsed; 161 is the gate fix rather than a check):

1. From MGIT-159 — does the guest resolve localhost WITHOUT DNS? The incident: the guest shipped no /etc/hosts, so every localhost lookup went to DNS and died under deny-all egress, taking vitest/vite/jest and every JS project with it. The check is one command in a live guest. Remedy: recompose the base.

2. From MGIT-157 — does this repository's recorded tree contain a nested .git? The incident: a .git below the root was absorbed into the base and then broke every subsequent `mgit work`, detectable only when it failed. This is detectable AT REST, before anything fails. Remedy: the recorded recovery (move .mgit aside, re-init) — already verified against a real poisoned repo.

3. From MGIT-161 — not a doctor check but the same rule-5 shape: a gate asserted a third party's behaviour (bytes from 1.1.1.1:80) rather than mgit's own property (raw-IP reachability). Fixed in the gate itself, which is where that class belongs.

NOT IN SCOPE HERE: the MGIT-160 check. "Can this daemon answer its largest plausible response" is a PROPERTY, not a state, and the right shape for it is on the sitting's R-H300 agenda.
nodes.acceptance:
- `mgit doctor` exists, runs every applicable check, and exits non-zero when any check FAILS (never merely because one could not run).
- Every check reports one of: ok / failed / not-checked-and-why. A check that cannot run never reads as a pass.
- Every failure names a remedy the reader can act on.
- `--json` emits the same verdicts for a harness.
- The localhost check runs against a live guest and states plainly when there is no sandbox to check.
- The nested-.git check runs at rest, needs no sandbox, and names the verified recovery.
- The MGIT-161 gate asserts reachability rather than a third party's bytes, with the distinction stated in the test so it is not re-tightened later.
- Each check names the incident it came from, so the reason it exists survives the people who remember it.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: CI re-downloads a 145 MB pinned kernel tarball on every libkrun run, and a runner network hiccup blocks unrelated PRs
nodes.description:
Blocked PR #65 (an unrelated doctor-verb change) three times in a row:

    curl: (18) transfer closed with 147244176 bytes remaining to read
    make: *** [Makefile:103: tarballs/linux-6.12.91.tar.xz] Error 2
    guard-fetch[libkrunfw-build]: failed (exit 2) on attempt 2/2

The libkrunfw build fetches linux-6.12.91.tar.xz (~145 MB) from cdn.kernel.org on EVERY run of the libkrun jobs, and compiles a guest kernel from it.

NOT KERNEL.ORG. Tested directly from a developer machine at the same time: HTTP/2 200, correct content-type, and a ranged fetch of the first 2 MB succeeded immediately. The CDN is healthy; the runner's network is where the transfer dies. The identical remaining-byte count across three separate runs (147244176 every time) says the transfer dies almost immediately rather than randomly mid-stream.

THE GUARD WORKED AS BUILT and is not the problem: bounded retry, a fresh artifact per attempt (MGIT-143's clause 3 — the partial file is removed between tries, so a retry is a real attempt rather than a re-extraction of the same corrupt bytes), and a legible failure naming attempt counts. It did everything it could; the fetch simply cannot succeed right now.

THE ACTUAL FRAGILITY. A 145 MB third-party download on the critical path of every libkrun CI run is a single point of failure for the whole repository — an unrelated PR cannot merge because a CDN transfer to a rented runner is unhappy. It also costs 4-5 minutes of every run even when it succeeds.

AND THE FIX IS THE ONE THIS REPO ALREADY KNOWS. The tarball is PINNED — a specific version, verified before use. Identity is therefore content, and content-addressed things are cacheable by construction: that is exactly the MGIT-147 base-cache argument, applied to CI. Cache it keyed by the pinned version (and its digest), and a CDN outage costs nothing after the first successful fetch, on top of saving the download every run.

Worth noting this is the SECOND external-dependency CI failure in two days, after MGIT-161 (a gate asserting a third party's bytes). Different mechanisms, same lesson: the parts of CI that depend on someone else behaving deserve the same scrutiny as the parts that test us.
nodes.acceptance:
- The pinned kernel tarball (and any comparably large pinned artifact on the libkrun path) is cached across CI runs, keyed by the pinned version and verified by digest before use — a cache hit must never weaken the verification that already exists.
- A cold cache still works: the fetch remains, with its existing guard, as the fallback.
- Measured: the libkrun jobs no longer spend 4-5 minutes downloading on a warm cache.
- A corrupted or truncated cache entry is detected by the same digest check and refetched rather than compiled.
- Review whether any other CI step pulls a large third-party artifact on every run; same treatment where it does.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Worktree sync reports success while the guest tree lacks the files — silent-destruction class, NOT REPRODUCED here
nodes.description:
From the founder's leg-4 run. `mgit sandbox sync` reported success while the guest tree did not receive file-creation operations: a `git apply` in a fresh worktree created CapacityCalculator.test.tsx and modified the sibling .tsx, and the guest could read neither. hyperswe's own stale-copy check refused the verdict, which is how it was caught rather than believed.

Founder's door text, verbatim: "The substrate reported the sync while silently dropping the operation."

WHY P1 REGARDLESS OF REPRO. This is the silent-destruction class. A sync that fails loudly costs a retry; a sync that reports success while dropping work sends an agent on to build against a tree that does not contain its own changes, and every later result is derived from a lie. It was caught by a judged-tree discipline ONE LAYER UP, not by mgit — mgit had no idea.

NOT REPRODUCED on macOS/libkrun with current main. Four shapes tested live, all behaved correctly; recording them so the next attempt does not re-walk them:

1. Booted guest, host CREATES a new file and MODIFIES an existing one, single `sandbox sync`. Reported "2 updated" and the guest read both, contents correct.
2. Lazy path: worktree registered, guest NOT booted, `git apply` a patch that CREATES a file, then sync. Sync correctly refused with "the sandbox has not booted yet; it stages the current worktree when it boots" — and the subsequent boot delivered the file.
3. `git apply` of a real create-file patch (new file mode 100644, /dev/null source) rather than a plain write. Delivered.
4. A SECOND sync round on the same sandbox after a completed first round — the shape "round sync" suggests. Delivered.

CODE READ, and both suspects cleared:
- `staging.Build` copies every worktree entry and excludes ONLY `.git`/`.mgit` store directories. There is no .gitignore filtering, so a newly created file cannot be dropped by an ignore rule.
- `Syncer.Sync` computes a plan from three manifests (host candidate, last delivered, guest), and `plan.Empty()` is the only path that reports done without doing anything. For that to fire wrongly, the freshly staged `host` manifest must already agree with `guest` — i.e. the candidate tree must be built from something other than the worktree the user changed, or the guest tree read must not be the tree the guest actually mounts.

THE TWO HYPOTHESES THAT SURVIVE, both consistent with "reported the sync while silently dropping it":
(a) sync stages from, or applies to, a DIFFERENT path than the one the guest mounts — a mismatch would make every sync truthful about what it did and useless to the guest. A resolved-vs-unresolved path difference is one way to get there.
(b) version skew across the sandbox's lifetime: a sandbox launched by one mgit and synced by another, where the staged-tree location or manifest convention differs. Note the reporter's sandbox may predate their current binary.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, in the order that most cheaply discriminates:
1. `mgit --version` AND the version that LAUNCHED that sandbox (was it registered before the current binary was installed?).
2. The backend: libkrun, vzf, or firecracker. Note firecracker REFUSES sync outright, so a firecracker sandbox reporting sync success would itself be a finding.
3. The exact sync invocation and its full output, including whether it said "N updated" or "already up to date" — those are different bugs. "already up to date" means the plan was empty; "N updated" means Apply ran and the guest still cannot see the result.
4. Whether the worktree path contains a symlinked component (/tmp, /var, a home-directory symlink).
5. `mgit sandbox status <task>` for the affected task, and the daemon log around the sync.

MGIT-160's refusal working in the field is recorded on its own merits: the first live failure after it shipped produced a one-screen diagnosis instead of an EOF.
nodes.acceptance:
- The reported failure is reproduced from a written recipe, or the reason it cannot be is established (e.g. it needed a state that current code cannot enter).
- Whatever the mechanism: a sync that does not deliver its plan must not report success. The report must describe what the GUEST can now read, not what the host intended.
- A verification step exists that compares the guest tree against the delivered manifest after apply, so the substrate catches this itself rather than depending on a consumer's stale-copy check one layer up.
- Converted into a doctor check per R-H300 rule 5: something that asks "does the guest's tree match what was last delivered to it".
- Covered by a test that fails against whatever code path is found.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: sync flattens a worktree symlink, and the MGIT-164 read-back then refuses the whole sync
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign (red-first probe), reproduced at the unit layer on macOS/arm64.

A worktree containing an ordinary internal symlink cannot be synced into a running guest at all. Every `mgit sandbox sync` on such a worktree fails.

MECHANISM, three hops that each look correct alone:

1. `staging.Build` PRESERVES an internal symlink (`copyStagingEntry` -> `os.Symlink(target, dst)`). Correct: only ESCAPING links are refused.
2. `worktreesync.BuildManifest`/`entryFor` records that path by its TARGET TEXT — `sha256("symlink:"+target)`, `Mode` carrying `os.ModeSymlink`. Correct, and covered by TestBuildManifest_Symlink_IsHashedByTargetNotContent.
3. `worktreesync.Apply` -> `copyInto` FOLLOWS the link: `os.Stat(src)` and `os.Open(src)` both resolve it, so a REGULAR FILE holding the target's bytes is written into the guest.

So the guest tree's read-back manifest records a regular file whose hash is the content hash, while the intended manifest holds the link hash. `VerifyDelivery` (MGIT-164, PR #69) correctly calls that "stale content" and refuses.

Note what changed: before PR #69 this silently delivered the WRONG THING (a copy where a link belongs, so an edit through the link no longer aliases). After PR #69 it is a hard failure. #69 did its job — it made the class loud — and this is one of the instances it exposed.

REPRO (unit layer, no VM needed):

    wt, store, state, guest := t.TempDir(), t.TempDir(), t.TempDir(), t.TempDir()
    os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(wt, "real.txt"), []byte("hello"), 0o644)
    os.Symlink("real.txt", filepath.Join(wt, "link.txt"))
    os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(store, "cfg"), []byte("x"), 0o644)
    _, err := worktreesync.Sync(worktreesync.Request{
        WorktreePath: wt, PrivateStorePath: store, StateDir: state, GuestTree: guest})

Observed:

    worktree sync: the guest's tree does not contain what was just synced into
    it: link.txt (stale content). Nothing is reported as delivered, because it
    was not. ... if it fails the same way the guest's tree is not the one being
    written to

The message misdirects: the guest's tree IS the one being written to. Nothing about a symlink appears anywhere.

SEVERITY: high. Symlinks are ordinary repo content — monorepo package links, `docs/x.md -> ../x.md`, a `.bin` shim checked in. Any such repo can be launched (staging succeeds) but never synced, and the refusal names neither the cause nor a recourse.

The fix belongs to the lane that owns worktreesync; the campaign only reproduces and reports. Both directions are defensible and it is a design call: recreate the symlink in the guest (`copyInto` handling `ModeSymlink` via Readlink/Symlink, matching what staging already does), or decide sync flattens links and make BuildManifest agree. They must agree — the bug is that they do not.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `worktreesync.Sync` over a worktree holding an internal relative symlink succeeds.
2. The guest tree's entry for that path agrees with what `BuildManifest` recorded for it — whichever representation is chosen, the producer and the verifier agree.
3. A regression test at the syncer layer, not only at BuildManifest: the existing per-function tests each pass while the composition is broken, which is how this survived.
4. An ESCAPING symlink is still refused (negative control).
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: SEC-03 symlink check falsely rejects an in-tree dangling link when the worktree root sits under a symlinked prefix
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign (red-first probe), reproduced and root-caused at the unit layer on macOS/arm64. This is a FALSE POSITIVE on a containment guard — it refuses safe content with a security-sounding error, and it hits the exact path CLAUDE.md tells every agent to use.

`staging.AssertSymlinkWithin`'s own doc comment promises:

    A link to a not-yet-existing in-root path is allowed; one pointing outside
    root (absolute or via ..) is rejected.

The code falsifies the first half whenever the worktree root resolves through a symlink — which on macOS is `/tmp` and `/var/folders` (the default TMPDIR).

ROOT CAUSE — an asymmetry in the two EvalSymlinks calls:

    resolved = filepath.Clean(resolved)                       // /var/folders/.../wt/not-yet.txt
    if eval, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(resolved); err == nil {
        resolved = eval                                       // FAILS: the target does not exist -> stays /var/...
    }
    cleanRoot := filepath.Clean(root)
    if eval, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(cleanRoot); err == nil {
        cleanRoot = eval                                      // SUCCEEDS -> /private/var/...
    }

The root is canonicalised and the target is not, so `filepath.Rel` compares `/private/var/...` against `/var/...` and returns a `../../..`-prefixed path. The guard reads that as an escape.

The root-side EvalSymlinks was added deliberately (its comment names the macOS /var -> /private/var case) to make the check compare like with like. It does — but only when the TARGET also resolves, i.e. only when it exists.

MEASURED, three runs, same code:

| root | link | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `t.TempDir()` (under /var/folders, a symlink) | `l -> not-yet.txt` | REJECTED as an escape |
| a real path with no symlinked prefix | `l -> not-yet.txt` | accepted (correct) |
| `t.TempDir()` | `bad -> /etc/passwd` | rejected (correct — negative control holds) |

So the containment guarantee itself is intact: no real escape is let through. What is broken is that a safe tree is refused, and the refusal says "escapes the worktree".

BLAST RADIUS. `staging.Build` fails closed on the first offending link, so the whole launch or sync is refused. CLAUDE.md's own instruction is

    mgit work /tmp/mgit-<N>-wt --task-id MGIT-<N> ...

which puts every dogfooded agent worktree under a symlinked prefix on macOS. A repo with a link to a generated-but-not-yet-built path (`dist -> build/out`, a `node_modules/.bin` shim, a link to a gitignored artifact) cannot be worked there at all — while the identical repo under `~/` works.

This is the hypothesis PR #59 correctly FALSIFIED for MGIT-157 — /tmp -> /private/tmp breaking a path comparison. It was not the cause of that bug. It is the cause of this one, one layer over.

REPRO:

    root := t.TempDir()                                  // macOS: under /var/folders
    os.Symlink("not-yet.txt", filepath.Join(root, "l"))
    err := staging.AssertSymlinkWithin(root, filepath.Join(root, "l"))
    // err != nil: "worktree symlink target escapes the worktree: symlink .../l -> not-yet.txt"

SEVERITY: high — a false refusal on the documented agent path, with a message that sends the reader hunting a containment breach that does not exist.

Directional fix (the owning lane's call, not the campaign's): canonicalise the target's nearest EXISTING ancestor rather than the target itself, so a not-yet-existing leaf is judged in the same namespace as the root.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `AssertSymlinkWithin` accepts a link to a not-yet-existing in-root path whether or not the root resolves through a symlink — the case its doc comment already promises.
2. Negative controls unchanged and asserted in the same table: an absolute out-of-root target, a `..` target, and a multi-hop chain that steps outside are all still rejected.
3. A test whose root deliberately sits under a symlinked prefix, since a test using only real paths cannot see this.
4. `staging.Build` over a worktree holding such a link succeeds and delivers the link.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: sync --force dies on a host-deleted path the guest modified; Plan.Forced() does not do what its own comment says
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign (red-first probe), reproduced at the unit layer.

`worktreesync.Plan.Forced()` carries this comment on its only loop:

    // A conflict is an update unless the host no longer has the path, in
    // which case honoring the host means deleting it.
    out.Update = append(out.Update, c.Path)

The comment describes two cases; the code implements one. EVERY conflict becomes an Update, including the conflicts `appendDeletes` produced for paths the host no longer has.

CONSEQUENCE. Host deletes a file, guest had modified it -> `appendDeletes` records `ReasonModifiedInGuest`. That is precisely the situation `--force` exists for: "yes, destroy the guest's copy, honour the host". Under `--force` the path is promoted to an Update, `Apply` -> `copyInto` stats it in the candidate tree where it no longer exists, and the whole sync dies:

    worktree sync: deliver doomed.txt: stat /.../worktree-sync-candidate/doomed.txt:
    no such file or directory

Two failures in one. `--force` cannot complete the one operation it is asked for; and the error is a raw `stat` on an internal candidate-tree path the user has never heard of and cannot act on — the MGIT-104 class.

Note the all-or-nothing contract makes this worse than a partial: the forced sync applies nothing, so a user who deletes a file and forces gets neither the deletion nor a usable diagnosis, and re-running fails identically.

REPRO (unit layer):

    f := newFixture(t, map[string]string{"doomed.txt": "V1", "keep.txt": "K"})
    os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(f.guestTree, "doomed.txt"), []byte("GUEST"), 0o600) // guest modifies
    os.Remove(filepath.Join(f.worktree, "doomed.txt"))                             // host deletes
    _, err := f.sync(true)                                                          // --force
    // err: worktree sync: deliver doomed.txt: stat .../worktree-sync-candidate/doomed.txt: no such file

Post-MGIT-164 note: `VerifyDelivery` would have skipped this path anyway (`intended` has no entry, so the `!planned` branch continues), so the read-back does not catch it either — `Apply` fails first. The verification is not at fault; the plan is malformed before it gets there.

SEVERITY: medium-high. It needs `--force` plus a host deletion of a guest-modified path, so it is not the common lane — but it is a data-losing verb failing in the one mode where the user has already accepted the loss, and the diagnosis is unusable.

The fix belongs to the lane that owns worktreesync. Directionally: route a conflict whose path is absent from the host manifest into `Delete` rather than `Update`, which is what the comment already says. `Forced()` currently has no access to the host manifest, so the split most likely belongs in `Compute`, where the classification is already made.
nodes.acceptance:
1. A forced sync over a host-deleted, guest-modified path succeeds and removes the path from the guest tree.
2. The path appears in `Result.Deleted` and in `Overridden` (destroying un-landed guest work stays audited).
3. Forced updates over guest-modified paths that the host STILL has are unchanged (regression control).
4. A table-driven test at the `Compute`/`Forced` layer plus one end-to-end through `Sync`, since the unit and the composition disagreed here.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: deleting a symlink empties its target: silent data destruction that reports success, through the door MGIT-164 left open
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign (red-first probe), reproduced end-to-end through `worktreesync.Sync` at the unit layer. This is the silent-destruction class MGIT-164 exists to close, arriving through the one door that verification deliberately leaves open.

`worktreesync.removeForGuest` truncates before it unlinks — correctly, and for a well-argued reason (MGIT-90: a guest's cached dentry keeps resolving a deleted name for ~5s on libkrun's virtio-fs, so the file is emptied first to make a stale read fail loudly instead of returning deleted code).

`os.Truncate` FOLLOWS SYMLINKS. So when the planned delete is a symlink, the truncate lands on the LINK'S TARGET — a path the plan never named — and then the unlink removes only the link. The target survives as a zero-byte file.
