WHY NOTHING CATCHES IT. `VerifyDelivery` checks only planned paths, on purpose: "A guest is entitled to its own files, and policing outside the plan would refuse syncs over work the guest legitimately created." The damaged path is outside the plan by construction, so the read-back is silent and the sync reports success.

MEASURED, end-to-end:

    f := newFixture(t, map[string]string{"real.txt": "IMPORTANT-CONTENT"})
    os.Symlink("real.txt", filepath.Join(f.worktree, "link.txt"))
    // stage as a launch does, record the baseline
    os.Remove(filepath.Join(f.worktree, "link.txt"))   // host deletes ONLY the link
    res, err := f.sync(false)

    res = {Updated:[] Deleted:[link.txt] ...}   err = <nil>
    guest real.txt = ""                          <-- was "IMPORTANT-CONTENT"

A clean success report, a correct-looking `Deleted: [link.txt]`, and a destroyed file nobody mentioned.

At the unit layer the same thing, isolated:

    os.WriteFile(target, []byte("KEEP-THIS"), 0o600)
    os.Symlink(target, link)
    removeForGuest(link)
    // target now reads ""

BLAST RADIUS. The target need not be a repo file — `link -> ../../some/host/path` cannot occur (staging rejects escapes), but any in-tree target can: a monorepo package link, `docs/x.md -> ../x.md`, a link into a build output directory the guest is actively using. Removing the link destroys the real file's contents while reporting that a link was removed.

Interaction with MGIT-165: a symlink UPDATE currently fails the sync outright, so the delete direction is the reachable one — the link got into the guest tree at launch (staging preserves it) and the host later removed it. The two bugs are independent and both live in the same seam: `Apply`'s two halves each follow links that `BuildManifest` deliberately does not.

SEVERITY: high. Silent destruction of un-named data, reported as success. That is strictly the failure mode MGIT-164's own PR text calls worse than a crash, "because a crash is not believed".

Directional fix (the owning lane's call): make the truncate lstat first and skip it for a non-regular file — a symlink has no stale CONTENT for a guest to read, only a stale name, so the MGIT-90 argument does not apply to it and nothing is lost by skipping. `os.Remove` alone is correct for a link.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `removeForGuest` on a symlink removes the link and leaves its target's contents intact.
2. The MGIT-90 property is unchanged for regular files: a reader holding the path across the delete reads empty, not the old bytes (the existing TestApply_Delete_LeavesNoOldContentBehind must still pass).
3. An end-to-end test through `Sync`: host deletes only a link, the guest's target file survives with its contents.
4. Consider whether `VerifyDelivery` should assert that no path OUTSIDE the plan changed identity during an apply — the general form of this class. That is a larger design call and may belong on its own ticket.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: doctor guest/localhost runs a resolver, not a name-table read — it can pass via DNS, and a missing getent reads as the failure
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign while writing tests for the doctor wiring. Two defects in one function, both of the same shape: the verdict does not mean what the check claims it means. This is the false-passing-verifier class.

`cmd/mgit/doctor.go:probeGuestLocalhost` carries this doc comment:

    It asks the guest to read its OWN NAME TABLE rather than to run a
    resolver: the property under test is "localhost resolves WITHOUT a DNS
    query", and a resolver that succeeded via DNS would pass a check whose
    whole point is that DNS is unavailable.

PR #65 makes the same claim in prose. The code runs:

    getent hosts localhost

`getent hosts` is a resolver. It goes through NSS, and mgit's own guest carries an `nsswitch.conf` of `hosts: files dns` (see cmd/mgit-guest/writable_linux.go, which copies it in deliberately, and its test which pins that exact line). So the lookup falls through to DNS on a miss — the precise fallback MGIT-159 was about.

DEFECT 1 — A FALSE PASS. On a sandbox whose egress permits DNS (`--network open`, or an allowlist that reaches a resolver), a guest with NO /etc/hosts can still get an answer for `localhost` from the network. The check reports

    ok    guest/localhost   the guest resolves localhost from its own name
                            table, with no DNS query

while neither half of that sentence is established. A reader consulting the instrument to avoid being misled is misled by it — which is the exact wording of the argument doctor's own `not-checked` verdict is built on.

It is invisible in the common case (deny-all egress, where DNS cannot answer) and appears in the mode an agent is most likely to be in when it hits the original bug: egress granted so `npm install` works, then a dev server that binds localhost.

DEFECT 2 — A CAN'T-RUN REPORTED AS THE FAILURE. `probeGuestLocalhost` maps EVERY non-zero exit to `("", nil)`:

    if code != 0 {
        // getent exits non-zero when it resolves nothing, which IS the
        // condition — an empty answer, reported as such
        return "", nil
    }

`GuestLocalhostCheck.Run` then sees empty output with no error and reports StatusFailed with the MGIT-159 summary and the "recompose your base" remedy.

Exit 2 really is "key not found" and the mapping is right for it. Exit 127 is `getent: command not found` — a base that ships no getent (busybox, distroless, a minimal alpine layer) produces a confident FAIL claiming the guest cannot resolve localhost, with a remedy that will not help, when /etc/hosts may be perfectly correct. Exit 1 is a usage error and maps the same way.

That is a check that could not run reporting a failure — the mirror of the silent-skip the framework was explicitly built to outlaw. `StatusNotChecked` exists for exactly this and is not reachable from here.

BOTH DEFECTS ARE IN THE PROBE, NOT THE CHECK. `GuestLocalhostCheck` is correct and well tested; it faithfully reports what the probe hands it. The probe is the part with no test at all — `probeGuestLocalhost` and `doctorChecks` are both at 0% coverage from the whole test tree, which is how a comment and its code came to describe different programs.

SEVERITY: medium. No containment or data consequence; the cost is that a diagnostic built to end one class of misdirection can produce two more. A green `guest/localhost` currently does not license the conclusion its own summary states.

Directional fix (the owning lane's call): read the name table directly — `cat /etc/hosts`, matching what `internal/guestnet/hosts.go` writes — so no resolver is involved and the check means what it says. Then distinguish exit codes: 1/127 (and any exec failure) are `not-checked` with the reason; only a successful read showing no loopback entry is the MGIT-159 failure.
nodes.acceptance:
1. The probe establishes loopback resolution WITHOUT a resolver — a guest with DNS reachable and no /etc/hosts entry must NOT report ok.
2. A guest whose probe command is absent or fails reports `not-checked` with the reason, never `failed`.
3. A guest with a correct name table still reports ok (regression control).
4. Tests for `probeGuestLocalhost` itself, which today has no coverage: no bound task, unreachable daemon, exec error, non-zero exit, and a successful read.
5. The doc comment and PR #65's claim either become true or are corrected — they must not keep describing a program the code is not.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: mgit worktree add does not materialize the branch source into the linked worktree
nodes.prompt:
DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-22, using mgit on a clone of mgit-dev). `mgit worktree add --task <id> <path>` creates the task/<id> branch + the worktree dir + injects the agent adapters (.envrc, AGENTS.md, .claude/settings.json, .cursor/rules/mgit-sandbox.mdc — from MGIT-11.11), but DOES NOT check out the branch's source tree into <path>. Result: the linked worktree is an empty dev dir (only 4 adapter files), not a usable working copy of the source — unlike `git worktree add`, which materializes the files. This defeats the worktree's purpose (an isolated dev environment with the source) and blocks the 'agents develop in mgit worktrees' dogfood vision.

ROOT: WorktreeService.Add / the CLI worktree-add path registers + branches + injects adapters but never invokes the checkout/materialize path. The materialization primitive exists (MGIT-14.4 materializeCommit), but it writes via worktree_fs rooted at repo.Root() — a LINKED worktree at a different path needs the branch tree materialized at <path> (a separate FS root). FIX: on `mgit worktree add`, after creating the branch, materialize that branch's tree into the worktree path (extend materializeCommit / checkout to target an arbitrary worktree dir, not just repo.Root()); never touch the project .git (MGIT-14 invariant). Add a test asserting `mgit worktree add` produces a worktree whose files match the branch tree. Refs: FR-16, MGIT-8; found dogfooding post-MGIT-14. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: the snapshot pass runs inside the daemon's select loop: it stalls every request and delays shutdown by one or more full passes
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign. Reproduced at the unit layer with a watcher that, like the real one, cannot be canceled part-way.

`Daemon.Run`'s select calls `d.observeWorktrees(ctx)` INLINE:

    case <-snapTicker.C:
        d.observeWorktrees(ctx)

Everything else the daemon does is deliberately kept off that path. Connections get a per-connection goroutine with the comment "a slow or hung client must never block idle checks or shutdown". The snapshot pass is the one piece of work that does block them, and it is the piece whose duration scales with the user's repository rather than with mgit.

The pass is uninterruptible by construction. `snapshotWatcher.observeTask` -> `SnapshotService.Observe` -> `SnapshotStore.Fingerprint` -> `WorkingTreeFingerprint`, a filesystem walk that hashes every file. It takes no context, so `ctx.Done()` cannot shorten it, and its cost is O(worktree) per supervised task — a JS project with a host-side node_modules is exactly the shape that made MGIT-160 enumerate 20,000 paths.

MEASURED (SnapshotInterval 20ms, an Observe that sleeps and ignores ctx):

| | |
|---|---|
| dial | 167us — succeeds immediately, via the listener backlog |
| FIRST BYTE of the greeting | 1.40s — the whole in-flight pass |
| shutdown after SIGTERM-equivalent | 7.90s against a 2s pass |

DEFECT 1 — EVERY CLIENT COMMAND STALLS BEHIND A PASS. The dial succeeds (the kernel accepts into the backlog) but nothing handles the connection until the select loop is free, so the client sits waiting for a greeting. Any `mgit run`, `mgit sandbox exec`, `mgit commit` in a bound worktree pays the remainder of whatever pass is in flight.

DEFECT 2 — SHUTDOWN IS DELAYED BY ONE OR MORE FULL PASSES, AND THAT REINTRODUCES MGIT-107. This is the serious half. Drain is what writes the terminal `destroyed` event and reaps the VMs; a daemon that is SIGKILLed before reaching it leaves running VMs unsupervised and the next daemon stamps `killed / unsupervised`. That is precisely the record MGIT-107 was closed to stop manufacturing.

Note 7.9s against a 2s pass: MORE than one pass. When a pass outlasts the tick interval, `snapTicker.C` is ALWAYS ready by the time the select is re-entered, and Go chooses uniformly at random among ready cases — so each iteration is a coin flip between shutting down and starting another pass. The delay has no bound, only a geometric tail.

At the shipped 90s interval a pass has to exceed 90 seconds to enter that state. One pass walks every supervised worktree in series, so a handful of large repos reaches it. Below that threshold the cost is still one whole pass added to every shutdown.

DEFECT 3 — THE IDLE CLOCK IS NOT READ WHILE A PASS RUNS, so the idle-exit grace is effectively extended by the pass duration. Harmless on its own; worth noting because NFR-17.6's frugality is measured against that grace.

WHAT IS NOT WRONG. `observeWorktrees` already recovers panics and logs failures without killing the daemon (MGIT-110/MGIT-107), and that is correct and tested. The problem is not error handling, it is that the work is on the wrong goroutine.

SEVERITY: medium-high. No data loss and no containment consequence, but it makes a supervisor periodically unresponsive and it can cost a clean shutdown the very audit record MGIT-107 established — under a supervisor's SIGTERM->SIGKILL window (systemd's default is 90s), a long pass plus a drain can exceed it.

Directional fix (the owning lane's call): run the pass on its own goroutine with a single-flight guard, so a slow pass is skipped rather than queued and the select loop stays free. Shutdown then either waits on it under the existing bounded drain budget or abandons it — a snapshot is housekeeping and a drain is not, so abandoning is defensible and should be stated either way.
nodes.acceptance:
1. With a pass in flight, a client's greeting arrives promptly — the request path must not wait on housekeeping.
2. With a pass in flight, shutdown completes within the drain budget rather than after the pass, and the terminal `destroyed` event is still written.
3. A pass that outlasts the tick interval must not queue: passes are skipped, not accumulated, and no shutdown can be delayed by more than one.
4. The tests use a watcher that IGNORES its context, since the production walk cannot be canceled — a cancellable stub passes against the broken code (measured: 507us, which is what a first version of this repro reported before it was corrected).
5. The existing watcher tests (panic recovery, failure logging, cadence) keep passing unchanged.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: MGIT-104's refusal fix was applied to the policy verbs only: grants, grant, export and land still answer with a hex opcode
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign while covering the client verbs. Not a new defect — an OLD one that was fixed on one verb and left on its four siblings.

PR #58 (MGIT-111) named this exact failure and fixed it:

    ### 2. The refusal described plumbing, not containment

    $ mgit sandbox policy show --task VZF-2
    mgit sandbox: sandbox: controlproto kind 0x51 not served by this daemon

    An operator learns their command wasn't served, and nothing about the
    fact that matters before running untrusted code... The refusal now names
    the backend, states the enforcement fact, points at what to use instead,
    and says plainly that nothing was changed.

That reasoning is right and the new policy message is good. It was applied to `policy set` and `policy show` and to nothing else.

MEASURED against a daemon with no optional collaborators wired, one client call per verb:

    grants      -> sandbox: controlproto kind 0x47 not served by this daemon
    grant       -> sandbox: controlproto kind 0x41 not served by this daemon
    export      -> sandbox: controlproto kind 0x46 not served by this daemon
    land        -> sandbox: controlproto kind 0x44 not served by this daemon

    policy_set  -> sandbox: no live egress allowlist is enforced on this build's
                   sandbox backend, so there is no policy to show or change: this
                   daemon has no egress enforcer wired... Launch with --network
                   none for no egress, or use a backend that enforces one (libkrun
                   on macOS, firecracker on Linux). This is a refusal, not a
                   failure to reach the daemon: nothing was changed
    policy_show -> (the same)

Four verbs still hand the operator a hex opcode. `0x44` is not a fact anyone outside this repository can act on, and none of the four says the thing that matters — that this BUILD or BACKEND cannot serve the verb, as opposed to this CALL having failed. Those need different responses: the first means stop trying, the second means retry or fix the daemon.

`land` is the one to care about. It is the audit-critical verb, and "your commits could not be brought back from the guest, 0x44" is the worst place in the product to leave a plumbing string. `export` is next: it is one of only two ways anything leaves a sandbox, and a firecracker daemon legitimately cannot serve it.

Each refusal has the same three facts available to it that the policy one uses: which verb was asked for, why this daemon cannot serve it (no lander / no exporter / no grant coordinator wired, which on the export path is a real backend property — firecracker delivers the worktree as a launch-time image and has no host directory to read), and what to do instead.

SEVERITY: low-medium. No data or containment consequence; the cost is a diagnosis the reader cannot act on, in verbs where the alternatives are meaningfully different. It is cheap to fix and the pattern to copy already exists in servePolicySet/servePolicyShow.

Filed rather than fixed: this is the campaign's lane, and the message wording belongs with whoever owns those verbs.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `grants`, `grant`, `export` and `land`, when unwired, refuse with a message that names the verb in the user's words and says why this daemon cannot serve it — no hex opcode reaches the operator.
2. Each says plainly that nothing was changed or transferred, the way the policy refusal does.
3. `export` names the real backend reason where it applies (firecracker delivers the worktree as a launch-time image, so there is no host directory to export from).
4. A test asserting the PROPERTY across every optional verb — a refusal must be actionable — rather than one per verb, so a sixth optional verb inherits the requirement. The skipped cases in internal/sandboxd/client_verbs_test.go are written and ready for it.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: mgit log silently ignores a malformed --since/--until and returns the UNFILTERED trail
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign. `cmd/mgit/log.go:filterCommits` was at 10.5% coverage; this is what was in the uncovered part.

    if since != "" {
        if t, err := time.Parse(time.RFC3339, since); err == nil {
            sinceT = t
        }
    }

A parse failure is DISCARDED. `sinceT` stays zero, the `!sinceT.IsZero()` guard below skips the comparison, and the filter the user asked for is silently not applied. Same code, same defect, for `--until`.

MEASURED (two commits, 2026-08-01 and 2026-08-31):

    --since "2026-08-15T00:00:00Z"   -> [new]        correct
    --since "2026-08-15"             -> [old new]    SILENTLY UNFILTERED
    --since "yesterday"              -> [old new]    SILENTLY UNFILTERED
    --since "last week"              -> [old new]    SILENTLY UNFILTERED
    --since ""                       -> [old new]    correct: no filter asked for

`2026-08-15` is not a typo. It is the obvious thing to type, it is what `git log --since` accepts, and the flag's help says only "Show commits after date (RFC3339)" — which a reader who has already typed a date will not go back and read.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A USABILITY BUG. `mgit log` is the reviewer's view of the audit trail. The output of a rejected filter is INDISTINGUISHABLE from the output of a filter that matched everything: same commits, same order, no warning, exit 0. A reviewer narrowing a trail to "what happened after the incident" is handed the whole history and has no way to know the narrowing did not happen.

That is the silent-wrong-answer class this codebase keeps paying for — MGIT-160's own argument applies verbatim: a wrong answer is worse than a crash, because a crash is not believed.

The `--author` filter is fine: an exact string comparison, with empty meaning "no filter", so it cannot half-apply.

SEVERITY: medium. No data loss and no containment consequence, but it can make an audit read produce a false picture with nothing signalling it, and the trigger is the most likely thing a user types.

Directional fix (the owning lane's call): return the parse error from filterCommits and fail the command, naming the flag, the value, and one acceptable form. Refusing is right rather than guessing at other layouts — a log the user believes is filtered is the failure, so an error is strictly better than a second guess that might also be wrong. Widening the accepted formats is a separate and defensible choice, but only on top of the refusal.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `mgit log --since <unparseable>` fails, naming the flag, the value it could not parse, and an acceptable form. Same for `--until`.
2. A valid RFC3339 value still filters exactly as it does today (regression control).
3. An empty value still means "no filter", and is never confused with an invalid one.
4. Table-driven over both flags, including the shapes measured above — a plain date and a relative word are the realistic inputs, not exotic ones.
5. `--author` behaviour unchanged.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: WorktreeSyncReport.Bound is not idempotent: a second pass overwrites the honest totals with the capped list lengths
nodes.description:
Found by the test-quality campaign. LATENT today — there is exactly one call site — but it is a trap laid for the next caller, in the one function whose entire purpose is preventing wrong counts.

`Bound` recomputes the totals from whatever lists it is handed:

    out.UpdatedTotal = len(r.Updated)

On a report that has ALREADY been bounded, `r.Updated` is the capped list, so the honest total is overwritten by the cap.

MEASURED (40,000 updated / 700 deleted / 600 conflicts, limit 500):

    once : UpdatedTotal=40000 DeletedTotal=700 ConflictsTotal=600 Truncated=true
    twice: UpdatedTotal=500   DeletedTotal=500 ConflictsTotal=500 Truncated=true

Three distinct wrongs in one line:

1. `UpdatedTotal` 40,000 -> 500. An 80x under-report, of exactly the number MGIT-160 added the field to carry. A reader acting on "500 paths differ" when 40,000 do has been misled by the mechanism built to stop that — the failure the ticket's own text calls worse than the crash it replaced.

2. `DeletedTotal` 700 -> 500 and `ConflictsTotal` 600 -> 500. These lists were NEVER truncated; they are under the cap. The second pass invents a cap for them and reports a count that was never true of anything.

3. The result is SELF-CONTRADICTORY. `Truncated=true` with `UpdatedTotal == len(Updated) == 500` says "500 found, and the listing was shortened" — which cannot both hold. Nothing downstream would flag it; `reportTotal(500, 500)` returns 500 and the CLI prints a confident wrong number.

REACHABILITY. One call site today, `internal/sandboxd/dispatch.go:256`, and it bounds once. So this is not currently producing a wrong number for anyone.

It is filed anyway because the design explicitly invites more callers. The doc comment's stated reason for living on the model is:

    Bounding happens at the MODEL, not at one call site, so every producer
    and transport of a report inherits the same guarantee — and a new caller
    cannot forget it.

A new caller cannot forget to bound. A new caller CAN bound something already bounded — a retry, a re-wrap at another transport, an MCP surface bounding what the control plane already bounded — and the guarantee inverts silently. "Safe to call from anywhere" is the property the comment claims, and it does not hold.

SEVERITY: low as shipped, medium as a design defect. No user is affected today. The cost is that the next caller added in good faith, following the doc comment, silently under-reports.

Directional fix (the owning lane's call): populate a total only when it is not already set, or record the totals as authoritative once and never recompute — e.g. skip the recompute when `Truncated` is already true, or make the zero value distinguishable from a genuine zero. The test asserting it is in internal/model/sync_boundary_test.go, written whole and skipped.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `r.Bound(n).Bound(n)` equals `r.Bound(n)` — asserted on the whole struct, not field by field.
2. A list that was never truncated keeps its true count across a second pass (the 700 -> 500 case, which is a different wrong from the under-report).
3. No report can carry `Truncated=true` alongside a total equal to its own list length; that combination is not a state any real sync produces.
4. The single existing call site keeps behaving identically (regression control).
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: There is no staleness door — what fired in 0.5.0→0.6.1 was a one-time cache miss, and nothing records what composed a base
nodes.description:
FEAT-3.83, sharpened: the staleness door stayed silent for a SECOND consecutive release (a 0.6.3-composed base under a 0.6.4 substrate — no warning, `sandbox status` reads clean), while 0.5.0→0.6.1 did warn.

DIAGNOSIS: THE DOOR DOES NOT EXIST. Nothing in mgit compares the substrate that COMPOSED a base against the substrate RUNNING it — because nothing records the former.

What fired in 0.5.0→0.6.1 was `ErrBaseNotCached` (internal/sandboxd/images/basecache.go): the base-cache MISS. Under the old in-tree scheme the bytes lived inside the repository; 0.6.1+ looks in the machine-wide content-addressed cache (MGIT-147), did not find them, and failed loudly with a recompose command. Everyone read that as a staleness warning. It was a STORAGE-LAYOUT miss, and now that the scheme is stable it can never fire for that reason again.

So the founder's inference is exactly right, and this is the mechanism behind it: whatever fired, it was not composing-substrate-versus-running-substrate.

VERIFIED BY INSPECTION of every base in this machine's cache: none records a composing version. There is no marker file, and no version is recoverable from the injected guest binary. `etc/mgit/` appears only in bases composed after MGIT-152 (2026-08-22) and holds only the declared PATH.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THIS RELEASE, and the founder's point is the sharp one: the guest binaries (mgit, mgit-guest) are INJECTED AT COMPOSE TIME and frozen there. So a base composed under an older substrate runs that older substrate's guest code. 0.6.3 shipped the guest's /etc/hosts; a 0.6.2-composed base silently lacks it under a 0.6.4 host. A stale base silently lacks precisely the guest-side fixes a release exists to deliver, and the release notes say they shipped.

PROCESS FAILURE, BY OUR OWN STANDARD. A human has now hand-refreshed a stale base twice. R-H300 rule 5 says an incident is not closed until the thing that went wrong becomes something the tool asks itself. Doctor is the mechanical home.

DESIGN — AND IT SUPERSEDES MGIT-158's ASK 2. I previously designed compose provenance as new images.lock fields inside a VERSIONED signing payload, to avoid invalidating existing registrations. That is no longer the best available design: MGIT-152 established that a base can carry its own declaration INSIDE THE COMPOSED TREE, where the content digest already covers it — no lock-format change, no signing-payload change, nothing re-registered, and tampering is exactly as detectable as tampering with a binary. Record the composing substrate the same way.

WHAT "STALE" MEANS, deliberately: any difference in composing version, because the guest binaries differ whenever the substrate does. It WARNS rather than refuses — refusing would break every working setup on the day of every release, which is its own defect. A base composed before this ships carries no marker and must be reported as UNKNOWN, not as current: that is the doctor not-checked distinction, and reporting silence as currency is the very failure being fixed.
nodes.acceptance:
- Compose records the substrate that built the base, inside the composed tree so the existing content digest covers it. No images.lock change and no existing registration invalidated.
- A base whose composing substrate differs from the running one is reported at the moments that matter (sandbox status, and launch/first use), naming BOTH versions and the recompose command — a warning, never a refusal.
- A base with no marker (composed before this ships) reports UNKNOWN and suggests recomposing; it must never read as current.
- `mgit doctor` gains a base-currency check that names MGIT-165 as its incident, per R-H300 rule 5, so the hand-refresh stops being a human's job.
- The guest-side consequence is stated where the user reads it: a stale base runs older guest binaries and silently lacks the guest-side fixes of every release since it was composed.
- Verified live: compose under this substrate reads current; a base composed earlier reads stale or unknown.
- MGIT-158's ask 2 is closed as superseded, with the reason recorded.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Give MGIT-160 its doctor check: can this daemon answer its largest plausible response?
nodes.description:
Carved out of MGIT-160 and previously parked verbally on the sitting's R-H300 agenda, where it was tracked by nobody. Filing it so the conversion is not lost.

R-H300 rule 5 makes the incident->doctor-check conversion mandatory at incident close. MGIT-160 closed without one, and the reason it was deferred is real rather than an excuse: every doctor check so far asks about a STATE — is there a nested .git in the tree, does the guest resolve localhost, was this base composed by this substrate. All of those are answerable by looking.

"Can this daemon answer its largest plausible response" is a PROPERTY, not a state. To answer it you have to know what the largest plausible response IS, and that depends on the repository: a worktree with a 40,000-path node_modules classifies into a report far over the 1 MiB control-response cap, while a two-file repo never comes close. So the check has to either measure something about this repository or provoke the condition, and those are very different designs.

THREE SHAPES WORTH WEIGHING, rather than picking one here:

(a) MEASURE THE INPUT. Count the paths a classification would enumerate for this repository's worktree and compare against the cap, at the same bytes-per-path the report actually costs. Cheap, no side effects, and it answers "would sync be able to reply about this tree". Wrong if the estimate drifts from the real encoder.

(b) PROVOKE IT. Ask the daemon for a deliberately over-sized response and assert a legible refusal comes back rather than an EOF. This tests the mechanism instead of estimating it, and it is exactly the MGIT-160 fix's contract. Needs a control verb that can be asked for an over-sized reply, which does not exist and would be a wire addition for a diagnostic — weigh that cost honestly.

(c) ASSERT THE INVARIANT ELSEWHERE. Since MGIT-164 bounds the sync report by construction, the interesting question may no longer be "can it answer" but "is every reply path bounded". That is a property of the code, not of a running daemon, so its home might be a test rather than doctor — which would mean the honest answer is that this incident's conversion is a test, not a check.

Note (c) is a live possibility and should not be dismissed to satisfy the rule. Rule 5 exists so an incident becomes something the tool asks itself; if the truest form of that is a bounding test rather than a doctor check, say so and record why, rather than building a check that measures an estimate to satisfy a ritual.
nodes.acceptance:
- A decision is recorded between measuring the input, provoking the condition, and asserting the invariant in a test — with the reason, not just the choice.
- If a doctor check is built: it names MGIT-160 as its incident, distinguishes cannot-tell from pass per the framework, and its estimate is validated against the real encoder rather than assumed.
- If the conclusion is that a test is the truer home, MGIT-160's conversion is recorded as satisfied by that test, and the reasoning is written down so a future reader does not re-open it as an oversight.
- Either way, a repository whose worktree would produce an unanswerable classification can learn that before a sync fails.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Preflight sweeps Go and not shell gates: a rendering change can break scripts/e2e invisibly
nodes.description:
A process gap, previously recorded only in one agent's memory. Filing it so it belongs to the repository rather than to whoever happens to remember.

`go test ./...` does not run `scripts/e2e/*.sh`. So the standard preflight — suite, -race, both lint targets, govulncheck — structurally CANNOT see an assertion living in a shell gate.

IT HAS ALREADY COST A RED CI. MGIT-155 changed `mgit log --task-id` from printing `pos=N` to printing commit subjects. The Go tests were swept for the old spelling; `scripts/e2e/course_correction.sh` asserted `pos=2` and was missed. CI caught it, and no local preflight could have.

TWO PARTS TO THE FIX, and the second matters more:

1. MECHANICAL: when a change alters command OUTPUT — a rendered line, a message, a status word, a JSON field — grep scripts/e2e for the old string and run the affected gate locally with the new binary first on PATH. A one-line sweep answers it; the sweep run after MGIT-155 found 87 assert_contains across the gates and no second instance, so the surface is small enough to check habitually.

2. STRUCTURAL: prefer fixing an assertion's SHAPE over its spelling. The repair to course_correction.sh was to count commit lines rather than match a rendered position, because what that step means is "all three commits are indexed" — which survives any future change to how a line is spelled. An assertion bound to presentation is the MGIT-161 class (a gate asserting someone else's behavior) turned inward: a gate asserting our own presentation rather than our own property.

WORTH CONSIDERING, since a mechanical rule a human must remember is the weaker half: whether the preflight can run the shell gates itself, or whether a cheap linter can flag an e2e assertion that matches a rendered-output shape. Either would move this from discipline to structure, which is the direction everything else in this repo has gone.
nodes.acceptance:
- The gap is documented where a contributor reads it (CLAUDE.md's verification checklist or the e2e README), not only in an agent's memory.
- The two-part rule is stated: sweep scripts/e2e when output changes, AND prefer asserting the property over the presentation.
- A judgement is recorded on whether this becomes structural — preflight running the gates, or a check that flags presentation-bound assertions — rather than remaining a rule someone must remember.
- The existing gates are swept once for presentation-bound assertions and the result recorded (done once after MGIT-155: 87 assertions, none bound to prose or rendered counts).
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Sweep the codebase for the wrong-layer question: which layer owns this fact?
nodes.description:
A named class with two confirmed instances a week apart, and only one layer audited. Filing the rest of the sweep.

THE CLASS: a component reaches past the layer that OWNS a fact to a lower layer that can answer a similar-looking question, and gets an answer that is true of the lower layer and false of the system.

  MGIT-107: the daemon's shutdown drain called the backend manager directly, while the terminal `destroyed` event is written by the service. An orderly stop therefore left no terminal event, and the next daemon stamped it `killed / unsupervised` — a crash record for a deliberate shutdown, on the daemon's own idle-exit path, which is the common case.

  MGIT-154: the daemon's idle check asked the backend whether anything was registered. The backend knows only BOOTED VMs; registration is a service fact. So a registered-but-unbooted task did not count, and the daemon exited while a live task was bound to it.

Both had a tell worth naming: MGIT-154's doc comment already said "registered" while the code asked the backend. The comment was right and the code had drifted beneath it, with nothing to make them disagree out loud. That is the quiet form of a decorative declaration, and it argues that comments asserting a LAYER CONTRACT deserve the same pinning as posture claims.

WHAT HAS BEEN AUDITED: the daemon only. After MGIT-154 I grepped every `d.cfg.Manager.*` call in internal/sandboxd and found four, all inside the two service-less FALLBACKS (hasSandboxes' else-branch and drainViaManager) where there genuinely is no registry to consult, and both say so. No third instance in the daemon.

WHAT HAS NOT: everything else. The question — which layer owns this fact? — has not been asked of the CLI reaching past services into stores, the MCP surface, the REST handlers, or the backends reaching into staging. CLAUDE.md's dependency rule (handlers never touch stores; cmd -> service -> store -> model) is exactly this law stated forwards; the two instances are it violated backwards, in a component that was allowed a lower-layer handle for a legitimate reason and then used it for an illegitimate question.

Two instances in a week is a class, not a coincidence. The audit should be mechanical rather than vigilant: enumerate the places where a component holds a handle to a layer below the one that owns the fact it is asking about, and judge each.
nodes.acceptance:
- Every site where a component queries a layer below the owner of the fact is enumerated, beyond internal/sandboxd — CLI, MCP, REST, and backend-into-staging included.
- Each site is judged: correct (a genuine fallback with no owner available, stated as such) or a wrong-layer question to be fixed.
- Findings are filed individually rather than fixed in one sweeping change, so each carries its own reasoning and test.
- A judgement is recorded on whether the rule can be enforced structurally — a lint or an architecture test on the dependency direction CLAUDE.md already states — rather than re-audited by hand each time.
- Comments that assert a layer contract are considered for pinning, since in both known instances the comment was correct and the code beneath it had drifted.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: A PR merge is not a ticket close: make closing part of the merge ritual
nodes.description:
Founder ruling, 2026-08-24. Filed because the failure it fixes was mine and it will recur without a mechanism.

WHAT HAPPENED. Ten tickets whose work had shipped and merged were still open or in_progress on the board: 143, 147, 152, 154, 155, 159, 160, 161, 162, 163, 174. I had been treating the PR merge as the close and letting the ticket lag, closing only the few I happened to remember (107, 111, 149, 157).

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN TIDINESS, and this is what makes it worth a ticket rather than a habit:

1. The board is the only shared view of what is left. A board that lists shipped work as pending is not a slow board, it is a WRONG one — and it is wrong in the direction that wastes the most time, because the next person picks up something already done.
2. A parallel test campaign is now filing into this board. Drift that was merely untidy while one lane worked becomes actively misleading the moment two do: the campaign cannot tell a real gap from a stale row.
3. It is the same shape as the defects this repo keeps fixing. A ticket that says "open" about finished work is a record asserting something that is not true, with nothing making it disagree out loud. I have spent a week fixing exactly that pattern in the product while producing it on the board.

THE RULE: closing joins the merge ritual. Merging without closing is an incomplete merge, the same way shipping without a test is an incomplete change.

WORTH WEIGHING, because a rule that depends on remembering is the same weak half as MGIT-176's: whether this can be structural. Candidates — a commit-message trailer parsed on merge, a PR-template checkbox, or a check that flags a ticket referenced by a merged commit and still open. Any of those beats discipline; the strongest is probably deriving it from the `Refs: MGIT-x` trailer the commit convention already requires, because the information is present and nothing reads it.

Note the boundary that keeps this honest: a merge closes a ticket only when the ACCEPTANCE is met, not when the diff lands. MGIT-164 shipped its verification and stays open because the root cause is unreproduced; MGIT-110 stays open pending three continuous runs; MGIT-162 closed with an annotation recording a defect in what it shipped (tracked as MGIT-169). Automation must not flatten that distinction into "merged means done".
nodes.acceptance:
- The rule is written where contributors read it (CLAUDE.md's task workflow), stated as: a merge without a ticket close is an incomplete merge.

nodes.title: goreleaser is installed at @latest in CI and the release path — v2.18.0 needs Go 1.27 and broke an unrelated PR
nodes.description:
RELEASE-BLOCKING. Found when a documentation-only PR went red.

    go: github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/v2@latest:
        github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/v2@v2.18.0 requires go >= 1.27.0
        (running go 1.26.6; GOTOOLCHAIN=local)

goreleaser released v2.18.0, which raised its Go floor. Both places mgit uses it are UNPINNED, so the new version arrived by itself:

  .github/workflows/e2e.yml:112   go install github.com/goreleaser/goreleaser/v2@latest
  .github/workflows/release.yml   goreleaser-action@v6 with `version: latest`

The e2e one broke the release-archive install channel on a PR that changed only CLAUDE.md. The release.yml one is worse and had not yet been observed: the ACTUAL RELEASE PATH resolves `latest` too, so cutting v0.6.5 would fail the same way, at the worst possible moment — after the tag is pushed, which by R-H298 burns the number.

NOT A FLAKE, and the fetch guard was right to say so. It retried three times and reported "READ THIS AS AN OUTAGE... Do not re-run this without reading it. A red absorbed as noise is how a real failure eventually gets waved through." Reading it was how the Go-version requirement surfaced; three re-runs would have produced three identical failures and an hour of confusion.

THE FIX IS THE LAW THIS REPO JUST WROTE DOWN. CLAUDE.md's working laws include "pin the publisher's stated sum, never the bytes you received" and MGIT-163 already established that a pinned artifact is cacheable and a floating one is a liability. A build TOOL resolved at `@latest` is the same hazard in a different costume: an input nobody chose, changing under a build that must be reproducible.

COMPATIBLE VERSIONS, from the module proxy:
  v2.18.0 -> requires go 1.27.0   (breaks the runner)
  v2.17.1 -> requires go 1.26.5   (newest that works)
  v2.17.0 -> requires go 1.26.4

Pin both sites to v2.17.1 — the newest that builds on the runner's toolchain. Bumping the runner's Go instead is a bigger, separate decision: GOTOOLCHAIN=local is deliberate here, and a toolchain bump touches every build in the repo rather than one tool.
nodes.acceptance:
- Both goreleaser invocations are pinned to an explicit version: the e2e install channel and the release workflow's goreleaser-action.
- The pin is stated once with its reason, so the next bump is a decision rather than an accident, and the Go-floor constraint is recorded beside it.
- The release-archive install channel passes on a PR that changes nothing else.
- A judgement is recorded on where this pin belongs long-term — alongside the other pinned versions in scripts/sandbox-image/pins.env, or in the workflows — so tool pins are discoverable in one place rather than scattered.
- Consider whether any other `@latest` or unpinned action remains on a path that must be reproducible; fix or file what is found.

nodes.title: mgit show rejects the abbreviated hash that mgit log prints
nodes.prompt: DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-22, mgit on a clone of mgit-dev). `mgit log` prints 8-char abbreviated commit hashes (e.g. `f29d8601 [MGIT:MGIT-2] add c`), but `mgit show f29d8601` fails with `Error: show: commit not found: f29d8601`. Only the FULL 40-char hash works (`mgit show f29d8601e511...` succeeds). The log->show round-trip is broken: show does not resolve abbreviated/prefix hashes that its own log command emits. Likely the commit lookup does an exact-key match on the full SHA. FIX: resolve abbreviated hashes (prefix match against the object/index, error on ambiguity). Add a test: commit, take the abbrev from `log`, `show` it. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.

nodes.title: MGIT-179 has no standing check: nothing fails when a build tool is resolved at @latest
nodes.description:
Rule 5 conversion for MGIT-179. The pin landed in #81 (both goreleaser sites moved to v2.17.1), but the FIX IS THE ONLY THING THAT LANDED — nothing in the repo now notices when a new floating version appears. Pin one tool, and the next unpinned one arrives the same way.

MGIT-179's own acceptance saw this coming and left it undone: "Consider whether any other @latest or unpinned action remains on a path that must be reproducible; fix or file what is found." This is that filing, promoted from a one-off sweep to a standing check, because a sweep done once decays the moment someone adds a workflow step.

WHERE THIS CHECK LIVES IS THE WHOLE DESIGN QUESTION, and it is the "which layer owns this fact?" question from the working laws. The property is "are this repo's build tools pinned" — a CI property of THIS repository, not a property of a user's machine. `mgit doctor` runs on an installed binary on someone else's laptop, where there are no workflow files to inspect and the honest verdict would be StatusNotChecked forever. A check whose only possible answer is "not applicable here" is the phantom door in reverse: noise that trains people to skip the report.

So the recommendation is that this one is a PREFLIGHT/CI gate rather than a user-facing doctor check — a make target and a CI job that fails the build, run where the fact actually lives. Rule 5 is satisfied by the incident having a standing automated check, not by that check necessarily being a `doctor.Check`. If the reviewer disagrees and wants it in `mgit doctor` under a "repo checks only when run inside the mgit source tree" mode, that is a legitimate alternative and should be recorded as the decision — but it needs the StatusNotChecked path to be designed deliberately, not fallen into.

WHAT TO DETECT, at minimum:
  - `go install ...@latest` / `@master` / `@main` anywhere in .github/ or scripts/
  - GitHub Actions `uses:` on a floating ref (a branch or a bare major where the workflow needs exactness), and any action input named version/goreleaser-version set to `latest`
  - unpinned tool fetches in scripts/ (curl of a "latest" release URL)

The check must also state the Go-floor constraint that made v2.18.0 unusable, or the next person pins to whatever is newest and reproduces MGIT-179 exactly.

Note the asymmetry that makes this cheap to get wrong: the failure lands AFTER the tag is pushed on the release path, and by R-H298 a tag never points twice, so the cost of the missing check is a burned version number rather than a red CI run.
nodes.acceptance:
- A standing automated check fails when a build tool or action on a reproducible path is resolved at a floating ref (@latest/@master/@main, `version: latest`, "latest" release URLs) in .github/ and scripts/.
- The check runs in CI on every PR, so a newly added unpinned step is caught at the PR that adds it, not at the release that trips on it.
- A negative control exists: introduce a floating ref in a scratch copy and prove the check FAILS on it, per the working law that a test which passes with its subject deleted tests nothing.
- The decision on where the check lives — CI/preflight gate vs. a `mgit doctor` repo-mode check — is recorded with its reason, including why StatusNotChecked-on-every-user-machine was or was not acceptable.
- The current tree passes the check, and any additional floating refs it finds are fixed in the same change or filed.
- The Go-floor constraint (goreleaser v2.18.0 requires Go 1.27; the runner is on 1.26.x with GOTOOLCHAIN=local) is recorded beside the pin so the next bump is a decision.
- MGIT-179's remaining acceptance item (the sweep) is satisfied by this work, and MGIT-179 is closed citing #81 plus this check.

nodes.title: VerifyDelivery's general form: should a sync refuse when a path OUTSIDE its plan changed identity during the apply?
nodes.description:
Carved out of MGIT-168's acceptance item 4, which asked the owning lane to "consider whether VerifyDelivery should assert that no path outside the plan changed identity during an apply — the general form of this class" and allowed that it may belong on its own ticket. It does: the fix for MGIT-168 holds at the syscall (a delete never follows a link), and the general assertion is a design call with a real false-refusal cost, so it is recorded here rather than decided inside a data-loss fix.

WHAT THE GENERAL CHECK WOULD BE. Sync already builds the guest manifest twice — before the apply (the `guest` view) and after it (the MGIT-164 read-back). Comparing the two on every path NOT in plan.Update/plan.Delete costs nothing extra and would have caught MGIT-168 without knowing its mechanism: real.txt's identity changed during an apply that never named it.

WHY IT IS NOT OBVIOUSLY RIGHT. VerifyDelivery checks only planned paths ON PURPOSE: "a guest is entitled to its own files, and policing outside the plan would refuse syncs over work the guest legitimately created." The sync lock stops execs during an apply, but it does not stop a guest process that is already running — a dev server writing a log, a watcher rebuilding, a package manager mid-install. Any of those changes an unplanned path between the two manifest builds, and the general check would refuse a sync that delivered everything it promised, with an error blaming the substrate for the guest's own activity. That is a false refusal on the documented agent path, the MGIT-166 shape.

SHAPES WORTH WEIGHING:
(a) Refuse on any unplanned change — simplest, catches the whole class, refuses legitimately busy guests.
(b) Refuse only when an unplanned path changed to EMPTY or VANISHED — narrower, matches the destruction shape, still races a guest that legitimately truncates or deletes its own files.
(c) Report, do not refuse: name unplanned changes in the Result as an audit line ("N paths changed outside the plan during this sync") so a reviewer can see it without the sync failing. Loud without being wrong.
(d) Keep it at the syscall (the MGIT-168 fix) and rely on per-primitive guards. Cheapest; catches nothing new.

(c) is the candidate that satisfies R-H300 rule 4 (nothing silent) without manufacturing refusals, and it can be promoted to (a)/(b) once field data says how often busy guests change unplanned paths.
nodes.acceptance:
- A decision between the shapes above is recorded with its reason, including the false-refusal cost of policing unplanned paths against a guest that may be running.
- If any check is built: it is exercised by a test that injects an unplanned change during the apply (through the applyPlan seam PR #71 introduces), and a negative control shows a busy-but-honest guest is not refused.
- If the decision is to keep it at the syscall, MGIT-168's acceptance item 4 is recorded as settled by this ticket so it is not re-opened as an oversight.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: pre-push hook refuses every push from a linked git worktree: branchguard cannot resolve the branch when --repo is the worktree path
nodes.description:
Hit 2026-09-02 while pushing the MGIT-168 branch from a linked worktree created with `git worktree add -b fix/mgit-168-symlink-delete ../mgit-168 origin/main`.

    $ git push -u origin fix/mgit-168-symlink-delete
    branchguard: resolve branch "fix/mgit-168-symlink-delete": reference not found
    exit status 1
    error: failed to push some refs to 'https://github.com/hyper-swe/mgit.git'

scripts/hooks/pre-push runs `go run ./scripts/branchguard --repo "$root" --branch "$branch"` with `root=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)`. In a linked worktree that is the worktree's own path, whose `.git` is a FILE pointing at the main repository's `.git/worktrees/<name>`. go-git's PlainOpen there does not see refs/heads/*, so the branch that is being pushed reads as nonexistent and the guard refuses with exit 1 — the hook's refusal path, not its "could not run" path.

The identical command from the main checkout passes:

    $ go run ./scripts/branchguard --branch fix/mgit-168-symlink-delete --base origin/main
    (exit 0)

Two things wrong, in R-H300 terms:
1. A check that cannot run reads as a FAILURE (rule 2: it says "reference not found" as if the branch did not exist; the branch exists and is clean). The hook already has a "could not run" door for a missing Go toolchain that exits 0 with a note; a repository it cannot read should take that door, not the refusal one.
2. Every linked-worktree workflow is blocked at the push, including the one CLAUDE.md prescribes for parallel tasks (`mgit work` provisions a linked worktree too — check whether `mgit work` trees hit the same refusal; if they do, the dogfood path has been pushing with --no-verify or not at all).

Workaround used: push from the main checkout. Note the CI backstop (Branch scope job) still runs the guard on the PR, so nothing unguarded reaches main.
nodes.acceptance:
- `git push` of a clean branch from a linked worktree passes the pre-push hook (branchguard resolves the branch through the worktree's commondir, or the hook resolves the main repository root — e.g. `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` — before invoking it).
- A repository the guard cannot read reports not-checked (exit 0 with the reason on stderr, like the missing-Go door), never a refusal that names the branch as nonexistent.
- A test that opens the guard on a linked worktree, since a test using only the main checkout cannot see this.
- Confirmed against an `mgit work` worktree as well as a plain `git worktree add` one.

nodes.title: CLAUDE.md does not state the repo's tool-silence rule (no AI-attribution trailers, no generated-with footers) — a fresh session learns it from a red verdict
nodes.description:
Hit 2026-09-02. A fresh agent session opened five PRs whose commits carried Co-Authored-By / session trailers and whose bodies carried a "generated with" footer, because the agent harness asks for exactly those. The gate reviewer failed the first PR on the repository's convention: 0 of 517 commits on main carry such trailers, a ticket in this repo (MGIT-61.14's prompt) says "no AI-attribution trailers", and the product's tool-silence scan rejects them. All five had to be amended (message-only, tree unchanged) and force-pushed with a lease; the sixth was opened clean.

The rule exists and is enforced, but it is written nowhere a new session reads before its first commit: CLAUDE.md's "COMMIT MESSAGE FORMAT" section shows the type/scope/Refs shape and says nothing about attribution, and the working laws do not mention it either. A convention that lives only in history and in a reviewer's checklist is learned by every new session the expensive way — once per session, at the cost of a review round trip and a force-push.

Also learned the same way, same session: every ticket gets an annotation naming the PR, branch and scenario tests when its PR opens (the reviewer's line 3). That belongs in the merge ritual text too.
nodes.acceptance:
- CLAUDE.md's commit-message section states plainly: no AI-attribution trailers (Co-Authored-By naming a model/tool, session links) in commits, and no "generated with" footer in PR bodies — with the one-line reason (public surfaces stay tool-silent) and a pointer to the scan that enforces it.
- The PR/merge ritual text names the ticket annotation (PR, branch, scenario tests) as part of opening a PR, beside "a PR merge is not a ticket close".
- A session that reads CLAUDE.md before its first commit produces a commit the reviewer's checklist accepts on the first try — verified by the next fresh session's first PR.

nodes.title: real-process command tests die as "signal: killed" at a fixed 10s budget under host load — a false red that reads exactly like a product failure
nodes.description:
Hit 2026-09-02, four times across three branches, while two other `go test ./...` runs shared the machine:

    --- FAIL: TestCodexHook_RealProcess_UnavailableSandboxIsDeniedNotAsked (16.97s)
        agent_hooks_realprocess_test.go:27: mgit [init]: signal: killed
    --- FAIL: TestCommit_JustUnderLimit_Unaffected (10.83s)
        commit_large_file_test.go:104: mgit [init]: signal: killed
    --- FAIL: TestCommit_OversizedFile_EscapeHatchesWork/... (10.65s, 10.11s)
    --- FAIL: TestCommit_MessageFileStdin_RecordsBytesVerbatim (10.64s)
        commit_message_file_test.go:125: mgit [init]: signal: killed

Every one of them passes alone on a quiet machine in 1.4s–3.7s. The cause is the harness: cmd/mgit/claude_hook_realprocess_test.go runs the built binary under `context.WithTimeout(…, 10*time.Second)` (runMgitTest at line 83, runMgitTestStdin at line 119; runMgitTestExit uses 30s), and `exec.CommandContext` SIGKILLs the child when the deadline passes. Under load `mgit init` — go-git init + SQLite schema — crossed 10s and was killed.

TWO THINGS WRONG, in R-H300 terms:
1. A fixed budget nobody measured. The fetch guard (MGIT-143) derives every timeout from the step's own worst success in history and says so at the site; these budgets are a round number. A budget that is right on a quiet laptop and wrong on a loaded one manufactures the red it exists to prevent.
2. The failure names nothing. "mgit [init]: signal: killed" is what a crash looks like; it does not say the TEST killed the process because its own deadline passed. A reader — human or agent — starts diagnosing mgit. This session did: three branches' gate logs went red before the pattern (10.x seconds, every time) gave it away.

Not the same class as a flaky test: the product did nothing wrong, and the tests are deterministic on a quiet machine.
nodes.acceptance:
- The kill is reported as what it is: "test budget of Ns exceeded (the harness killed the process; a loaded host does this) — not a crash", with the budget and the elapsed time in the message.
- The budget is derived from a measurement recorded at the site (worst observed success × a stated factor), or the real-process tests take an explicit, generous budget with the reason stated — not a bare 10s.
- The real-process tests do not run in parallel with each other (t.Parallel absent, or the binary build shared and the runs serialised), so the budget is not spent on each other.
- Reproduced before fixing: run the suite with a concurrent `go test ./... -race` on the same machine and show the kill; after the change, the same run passes or fails with the budget message.

nodes.title: Two sandbox daemons from test scratch repositories have been running for 12 days: nothing reaps a sandbox whose repository was a temp dir
nodes.description:
Observed 2026-09-02 21:02Z on the development mac while checking whether a dev-build doctor run could touch other lanes' daemons (`pgrep -fl mgit-sandboxd`, then `ps -o pid,etime,rss,command`):

    4641 12-13:35:14  9808  .../mgit-dev/build/mgit-sandboxd --socket .../T/mgit-501/07f2fa78e774/d.sock --host-root .../T/tmp.iAIYqjRBwV/.mgit/sandbox --repo-root .../T/tmp.iAIYqjRBwV ...
    4644 12-13:35:13 10960  .../mgit-dev/build/mgit-sandboxd __krun-vm
    4870 12-04:59:38  8432  /private/tmp/m152-pair/mgit-sandboxd --socket .../T/mgit-501/9307191f6518/d.sock --host-root .../T/tmp.DrtEkF6tg8/.mgit/sandbox --repo-root .../T/tmp.DrtEkF6tg8 ...
    4873 12-04:59:38 11312  /private/tmp/m152-pair/mgit-sandboxd __krun-vm

Both repositories are `mktemp -d` scratch dirs from the 2026-08-21 session (the MGIT-152 live pair, and an e2e run from this repo's build/ daemon). Each still exists with one entry (the .mgit store), each daemon still supervises one libkrun VM (`__krun-vm` child), and both have been alive for over twelve days. The idle exit (NFR-17.6) never fires because a sandbox is registered, and nothing else asks whether the repository the sandbox serves is still a place anyone works.

Not killed here: stopping them is a founder action (a running VM is someone's state until proven otherwise, and the contract forbids destructive-path mutations from a lane), and `pkill mgit-sandboxd` would also stop the coverage lane's live daemon (pid 4922, swe-go-cov).

WHAT IS WRONG, in R-H300 terms: silence. Twelve days of two VMs on a laptop with no line anywhere saying so. `mgit sandbox list` is per-repository, so from any real repository these do not show; `mgit doctor` runs per-repository too. There is no host-wide view that would have surfaced "you have N daemons, M of them serving repositories under $TMPDIR".

CANDIDATE SHAPES (the owning lane's call):
(a) A host-wide `mgit sandbox list --all` / doctor check that enumerates every daemon socket under the runtime base and flags ones whose --repo-root is under the temp dir or no longer exists — loud, no behaviour change.
(b) The daemon periodically checks that its --repo-root still exists and drains itself when it does not (a deleted repo cannot want its sandbox); for a repo that still exists under $TMPDIR, only (a) can say anything.
(c) The e2e/test harnesses that launch real sandboxes always remove them (t.Cleanup / trap), which is the cheapest fix for THESE two but not for the class.

Do (a) at least: R-H300 rule 4 — whether it is running must never require a second terminal and ps.
nodes.acceptance:
- A host-wide view exists (a doctor check or a `sandbox list --all`) that names every daemon on the host with its repository root, age and sandbox count, and flags roots under the temp directory or roots that no longer exist.
- A daemon whose --repo-root has been deleted drains itself within one idle-check interval and writes the terminal record (the MGIT-107 law).
- The live-sandbox e2e harnesses in this repo remove what they launch, verified by running one and checking `pgrep mgit-sandboxd` afterwards.
- The two daemons above are stopped by the founder and the fact recorded here (pids and ages are evidence, not something to tidy).

nodes.title: UndeliveredError's advice names one cause for a whole class: "the guest's tree is not the one being written to" misdirected the symlink case
nodes.description:
Residual from MGIT-165 (PR #84), raised by the gate reviewer at PASS: the read-back refusal quoted in the ticket —

    worktree sync: the guest's tree does not contain what was just synced into it: link.txt (stale content). Nothing is reported as delivered, because it was not. The host worktree is unchanged and safe; re-run the sync, and if it fails the same way the guest's tree is not the one being written to

— is still the text UndeliveredError renders. In the symlink case the guest's tree WAS the one being written to; the delivered entry was a regular file where the manifest expected a link, and the advice sent the reader to check paths. The MGIT-165 fix removes that particular cause, but the sentence still asserts a single cause for a refusal that VerifyDelivery raises for several: a path absent, content that does not hash to what was staged, a mode that differs, a delete that did not land.

R-H300 rule 2: an error states what it verified, never what it guesses. The refusal verifies "the guest's tree does not hold what was staged, at these paths, in this way" (it already names the way: absent / stale content / mode / still present). The advice should list the candidates that distinction leaves open rather than name one:
  - absent or still present → the tree being written is not the tree the guest mounts (the original suspicion), or the guest removed/recreated it during the apply;
  - stale content → what was staged and what the guest holds are different KINDS of entry (a link vs a file, MGIT-165's shape), or the guest rewrote the file during the apply;
  - mode → the destination's umask or filesystem dropped the bits (MGIT-81's class).

A doctor check per R-H300 rule 5 is not owed here (the check that catches the class is the read-back itself); the owed change is the sentence.
nodes.acceptance:
- UndeliveredError's advice lists the candidates each failure kind leaves open (absent/still present, stale content, mode) instead of asserting one cause for all.
- A test asserts the advice for each kind names its candidates (drawn from the list above, not from the implementation).
- The MGIT-165 shape (a link staged, a file read back) would, on the pre-#84 code, have produced advice naming "a different kind of entry" — checked by constructing that manifest pair directly against VerifyDelivery.

nodes.title: Core Model & Storage
nodes.description: Domain types, go-git wrapper, SQLite index, task-commit mapping.
nodes.prompt:
CONTEXT: Core Model & Storage — Waves 2-4

You are building the foundational data layer for mgit. This story covers domain model types, the go-git repository wrapper, and the SQLite task-commit index. Everything in later stories (services, CLI, API, MCP) depends on this being correct.

ARCHITECTURE:
  internal/model/ — Pure types: Commit (16 fields per FR-3), Branch (9 fields per FR-5), TaskID (dot-notation per FR-4), FileDiff (per FR-11), sentinel errors (15+ per model/errors.go). NO I/O in model/.
  internal/store/git/ — go-git wrapper: Repository, CommitStore, TreeStore, BranchStore, DiffStore, WorktreeStore, SyncingStorer. Uses plumbing API (not porcelain) for determinism. Wraps all go-git types — never expose *object.Commit or *git.Repository to callers.
  internal/store/index/ — SQLite: schema.go, migration.go, store.go (dual connection pools: 1 writer, 5 readers), task_commits.go (APPEND-ONLY), branches.go.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINTS:
  - DUAL-HASH MODEL (ADR-002): SHA-1 for go-git object IDs (protocol requirement) + SHA-256 for mgit content_hash (integrity/compliance). Store BOTH in SQLite.
  - APPEND-ONLY (FR-12): task_commits table is INSERT-only. No UPDATE, no DELETE. Ever. Rollbacks create revert commits.
  - CLOCK INJECTION: Never call time.Now() directly. Accept func() time.Time parameter for deterministic testing.
  - FSYNC (NFR-3.3a): SyncingStorer wraps go-git filesystem.Storage with explicit fsync() after every write — crash safety for hospital/airline deployments.
  - SQL SAFETY: Parameterized queries ONLY (?). No fmt.Sprintf in SQL. PRAGMAs: JOURNAL_MODE=WAL, SYNCHRONOUS=FULL, FOREIGN_KEYS=ON, BUSY_TIMEOUT=5000.

DEPENDENCY ORDER: Model types (Wave 2) → go-git wrapper (Wave 3) → SQLite index (Wave 4) → Integration tests (Wave 4).

nodes.title: Domain Model Types
nodes.description: Implement core domain models: Commit, Branch, TaskID, FileDiff, and error types.
nodes.prompt:
SCOPE: Implement the pure domain model types in internal/model/. These types have NO I/O dependencies — they import only stdlib and define the data structures used everywhere in mgit.

TYPES TO IMPLEMENT:
  Commit (commit.go) — 16 fields per FR-3: commit_id, task_id, agent_id, session_id, timestamp, message, parent_id, tree_hash, file_diffs, metadata, content_hash, signature, status, created_by, branch. Must implement Validate(), String(), JSON marshal/unmarshal.
  Branch (branch.go) — 9 fields per FR-5: branch_id, name, commit_id, task_id, created_at, locked_by, locked_until, merged_to, is_merged. Must implement Lock(), Unlock(), Validate().
  TaskID (taskid.go) — Dot-notation per FR-4: Parse("MGIT-1.2.3") → TaskID. Regex: ^MGIT-\d+(\.\d+)?(\.\d+)?$. Must be comparable (map key).
  FileDiff (filediff.go) — Per FR-11: path, status (Added/Modified/Deleted/Renamed), old_hash, new_hash, hunks ([]Hunk), binary_diff. Must implement Statistics().
  Errors (errors.go) — 15+ sentinel errors: ErrCommitNotFound, ErrBranchNotFound, ErrTaskNotFound, ErrBranchInUse, ErrTaskAlreadyBound, ErrTaskMismatch, ErrWorktreeNotFound, ErrAppendOnlyViolation, etc. All errors.Is() compatible.

WAVE GATE: All types compile, validation methods pass, JSON serialization correct.

nodes.title: go-git Repository Wrapper
nodes.description: Implement repository and storage abstractions wrapping go-git library.
nodes.prompt:
SCOPE: Implement the go-git repository wrapper in internal/store/git/. This layer wraps go-git v5 plumbing API to provide deterministic, auditable git operations. NEVER expose go-git types to callers — wrap everything in model types.

STORES TO IMPLEMENT:
  Repository (repository.go) — Init/Open/Close .mgit/ directory. Clock injection for deterministic timestamps.
  CommitStore (commit.go) — CreateCommit (go-git objects + SHA-256 content_hash), GetCommit, ListCommits, DeleteCommit (returns ErrAppendOnlyViolation always).
  TreeStore (tree.go) — BuildTree (from FileDiffs), GetTree, TraverseTree.
  BranchStore (branch.go) — CreateBranch, GetBranch, ListBranches, SwitchBranch, DeleteBranch. Locking support per FR-5.
  DiffStore (diff.go) — FileDiff (between two commits), RangeDiff (over commit range), DiffStats.
  WorktreeStore (worktree.go) — Status, Checkout, Clean.
  SyncingStorer (storer.go) — Wraps go-git filesystem.Storage with fsync() after every write per NFR-3.3a. Critical for crash safety.

KEY RULES:
  - Plumbing API (not porcelain) for determinism and auditability
  - All go-git types wrapped in model types before returning
  - go-git errors converted to mgit domain errors (ErrCommitNotFound etc.)
  - Dual-hash: SHA-1 for go-git object IDs + SHA-256 for mgit content_hash

WAVE GATE: All go-git operations pass against temp repos, no external git binary usage.

nodes.title: SQLite Index Store
nodes.description: Implement SQLite schema, migrations, and task-commit index operations.
nodes.prompt:
SCOPE: Implement the SQLite index store in internal/store/index/. This is the task-commit mapping database — the source of truth for which commits belong to which tasks.

COMPONENTS:
  schema.go — Table definitions: commits, tasks, task_commits (APPEND-ONLY), branches, branch_locks, worktrees.
  migration.go — Schema versioning and incremental migration support.
  store.go — IndexStore: dual connection pools (1 writer, 5 readers), PRAGMA configuration, ReadTx/WriteTx transaction helpers.
  task_commits.go — AddCommitToTask, GetTaskCommits, GetCommitTask (bidirectional), DeleteFromTask (always fails — append-only).
  branches.go — CreateBranch, GetBranch, UpdateBranchHead (forward-only), LockBranch, UnlockBranch.

CRITICAL SQL RULES:
  - PARAMETERIZED QUERIES ONLY (? placeholders). No fmt.Sprintf near SQL.
  - PRAGMAs: JOURNAL_MODE=WAL, SYNCHRONOUS=FULL, FOREIGN_KEYS=ON, BUSY_TIMEOUT=5000.
  - Separate read/write connection pools: writeDB.SetMaxOpenConns(1) for mutual exclusion.
  - All writes in transactions via withTx() helper.
  - task_commits is INSERT-only. No UPDATE, no DELETE. Ever.

WAVE GATE: Store layer at 95% coverage, append-only enforced, concurrent access safe.
nodes.creator: cli

All tables must be append-only per FR-12. Implement migration runner supporting schema versioning.

nodes.title: Commits do not appear in mgit audit (No audit entries found)
nodes.prompt: DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-22). After 3 `mgit commit`s, `mgit audit` reports `No audit entries found`. Commit operations are not recorded in the audit trail. For a safety-critical tool whose premise is provenance + auditability (DO-178C/IEC 62304), commit operations not being auditable is a real gap. EXPECTED: each commit (and squash/rollback) appends an audit entry surfaced by `mgit audit`. VERIFY whether the commit path was ever wired to the AuditService, or whether the MGIT-14 plumbing-rework of CreateCommit dropped an audit-log write that the prior go-git-worktree path performed. Add a test: commit -> `mgit audit` shows the entry. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: mgit verify exits 0 even when it reports issues
nodes.prompt: DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-22). `mgit verify` printed `WARNING: git commit 568e2bdb has no index entry` / `1 issues found` but exited with code 0. A verification command that finds issues must exit non-zero so CI and scripts can detect failures (the whole point of `mgit verify` in a safety-critical pipeline). EXPECTED: exit non-zero (e.g. 1) when any verification issue is found; exit 0 only on a clean verify. Add a test asserting the exit code on a repo with a known verification issue. (Separately, consider whether the initial commit legitimately having no index entry should even be flagged as an issue.) Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.

nodes.title: Clarify/verify mgit squash semantics (originals retained, squash placed above unrelated commit)
nodes.prompt: DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-22). With history: 82a58fd7 [MGIT-1] add a, e478a13f [MGIT-1] extend a+b, f29d8601 [MGIT-2] add c (tip). `mgit squash --task-id MGIT-1` produced `[4c1a1739] [MGIT-1] Squashed from 2 micro-commits` — but `mgit log` afterward still shows BOTH the squash commit (4c1a1739, now the tip, ABOVE the unrelated MGIT-2 commit) AND the original MGIT-1 micro-commits (82a58fd7, e478a13f). So squashing MGIT-1 appended a squashed commit on top of an unrelated task's commit while leaving the originals in place. This is confusing: it's unclear what the branch state means, whether MGIT-1's changes are now represented twice, and why the squash sits above MGIT-2. EXPECTED: define + document the intended squash semantics (append-only? does it rewrite the task's commits? where does the squashed commit land relative to other tasks' commits?) and make `mgit log`/behavior reflect it unambiguously. VERIFY against FR-2.x squash requirements + the append-only law; add tests pinning the resulting branch shape. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.

nodes.title: CLI UX inconsistencies (dogfood sweep): branch list, rollback positional, gc count
nodes.prompt:
DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-22), grouped CLI polish:
(1) `mgit branch list` fails with `Error: branch switch: branch not found: list` — it treats `list` as a branch to switch to (listing is bare `mgit branch`). Inconsistent with `mgit worktree list`/`mgit sandbox list` which DO take a `list` subcommand. Add a `branch list` subcommand or a clear error.
(2) Arg-convention inconsistency: `mgit show <hash>` takes a POSITIONAL hash, but `mgit rollback <hash>` rejects it (`Error: --task-id or --commit is required`) and requires `--commit <hash>`. Standardize: accept a positional commit hash where a command takes one, or document the convention.
(3) `mgit gc` reported `no-op: 480 -> 480 loose objects` in a repo with only ~4 tiny commits (a.go/b.go/c.go). 480 loose objects is implausibly high — verify gc is counting mgit's `.mgit` store (not the project `.git`) and that the count is correct.
These are low-severity polish, but they're the friction a new user hits immediately. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.

nodes.title: Linked-worktree command routing: run mgit (commit/log/status) from within a worktree
nodes.prompt:
DOGFOOD-FOUND (2026-06-23, using mgit worktrees to run parallel dev agents post-MGIT-17). VERDICT: implementation flaw / incomplete feature, NOT by design — the design explicitly INTENDS worktree-local commits (CLAUDE.md WORKTREE CONVENTIONS: "Commits from within a worktree auto-inherit the bound task ID"; FR-16 is for multi-agent parallel development), but the store linkage + command routing was never built. MGIT-17 only materialized the branch SOURCE into the worktree dir.

Two distinct gaps (both confirmed empirically against main f0f0715):

GAP 1 — No store-discovery walk-up. cmd/mgit/main.go openAppFromCwd → OpenApp(cwd) → repository.Open looks for .mgit ONLY in cwd (filepath.Join(path, ".mgit")); there is no walk up the directory tree. So `mgit log` (or any command) run from ANY subdirectory of the repo fails with "repository does not exist" — unlike git, which walks up to find .git. PROVEN: init mgit, `cd sub/deep`, `mgit log` → error. This is independently a usability bug and a prerequisite for worktree resolution. [Being fixed first as slice 1 — see annotations.]

GAP 2 — No linked-worktree store binding + per-worktree HEAD. internal/store/git Repository has a single `root` (project dir) and a single shared `.mgit/HEAD`. A linked worktree needs: (a) a MARKER in the worktree (analogous to git's `.git` gitfile) recording the parent .mgit store path + bound branch + task; (b) OpenApp/Open to detect the marker and open the PARENT's shared object store + refs + index.db while setting `root` = the worktree dir (so working-file reads + materialization target the worktree); (c) a PER-WORKTREE HEAD = the bound task branch, overriding the shared .mgit/HEAD, because two worktrees on different branches cannot share one HEAD (this is the architectural crux — many call sites use goRepo.Head() directly, e.g. commit.go/merge.go; they must respect the worktree's bound branch); (d) commits auto-inherit the bound task ID (the worktree registry already maps path→branch→task via index.GetWorktree); (e) concurrency: two mgit processes committing to one shared .mgit/index.db from two worktrees — already partly covered by SQLite WAL + the .mgit file lock + CAS refs, but verify the lock targets the shared parent .mgit. Today the MGIT-17 worktree has only a `.mgit/shims` dir (agent-adapter injection from MGIT-11.11), which is NOT a valid store — so `mgit commit` from a worktree fails.

ACCEPTANCE: `mgit commit`/`log`/`status`/`add` run from within a linked worktree operate on the bound task branch, share the parent's object store + index, materialize into the worktree dir, never touch the project .git (MGIT-14 invariant), and auto-inherit the bound task ID (CLAUDE.md). Add e2e: `mgit worktree add` then `cd <wt> && mgit add . && mgit commit` lands a commit on task/<id> visible from the parent, with two worktrees committing to disjoint branches without corruption. Likely needs an ADR for the per-worktree-HEAD model. Touches cmd/mgit (openAppFromCwd/OpenApp), internal/store/git (Repository: root vs store split, HEAD override, a linked-open constructor), internal/service/worktree (write the marker on Add). Standalone — gates nothing already shipped. Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.

nodes.title: rollback by commit-hash opens the App twice and self-contends on the file lock
nodes.prompt:
FOUND by adversarial review during MGIT-24 (2026-06-23). PRE-EXISTING (not introduced by the linked-worktree work) but real and reachable.

cmd/mgit/rollback.go RunE: when a commit hash is supplied (positional arg, --commit, or --to-commit) and --task-id is not, it calls openAppFromCwd() at ~line 34 to resolve the task ID from the commit, with `defer app.Close()`. It then falls through and calls openAppFromCwd() AGAIN at ~line 52 — while the first App (and its process-level file lock, lock.DefaultTimeout = 30s) is still held by the deferred Close that only fires when RunE returns. The second lock.Acquire contends with the first (flock on a second fd of the same lock file blocks), so `mgit rollback <hash>` stalls ~30s and then fails with a lock-held error instead of rolling back. The plain `mgit rollback --task-id X` path opens once and is unaffected. The MGIT-24 shared-lock change (worktrees lock the parent store) amplifies this class but did not cause it.

FIX: open the App once and reuse it — resolve the task from the commit hash and perform the rollback with the SAME App instance (move the resolve step after a single openAppFromCwd, or pass the resolved taskID forward without re-opening). Add a test: `mgit rollback <hash>` (and --commit / --to-commit) completes promptly and creates the revert, with no second lock acquisition. VERIFY against the lock model (single open per command invocation). Commit Refs to this ticket; no trailers.
