nodes.title: Detect Homebrew formula-body drift: the tap's automation updates version + checksums but never the body
nodes.description: hyper-swe/homebrew-tap's update-formula.yml rewrites ONLY the version and the four sha256 lines in Formula/mgit.rb, by literal text regex. It never touches install/, caveats or depends_on. So every time mgit's install shape changes, the live formula body silently drifts from brew/mgit.rb and nothing detects it — the drift is only ever discovered by a user. That is exactly how the tap came to install both binaries but NOT the guest/ payload, leaving `mgit sandbox base from` broken for every brew user while CI stayed green.
nodes.prompt:
Add a check that makes formula-body drift a visible CI failure instead of a user-facing one.

BACKGROUND, verified 2026-08-05/06:
- The tap update is automated but PARTIAL. release.yml's `homebrew` job sends a repository_dispatch carrying only {"tag", "project"}. The tap's own .github/workflows/update-formula.yml then downloads that release's checksums.txt and rewrites ONLY `version "..."` and the four `sha256 "..."` lines in its existing Formula/mgit.rb, via literal text regex. install/, caveats and depends_on are never touched by anything.
- brew/mgit.rb in THIS repo is the single source of truth for the body (docs/release/homebrew-tap-formula.md was deleted as redundant in PR #3), but nothing pushes it.
- Consequence already realised: the live formula installed mgit + mgit-sandboxd but NOT the archive's guest/ payload, so `mgit sandbox base from` fell through to source-building and failed for every brew user (no Go toolchain). The body was hand-synced on 2026-08-06 (tap commit 358a2d19). It WILL drift again.

WHAT TO BUILD:
A CI check (this repo) that fetches the live Formula/mgit.rb from hyper-swe/homebrew-tap and compares its BODY against brew/mgit.rb, ignoring exactly the fields the tap owns: the `version "..."` line and the four `sha256 "..."` lines. Everything else — install/, caveats, depends_on, desc, license, test — must match. Fail loudly with a diff naming what drifted and the remedy (sync brew/mgit.rb's body into the tap).

REQUIREMENTS:
- Normalise only what the automation legitimately rewrites. Do NOT normalise comments away — a stale comment in the tap is drift worth seeing.
- The tap is public, so an unauthenticated fetch works; do not require a token, and do not fail the build when GitHub is unreachable (skip loudly with the reason — a network blip must not look like drift).
- Run it in the normal CI job, and add it to the release checklist as a pre-tag gate.
- BETTER, IF CHEAP: instead of only detecting drift, have release.yml PUSH the body too, so the tap is fully generated rather than half-generated. Assess this — it removes the manual step entirely rather than policing it. If you take it, the dispatch payload or a follow-up API call needs to carry the body, and the tap's workflow must apply it without clobbering the checksums it just wrote. Say which approach you chose and why.

TESTS: the check fails when the body differs (mutate a copy and prove it); passes on an in-sync pair; skips loudly (not fails) when the tap cannot be fetched.

Refs: MGIT-65, MGIT-64, MGIT-44, brew/mgit.rb, brew/TAP-SETUP.md, docs/release/RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md step 3, tap commit 358a2d19.
Constraints: never touch the mtix formula in the tap repo; no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`.
nodes.acceptance: A CI check compares the live tap formula's body against brew/mgit.rb, ignoring only the version and the four checksum lines, and fails with an actionable diff when they drift; it skips loudly rather than failing when the tap cannot be fetched; tests prove it catches a mutated body, passes when in sync, and skips on fetch failure; the release checklist lists it as a pre-tag gate; and the decision between detecting drift and fully generating the tap body is recorded with its rationale.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: P0 REGRESSION in v0.4.0: guest egress is non-functional on macOS/libkrun — the guest NIC is never configured
nodes.description: Reported by the HyperSwe lane (hyper-swe/swe PR #66) and confirmed by our own RCA: in allowlist mode guest DNS fails EAI_AGAIN, and in --network open a connection to a RAW IP fails ENETUNREACH. The guest has no route out in any mode. Blocks HyperSwe's in-guest provisioning (npm install, curl). Shipped in v0.4.0.
nodes.prompt:
Reported externally; RCA done here — treat the reporter's diagnosis as directional and re-verify, but the cause below was established by reading the shipped code, not inferred from symptoms.

ROOT CAUSE: NOTHING CONFIGURES THE GUEST'S NIC.
- cmd/mgit-guest (the real PID 1) contains no address/route configuration at all: no SIOCSIFADDR, no SIOCADDRT, no netlink, no DHCP client (grep returns nothing).
- The netstack gateway (internal/sandboxd/backend/libkrun/netgw.go) serves no DHCP.
- Under libkrun there is no kernel command line of ours to carry `ip=` — libkrunfw supplies the cmdline, which is why the boot descriptor travels in the guest ENV (see BootTokens).
So the guest boots with eth0 PRESENT but UNADDRESSED and with NO DEFAULT ROUTE. That single cause produces both reported symptoms: ENETUNREACH for a raw IP in open mode, and EAI_AGAIN for DNS because the gateway's :53 is equally unreachable.

THE GATEWAY IS NOT THE PROBLEM. It is proven working against a real libkrun VM (allowlisted destination spliced with a real byte round-trip; off-allowlist RST). What is missing is the GUEST side of the wire. The joined spike DID prove the allow path end to end — but its guest binary configured eth0 itself via SIOCSIFADDR/SIOCADDRT. That was TEST SCAFFOLDING and never shipped. Preserved at ~/mgit-vz-cache/libkrun-netstack-spike/netstack-spike/guest/ — read it; it is the shape of the fix.

WHY CI AND THE LITMUS DID NOT CATCH IT — fix this too, or the next regression hides the same way:
TestE2E_Libkrun_RealVM_NoneMode_NoEgress and TestE2E_Libkrun_RealVM_Allowlist_DefaultDeny assert ONLY `GUEST-RESULT OFF_ALLOWLIST = DENIED`. An unconfigured NIC produces exactly that, so both tests passed for the wrong reason. There is NO real-VM assertion that an ALLOWED flow succeeds. Litmus legs 2 and 3 used the simulated guest netstack, which the test configures itself.

WHAT TO BUILD:
1. Give the guest an address and a default route. Pick ONE and record why:
   (a) DHCP served by the gateway — netstack can do it; keeps the guest generic and works for any base image, including ones whose init expects DHCP.
   (b) mgit-guest configures eth0 itself from boot tokens the host already sends (the BootTokens env channel is established and tested), using the ioctl sequence from the spike.
   Prefer (a) if a stock base image's own tooling would otherwise fight us; prefer (b) if we want zero dependence on guest userspace. State the trade-off.
2. Make the gateway address/prefix and the guest address a single source of truth (netgw.go already has guestIP/gatewayIP/gwPrefixLen — the guest side must agree with them, not restate them).
3. Verify DNS: the guest needs a resolver pointing at the gateway (resolv.conf or equivalent). EAI_AGAIN will persist otherwise even with a route.

REQUIRED TESTS — the gap is the point:
- A real-VM test asserting an ALLOWED destination SUCCEEDS (real bytes returned), not merely that a denied one fails. This is the assertion whose absence let this ship.
- A real-VM test that DNS resolves an allowlisted NAME through the host resolver and connects to the pinned IP.
- Keep the deny assertions, but make them distinguishable from "no network at all": assert the denial reason (RST/refused) rather than any failure.
- open mode: a raw-IP connection SUCCEEDS.

Refs: ADR-010, MGIT-61.15, MGIT-61.6 annotations (guest addressing was flagged repeatedly as unresolved and never closed), hyper-swe/swe PR #66.
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`; this needs a v0.4.1.
nodes.acceptance: A guest booted by mgit-guest under libkrun obtains an address and default route without test scaffolding; DNS resolves through the gateway resolver; a real-VM test asserts an ALLOWED flow succeeds with real bytes returned; a real-VM test resolves an allowlisted NAME and connects to the pinned IP; open mode reaches a raw IP; deny assertions distinguish a policy refusal from a dead network; the HyperSwe repro (compose an image, run a command needing network) succeeds; and the addressing choice (DHCP vs guest-side config) is recorded with its rationale.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: firecracker guests get a route but no /etc/resolv.conf — the default-resolver path is unasserted
nodes.description:
Found while fixing MGIT-68. On firecracker the guest DOES get an address and default route (firecracker-go-sdk renders IPConfiguration into an `ip=` kernel boot param and the guest kernel applies it), so routing works. But nothing writes /etc/resolv.conf, and the allowlist e2e only ever resolves with the DNS server named explicitly (`nslookup <name> <gateway>`) — so the default-resolver path a real getaddrinfo caller uses (npm, curl, apt) is unasserted and may fail EAI_AGAIN exactly as libkrun did. VERIFY on KVM before changing anything; not fixed in the MGIT-68 PR because it could not be live-validated there and an unvalidated change to the working Linux backend does not belong in a P0 hotfix.</description>
</invoke>
<parameter name="title">firecracker guests get a route but no /etc/resolv.conf — the default-resolver path is unasserted
nodes.acceptance: Either evidence that a firecracker guest resolves names through its default resolver today (with a test asserting it), or the fix plus a real-VM test that resolves an allowlisted NAME with no explicit server and connects to the pinned IP, live-validated on KVM.

nodes.title: BLOCKING (HyperSwe): host worktree edits must reach a running guest — re-stage on exec, not a live mount
nodes.description: The guest is a launch-time COPY: host edits (raw writes or mgit commits) never reach a booted guest. HyperSwe verified this on the real substrate (hyper-swe/swe PR #68 — a host file written, read back through the guest, mismatch every time) and have stopped their sandboxed dev/review loop with a canary check, because every round after the first would test stale code. This is correct behaviour per the SEC-03 design, not a defect — but it blocks the agent loop the sandbox exists to serve, so the capability gap is real.
nodes.prompt:
HyperSwe's finding is accurate and the current behaviour is BY DESIGN. Do not "fix" it by making the share bidirectional — read the design note first (internal/sandboxd/backend/vzf/hypervisor_darwin.go, "DESIGN TRADE-OFF (copy vs. live)"):

  a virtiofs share could follow the guest's writes back to the live worktree, but it cannot host-side EXCLUDE an in-worktree .mgit/.git, REBIND .mgit to a sandbox-local store, or REJECT an escaping symlink before the guest follows it — all SEC-03 delivery invariants the guest (the attacker) must never violate. virtiofs has no per-entry deny or symlink-resolution-boundary control, so a live share CANNOT FAIL CLOSED. The staged copy enforces every invariant host-side before the guest boots.

So the constraint is: any host->guest propagation must go through the SAME host-side staging that enforces those invariants. That rules out a live mount and rules IN re-staging.

APPROACH TO EVALUATE (pick one, record why):
(a) RE-STAGE ON EXEC — before serving a command, if the host worktree changed, rebuild the staged tree through internal/sandboxd/staging (the existing, tested path that drops in-worktree stores and rejects escaping symlinks) and make the guest see it. Cheapest conceptually because it reuses the enforcement wholesale. Cost: staging on every exec, and deciding what happens to guest-side writes that are not yet landed — they must NOT be silently clobbered.
(b) AN EXPLICIT SYNC VERB — `mgit sandbox sync` (or a flag on run) that re-stages on demand. Predictable and cheap, but the agent loop has to remember to call it; a stale round is then a user error rather than a silent wrong answer.
(c) INCREMENTAL RE-STAGE — only changed paths, same invariant checks. Better steady-state cost, more machinery.

Whatever is chosen: the guest must never observe a partially-updated tree mid-exec, and re-staging must not resurrect files the guest deleted or overwrite guest work that has not been landed. Define that collision policy explicitly — it is the hard part, not the plumbing.

REQUIRED TESTS: a host edit between two execs is visible to the second (the exact HyperSwe repro — write a host file, read it back through the guest, expect a MATCH); the SEC-03 hostile-guest tests still pass unchanged (shared store unreachable, escaping symlink rejected, land is the only bridge) — if any of those weaken, the approach is wrong; guest-side uncommitted work is not silently destroyed; no partially-updated tree is observable.

ALSO: document the semantics wherever the sandbox is described. "The guest is a launch-time copy" is currently discoverable only by probing, which is how HyperSwe found it.

Refs: hyper-swe/swe PR #68, SEC-03, ADR-005, internal/sandboxd/staging, MGIT-61.15.
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`.
nodes.acceptance: A host edit made between two execs is visible to the guest on the next exec, verified with HyperSwe's exact repro (host write -> guest read -> match); every SEC-03 hostile-guest test passes unchanged; the collision policy for un-landed guest-side work is defined, documented and tested; no partially-updated tree is observable mid-exec; the chosen approach and its rationale are recorded; and the copy-vs-live semantics are documented where users read about the sandbox rather than being discoverable only by probing.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Live policy revoke: mutate a running sandbox's egress allowlist without relaunch
nodes.description: HyperSwe's provisioning design grants package-registry egress during setup and revokes it before dev/test runs. Today the only revoke is relaunch, which destroys the provisioned environment — so they run "held-for-the-run" egress with disclosure, a weaker posture than their design intends. A runtime allowlist mutation on the daemon's task binding restores the strict design.
nodes.prompt:
Add the ability to change a RUNNING sandbox's egress policy without relaunching it.

WHY THIS IS TRACTABLE: the authorizer is consulted PER CONNECTION. netgw.go's handleForward calls flowAuthorizer.Authorize for every inbound connection request before completing the handshake, and firecracker's proxy does the equivalent. So a mutated allowlist takes effect on the NEXT flow with no VM involvement — this is a control-plane change, not a data-path one. Established connections are the design question, not the plumbing.

DESIGN DECISIONS TO MAKE AND RECORD:
1. ESTABLISHED FLOWS. Does revoke kill in-flight connections or only refuse new ones? Killing is the stronger guarantee and the one a security-minded caller expects from "revoke"; letting them drain is friendlier and matches how firewalls usually behave. Whichever is chosen must be DOCUMENTED at the verb, because a caller who assumes the other is exposed. Consider making it explicit (--drain vs --kill) rather than picking a default nobody can predict.
2. ATOMICITY. A partially-applied policy must never be observable — a flow must be authorized against the old policy or the new one, never a mixture.
3. AUDIT. Every mutation is an append-only audit event: who, when, what changed, on which task binding. A policy that can change at runtime without a record is worse than one that cannot change at all — this is the thing a reviewer must be able to reconstruct.
4. SURFACE. Likely `mgit sandbox policy set/revoke --task <ID>` plus the equivalent on the daemon control protocol and the MCP tool surface, since an agent is the intended caller. Follow the existing sandbox subcommand conventions.
5. AUTHORITY. Only the HOST may mutate policy. The guest must have no path to widen its own allowlist — verify no control-plane route exposes this to the guest side (SEC-05: host-observed, never guest-asserted).

TESTS: a running sandbox refuses a destination after revoke, with the denial distinguishable by reason (not a dead network — see MGIT-68); it ALLOWS after a grant, returning real bytes; established-flow behaviour matches whatever was chosen and is asserted; the audit record exists and names the change; a guest-side attempt to mutate policy is refused. Real-VM coverage for at least the grant-then-revoke round trip, since that is the sequence HyperSwe runs.

Refs: hyper-swe/swe lane request, SEC-04, SEC-05, FR-17.8, internal/sandboxd/egress/authorizer.go, netgw.go handleForward.
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`.
nodes.acceptance: A running sandbox's egress allowlist can be granted and revoked without relaunch; the next flow is authorized against the new policy; established-flow behaviour is an explicit, documented choice and is tested; mutations are atomic and appear in the append-only audit trail with task binding and change detail; the guest cannot mutate its own policy; and a real-VM test covers the grant-then-revoke round trip HyperSwe actually runs.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Artifact export guest→host: bring guest-built artifacts out without weakening the land airlock
nodes.description: The guest works on a staged copy, so guest-built artifacts (node_modules, build caches) never reach the host. HyperSwe's provisioning cache depends on a once-per-lockfile reuse promise that this breaks: every round re-does work the previous round already did. An explicit "export path from guest to host" verb restores it. Sibling of MGIT-71 (host→guest); this is the other direction.
nodes.prompt:
Add an explicit way to bring a path OUT of a running guest onto the host.

THE SHAPE ALREADY EXISTS: land is the verified guest->host bridge for COMMITTED OBJECTS — the guest writes into a private store and the host pulls, verifies and attests. Artifact export is the same shape for FILES. Reuse that thinking; do not invent a second, weaker bridge. In particular land is currently "the only bridge", and the hostile-guest tests assert exactly that (TestE2E_*_HostileGuest_LandIsOnlyBridge) — those tests will need to be re-stated deliberately rather than deleted, and the new bridge must be as fail-closed as the old one.

THE SECURITY PROBLEM IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM. The guest is the untrusted side. An export verb is a guest->host write path, so:
- The HOST names what to export and where it lands. The guest must not choose the destination — a guest-supplied path is a host-filesystem write primitive.
- Reject escaping symlinks, hardlinks out of the exported subtree, and absolute paths, host-side, BEFORE anything is written. internal/sandboxd/staging already does this in the other direction; reuse its checks rather than writing new ones.
- Decide and document what happens on collision with existing host files (refuse? overwrite? into a quarantine dir the caller moves?). Refusing is the safe default.
- Bound it: size and file-count limits, so an export cannot fill the host disk (T7 resource abuse).
- Audit every export: task binding, path, byte count, when. A file crossing the boundary without a record defeats the audit trail.

ALSO CONSIDER, and record the decision: should exported artifacts carry provenance the way commits do (which sandbox produced them)? The base-digest attestation work (MGIT-61.15 req 7) established the pattern. A node_modules tree with no provenance is a supply-chain artifact of unknown origin sitting in a host cache.

SURFACE: likely `mgit sandbox export --task <ID> <guest-path> <host-path>` plus the MCP equivalent, since an agent is the caller. Follow existing sandbox subcommand conventions.

TESTS: a guest-built tree lands on the host intact; an escaping symlink is refused before any host write; an absolute or traversing guest path is refused; collision policy behaves as documented; limits are enforced; the audit record exists; and the hostile-guest suite still proves the guest cannot write outside the exported destination.

Refs: hyper-swe/swe lane request, MGIT-71 (host->guest, the other direction), SEC-03, SEC-10, internal/sandboxd/staging, the land airlock.
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`.
nodes.acceptance: A host-initiated verb exports a named guest path to a host-named destination; escaping symlinks, hardlinks out of the subtree, and absolute/traversing guest paths are refused host-side before any write; collision policy and size/count limits are documented and enforced; every export is in the append-only audit trail with task binding, path and size; the hostile-guest tests are re-stated deliberately (not deleted) and still prove the guest cannot write outside the destination; and the provenance decision for exported artifacts is recorded.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: libkrun host↔child control channel: the daemon cannot reach the in-child egress authorizer
nodes.description: MGIT-72's premise — that live policy revoke is "a control-plane change, not a data-path one" — holds only where the daemon owns the egress stack. On libkrun, the MACOS DEFAULT backend, the authorizer is built and consulted inside the VM CHILD PROCESS (a consequence of krun_start_enter consuming the process, MGIT-61.8), and wireEgress is a no-op off Linux. So the daemon has no route to the running policy and live revoke cannot work there at all. This is the same backend asymmetry that MGIT-71 hit, and it blocks the capability on the platform HyperSwe actually runs.
nodes.prompt:
Design and build a host->child control channel for the libkrun backend, so the daemon can act on a RUNNING sandbox's in-child state.

THE STRUCTURAL CAUSE, so nobody re-derives it: krun_start_enter never returns and consumes the process, so each libkrun VM runs in a re-exec'd CHILD (MGIT-61.8). The netstack egress gateway and its authorizer live in that child — which is correct, because the gateway's lifetime must match the VM's exactly. The consequence is that the daemon, which owns the CLI/MCP surface and the task bindings, has no way to reach the thing enforcing policy. `wireEgress` is a no-op off Linux for the same reason.

FIRST USE CASE: MGIT-72 (live policy revoke). Do not build only for that — the same channel is what any future "act on a running sandbox" verb needs, and getting the shape wrong once costs twice.

DESIGN CONSTRAINTS:
- HOST-INITIATED ONLY. The child must never be able to push state the daemon then trusts, and the GUEST must never reach this channel at all. MGIT-72 proved the guest cannot widen its own policy by a dependency assertion; that property must survive this change — re-run that assertion, and make sure its positive control still fires.
- The channel is a per-VM host-side artifact with the same lifetime and residue rules as the rest (SEC-10: nothing left after teardown). Note the existing per-VM unix sockets already hit the sun_path length limit once — reuse the state-dir path discipline rather than inventing new paths.
- Fail closed: if the channel is unavailable, a policy mutation must REPORT FAILURE, never silently succeed while the running VM keeps the old policy. A revoke that reports success without taking effect is worse than one that errors.
- The child applies mutations atomically — a flow is authorized against the old ruleset or the new one, never a mixture. The daemon-side equivalent already works this way; match it.

ALSO SETTLE: whether the same channel serves MGIT-73's artifact export on libkrun, or whether export uses a different path. MGIT-71 established "the host decides WHAT, the backend decides HOW" — check whether export hits the same asymmetry before assuming one mechanism fits both. Firecracker delivers the worktree as an ext4 image built at launch, so it will not.

TESTS: a policy mutation on a RUNNING libkrun sandbox takes effect on the next flow, proven on a real VM (allow -> revoke -> refused -> re-grant -> admitted, with the denial distinguishable by reason from a dead network); an unavailable channel fails closed with an actionable error; no residue after teardown; the guest still cannot reach the channel or widen its policy; concurrent mutation and authorization are race-free (-race).

Refs: MGIT-72, MGIT-71, MGIT-61.8 (the re-exec child), ADR-010, ADR-011, SEC-04, SEC-05, SEC-10.
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`.
nodes.acceptance: The daemon can mutate a running libkrun sandbox's egress policy and the change takes effect on the next flow, proven on a real VM with allow/revoke/re-grant all asserted and the denial distinguishable by reason; an unavailable channel fails closed with an actionable error rather than reporting false success; mutations are atomic in the child; nothing is left after teardown; the guest can neither reach the channel nor widen its own policy, with the existing dependency assertion and its positive control still passing; concurrency is race-clean; and whether artifact export shares this channel is decided and recorded.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: brew install of mgit fails for a fresh macOS user: untrusted libkrun tap
nodes.description:
The Homebrew formula declares `depends_on "libkrun/krun/libkrun"`. Homebrew refuses to LOAD a formula from an untrusted third-party tap, so resolving that dependency on a machine that does not already have libkrun installed fails before anything is built.

Observed on 2026-08-09 against the freshly-synced v0.4.2 tap:

    $ brew info hyper-swe/tap/mgit
    Error: Refusing to load formula libkrun/krun/libkrun from untrusted tap libkrun/krun.
    Run `brew trust --formula libkrun/krun/libkrun` or `brew trust libkrun/krun` to trust it.

Note the shape of this bug: `brew install --dry-run hyper-swe/tap/mgit` PASSED on the same machine, because libkrun 1.19.4 was already installed and the dependency formula therefore never had to be loaded. Any check run on a developer machine that has already provisioned libkrun is a false green. This is the same species as the release-CI gap in MGIT-69/70 — the state that makes the check pass is exactly the state a first-hour user does not have.

We already know about the trust requirement: .github/workflows/release.yml runs `brew tap libkrun/krun && brew trust libkrun/krun && brew install libkrun` before GoReleaser. The USER-FACING install path never got the same treatment. The formula caveats describe libkrun's NET=1 requirement but print only AFTER a successful install, which is precisely the install that cannot happen.
nodes.prompt:
Fix the first-hour macOS install. Read the description and acceptance criteria in full.

The trap in this ticket is the verification, not the fix. The bug is invisible on any machine that already has libkrun — which is every machine that has ever developed or tested mgit's sandbox, including the one that found it. Establish libkrun-absence explicitly and say how you established it.

Recommend which remedy to take (documented `brew trust` prerequisite vs. making libkrun optional) with your reasoning, and confirm the direction before implementing. The formula caveats already promise "Core mgit (init, commit, worktrees, squash, land) is ready to use" — a user who wants only the commit substrate should not be blocked by a VMM they will never run.

Refs: MGIT-69, MGIT-70 (same species — the state that makes the check pass is the state a first-hour user lacks).
nodes.acceptance:
1. A fresh macOS machine with NO libkrun installed and the libkrun/krun tap NOT trusted can get to a working `mgit` by following the documented install path, with no unexplained Homebrew error.

2. Verified on a machine (or a container/VM/fresh Homebrew prefix) where libkrun is genuinely absent. A pass on a machine that already has libkrun is NOT evidence and must not be accepted as one — state explicitly in the report how libkrun-absence was established.

3. Whichever remedy is chosen is reasoned about rather than defaulted:
   - Document the `brew trust libkrun/krun` prerequisite ahead of the install command in README.md and docs/INSTALL-SANDBOX.md, so the user runs it before hitting the wall; and/or
   - Make libkrun an OPTIONAL dependency so core mgit (init/commit/worktree/squash/land) installs cleanly with no third-party tap at all, and the sandbox is activated as a documented second step.
   The second is likely correct and matches what the caveats already claim ("Core mgit is ready to use") — core mgit does not need libkrun, and today a user who wants only the commit substrate is blocked by a VMM they will never run. Confirm before implementing.

4. Whatever the fix, the failure mode is checked in CI on a runner that does not pre-install libkrun, so this cannot regress silently.

5. If the fix changes the formula body, remember the tap's formula body is MANUAL — brew/mgit.rb in this repo is the source of truth and must be hand-synced. Never touch the mtix formula.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Ship `mgit sandbox sync` — ADR-011 documents a verb the CLI never got
nodes.description:
ADR-011 line 98 states worktree sync runs "automatically before an exec when the host worktree has changed ... plus an explicit `mgit sandbox sync` for control." The automatic half shipped in v0.4.2 and is live-validated. The explicit verb does not exist: `mgit sandbox --help` lists base, exec, grant, grants, image, land, launch, list, published, remove, shell, status — no sync.

Reported by the HyperSwe lane while integrating v0.4.2, and reproduced here against the CLI on main (2026-08-09). No urgency from their side: their integration does not need the verb, and everything else in MGIT-71 verified live against the release — conflict refusal, all three collision classes, and guest-created preservation.

WHY SHIP IT RATHER THAN JUST DELETE THE SENTENCE. HyperSwe's workaround is the argument for the verb: they force a re-stage with a probing no-op exec each round. That IS the verb, spelled awkwardly, and it costs a guest process per round to express. Two things only the explicit verb gives you:
  - re-stage without running anything in the guest;
  - get the conflict report (which paths diverged) WITHOUT an exec — today the only way to discover a conflict is to attempt work and be refused.

ADR-011 has been amended to describe what actually shipped and to point here, so the document stops claiming a verb that does not exist. That amendment is not the fix; this ticket is.
nodes.prompt:
Ship the explicit sync verb ADR-011 already promises.

Read MGIT-71 first — the collision policy, the exec lock, and the truncate-and-rewrite requirement (host-side rename is invisible to a guest on a live virtiofs share) are all settled there and this verb inherits every one of them. You are adding a caller, not a mechanism: if you find yourself writing a second staging path, stop, because that is the drift this ticket is specifically trying to avoid.

The interesting design question is the conflict report, not the copy. HyperSwe cannot currently discover a conflict without attempting an exec and being refused. `--dry-run` should give them the classification for free.

Validate on a real libkrun VM. A green unit suite is not evidence for anything in this subsystem.
nodes.acceptance:
1. `mgit sandbox sync --task <ID>` re-stages the host worktree into a running sandbox and reports what it did: counts per collision class (updated / guest-created preserved), and on conflict, refusal naming every conflicting path.

2. It shares ONE implementation with the pre-exec path — no second staging code path that can drift from the one exec uses. A sync must never be able to deliver what a launch or a pre-exec stage would have refused; that invariant is the whole security argument for staging over a live mount.

3. `--force` matches the pre-exec semantics exactly (overwrite, reporting each path destroyed), and `--dry-run` reports the classification without touching the guest — the conflict report HyperSwe currently cannot get without an exec.

4. Unchanged worktree is a genuine no-op (cheap manifest comparison, no re-stage), and says so rather than reporting phantom work.

5. On firecracker it fails closed with the backend limitation named — the worktree is an ext4 image built at launch and cannot be written into. It must not silently no-op and report success; a sync that claims to have run is how stale code gets executed.

6. MCP parity: an agent is a first-class caller. Update docs/MCP-PARITY.md.

7. Real-VM validation on libkrun: host edit -> sync -> guest reads new content, with the no-op and conflict-refusal cases proven too. And a positive control — a sync that DOES deliver — so a refusal is distinguishable from a broken path.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: mgit commit silently creates an EMPTY commit when nothing is staged — agents lose their work
nodes.description:
Found while dogfooding an mgit worktree for MGIT-75 (worktree /tmp/mgit-75-wt, mgit v0.4.3-0.20260809022710-9d5e21860be7).

`mgit commit -m "..."` with NOTHING staged reports SUCCESS — prints a commit hash, exits 0 — and creates a commit whose tree is byte-identical to its parent. The work is not recorded. Reproduced deliberately, minimal case:

    $ echo friction-probe > FRICTION.txt
    $ mgit commit -m "friction probe: unstaged commit"
    [d0ae42ff] [MGIT:MGIT-75] friction probe: unstaged commit
    $ echo $?
    0
    # FRICTION.txt is absent from the commit tree; `git ls-tree <commit> FRICTION.txt` is empty.

`mgit commit --help` documents `--allow-empty  Allow commit with no staged changes`, which states the intended default: refuse. The default does not refuse. It does the opposite of what the flag implies, without a word.

WHY THIS IS P1 AND NOT A PAPERCUT

1. It is silent and it destroys the substrate's whole value proposition. Two full commits of MGIT-75's work went into empty commits before it was noticed; only a manual `git ls-tree` over the .mgit store caught it. An agent that trusts the exit code has no way to detect this.

2. The generated agent instructions walk agents straight into it. The `mgit work`-generated block in a worktree's CLAUDE.md says:

     "Commit after every coherent step. Run `mgit commit -m "<what changed>"` once a step compiles/passes — the task ID is auto-inherited from this worktree"

   It never mentions `mgit add`. An agent following the instructions mgit itself generates produces a branch of empty commits and a squash patch with zero hunks.

3. The downstream signal is also empty, not wrong. `mgit squash --task-id <ID> --to-git` on such a branch emits a well-formed git format-patch with NO diff hunks, and `git apply` accepts it happily. So the land step succeeds and lands nothing. There is no error anywhere in the chain.

4. `mgit status` reports the files as modified the whole time, so the tool shows the user their changes are pending while commit quietly declines to take them.

SECONDARY: status output is ambiguous about staging. Before `mgit add` the entries render as `  M path` and after as `M   path` — a column shift is the only difference between "will be committed" and "will be silently dropped".
nodes.prompt:
Make `mgit commit` refuse to create an empty commit unless `--allow-empty` is passed, and make the agent-facing instructions mgit generates match how commit actually works.

Reproduce first (do not fix from this description alone — see the bug-report RCA discipline): create an mgit worktree, modify a file WITHOUT `mgit add`, run `mgit commit`, and confirm the resulting commit's tree equals its parent's while the command exits 0.

Scope to consider:
1. `mgit commit` with no staged changes must fail with a non-zero exit and an actionable message naming `mgit add` (and `--allow-empty` for the deliberate case). This is the core fix.
2. The `mgit work`-generated CLAUDE.md block must tell the agent to stage. Either document `mgit add -A` (or explicit paths) before `mgit commit`, or give `mgit commit` a stage-and-commit flag and document that. Decide which, and say why — an agent loop that needs two commands per step will drop one.
3. Consider whether `mgit squash --to-git` should warn when it produces a patch with no hunks. A land step that silently lands nothing is the same failure one layer down.
4. Consider making `mgit status` state the staged/unstaged split in words rather than by column position.

Refs: MGIT-75 (found during), MGIT-26 (dogfood pilot), MGIT-32/33 (previous defects found the same way)
nodes.acceptance:
1. `mgit commit` with no staged changes exits non-zero and names the remedy (`mgit add`), with a test that pins the exit code AND the empty-tree condition — not just the message.

2. `mgit commit --allow-empty` still succeeds with no staged changes (the flag keeps its documented meaning).

3. A regression test proves the positive path records content: after `mgit add <path>` + `mgit commit`, the commit's tree DIFFERS from its parent and contains the file. The bug shipped because nothing asserted that a commit actually carries a change.

4. The CLAUDE.md block generated by `mgit work` describes a sequence that, followed literally by an agent with no other knowledge, produces commits that contain the work. Verify by following it literally in a fresh worktree.

5. Verified end-to-end: in a fresh mgit worktree, make a change, follow the generated instructions verbatim, then `mgit squash --task-id <ID> --to-git` and confirm the patch has the expected diff hunks.

nodes.title: Live-validate firecracker live egress policy revoke on real KVM hardware
nodes.description: MGIT-72 shipped live egress policy mutation (grant/revoke without relaunch) with kill-by-default and --drain opt-in. The libkrun backend is proven on hardware. The firecracker backend is implemented, unit-tested, and has a full mirror e2e test written and compiling, but that test has never been run on hardware because it needs a Linux KVM host with a guest image and net-root.
nodes.prompt:
Run the firecracker real-VM live-policy e2e on the Linux KVM box and record the output.

The tests already exist and compile (GOOS=linux go vet passes); nothing needs writing unless they fail:

  internal/sandboxd/backend/firecracker/livepolicy_e2e_linux_test.go
    TestE2E_Firecracker_Revoke_KillsEstablishedFlow
    TestE2E_Firecracker_Revoke_DrainKeepsEstablishedFlow

They are gated by requireGuestImage + requireNetRoot, so they SKIP on any host without a firecracker guest image and net-root — confirm they actually RAN rather than skipped, because a skip reads as a pass in CI summaries.

WHY THIS IS NOT COVERED BY THE LIBKRUN PASS. The two backends enforce egress by different mechanisms: libkrun terminates the guest's TCP in a userspace netstack inside a re-exec'd VM child, while firecracker steers the guest through tap + iptables REDIRECT into a host-side transparent proxy in the daemon's own process. The FlowRegistry is shared, but what populates it and when is not. A pass on one is not evidence for the other — which is exactly the reasoning that made MGIT-72's own killed=0 result a GA blocker.

ASSERT BOTH HALVES, as on libkrun:
  kill  (default) - the held, data-carrying flow DIES,     host reports killed>=1
  drain (--drain) - the same held flow SURVIVES,           host reports killed=0
and in both cases the NEXT flow is refused by policy (not by a dead network), so "survived" can never be a revoke that silently did nothing.

Note the denial observable differs by construction here: firecracker's redirect completes a handshake with the local proxy which then resets, so the guest sees connect-then-reset rather than libkrun's connect-refused. Assert the CLASS of outcome, not an errno.

ON COMPLETION: update the "Live-VM evidence" section of docs/adr/012-live-egress-policy-mutation.md, which currently states plainly that firecracker is "implemented and reviewed, not proven". Paste the real assertion lines there as was done for libkrun.

Refs: MGIT-72, SEC-04, ADR-012, FR-17.8
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; ADR-010 stays untracked; never `git add -A`.
nodes.acceptance: Both firecracker live-policy e2e tests are shown RUNNING (not skipped) on real KVM hardware with their assertion output recorded; the kill case reports killed>=1 with the guest's held connection dying, the drain case reports killed=0 with it surviving, and both show the next flow refused by policy; ADR-012's evidence section is updated from "not proven" to the actual result.

nodes.title: Coverage is below the CLAUDE.md bar in three real places — and the headline number is partly a measurement artifact
nodes.description:
Measured on main (post MGIT-76/72 merge, macOS arm64, 2026-08-10) with `go test ./... -count=1 -cover`. Whole-tree total from a single profile: **72.5%** against a 90% overall bar. The previously-reported 79.3% and this 72.5% are the same finding measured slightly differently; neither should be acted on before separating the artifact from the shortfall, which this ticket does.

ARTIFACT, not a gap — do not "fix" these:
- `cmd/mgit-guest` 0.0%. The guest supervisor is `*_linux.go`; on macOS its tests do not build, so the package reports zero. It HAS tests (bridge_linux_test.go, net_linux_test.go, serve_linux_test.go) and they run on Linux. Any coverage number taken on a Mac understates the tree by this whole package.
- `internal/sandboxd/backend/vzf` 66.2%, `internal/sandboxd/backend/libkrun`, `internal/sandboxd/backend/firecracker`: their real-VM e2e are env-gated (MGIT_E2E_*) and skip in an ordinary run. The uncovered statements are exercised, just not by the run that produced the number.
- `scripts/e2e/mcpdrive` 0.0% — a test driver, not shipped code.

GENUINE SHORTFALL against the bar in CLAUDE.md:
- `internal/store/git` **76.2%** vs the 95% Store bar. The largest real gap, in the layer with the strictest bar.
- `cmd/mgit` **64.1%** vs the 90% CLI bar.
- `cmd/mgit-sandboxd` **33.0%** — daemon wiring; arguably CLI-tier, and the wiring is what a first-hour user hits.
- `internal/service` **90.3%** vs the 95% Service bar — close, but under.
- `internal/store/index` 81.0%, `internal/store/gitref` 81.0% vs 95%.
- `internal/sandboxd/imageinstall` 61.2%, `provision` 74.7%, `staging` 76.2% — staging is load-bearing for SEC-03 and deserves better than 76%.

Not release-gating: the shipped behaviour is covered by real-VM e2e that a coverage profile cannot see. It is a standing quality debt in the layers whose bar is highest.
nodes.prompt:
Close the coverage gap where it is real, and make the number honest where it is not.

FIRST, fix the measurement so the next person does not re-litigate this. A single `go test ./... -coverprofile` on macOS cannot see the Linux-only guest package or the env-gated real-VM suites, so it reports a number nobody should act on directly. Produce a measurement recipe (a make target is the obvious home) that either runs on Linux with the e2e env set, or excludes what it provably cannot measure and SAYS which packages it excluded and why. A coverage number that silently omits a package is the same species of defect as a test that skips and reads as a pass.

THEN raise the three that matter, in this order — depth first, not breadth:
1. `internal/store/git` (76.2% -> 95%). Strictest bar, largest gap, and the layer where a defect is a lost-history defect.
2. `internal/sandboxd/staging` (76.2%). Every SEC-03 invariant is enforced here; the uncovered branches are the refusal paths.
3. `cmd/mgit` (64.1%) and `cmd/mgit-sandboxd` (33.0%). Command wiring is what a first-hour user meets.

Do NOT write coverage-chasing test files — CLAUDE.md rule 12. Name tests after the behaviour they verify. If a branch is genuinely unreachable, say so at the branch rather than contorting a test to enter it. The MGIT-9 fault-injection harness (faultStorer, idx.Close()) already exists for the defensive-wrap tail; reuse it rather than inventing a second one.

Refs: MGIT-9 (the earlier coverage sprint and its harness), CLAUDE.md coverage table

nodes.title: Agent Worktrees (Multi-Agent Parallel Development)
nodes.prompt:
CONTEXT: Agent Worktrees (Multi-Agent Parallel Development) — Wave 11

You are building linked worktree support so multiple LLM coding agents can work in parallel on different tasks without interfering with each other. The CLI mirrors standard git worktree semantics so agents trained on git documentation can use them without friction.

DESIGN DECISION (ADR-004): Pluggable WorktreeManager interface. v1 is mgit-managed (filesystem + SQLite registry). v2 will swap in go-git v6 native worktrees when v6 matures (currently too new — 3 weeks old, experimental x/ prefix, known bugs #1406/#1190).

ARCHITECTURE:
  internal/model/worktree.go — WorktreeInfo struct, WorktreeAddOptions, WorktreeManager interface (Add/List/Remove/Prune/Resolve).
  internal/store/index/worktrees.go — SQLite worktrees table: path TEXT PK, name TEXT UNIQUE, branch TEXT, task_id TEXT UNIQUE, agent_id TEXT, created_at TEXT, last_commit_at TEXT.
  internal/worktree/manager.go — v1 WorktreeManager implementation. Creates .mgit/worktrees/<name>/ directories with HEAD, task_binding, agent_id, created_at, locked files.
  internal/service/worktree_service.go — Lifecycle orchestration: auto-create branch on worktree add, task binding enforcement, commit integration (auto-inherit task ID), squash/rollback hooks.
  cmd/mgit/worktree.go — CLI: mgit worktree add/list/remove/prune.
  internal/mcp/ — MCP tools: mgit_worktree_add, mgit_worktree_list, mgit_worktree_remove.

KEY RULES (FR-16):
  1. Every worktree bound to exactly one task (ErrTaskAlreadyBound if duplicate).
  2. No branch sharing between worktrees (ErrBranchInUse).
  3. Commits from worktree auto-inherit bound task ID (ErrTaskMismatch if --task conflicts).
  4. Auto-remove worktree on squash completion (FR-16.7).
  5. Main worktree always present, no implicit task binding (FR-16.12).

nodes.title: `mgit commit -a` sweeps mgit's OWN generated scaffolding into the landed patch
nodes.description:
Found while verifying the MGIT-77 fix end to end (2026-08-10, mgit built from main after the MGIT-77 merge).

`mgit work <path> --task <ID>` writes a GENERATED, worktree-specific block into the worktree's `CLAUDE.md` (`<!-- BEGIN mgit-sandbox (generated; do not edit) -->`) plus `.claude/settings.json`. Neither is ignored. MGIT-77 now prescribes `mgit commit -a` as THE agent loop — and `-a` stages every change including new files — so the scaffolding is committed to `task/<ID>` and appears in the exported patch:

    $ mgit work /tmp/wt --task-id T-3
    $ cd /tmp/wt && echo 'func Answer() int { return 42 }' > feature.go
    $ mgit commit -a -m "add feature"        # the instruction mgit itself generates
    $ cd /tmp/proj && mgit squash --task-id T-3 --to-git
    diff --git a/CLAUDE.md b/CLAUDE.md       <-- mgit's own scaffolding, landing
    @@ -0,0 +1,16 @@
    diff --git a/feature.go b/feature.go
    @@ -0,0 +1 @@
    +func Answer() int { return 42 }

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW rather than before. Until MGIT-77 the loop was a bare `mgit commit`, which recorded nothing at all — so nobody noticed, and the two agents working MGIT-72 and MGIT-73 in mgit-dev worktrees BOTH reported, unprompted, that they had deliberately left CLAUDE.md unstaged. They were working around this by hand. With `-a` prescribed they cannot: the instruction mgit generates now guarantees mgit's scaffolding lands in the user's repository.

The landed content is also WRONG for the destination, not merely noisy: the block describes one worktree's task binding and this host's sandbox availability ("containment is unavailable here"), which is meaningless on main.

This is the same species as MGIT-77 itself — the generated instructions and the tool's real behaviour disagreeing — and it was introduced by MGIT-77's own remedy, which is exactly when it is cheapest to fix.</parameter>
</invoke>
nodes.acceptance: In a fresh worktree AND in a repo with a pre-existing CLAUDE.md: `mgit work` then edit a source file then `mgit commit -a` produces a commit containing ONLY the user's change, and `mgit squash --to-git` produces a patch with no mgit-generated scaffolding in it. `.claude/settings.json` is covered too. A regression test pins both shapes, and the behaviour for a user who deliberately wants to commit their own CLAUDE.md edits is decided, documented and tested.

nodes.title: Exported artifacts lose their executable bit on macOS/libkrun (virtio-fs mode mapping)
nodes.description: Measured while building MGIT-73's real-VM export e2e on macOS/HVF with libkrun 1.19.4: a file the guest writes with mode 0755 is presented to the HOST on the virtio-fs share as 0600. Artifact export reproduces the modes the host observes (deliberately — inventing the guest's intended mode would be worse), so an exported node_modules tree's .bin scripts arrive on the host non-executable. This blunts the provisioning-cache reuse MGIT-73 exists to enable, for any artifact whose value includes executables. See the annotation for the full investigation brief.
nodes.acceptance: The cause is established by measurement (not inference) on at least libkrun/macOS, the vzf behaviour is checked, and either the modes survive an export or the limitation is documented at the verb and in ADR-011 with the reason. No exported file is given a mode that was not observed somewhere real.

nodes.title: `mgit checkout -b` can refuse inside a worktree because of mgit's OWN generated block
nodes.description:
Identified while fixing MGIT-80 (2026-08-10) and deliberately left out of that fix's scope; recorded in ADR-013's consequences.

MGIT-80 stopped mgit's generated scaffolding from being BULK-STAGED, which is the right choke point for `add -A` / `add .` / `commit -a`. It does not change what the store considers DIRTY. So a tracked `CLAUDE.md` carrying mgit's generated block still counts as a dirty tracked path for the checkout guard (`dirtyTrackedPaths`), and `mgit checkout -b <branch>` from inside such a worktree can refuse.

The irony is the point: `mgit checkout -b` is the course-correction step that the very same generated block instructs the agent to use — "Course-correct, don't restart... `mgit checkout -b <branch>` to fork a new line from a good commit". mgit's own instructions can be blocked by mgit's own file.

Only affects a repository that already TRACKS the file mgit injects into (mgit-dev itself, and any project with its own CLAUDE.md). In a fresh worktree the generated file is untracked and the guard does not fire.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Make the checkout guard agree with the staging filter about mgit's generated scaffolding.

Reproduce first: in a project that TRACKS CLAUDE.md, `mgit work` a worktree (so mgit injects its block into the tracked file), then run `mgit checkout -b scratch` from inside that worktree and observe the refusal.

WHY THIS IS NOT A ONE-LINE EXTENSION OF MGIT-80. Bulk-stage filtering is safe because skipping a path only means "do not stage it" — the file on disk is untouched and `mgit status` still tells the truth. The checkout guard is different: it protects against CLOBBERING uncommitted work when the worktree materializes a different commit. Exempting a path from the guard means deciding what happens to that path's content during the checkout, and there are only two honest answers:

1. Materialize the new commit and RE-INJECT the generated block afterwards, so the worktree keeps working wiring for its bound task. mgit owns the block and knows how to regenerate it (internal/agentadapter), so this is coherent — but it must not clobber the USER's own content in the same file. The block has BEGIN/END markers; a merge that preserves everything outside them is the shape to aim for.
2. Keep refusing, but make the refusal actionable — name the generated file, say why it is dirty, and give the exact command that proceeds.

Prefer (1) if the marker-preserving merge is genuinely safe, because it makes the prescribed course-correction loop work without the agent understanding mgit's internals. Fall back to (2) rather than shipping something that can silently eat a user's edits. Whichever you choose, a user edit OUTSIDE the markers must survive; prove it with a test.

Read ADR-013 first — MGIT-80's decision record — and extend it rather than contradicting it. Reuse `agentadapter.GeneratedWorktreeFiles` and the `<worktree>/.mgit/generated` provenance manifest; do not introduce a second notion of what mgit generated.

Refs: MGIT-80, ADR-013, MGIT-24 (linked-worktree commit), internal/store/git/worktree.go (dirtyTrackedPaths)
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">In a project that tracks CLAUDE.md, `mgit checkout -b <branch>` from inside an `mgit work` worktree either succeeds with the generated block correctly present afterwards and any user content outside the markers preserved, or refuses with a message naming the generated file and the exact command to proceed. A regression test covers the tracked-file shape and proves user content outside the markers survives. ADR-013 records the decision.

nodes.title: mgit-sandboxd has no --version flag, and the release checklist assumed it did
nodes.description:
Found running the v0.4.3 post-publish brew smoke test (2026-08-10) against the real tap install.

`mgit-sandboxd --version` is not a flag. The daemon answers:

    flag provided but not defined: -version
    Usage of mgit-sandboxd: ...

and exits 2. `mgit --version` works; only the daemon lacks it.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A MISSING CONVENIENCE. The release checklist's Gatekeeper smoke step (MGIT-64) ran `./mgit --version && ./mgit-sandboxd --version`, whose entire purpose is to distinguish "the binary executed" from "Gatekeeper SIGKILLed a quarantined ad-hoc-signed binary". A spurious non-zero exit is indistinguishable, to anyone following the checklist, from the failure the step exists to catch — and it would be read as "the archive shipped broken again". The checklist has been corrected to use `--help` (exit 0), with the reason recorded inline.

Operationally it is also just a gap: the daemon is shipped in every archive and installed by Homebrew beside `mgit`, and an operator debugging a sandbox cannot ask the running daemon what build it is.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Give `mgit-sandboxd` a `--version` flag that matches `mgit`'s.

Read how `cmd/mgit` builds its version string (the same ldflags-stamped commit/date the release sets) and mirror it exactly, so the two binaries from one archive report the same build in the same format. They are released together and a mismatch is its own confusion.

The daemon parses flags with the stdlib `flag` package, so this is a small addition — but note the daemon's flags are also its operational surface, and the version path must print and exit 0 WITHOUT starting a daemon, binding a socket, or touching the host root.

While you are there, check whether `--version` should also report the backend the binary links (libkrun vs firecracker vs none). An operator diagnosing "why does my sandbox not launch" is usually asking exactly that, and the daemon already verifies its VMM capabilities at startup (`vmm_capabilities`). Decide and say why.

AFTER IT LANDS: `docs/release/RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md`'s downloaded-archive smoke step currently uses `./mgit-sandboxd --help >/dev/null` with a note explaining why; put it back to `--version` and drop the note.

Refs: MGIT-64 (the Gatekeeper smoke this broke), MGIT-44, cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">`mgit-sandboxd --version` prints the same version/commit/date format `mgit --version` does and exits 0 without starting the daemon or binding anything; a test pins both the exit code and the format's agreement with `mgit`; the backend-reporting question is decided and recorded; and the release checklist's smoke step is restored to `--version` with the explanatory note removed.</parameter>
</invoke>

nodes.title: The post-publish smoke steps are prose nothing executes, and they have drifted three times
nodes.description:
Three separate instances in one release cycle (2026-08-10/11) of a release-checklist instruction not matching the binaries it describes:

1. **`mgit-sandboxd --version` did not exist** (MGIT-83). Step 7's Gatekeeper smoke chained it with `&&`, so it exited 2 — and that step's whole job is distinguishing "the binary ran" from "Gatekeeper SIGKILLed it", making a missing flag indistinguishable from the failure being tested.
2. **Then the fix re-broke it in the other direction.** The step was restored to `--version` immediately after MGIT-83 landed, but steps 6-8 are POST-PUBLISH — they verify the artifact just released, which for v0.4.3 predates the flag. Corrected by splitting the liveness probe (`--help`, works on every version ever shipped) from the build cross-check (`--version`, v0.4.4+).
3. **`MGIT_GUEST_CMDLINE` was omitted** from the documented posture invocation (found by MGIT-78). An image registered without it boots a kernel with no `root=` and no `init=`, and the only symptom is `guest vsock not ready within 15s` — a failure that looks like a broken sandbox rather than a bad instruction.

Plus the standing one MGIT-78 already fixed: the checklist asserted "CI cannot run these" for the Linux live pass, which had been false since GitHub enabled nested virtualization on hosted runners.

THE COMMON CAUSE. These steps are prose in a markdown file. Nothing runs them, so nothing can notice when the binaries move underneath. Every instance was found by a human (or agent) hand-executing the step and hitting the failure — which is exactly the discovery path a release checklist exists to avoid. Note that the parts of the release gate that ARE scripts (`scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh`, the install-channel e2e, the new `sandbox-live-linux` job) have not drifted, because CI runs them every time.

This matters more than a documentation nit: a checklist step that fails spuriously trains the operator to ignore it, and these particular steps are the last line before users get the artifact.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Turn the post-publish smoke steps into a script the release runs, so they cannot drift from the binaries.

Read `docs/release/RELEASE-CHECKLIST.md` steps 6-8 and `scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh` first — the latter is the model: it gates gracefully, prints an unambiguous PASS line, and CI asserts on that line rather than on an exit code alone.

SCOPE, and the honest constraint on it. Not all of steps 6-8 can run in CI, and pretending otherwise would repeat the mistake this ticket is about:
- **Step 7's Gatekeeper quarantine check genuinely cannot run on a hosted runner** — it needs a real download onto a Mac that did not build the release, and `com.apple.quarantine` is not set by `scp` or a build directory. What CAN be scripted is the *invocation*, so a human runs one command instead of hand-copying four; and the script can set the quarantine attribute explicitly to at least exercise the kill path deterministically. Decide what is honestly automatable and say plainly what is not.
- **Step 6 (`brew install` on a clean machine)** is partly covered by `scripts/brew-install-no-libkrun.sh` in ci.yml. Check what it does and does not assert, and extend it rather than writing a second one.
- **Step 8 (libkrun `NET=1`)** is a one-line `nm` check and is trivially scriptable.

REQUIREMENTS for whatever you write:
- A version-liveness probe must NOT depend on a feature flag the artifact might predate. That is the specific defect in instance 2 above: the probe answers one bit (did it execute), so use something every shipped version supports, and keep feature-dependent assertions separate and explicitly version-gated.
- Print one unambiguous PASS line and make a SKIP loud, on the `sandbox_posture.sh` pattern — a skip that reads as a pass is the recurring failure in this repo.
- Where a step stays manual, the checklist should point at the script and say WHY the rest cannot be automated, so the boundary is a recorded decision rather than an omission.

Refs: MGIT-83, MGIT-78, MGIT-64, MGIT-65, scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh, scripts/brew-install-no-libkrun.sh
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">The scriptable parts of post-publish steps 6-8 run from a script with an unambiguous PASS line and a loud SKIP; the version-liveness probe works against every shipped release including ones predating `mgit-sandboxd --version`; feature-dependent assertions are separately version-gated; the checklist points at the script and records why any remaining step must stay manual; and whatever can run in CI does.</parameter>
</invoke>

nodes.title: Sync/export capability is inferred from a directory's existence, not declared by the backend
nodes.description:
Noticed while verifying the backend matrix for a customer deployment (2026-08-11). Not a live defect — the current behaviour is correct — but the correctness rests on a coincidence that nothing enforces.

`microvm.stagedTreePath(stateDir)` decides whether a backend can propagate host changes into a running guest by checking whether `<stateDir>/worktree-staging` exists as a directory. `syncLocked` and `ExportArtifact` both gate on it, and `syncBeforeExec` treats an empty result as "launch-time-copy backend, unchanged behaviour".

firecracker ALSO creates `<stateDir>/worktree-staging` — it is the input tree mke2fs packs `worktree.ext4` from (backend/firecracker/worktree_image.go, same constant name, same parent directory). It happens to remove it on a `defer` once the image is built, so by the time a VM is running the directory is gone and sync correctly reports ErrSyncUnsupported.

THE FRAGILITY: if that `defer os.RemoveAll(stagingDir)` were ever dropped, reordered, or failed, `stagedTreePath` would return a real path on firecracker and the manager would conclude the backend supports sync. It would then write into the mkfs INPUT directory — which the guest does not mount, because the guest mounted an ext4 image built at launch — and report success with a list of updated paths.

That is precisely the failure ADR-011 names as the reason the verb must fail closed: "a sync that claims to have run is how stale code gets executed." The guard against it is currently one deferred cleanup in a different package that shares a constant's value by coincidence rather than by reference.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Make the sync/export capability something a backend DECLARES, not something the manager infers from a filesystem side effect.

Reproduce the fragility first so the fix is aimed at something real: comment out the `defer os.RemoveAll(stagingDir)` in internal/sandboxd/backend/firecracker/worktree_image.go, launch a firecracker sandbox, and run `mgit sandbox sync`. It should report success while the guest sees nothing.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIX. microvm.Config already carries a Backend name and the Hypervisor seam. Add an explicit capability — a field on Config, or a method on the Hypervisor/VM interface — that says whether the worktree is delivered as a shared host directory or as a launch-time image, and have syncLocked/ExportArtifact/syncBeforeExec gate on THAT. `stagedTreePath` can still resolve the path once the capability says there is one; it must stop being the thing that decides.

Note the two constants named `stagingDirName`/`stagedTreeName` in different packages share a value but not a definition. Whatever you do, make the relationship explicit — either one exported constant both use, or two clearly independent names. A silent agreement between packages is what makes the current arrangement look safe when it is only lucky.

TESTS: a fake backend that declares "launch-time image" is refused even when a `worktree-staging` directory exists beside it; a fake that declares "shared directory" is served; and the firecracker manager reports the image capability regardless of what is on disk mid-launch.

Refs: MGIT-71, MGIT-73, MGIT-76, ADR-011, internal/sandboxd/backend/microvm/sync.go, internal/sandboxd/backend/firecracker/worktree_image.go
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">Backend worktree-delivery capability is declared explicitly and sync/export/pre-exec-stage gate on the declaration rather than on the presence of a directory; a test proves a launch-time-image backend is refused even with a `worktree-staging` directory present on disk; the shared constant relationship between the microvm and firecracker packages is made explicit or eliminated.</parameter>
</invoke>

nodes.title: AUTHORISED, held: firecracker parity for sync + export — fires only if Path A hits an unbounded upstream wall
nodes.description:
Scoping ticket raised 2026-08-11 while deciding whether the HyperSwe lane can proceed on a customer deployment. Not a defect — both capabilities fail closed correctly, with the backend named — but it is the gap that decides which backend a deployment can use.

WHAT WORKS WHERE TODAY, verified against v0.4.3:
  launch / exec / land          libkrun: yes    firecracker: yes (CI-gated)
  live egress policy            libkrun: yes    firecracker: yes (MGIT-78, hardware-proven)
  host edits -> running guest   libkrun: yes    firecracker: REFUSED
  artifact export               libkrun: yes    firecracker: REFUSED

WHY. libkrun and vzf share the worktree as a host DIRECTORY over virtio-fs, so the host can re-stage into it (MGIT-71/76) and read out of it (MGIT-73). firecracker packs the worktree into an ext4 image at launch (backend/firecracker/worktree_image.go) and the guest mounts that; the host cannot write into a mounted image without corrupting it, and there is no host directory to export from.

WHAT IT COSTS THE AGENT LOOP ON FIRECRACKER. Every exec after launch runs against the launch-time copy. A loop that edits the host worktree between rounds tests stale code — which is exactly the failure HyperSwe reported in MGIT-71 and stopped their sandboxed loop over. Their workaround there (a probing no-op exec to force a re-stage) does not help here either: there is no re-stage on this backend at all. The MGIT-73 provisioning cache (node_modules reuse across rounds) is likewise unavailable.

OPEN QUESTION THAT SETS THE PRIORITY, and it should be answered before any code: does the customer loop actually need per-round re-stage and the artifact cache, or is launch-time-copy plus land sufficient for it? If a fresh sandbox per round is acceptable, this is a performance and ergonomics gap rather than a correctness one, and the honest answer may be "deploy on libkrun" rather than "build this".</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Decide, then scope. Do not start implementing until the first question is answered.

FIRST: establish what the deployment actually needs. Ask the HyperSwe lane directly whether their loop requires (a) host edits reaching an ALREADY-RUNNING guest, and (b) artifact export for the provisioning cache — or whether relaunching a sandbox per round, plus land, covers it. A relaunch is not free (it destroys the provisioned environment, which is the whole reason MGIT-72 exists) but it is a legitimate answer for some loops. Record the answer here.

IF THE ANSWER IS "DEPLOY ON LIBKRUN": close this and document the backend recommendation prominently, including on Linux where firecracker is the default. That is a real outcome, not a cop-out — note that Linux libkrun (`-tags libkrun`) is NOT a validated path today (see the CHANGELOG's standing limitation), so "use libkrun on Linux" is itself work: it would need the same live-VM validation firecracker got in MGIT-78.

IF THE ANSWER IS "FIRECRACKER MUST HAVE PARITY", the mechanism is a guest-mediated stream, and the design constraints are already settled elsewhere — read them before proposing anything:
- SEC-03 says the guest is the untrusted side. MGIT-73's annotation is explicit that export on the virtiofs backends is a host-side READ precisely so the guest gets no say in what leaves. A guest-mediated stream gives it a say, so every invariant must be re-established host-side: the HOST names what is exported and where it lands, escaping symlinks / hardlinks out of the subtree / absolute and traversing paths are rejected before any host write, collisions refuse, and size and file-count ceilings hold.
- The inbound direction has the mirror problem: a guest-mediated re-stage means the guest receives a stream, so the host must still enforce the staging invariants (in-worktree store excluded, .mgit rebound to the sandbox-local store, escaping symlinks rejected) BEFORE the bytes reach the guest.
- MGIT-74's finding stands: do NOT extend the vmctl host→child control channel for this. It is a policy-control hop and this is a data path.
- The hostile-guest suites must be re-stated deliberately, as MGIT-73 did, never deleted.

Whatever is chosen, the capability must remain DECLARED rather than inferred — see MGIT-85, which should land first so the new path cannot accidentally be enabled by a directory appearing on disk.

Real-VM validation on KVM is mandatory: the Linux live gate exists now (MGIT-78, `sandbox-live-linux` in e2e.yml), so there is a place to run it.

Refs: MGIT-71, MGIT-73, MGIT-74, MGIT-78, MGIT-85, SEC-03, ADR-011, internal/sandboxd/backend/firecracker/worktree_image.go
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">The HyperSwe lane's actual requirement is recorded (per-round re-stage and artifact cache needed, or launch-time-copy sufficient). If parity is required: host→guest sync and artifact export work on firecracker through a guest-mediated stream with every SEC-03 invariant enforced host-side, the hostile-guest suites re-stated and passing, and both directions validated on real KVM hardware in the Linux live gate. If not required: the backend recommendation is documented wherever a deployment chooses one, and the Linux-libkrun validation gap is either closed or explicitly scoped.</parameter>
</invoke>

nodes.title: NOW: validate the FULL libkrun column on Linux/KVM — boot, exec, land, policy, sync, export — as a continuous CI gate
nodes.description:
Raised 2026-08-11 as the direct consequence of MGIT-86's decision. The founder accepted "deploy on libkrun" as the near-term answer for the loop that needs host-edits-to-running-guest and artifact export — both of which are libkrun/vzf only. That answer is sound for a macOS pilot and does NOT extend to Linux, because Linux libkrun is unvalidated.

WHAT IS AND IS NOT TRUE TODAY:
- macOS / libkrun (Apple Silicon): live-validated. Full real-VM e2e suite plus the release posture pass.
- Linux / firecracker: live-validated, and CI-gated on every release since MGIT-78.
- Linux / libkrun (`-tags libkrun`): NEVER BOOTED IN VALIDATION. It is not the Linux default. ci.yml's libkrun-linux job build+vets the tagged path so a compile or link regression is caught early — that is a compile check, and it says nothing about whether a VM starts. The CHANGELOG has carried this as a standing limitation since 0.4.2.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW rather than as background debt: before MGIT-86, "which backend on Linux" had one answer (firecracker, validated). After it, a Linux deployment that needs per-round re-stage or the artifact cache has no validated option at all — firecracker cannot do those, and libkrun on Linux is unproven. That is a real fork with no safe branch, and it should be visible before someone hits it during a deployment rather than after.

The good news is that the hard part is already built: MGIT-78 established that GitHub-hosted runners expose /dev/kvm and added the `sandbox-live-linux` job, so there is a place to run this without the dual-boot box.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Establish whether Linux libkrun actually works, on real KVM, and record the answer either way.

This is a validation task first and a fix task only if it fails. Do not start by changing code.

THE SHAPE IS ALREADY SET by MGIT-78 — read that job before writing anything. `e2e.yml`'s `sandbox-live-linux` boots real firecracker microVMs on a hosted ubuntu runner after a udev rule grants access to /dev/kvm. The same runner can host libkrun: it is a linked VMM rather than a separate binary, so the daemon must be built with `-tags libkrun` and libkrun itself installed (built from source on Linux — there is no tap; check what `make test-libkrun` documents).

WHAT TO PROVE, in this order, stopping at the first failure and reporting it rather than working around it:
1. A libkrun microVM BOOTS on Linux/KVM at all — the thing no test has ever asserted.
2. The posture pass: launch -> exec inside the guest -> land round-trip.
3. The two capabilities that motivated this: `mgit sandbox sync` delivers a host edit into a RUNNING guest, and `mgit sandbox export` brings a guest-built tree out. These are the whole reason the question is being asked, so a green boot without them is not an answer.
4. SEC-03 hostile-guest containment, unchanged. A backend that boots but leaks is worse than one that does not boot.

ASSERT IT RAN. Every one of these suites skips gracefully without its prerequisites, and a skip that reads as a pass is this repo's recurring defect — grep for the PASS lines explicitly, as `sandbox-live-linux` does.

IF IT WORKS: wire it as a CI gate alongside the firecracker one, update the CHANGELOG's standing limitation, and document Linux libkrun as the supported backend for loops that need sync/export. That closes MGIT-86's dependency.

IF IT DOES NOT WORK: report precisely where it fails and stop. The decision that follows is the owner's — fix Linux libkrun, or build the firecracker guest-mediated stream (MGIT-86), or tell Linux deployments that per-round re-stage is unavailable. Do not pick one silently by fixing whatever is nearest.

Refs: MGIT-86 (the decision that created this dependency), MGIT-78 (the live gate and the /dev/kvm finding), MGIT-61.13, ADR-010, the CHANGELOG's "Linux libkrun is still not a validated path" limitation
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">Whether a libkrun microVM boots on Linux/KVM is established by a real run and recorded here with output. If it does: the posture pass, sync, export and the SEC-03 hostile-guest suite all pass on Linux/libkrun, asserted to have RUN rather than skipped, wired as a CI gate, and the CHANGELOG's standing limitation is updated. If it does not: the failure point is recorded precisely and the follow-on decision is left to the owner with the options stated.</parameter>
</invoke>

nodes.title: Six sandbox subcommands are unit-only — no e2e script ever invokes them
nodes.description:
Reported 2026-08-11 by a lane that audited the Linux backend end to end, and confirmed against docs/E2E-MATRIX.md.

`mgit sandbox exec`, `shell`, `grants`, `list`, `status`, `remove`, and `image install` are covered by unit tests only. None is invoked by any e2e script — not sandbox_posture.sh, not the install-channel e2e, not the new release smoke.

WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY A COVERAGE NUMBER. Every one of them is a command a user or agent types at a real installed binary, and unit tests exercise the service beneath the CLI rather than the CLI itself. That is exactly the seam where this project's defects keep appearing: MGIT-77 (`mgit commit` reported success for work it never recorded), MGIT-83 (`mgit-sandboxd --version` did not exist while a release-checklist step invoked it), MGIT-65 (the archive shipped no guest binaries, so `sandbox base from` could not compose — the unit tests passed because they ran inside a source checkout). In each case the unit layer was green and the command was broken for a user.

`sandbox status` and `sandbox list` are the ones an operator reaches for FIRST when something is wrong, and `remove` is what they reach for second. A defect in those is discovered at the worst possible moment.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Drive the seven unit-only sandbox subcommands through a real binary in an e2e script.

The point is the CLI surface against a REAL install, not more service-layer tests. Model it on scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh, which already launches a live sandbox — most of these can ride on that same running VM rather than paying for another boot:

  sandbox list      — the launched sandbox appears, with its task binding
  sandbox status    — reports running, and the fields a user acts on
  sandbox exec      — runs a command in the guest and propagates its exit code
  sandbox shell     — proxies stdin/stdout (the posture script's `mgit run` path
                      covers exec indirectly; shell has its own transport)
  sandbox grants    — lists pending capability requests (drive one by attempting
                      an off-allowlist connection first, so the list is non-empty)
  sandbox remove    — tears down, and `list` afterwards shows it gone
  sandbox image install — its own flow; needs a bundle, so it may belong in the
                      install-channel e2e instead. Decide and say which.

ASSERT OBSERVABLE BEHAVIOUR, not exit codes alone. `assert_ok` on a command that
prints nothing useful is how the posture script's own `land` assertion ended up
weaker than its comment claimed (E2E-MATRIX line 88 records exactly that). Check
the output says what the user needs: that `status` names the task, that `remove`
actually removed, that `exec` propagated the guest's exit status rather than the
CLI's.

WHERE IT RUNS: the Linux live gate (`sandbox-live-linux` in e2e.yml) already
boots a real firecracker VM on every push/PR/release, so this can be continuous
rather than manual. Follow its conventions — assert the literal PASS line, and
fail on a SKIP, because a skip that reads as a pass is this repo's recurring
defect.

defects at exactly this seam), docs/E2E-MATRIX.md
