nodes.title: Linux/libkrun: the guest's root overlay is not writable (EOPNOTSUPP), which kills every networked sandbox
nodes.description:
Found by MGIT-87's live validation of Linux/libkrun on real KVM.

On Linux/libkrun a guest process CANNOT create a file anywhere under its writable-root overlay; the create fails with EOPNOTSUPP ("operation not supported"). /tmp (tmpfs) and the mounted worktree share are writable and behave normally.

Measured through the PRODUCTION path (mgit work --sandbox, real debian:12 base composed with `mgit sandbox base from`, read-only root as FR-17.17 intends), not only in a test fixture:

  echo hi > /etc/probe         -> /bin/sh: cannot create /etc/probe: Operation not supported
  echo hi > /tmp/probe         -> ok
  echo hi > ./probe (worktree) -> ok

Guest mount table at the time:
  overlay on / type overlay (rw,relatime,lowerdir=/,upperdir=/mnt/upper,workdir=/mnt/work,uuid=on)
  tmpfs on /tmp type tmpfs (rw,relatime)
  work on <worktree> type virtiofs (rw,relatime)

THE CONSEQUENCE THAT MAKES THIS P1: mgit-guest writes the resolver into /etc/resolv.conf while configuring the guest network (internal/guestnet/guestnet.go writeResolvConf, called from cmd/mgit-guest/serve_linux.go), so it dies on this refusal before it serves:

  {"level":"ERROR","msg":"mgit-guest exited with error","error":"mgit-guest: write /etc/resolv.conf: open /etc/resolv.conf: operation not supported"}

Every --network allowlist and --network open sandbox therefore exits at startup on Linux/libkrun; nine real-VM e2e tests fail on it (the whole net + live-policy set). --network none is unaffected. `mgit work --sandbox --network allowlist` still reports a launched sandbox, and only the first exec fails — worth deciding whether launch should fail closed instead.

Reproduced identically in three environments, so it is not an artifact of one: a hosted runner inside an ubuntu:20.04 container with /dev/kvm passed through, a hosted runner on the bare host as an unprivileged user, and a bare-metal KVM box. macOS/libkrun is unaffected — the same code path works there.

NOT ROOT-CAUSED, deliberately: MGIT-87 was a validation task and stopping at the failure was the instruction. The obvious suspect is overlayfs's upper/work layer landing on a filesystem that cannot support it (libkrun's Linux virtio-fs) rather than on the tmpfs the scratch mounter intends — see makeRootWritableWith + mountScratch in cmd/mgit-guest/serve_linux.go. Confirm where /mnt/upper actually lives inside the guest before changing anything.
nodes.prompt:
Establish why creating a file under the guest's root overlay returns EOPNOTSUPP on Linux/libkrun, then fix it or record why it cannot be fixed.

Start by MEASURING, not patching: boot a sandbox on Linux/libkrun and determine which filesystem /mnt/upper and /mnt/work are really on (the scratch mounter intends tmpfs; if the tmpfs mount silently did not happen, the overlay upper is the virtiofs root share, and overlayfs over such an upper is exactly where EOPNOTSUPP comes from). `mgit run -- /bin/sh -c 'cat /proc/mounts'` inside the guest, before and after switch_root if you can.

If it is the scratch mount: fix it and the networked column opens up with it — re-run the KNOWN_GAP tripwire in scripts/e2e/libkrun_linux_column.sh, which will go RED on success by design, and move the network tests into VALIDATED along with the tables in README.md, docs/INSTALL-SANDBOX.md and the CHANGELOG in the same commit.

If it is libkrun's virtio-fs itself, say so with the evidence and propose the alternative (e.g. a disk-backed COW upper, or writing the resolver somewhere that is not the image root).

Refs: MGIT-87 (the validation that found it), FR-17.17, MGIT-68, ADR-010
nodes.acceptance: The filesystem backing the overlay upper on Linux/libkrun is established by measurement and recorded. Either a guest can create files under its root (and the networked e2e set passes, with the CI column and the shipped tables updated together), or the reason it cannot is recorded with the evidence and the alternative is proposed.

nodes.title: Linux/libkrun: `sandbox sync` delivers content but not creates/deletes — the guest reads a file the sync reported deleted
nodes.description:
Found by MGIT-87's live validation of Linux/libkrun on real KVM, by the new collision-class e2e written for that task.

On Linux/libkrun, a `mgit sandbox sync` that CHANGES an existing file's content reaches the running guest correctly (TestE2E_Libkrun_RealVM_Sync_HostEditReachesTheRunningGuest passes there). A sync that CREATES or DELETES a path does not: the verb reports the delete as applied, and a guest process reading that path still gets the old file.

Evidence, from TestE2E_Libkrun_RealVM_Sync_RefusesADeleteOfAPathTheGuestChanged on Linux/KVM:

  report.Deleted == ["seed.txt"]   (the production verb's own report)
  guest /bin/cat <worktree>/seed.txt -> exit 0, "host work"

The same test passes on macOS/libkrun, where the guest's reader exits 1 for the removed path. So this is a Linux-specific difference in what a running guest observes through the virtio-fs share, not a defect in worktreesync's plan (the plan is right — it is the guest's view that is stale).

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS: this is precisely the silent-staleness failure MGIT-76's real-VM e2e exists to catch — the host tree is correct, the report says success, and the agent executes stale code. A loop that removes a file and re-runs tests would test the removed file.

Reproduced identically on a hosted runner (inside a container as root, and on the bare host as an unprivileged user) and on a bare-metal KVM box.

Gated: `TestE2E_Libkrun_RealVM_Sync_RefusesADeleteOfAPathTheGuestChanged` is a KNOWN_GAP tripwire in scripts/e2e/libkrun_linux_column.sh, so CI fails if this starts passing without the shipped tables being updated.

NOT ROOT-CAUSED, deliberately (MGIT-87 was a validation task). First suspect is guest-side dentry caching over libkrun's Linux virtio-fs — a namespace change made host-side is not invalidated in the guest, while a content change is picked up. Compare the FUSE entry/attr timeouts libkrun's Linux fs device uses with its macOS one before changing mgit code.
nodes.prompt:
Establish why host-side creates and deletes in the staged tree are invisible to a RUNNING guest on Linux/libkrun, while content changes are not, then either fix it or state the limit precisely enough for the docs to stand on.

Measure first. Inside a live sandbox, have the guest stat a delivered path, delete it host-side, and stat again — with and without dropping the guest's caches — to separate "the host write never reached the share" from "the guest cached the dentry". libkrun's Linux virtio-fs FUSE timeouts are the first place to look; mgit may have no say in them.

If mgit can fix it (a different staging write strategy, an explicit invalidation, a mount option): the tripwire in scripts/e2e/libkrun_linux_column.sh will go RED when the test starts passing, by design — move it to VALIDATED and update README.md, docs/INSTALL-SANDBOX.md and the CHANGELOG in the same commit.

If it cannot be fixed at our layer, the honest outcome may be that `sandbox sync` must REFUSE (or loudly warn) on Linux/libkrun when the plan contains creates or deletes, rather than report success for work the guest will not see. A sync that claims to have run is how stale code gets executed — that is this feature's stated failure mode.

Refs: MGIT-87 (the validation that found it), MGIT-76, MGIT-71, ADR-011
nodes.acceptance: Why creates/deletes do not reach a running guest on Linux/libkrun is established by measurement and recorded. Either they do reach it (with the CI column and the shipped tables updated together), or the verb no longer reports success for a plan whose creates/deletes the guest will not observe.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Linux/libkrun: `mgit run -- <bare command>` resets the guest exec channel; only absolute paths work
nodes.description:
Found by MGIT-87's live validation of Linux/libkrun on real KVM, and it is the reason scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh fails there.

A command that needs resolving against the guest's PATH kills the exec connection. The same sandbox, moments apart, on a real debian:12 base:

  mgit run -- echo ok
    mgit run: sandbox exec: sandbox exec: libkrun exec: guest exec: read frame:
    read unix @->/tmp/mgit-0/.../v1024.sock: read: connection reset by peer   (rc=1)

  mgit run -- /bin/echo ok        -> "ok"  (rc=0)
  mgit run -- /bin/sh -c 'echo ok'-> "ok"  (rc=0)

Reproduced twice in the same run, and it is what made the posture script die immediately after "== launch a task sandbox and exec inside it ==" on both a hosted runner and the bare-metal box.

WHY IT MATTERS: this is the everyday form. `mgit run -- npm test`, `mgit run -- go build`, and every agent shim that routes a plain command through `mgit run` take this path. An agent on Linux/libkrun would see its very first command fail with a transport error that names nothing it can act on.

WHAT IS KNOWN:
- The VM SURVIVES: the next exec on the same sandbox succeeds, so mgit-guest as a whole is not dying — only that connection's handler.
- The only code difference between the working and failing forms is internal/guest/supervisor.go's lookPathIn(): a program containing a path separator is returned unchanged, anything else is resolved by os.Stat-ing each PATH entry (/usr/local/sbin, /usr/local/bin, /usr/sbin, /usr/bin, /sbin, /bin) with isExecutable().
- A "not found" outcome is supposed to be a clean start-failure Result frame, not a dropped connection, so the reset points at something worse than a failed lookup — a panic in the connection handler is the obvious suspect.
- macOS/libkrun is unaffected; the posture pass uses this exact bare form there.

NOT ROOT-CAUSED, deliberately: MGIT-87 was a validation task. The next step is cheap — read the per-VM console log (mgit-guest's stderr) right after a failing bare exec; an unrecovered panic will be sitting in it.

Gated: the posture script is run by e2e.yml's sandbox-live-linux-libkrun job as a KNOWN-GAP tripwire, asserting it still fails with this signature, so a fix turns CI red until the capability tables are updated.
nodes.prompt:
Find out why resolving a bare command against the guest PATH drops the exec connection on Linux/libkrun, then fix it.

Reproduce first (it is reliable): launch a sandbox on Linux/libkrun with a real OCI base and run `mgit run -- echo ok`, then `mgit run -- /bin/echo ok`. Immediately read the per-VM console log — mgit-guest's stderr lands there, and an unrecovered panic in the exec connection handler would explain a reset that leaves the VM alive.

Look hard at internal/guest/supervisor.go's lookPathIn/isExecutable running over an overlay-backed root, and at whether the guest's connection handler recovers panics at all. A failed lookup must come back as a start-failure Result frame — the caller cannot act on "connection reset by peer".

When it is fixed: scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh will start PASSING on Linux/libkrun, which turns the tripwire in scripts/e2e/libkrun_linux_column.sh RED by design. Promote the posture back to a required step and update the capability tables in README.md, docs/INSTALL-SANDBOX.md and the CHANGELOG in the same commit.

Refs: MGIT-87 (the validation that found it), FR-17.11, ADR-010
nodes.acceptance: `mgit run -- <bare command>` either executes in the guest on Linux/libkrun, or fails with a classified, actionable error rather than a dropped connection — and scripts/e2e/sandbox_posture.sh passes there, with the CI gate and the capability tables updated together.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: `mgit work --sandbox` reports a launched sandbox whose guest never started — launch must fail closed
nodes.description:
Raised from MGIT-89, where this was the thing that made a broken backend look fine for weeks.

`mgit work --sandbox` (and `mgit sandbox launch`) return success as soon as the VMM is up. Manager.Launch does not wait for the guest to bind its vsock listener — the sync e2e says so in a comment and works around it with its own waitGuestBooted. So when mgit-guest dies during startup, the CLI prints "Launched sandbox <id> for task <T> (created)" and the operator believes containment is established. The first `mgit run` then fails with a transport error that names a socket, not a cause.

That is exactly how MGIT-89 presented: every networked sandbox on Linux/libkrun was dead on arrival, and the launch command said nothing.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: the substrate's contract is fail-closed. `mgit run` already refuses to fall back to the host when a sandbox is unavailable (NFR-17.6) precisely because a silent host execution would be a containment breach. A launch that reports success for a guest that is not serving breaks the same contract one step earlier, and it is the step the operator reads.

THE DECISION TAKEN (MGIT-89, and the reasoning, so it is not relitigated from scratch): launch SHOULD fail closed. Not by guessing — by confirming. Launch already waits for the VMM; it should additionally wait, bounded, for the guest to bind its exec port, and on timeout tear the sandbox down and report the failure with the tail of the per-VM console log, which is where mgit-guest's own error already lands ("mgit-guest exited with error: ...").

The cost is ~1s of launch latency, which is small against an operator or agent proceeding against a sandbox that does not exist. The obvious objection — that a slow guest would now fail a launch that used to "work" — is not a real loss: that launch produced a sandbox no exec could use.

NOT IN SCOPE HERE: changing Manager.Exec's own readiness wait, which is correct and should stay.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Make a launch that produces a non-serving guest fail, loudly, instead of reporting success.

Manager.Launch should wait — bounded, a few seconds — for the guest's exec port to accept, then return. On timeout: stop the VM, remove the sandbox, and return an error carrying the TAIL OF THE CONSOLE LOG, because mgit-guest's own startup error is already sitting there and is the actual diagnosis (MGIT-89's was "mgit-guest: write /etc/resolv.conf: operation not supported").

Reuse rather than reinvent: Manager.Exec already has a guest-readiness wait, and the libkrun sync e2e has waitGuestBooted. One implementation, used by both, is the right shape — and once Launch guarantees readiness, the e2e helpers that poll for it can go.

Test it with a guest that deliberately never serves (a base whose init exits immediately), and assert the error names the guest's own failure rather than a socket path. A test that only checks "launch returned an error" would pass for the wrong reason.

Watch the backends: firecracker, vzf, libkrun and the container fallback all launch through the same manager, so the wait must be expressed once, in the manager, not per backend.

Refs: MGIT-89 (where this hid a dead backend), NFR-17.6, FR-17.11</prompt>
<parameter name="acceptance">A sandbox whose guest never binds its exec port fails the launch, tears itself down, and reports the guest's own startup error from the console — on every backend, with a test that would fail if the error were merely a transport or socket message.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Same-second host write after a guest read can be missed on BOTH platforms (cached size+mtime unchanged)
nodes.description:
Found while fixing MGIT-90, deliberately not fixed there (different mechanism, and MGIT-90 was already scoped).

A host write that lands in the SAME SECOND as a previous guest read can be missed by the guest — on macOS/libkrun as well as Linux/libkrun. The guest's cached attributes show an unchanged size and an unchanged mtime (1-second granularity), so nothing invalidates its page cache and it serves the old bytes.

THIS IS NOT THE MGIT-90 DEFECT. That one was a lingering NAME lookup after an unlink, Linux-only, and is fixed by emptying the file before unlinking. This is a CONTENT update going unobserved, and it is cross-platform — including the backend the pilot runs on.

WHY IT HAS NOT BITTEN: no sync test is tightly spaced enough to hit it. A real agent loop can be: edit, sync, exec, read — well within a second on a fast machine, especially for a small file whose length does not change (a one-character fix, a flipped boolean, a version bump of equal width).

WHY IT MATTERS ANYWAY: it is the same silent-staleness class the sync verb exists to prevent — the host tree is correct, the verb reports success, and the guest executes stale code. The failure is invisible at every layer except the guest's own read.

SECOND NET ALREADY EXISTS ON THE CALLER'S SIDE: the integrating lane is upgrading their per-round canary to a modify+create+delete triplet probe, which would catch exactly this class at their door. That is a reason to know about it, not a reason to leave it — their canary stops a bad round, ours should stop a bad substrate.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Establish whether a same-second content update can be missed by a running guest, on each backend, then close it or document the bound precisely.

REPRODUCE FIRST, and make the reproduction deterministic rather than hoping to hit a race: have the guest read a delivered file, then within the same wall-clock second write NEW CONTENT OF THE SAME LENGTH host-side, then have the guest read again. Equal length is the point — it keeps the cached size identical, so only mtime could invalidate, and mtime has 1-second granularity. Do it on macOS/libkrun and Linux/libkrun; the MGIT-90 work left an in-guest `fsprobe` in testdata that already reads through the guest, which is the only vantage point that proves anything here.

IF IT REPRODUCES, the fix is likely ours rather than upstream, and cheaper than it sounds. Options to weigh, with the trade-off stated:
- Write with O_TRUNC + rewrite rather than in-place, so the size transiently changes.
- Bump the delivered file's mtime explicitly (utimes) to a value strictly greater than the guest's cached one — note MGIT-71's finding that a host-side RENAME is invisible to a guest holding the tree, so prefer in-place metadata changes over swap-in tricks.
- Give the sync a monotonic marker the guest can trust rather than relying on mtime granularity at all.
Whichever is chosen, it must not regress MGIT-90's truncate-before-unlink or MGIT-71's truncate-and-rewrite requirement — both exist because of how this share behaves, and a "cleaner" rewrite that ignores them will reintroduce a fixed defect.

IF IT DOES NOT REPRODUCE, say so with the measurement and close this — a hazard that cannot be demonstrated should not sit in the backlog implying otherwise.

Refs: MGIT-90 (found during), MGIT-71 (the rename-is-invisible finding), MGIT-76, ADR-011
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">Whether a same-second, same-length host content update is observed by a running guest is established by a deterministic measurement on both libkrun backends and recorded. Either the guest observes it (with a regression test that would fail without the fix, and MGIT-90/MGIT-71's behaviours preserved), or the ticket is closed with the measurement showing it does not reproduce.</parameter>
</invoke>
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: The firecracker CLI-surface gate asserts `shell` must run on Linux/KVM, but no daemon build serves it
nodes.description:
Found while validating MGIT-92, and only visible because MGIT-92 fixed a different bug in the same CI step.

THE STEP WAS DEAD. `.github/workflows/e2e.yml`'s "Sandbox CLI surface e2e" step (firecracker job) exported MGIT_GUEST_CMDLINE="$FC_CMDLINE" without sourcing scripts/sandbox-image/pins.env, which defines it. Under `set -u` that killed the step on an unbound variable before a single verb ran, so the gate had been reporting failure while validating NOTHING — on main, for at least two days (runs 31509560815, 31512727903, 31567336824 all fail on this same step). MGIT-92 sourced pins.env, and the gate finally ran.

WHAT IT FOUND, on the first real run. Every verb passes — list, list --json, status before boot (`created`), exec (triggering the lazy boot), exit-status propagation, status after boot (`running`), grants, grants --json, remove. Then the step fails on its OWN assertion:

    SANDBOX CLI SURFACE E2E: PASS (live) — NOT SERVED on this backend: shell
    FATAL: a verb reported NOT SERVED on the Linux/KVM gate, where both are expected to run

The assertion says shell and grants must RUN on Linux/KVM because their refusals are documented as platform gates. But sandboxd.Client.Shell returns ErrShellTransportUnavailable UNCONDITIONALLY in every build: its own comment says the bidirectional vsock-PTY transport "is KVM-gated guest infrastructure not served by this daemon build". So the gate encodes an expectation the product does not meet on any platform.

THE QUESTION TO DECIDE (this is why it is a ticket and not a drive-by fix): is the T2 interactive shell transport supposed to be served by the Linux/KVM daemon build, in which case the gate is right and the capability regressed or was never wired — or is the transport still unshipped (it is gated under MGIT-11.11.6), in which case the ASSERTION is wrong and should expect the documented refusal until the transport lands? Answering it by weakening the assertion would be guessing, and this project's defects keep landing exactly in that gap.

Not fixed in MGIT-92 deliberately: MGIT-92 fixed the unbound variable (a strict improvement — the gate now validates 13 verbs instead of nothing) and left the assertion alone.

Refs: MGIT-92, MGIT-88, MGIT-11.11.6
nodes.prompt:
Decide whether `mgit sandbox shell` is meant to be served by the Linux/KVM daemon build, then make the gate and the product agree.

Start by reading sandboxd.Client.Shell and the MGIT-11.11.6 transport work: the client returns ErrShellTransportUnavailable in all builds, so establish first whether the vsock-PTY transport is wired anywhere, gated behind a build tag, or simply not shipped.

If it is not shipped: the CLI-surface gate's "both must have RUN" assertion is wrong for `shell` and should expect the documented refusal, with a comment naming the ticket that will flip it back. Keep the assertion for `grants`, which does run.

If it IS meant to be served: the gate is right and this is a real capability gap on the Linux/KVM build — fix the wiring, and keep the assertion as the thing that would have caught it.

Either way, verify by running the gate live (the firecracker job, or scripts/e2e/sandbox_cli_surface.sh on the KVM box) rather than reasoning about it — the step spent two days reporting failure while executing nothing, which is precisely the failure mode to avoid repeating.
nodes.acceptance: The firecracker CLI-surface gate runs to completion and its pass/fail reflects the product's actual shell capability, with the decision (transport shipped or not) recorded in the step's comment and traceable to code.
nodes.creator: mcp

nodes.title: Per-sandbox resource caps declarable at launch, bounded by policy (R-H212) — the ceiling leaked into a customer's production build config
nodes.description:
Requested by the HyperSWE lane as R-H212, with consumer evidence.

THE MEASUREMENT: a real repository's production build peaks at 2.10 GB RSS. The guest's effective default is 2 vCPU / ~1.94 GB (mgit's policy default is CPUs 2, MemoryMB 2048; guest overhead accounts for the rest). The build aborts in-guest — V8 old-gen exhaustion, exit 134 — and succeeds on the host.

THE CONSEQUENCE, AND THE REASON THIS IS P1: caught in their review, the dev agent responded by RESHAPING THE PRODUCTION BUNDLER CONFIG to fit the ceiling. A posture-dependent fact — how much memory mgit's sandbox happened to grant — nearly became permanent product code in a customer's repository. That is the substrate corrupting the artifact it exists to protect. The agent behaved reasonably given what it could observe; it saw a build that OOMs and made it fit.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS (so this is a surface + bound problem, not new machinery):
- model.SandboxLaunchOptions already carries CPUs, MemoryMB and DiskQuotaMB, documented as "0 = policy default", and they flow all the way to VMConfig.
- service.applyPolicyDefaults fills the zeros from model.SandboxPolicy (defaults CPUs 2, MemoryMB 2048, and a TTL).
- Policy already enforces AGGREGATE limits: MaxConcurrentSandboxes 8 and MaxTotalMemoryPercent 50, plus the daemon's FR-17.26 --max-memory-mb ceiling.

WHAT IS MISSING:
1. NO CALLER SURFACE. Neither `mgit sandbox launch` nor `mgit work` exposes memory/cpu/disk flags. The fields exist in the API and nothing can set them. That absence is exactly why the lane's only route would have been editing a host policy file — which they refused, on the same routing-around principle as R-H197. They are right to refuse: a caller editing the operator's policy defeats the point of having one.
2. NO PER-SANDBOX MAXIMUM. Policy carries DEFAULTS and AGGREGATE caps, but nothing to validate a caller-declared request against. "Declarable by the workload, enforced by the daemon" needs an upper bound per sandbox, distinct from both the default and the fleet-wide total.

THE MODEL THE LANE ASKED FOR, and it is the right one: the workload sizes the guest, within a policy the operator sets. Caller declares; daemon bounds; neither can be bypassed by the other.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Let a launch declare its own resource caps, and have the daemon bound them.

MOST OF THE PLUMBING EXISTS — read it before adding anything. SandboxLaunchOptions.CPUs/MemoryMB/DiskQuotaMB already reach VMConfig, and applyPolicyDefaults already fills the zeros. The work is a caller surface and a per-sandbox bound, not a new resource path.

1. SURFACE. Add the flags to `mgit sandbox launch` AND `mgit work` (the lane starts agents with `work --sandbox`, so a flag only on `launch` would not reach them). Follow the existing sandbox subcommand conventions and mind the flag-naming inconsistency already in this tree (`exec` takes --task, `shell` takes --task-id — do not add a third spelling). Carry them over controlproto to the daemon; the launch options already serialise. Decide whether the MCP surface needs them: sandbox LIFECYCLE is deliberately CLI-only (docs/MCP-PARITY.md) with sync/policy/export as the reasoned exceptions, so adding launch flags to MCP would need the same kind of argument — make it or don't, but record the decision.

2. THE BOUND. Add a per-sandbox maximum to model.SandboxPolicy (e.g. MaxMemoryMB, MaxCPUs, MaxDiskQuotaMB) and validate a declared request against it in the service, BEFORE the backend sees it. A request over the bound must be REFUSED with a message naming the limit and the policy that set it — never silently clamped. Silent clamping would reproduce this ticket's own defect one level up: the caller would think it asked for 4 GB, get 2, and go back to reshaping the build. The aggregate FR-17.26 ceiling still applies on top; a launch may be individually legal and still refused because the fleet is full, and those two refusals must read differently.

3. THE DIAGNOSTIC, which matters as much as the cap and was not asked for. Even with declarable memory, the NEXT build to hit a ceiling will produce exit 134 and an opaque V8 message, and the next agent will again "fix" the bundler. When a guest process dies of memory exhaustion, mgit should say so and name the cap — the daemon knows the sandbox's MemoryMB, and an OOM kill is observable in the guest. Investigate what is detectable (guest dmesg/OOM killer, the exit signal, cgroup counters if any) and surface something an agent can act on: "the guest exceeded its 2048 MB cap; raise it with --memory-mb or reduce the workload" beats exit 134 every time. If it cannot be detected reliably, say so and instead make the cap VISIBLE — `mgit sandbox status` reporting the effective memory/cpu would at least let an agent check before concluding its build is wrong.

TESTS: a declared value reaches VMConfig; an over-bound request is refused naming the limit; an unset value still gets the policy default; the aggregate ceiling still refuses independently and distinguishably; and the CLI flags actually reach the daemon (assert through the CLI, not only the service — see MGIT-88 for why that distinction keeps mattering here).

Refs: R-H212, R-H197 (the routing-around principle), FR-17.26, NFR-17.5, MGIT-88
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">`mgit sandbox launch` and `mgit work` accept per-sandbox memory/cpu/disk caps that reach the VM; policy carries a per-sandbox maximum and the service REFUSES an over-bound request naming the limit rather than clamping it; unset values still take policy defaults; the aggregate FR-17.26 ceiling still applies and its refusal is distinguishable; a guest that dies of memory exhaustion produces a diagnostic naming the cap, or — if that is not reliably detectable — the effective cap is visible via `sandbox status` and that decision is recorded.</acceptance>
</invoke>

nodes.title: Firecracker kill-flow e2e races its own precondition — it waits for the host accept, not the guest's bytes
nodes.description:
RED ON MAIN, blocking the 0.4.5 release. Run 31571888379, job "Sandbox LIVE (Linux/KVM firecracker)", step "root-gated half".

    --- FAIL: TestE2E_Firecracker_Revoke_KillsEstablishedFlow (1.19s)
    the host counted killed=1 but the GUEST's established connection did not die
    PROBE-RESULT HOLD = CONNECTED-NO-DATA reason="EOF"

THE PRODUCT IS FINE — verified before filing. The host reported killed=1, the post-revoke flow was refused by policy, and the drain positive control passed in the same run with real bytes (`PROBE-HOLD ESTABLISHED bytes=40 head="REAL-BYTES-FROM-ALLOWLISTED-DESTINATION"`, `HOLD = SURVIVED after=20.039s`). The revoke worked. What failed is the test's own precondition.

THE RACE, and it is an asymmetry between two tests that claim the same property:

- firecracker (this test) calls `awaitHeldFlow(t, f.accepted, ...)`, which waits on the HOST LISTENER'S ACCEPT. Accepted is not the same as carrying data: if the revoke lands between the accept and the guest's first read, the probe reports CONNECTED-NO-DATA rather than DIED, and the assertion fires.
- libkrun (its twin, `e2e_realvm_livepolicy_test.go`) waits on the GUEST-SIDE streamed marker `PROBE-HOLD ESTABLISHED`, i.e. the guest reporting a connection carrying real bytes. Its own doc comment says why: "an unestablished flow would make every assertion after it vacuous, which is the exact defect this file fixes."

So the stronger precondition already exists, one directory over, written for exactly this hazard. The firecracker twin never got it.

WHY IT SURFACED NOW: timing. MGIT-92 made launch confirm guest readiness before returning, which shifts what happens when relative to the probe. The race was always there; the firecracker job had also been red for two days on an unrelated `$FC_CMDLINE` bug, so the root-gated half was not reaching this assertion.

MECHANICAL DIFFICULTY, so nobody starts down the wrong path: firecracker's `probe()` goes through `microvm.Manager.Exec`, which BUFFERS stdout and returns it when the command finishes — there is nothing to observe mid-flight. libkrun's `execProbe` dials the guest directly and passes an `io.Writer` to `guestexec.Run`, so it sees each frame as it arrives. Giving firecracker the same wait needs a streaming path, not just a different channel to select on.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Give the firecracker kill test the same precondition its libkrun twin already has: wait for the GUEST to report a connection carrying real bytes before revoking.

Do NOT weaken the assertion to accept CONNECTED-NO-DATA. The assertion is right — a revoke must kill a flow that is carrying data — and accepting a probe that never carried any would make the test vacuous, which is the precise defect libkrun's version was written to fix.

Read internal/sandboxd/backend/libkrun/e2e_realvm_livepolicy_test.go first: `markerWatcher`, `execProbe`'s streaming `writerFunc`, and `heldFlow.awaitEstablished` (note it also fails fast if the probe EXITS before establishing, which is a better failure than a timeout). Mirror that shape rather than inventing a second one — the two proofs should stay the same observation made twice.

The mechanical obstacle is that firecracker's probe path is buffered: `probe()` -> `guestProbe()` -> `microvm.Manager.Exec`, which returns stdout only when the command ends. Options, in the order I would try them:
1. Dial the guest directly in the test as libkrun does, if this package has (or can reach) a guest dialer — the closest mirror, and it keeps Manager out of the test's way.
2. Add a streaming exec entry to microvm.Manager (io.Writer sinks) and use it from both suites. Bigger, but it removes the asymmetry at the source and may be worth it — `Manager.Exec`'s buffering is a real limitation for any long-running guest command, not just this test.
Pick one and say why.

VERIFY BY REPETITION, not one green: this is a race, so a single pass proves nothing. Run the kill/drain pair enough times on real KVM to justify the claim, the same standard MGIT-91 was held to.

While you are there: check whether TestE2E_Firecracker_Revoke_DrainKeepsEstablishedFlow has the same weak precondition and merely gets away with it because a drained flow survives long enough to read its bytes. If so, fix both — a test that passes for the wrong reason is a defect waiting for a timing change.

Refs: MGIT-72, MGIT-78, MGIT-92 (the timing change that exposed it), SEC-04, ADR-012
Constraints: no AI-attribution trailers; never `git add -A`.</parameter>
<parameter name="acceptance">TestE2E_Firecracker_Revoke_KillsEstablishedFlow waits for the guest to report an established, data-carrying flow before the revoke — mirroring the libkrun twin — and fails fast if the probe exits first; the assertion that the flow DIED is unchanged; the drain twin's precondition is checked and fixed if it shares the weakness; and the kill/drain pair passes repeatedly on real KVM with the firecracker gate green on main.</acceptance>
</invoke>

nodes.title: microvm.Manager.Exec buffers guest stdout until the command exits — no streaming entry point
nodes.description:
Found while fixing MGIT-96. microvm.Manager.Exec -> execUntilTheGuestAnswers -> execOnce collects guest stdout/stderr into bytes.Buffer and returns them only when the command finishes, even though the layer underneath it (guestexec.Run) already streams frame by frame to io.Writers. So no caller of Manager can observe a long-running guest command mid-flight: not a build's progress, not a test's output, and not a probe that announces something before it blocks.

MGIT-96 needed exactly that (wait for the guest's "PROBE-HOLD ESTABLISHED" line while the probe is still holding its connection) and worked around it by dialing the guest exec channel directly from the test, mirroring what the libkrun suite already does. That is fine for a test whose fixture has already proven the guest is serving, but it leaves the asymmetry in place: libkrun's suite streams because it dials directly, firecracker's suite streams because it now dials directly, and anything that goes through Manager still cannot.

The fix is a streaming exec entry on Manager (io.Writer sinks for stdout/stderr, exit code returned as today) with Exec kept as the buffered convenience wrapper over it. It removes the asymmetry at the source and gives the daemon/CLI a path to stream long guest commands.</description>
<parameter name="prompt">Add a streaming exec entry point to microvm.Manager: same contract as Exec (whole-command routing, no host env, non-zero exit is a normal result, first-command retry semantics preserved) but with caller-supplied io.Writer sinks so output is delivered as frames arrive. Keep Exec as the buffered wrapper so no caller changes. Then consider moving the firecracker and libkrun live-policy suites onto it, so both backends observe their establishment marker through the SAME code path instead of each dialing the guest themselves.

Note the retry interaction carefully: execUntilTheGuestAnswers may re-send the whole command while the guest has never answered, and it may only do so when NOTHING was received. With streaming sinks, bytes already handed to the caller cannot be un-delivered — so the retry must remain gated on "no output at all reached the sink yet", or the streaming path must decline the retry and say so. Getting this wrong would replay a command that had already started producing output.

Refs: MGIT-96, MGIT-91, MGIT-61.15, FR-17.11
nodes.acceptance: microvm.Manager exposes a streaming exec that writes guest stdout/stderr to caller-supplied io.Writers as frames arrive; Exec is implemented on top of it and its behavior is unchanged (tests still pass); the first-command retry cannot replay a command whose output has already been delivered, proven by a test; and at least one live-policy suite observes its establishment marker through Manager rather than by dialing the guest itself.

nodes.title: The FR-17.26 aggregate MEMORY ceiling is inert in a default install — and declarable per-sandbox memory just raised the stakes
nodes.description:
Found while implementing MGIT-95 (declarable per-sandbox resource caps).

model.SandboxPolicy carries MaxTotalMemoryPercent (default 50) — the FR-17.26 host-wide memory ceiling. Nothing reads it. cmd/mgit-sandboxd/main.go wires the ceiling from FLAGS instead:

    flags.IntVar(&o.maxMemoryMB, "max-memory-mb", 0, "global sandbox memory ceiling in MB (0 until policy wiring resolves the FR-17.26 50% host default)")
    manager := sandboxd.NewCeilingManager(selected, opts.maxSandboxes, opts.maxMemoryMB, 0)

and the flag defaults to 0, which DISABLES that dimension in CeilingManager.reserve. The concurrency cap (--max-sandboxes 8) is live; the memory ceiling is not, unless an operator passes the flag by hand. The flag's own help text admits it ("0 until policy wiring resolves...").

Why it matters more now: before MGIT-95 every sandbox took the 2048 MB policy default, so 8 concurrent sandboxes was ~16 GB — self-limiting. With per-sandbox memory declarable up to max_memory_mb (default 16384), 8 sandboxes can now legally ask for 128 GB with no aggregate check to refuse them. The per-sandbox bound added in MGIT-95 is real protection, but it is a per-launch bound, not a fleet bound — exactly the distinction that ticket kept separate.

Note also that MaxTotalMemoryPercent is a PERCENT of host memory and the ceiling takes MB, so the wiring needs a host-memory probe (or a resolved absolute in policy).
nodes.prompt:
Wire the FR-17.26 aggregate memory ceiling from host policy instead of an off-by-default flag.

1. Resolve MaxTotalMemoryPercent against host physical memory at daemon start (per-platform probe: sysctl hw.memsize on darwin, /proc/meminfo MemTotal on linux) and pass the resulting MB to sandboxd.NewCeilingManager. Keep --max-memory-mb as an explicit override, not the only source.
2. Pass the policy's default MemoryMB as CeilingManager's defaultMemoryMB rather than the hardcoded 0 -> fallbackAccountedMemoryMB, so accounting matches the policy actually in force.
3. Test that a fleet exceeding the resolved ceiling is refused with ErrSandboxCeilingExceeded and that the refusal still reads as "the host is full" and NOT as MGIT-95's per-sandbox ErrSandboxResourceLimitExceeded — the two must stay distinguishable.
4. If a host-memory probe cannot be made reliable on some platform, fail closed to a conservative absolute rather than to "unlimited", and say so.

Refs: FR-17.26, MGIT-95, R-H212, SEC-09
nodes.acceptance: The daemon derives its aggregate memory ceiling from host policy (MaxTotalMemoryPercent) with no operator flag required; an over-fleet launch is refused with ErrSandboxCeilingExceeded whose message reads as a full host; the per-sandbox refusal stays separately identifiable; the accounted default matches the policy default.

nodes.title: A guest killed by its own kernel stays registered as `running` and every later exec fails with a raw vsock dial error
nodes.description:
Reproduced live on macOS/libkrun while implementing MGIT-95 (2026-08-12).

Steps: launch a sandbox at the 2048 MB default, then in the guest mount a tmpfs and dd 4 GB into it.

Observed:
1. The exec that triggered it fails with `libkrun exec: guest exec: read frame: EOF` — no exit code, because the guest supervisor (PID 1) was killed with everything else.
2. `mgit sandbox status <task>` still reports `running`. The service's in-memory registration says booted; nothing notices the guest is gone.
3. Every subsequent exec fails after a 15s timeout with:
   `libkrun exec: dial guest: guest vsock not ready within 15s: dial ... v1024.sock: connect: connection refused`
4. The only recovery is `mgit sandbox remove --force` + relaunch, which the message never suggests.

MGIT-95 added an advisory on both the EOF and the signal-exit paths naming the sandbox's memory cap, so the FIRST failure now explains itself. The stale state and the 15s-then-obscure-error on every subsequent command are untouched — an agent that keeps working in that worktree hits a wall it cannot read, 15 seconds at a time.

Related evidence and reasoning: docs/adr/014-guest-memory-exhaustion-is-not-detectable.md.
nodes.prompt:
Make a dead guest an honest, recoverable state instead of a stale `running` plus an opaque dial failure.

1. DETECT: when the exec transport fails in a way that means the guest is gone (channel EOF mid-exec, then a refused/timed-out control dial), the service should mark the sandbox's state accordingly rather than leaving `booted=true`. Consider a distinct state or reusing an existing one — but do NOT invent a state that the append-only sandbox_events vocabulary does not carry without extending it deliberately (FR-17.18 closes that vocabulary on purpose).
2. REPORT: `mgit sandbox status` must not claim `running` for a sandbox whose control channel is refused. A caller reading status to decide whether to retry is currently told to retry forever.
3. RECOVER: the error a user sees should name the remedy (`mgit sandbox remove --task-id <ID> --force` then relaunch, keeping any declared --memory-mb), and the 15s dial timeout should not be paid on every subsequent command once the guest is known dead.
4. Test the transition with a fake manager whose Exec returns a transport EOF and whose subsequent dials fail; assert status stops reporting running and the message names the remedy.

Refs: MGIT-95, R-H212, FR-17.9, FR-17.18, NFR-17.6, ADR-014
nodes.acceptance: A sandbox whose guest died is no longer reported as `running`; the failure names the remedy; a later exec fails fast instead of waiting out the dial timeout; covered by tests that drive the transport failure.
